2. The classification of sciences must govern the architecture

2.1 Practical knowledge and instrumental inquiry

The opening of al-Ḍarūrī does not support the simple identification “all uṣūl is universal practical science; all fiqh is particular application.” It supplies three coordinated distinctions.

First, knowledge can terminate in an assent or conviction in the soul, or it can terminate in action. His examples for the first kind concern the originatedness of the world and the indivisible part. The text speaks of the end of this knowledge as iʿtiqād; it does not thereby certify those examples as demonstratively true. Second, knowledge directed to action can be universal and comparatively remote from action, or particular and comparatively proximate to it. Particular examples include rules of prayer and zakāt; universal examples include the foundations on which such branches depend—Book, Sunna and consensus—and the classifications of rulings considered generally. Third, there is knowledge of the rules and conditions by which thought is guided correctly in the preceding inquiries. Ibn Rushd compares its service to the mind with the service of measuring instruments to the senses. al-Ḍarūrī, Arabic, PDF pp.17–18, printed pp.34–37, §§2–6; Ibn Rushd / Akl edition, PDF p.129, translation §2; PDF pp.341–344, commentary.

Thus we need three questions, not one ladder:

Dimension Question Application to this project
Finality Does the knowledge terminate in assent or in action? Practical knowledge is ordered toward conduct even when its immediate subject is abstract.
Generality How universal is its object, and how remote from a determinate act? A classification of obligation differs from the rule for a particular kind of ablution.
Function Does it state substantive principles or regulate the correctness of inquiry? The source-status of a report differs from the method for interpreting its imperative.

These axes can intersect. An instrumental rule may be universal; universal practical knowledge can concern the grounds of a source without being the rule for construing an expression within it. A chapter of fiqh can contain highly general propositions relative to its many instances. “Particular practical science” therefore does not mean an unorganized heap of isolated events. Conversely, a universally stated proposition is not necessarily a demonstration or a metaphysical first principle.

Ibn Rushd applies this analysis to the Mustaṣfā’s four-part arrangement: rulings, foundations, methods of derivation, and the qualified investigator. The distinctive instrumental part is the third. The remaining material belongs to practical knowledge; Akl interprets it within universal practical science. The fourth part’s placement there is an interpretive extension of the classification, since the initial examples do not explicitly mention it. The comprehensive historical discipline called uṣūl al-fiqh contains more than the narrower instrumental core singled out by this analysis. Ibn Rushd / Akl edition, PDF pp.130–132, §§5–9; PDF p.344, commentary §6; al-Ḍarūrī, Arabic, PDF pp.18–19.

The general/particular distinction therefore belongs at the foundation, with the instrumental dimension retained. Otherwise the very distinction that makes Ibn Rushd’s reorganization philosophically interesting disappears.

al-Ḍarūrī · method · Arabic / EnglishKnowledge, action and the work of legal method

2.2 Why the science becomes explicit

The discipline also has a history. Ibn Rushd explains the need for explicit rules against conditions of dispersed transmission and increased difficulty; he allows that the earlier community possessed the relevant powers before their systematic formulation. He relates universals to what can be recovered from prior judgments. He then considers an arrangement that would join interpretive methods with the positions and derivations of the jurists, rather than merely presenting one school. Akl reads this unrealized arrangement as anticipating the Bidāya’s structure. The textual proposal is primary evidence; the relation between the two books as a developmental program is Akl’s reconstruction, to be tested against their actual contents. al-Ḍarūrī, Arabic, PDF pp.17–19, §§3–9; Ibn Rushd / Akl edition, PDF pp.130–132; pp.343–345.

Ibn Khaldūn later gives a closely relevant, but historically distinct, account. Linguistic competence and proximity to transmitters once reduced the need for explicit technical disciplines; with the loss of those conditions, scholars formulated rules and sciences. His description of uṣūl includes validation of evidence, transmission, abrogation, legal semantics and analogy. It is not simply a general hermeneutics of everything. His description of juristic disagreement also identifies language, reports and new cases as sources of disagreement. Muqaddimah, PDF pp.576–577, VI.12; pp.585–587, VI.13.

The relation is recursive: competent practice makes the articulation of rules possible; articulated rules help reproduce competence after the original social conditions have changed. This is a defensible meaning of the city producing jurists and jurists forming the city. It does not entail that all legal theory was invented after the fact to rationalize settled rulings.

2.3 Four senses of uṣūl that must remain distinct

  1. Sources or foundations: the things on which rulings rest in the usage of the passage under study.
  2. The historical discipline of uṣūl al-fiqh: inquiry into legal proofs, their modes of indication and inference, and the relevant qualifications and conditions, with variations across authors.
  3. Ibn Rushd’s instrumental analysis of that discipline: its distinctive contribution to directing legal inference correctly.
  4. The project’s broader anthropological reconstruction: disciplined disclosure of the Lawgiver’s normative meaning through revealed language, contextual indication, relevant knowledge of reality and practical judgment, under conditions of human epistemic finitude; its anthropological correlate is discerning what acknowledgement requires here and now.

Only the fourth is our enlarged philosophical use. It must never be inserted into a historical author’s definition as though that author had defined his discipline in those words. Nor is every citizen thereby a mujtahid. A non-specialist’s warranted recourse to a qualified scholar can itself be a legitimate condition of responsible action, although the conditions and limits of that recourse require their own historical treatment.

The later Jamʿ al-Jawāmiʿ is a control for distinctions such as knowledge of general proofs, inference and the inferer, and for the definition of fiqh through detailed proofs. It must not be used to silently rewrite Ibn Rushd’s vocabulary or erase the difference between his analysis and later definitions. The matn and its editorial introduction also require separation. Jamʿ al-Jawāmiʿ, PDF pp.11–13, opening definitions.

2.4 Agency, capacity, coercion and the difference between compliance and acknowledgement

The anthropology cannot be inferred only from the classification of sciences. In §§54–55, Ibn Rushd criticizes the account he attributes to al-Ashʿarī in which human agency is merely concomitant with action rather than a near or remote cause. His comparison concerns the different relation to walking of someone with and without legs. He then rejects obligation to perform the impossible both rationally and on scriptural grounds: the commanded act must be intelligible and representable to the one commanding and the one addressed. These are Ibn Rushd’s arguments against a particular theological position as he presents it; they are not a neutral summary of every Ashʿarī theory of acquisition. Ibn Rushd / Akl edition, PDF pp.158–159, printed pp.148–149, §§54–55.

This supplies a primary basis for two requirements of our alchemy. The human being must have a real relation to the act, and formation must address an intelligible possibility within capacity. An account that makes practice causally inert cannot straightforwardly explain habituation; an account that treats impossible demands as ordinary formative exercises cannot explain the importance of capacity. These conclusions do not settle the whole Rushdian doctrine of freedom and divine causation. They establish the local anthropology presupposed by this practical inquiry.

The next passage is more difficult. Ibn Rushd distinguishes an act begun under coercion from the agent’s subsequent undertaking of it as obedience. Without that obedient orientation, he says, reward does not follow merely from performance; with it, reward can follow even when coercion initially moved the person. He also invokes coercion to faith under threat of death as an example. That historical claim must be included in a critical account, rather than concealed beneath contemporary language of self-realization. The Bidāya comparison is now explicit: Arabic II459 begins with a male apostate apprehended before fighting. Its reported penalty cannot be reconstructed only as a response to armed treason. The jizya discussion at I403–407 also retains unequal religious and political standing; representative commentary on preserves Ibn ʿĀshūr’s interpretation even where it resists this project’s preferred language of formation. The philosophical distinction between initial motive and later acknowledgement does not by itself justify the coercive example. Ibn Rushd / Akl edition, PDF pp.158–161, §§57–58.

Bidāya Arabic II, PDF p.459, before-fighting case; image checked Bidāya Arabic I, PDF pp.403–407, persons, assessment and fiscal status

The passage thereby creates a substantive tension with Ibn Khaldūn’s analysis of externally imposed discipline weakening fortitude. It also invites comparison with Aquinas’s account of persons beginning to refrain from wrongdoing through fear and later acting voluntarily through habituation. We have three different arguments: a legal-theological account of reward under coercive initiation; a political and psychological account of damaged or internalized restraint; and a theory of the gradual formation possible through human law. They must be compared for mechanism, limits and evidence rather than harmonized by the single word “habituation.” Muqaddimah, PDF pp.168–169, II.6; Aquinas, Treatise on Law, PDF p.36, printed pp.44–45, I–II q.95 a.1.

In §58, coercion to an unlawful act requires attention to degrees of threatened harm and to the act demanded; Ibn Rushd assigns the assessment to legal reasoning and ijtihād. In §59, he distinguishes kinds of omission and uses fasting as an example of an attributable, rewarded abstention, leaving the classification of individual cases to particular jurisprudence. Thus even “not doing” has a differentiated practical ontology. Mere bodily non-occurrence is not yet the same thing as a person’s abstention. Ibn Rushd / Akl edition, PDF pp.160–161, §§58–59.

The enlarged definition of discernment must therefore include four irreducible questions: can the person act; what act or abstention is legally constituted; how does the person undertake it; and what may others legitimately require or infer? Capacity, validity, reward and jurisdiction must never be collapsed into a single measure of spiritual achievement.

2.5 Reclassifying qiyās: the operation before the name

Ibn Rushd does not simply adopt the familiar aṣl–farʿ–ʿilla–ḥukm schema: an original case, a new case, a common legally relevant ground, and a ruling. He reports that account in §257, then says in §259 that the operation under examination is not qiyās in the relevant strict sense. Where the expression or its context indicates a meaning wider than the named case, the jurist recovers that intended general meaning and determines what falls under it. The distinction concerns the source of the transition, not whether the conclusion extends beyond the noun originally used. al-Ḍarūrī §§257–261, Arabic/French PDF pp.298–301

The Bidāya introduction makes the contrast explicit. Semantic extension moves from a revealed particular through an indicated general meaning to another instance. Qiyās sharʿī in the narrower classification extends the ruling of a particular intended as particular to an unmentioned case through resemblance or a proposed common cause. Ibn Rushd places the rival food predicates in ribā under the first operation; he places assimilation of the wine-drinking penalty to the penalty for false accusation, and of the minimum dower to the theft threshold, under the second. He says these operations are easily confused. We must consequently retain both his restrictive classification and his more conventional use of the word qiyās while reporting juristic arguments elsewhere. A word count cannot identify an inference. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.3–4; p.4 image checked

Operation Transition What must be established
Application of an already given general rule General norm → a verified instance That the facts satisfy the adopted criterion; this is not automatically an analogical extension.
Indicated semantic extension Revealed particular → intended general meaning → new instance The expression/context warrants that broader meaning, and the new case falls beneath it.
Residual qiyās / exemplum Established particular → another particular through relevant resemblance Why the resemblance supports transfer despite the absence of an independently established intended universal in the expression.
Means–ends reasoning Present act → likely course of events → legally significant end The causal assessment, the legal status of the end, and authority to regulate its means.

The residual inference is epistemically more exposed: an intelligible similarity does not by itself show that the Lawgiver assigned the same positive rule to both cases. In §§272–273 Ibn Rushd accepts the force of the Ẓāhirī objection that legal statuses are not essential natural properties apprehended by unaided reason. But he limits the objection: language includes implied meaning and contextual indication, so an expression can indicate its legally relevant ground without stating it in a separate formula. Restricting meaning to grammatical surface alone excludes legitimate Arabic discourse. His response redraws the boundary between interpretation and independent transfer; it neither embraces ordinary analogy without restriction nor adopts a comprehensive Ẓāhirī literalism. It also does not settle every question about the rational knowledge of moral goods. al-Ḍarūrī §§272–274, Arabic/French PDF pp.308–311 Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF p.4

The Aristotelian connection is explanatory, with a source limit. Akl reconstructs this distinction through al-Fārābī's treatment of mithāl/tamthīl, the rhetorical example: a common feature can remain attached to the known particular instead of functioning as a fully isolated universal premise. That is not inference between absolutely unrelated particulars, nor is every syllogism a demonstration. Akl discusses both a subjective explanation—an audience has not extracted the universal—and an objective explanation in terms of the kind of legal warrant available. He attributes the latter reading to Ibn Rushd. These are Akl's historical-philosophical arguments, including his translated extracts from al-Fārābī; the underlying Kitāb al-Qiyās has not been independently collated here. We therefore distinguish the primary Rushdian contrast, which is directly verified, from the proposed genealogy through al-Fārābī. Akl, study, PDF pp.67,73–80, printed pp.57,63–70; especially pp.78–80

Later theory did not simply adopt Ibn Rushd's restricted terminology. Jamʿ al-Jawāmiʿ defines qiyās through equality in the cause of a ruling, explicitly states that it has four pillars, and proceeds through the original case, its ruling, the branch and the cause. It also distinguishes cases in which the original proof already embraces the branch. This is a developed alternative taxonomy, not a crude theory of arbitrary resemblance. The fourfold model remains useful as a later control, but it must not erase Ibn Rushd's question about what actually does the inferential work. Jamʿ al-Jawāmiʿ, matn, Book IV, PDF pp.80–84; distinguish editorial notes

2.5.1 Semantic warrant requires knowledge of what is being signified

“Linguistic” describes the contrast with an autonomous transfer from case to case; it does not mean that the jurist reasons within a self-contained dictionary. In §260 Ibn Rushd explicitly allows entry beneath the universal to be established through ijtihād or sense-perception. In §§269–270 he distinguishes establishing that a wider meaning is intended from identifying which meaning it is. Context must belong to a kind of consideration recognized by the law, not any circumstance the interpreter finds attractive. These distinctions make room for relevant knowledge of reality without making that knowledge an independent source of sharʿī authorization. al-Ḍarūrī §§260–261,269–270, PDF pp.300–301,306–307

Three questions must be answered separately. Semantic warrant: what licenses moving beyond the named particular? Practical intelligibility: what feature of the act or object matters, how is it known, and how does it operate? Teleological coherence: how does this proposed interpretation fit the goods and constraints manifested in the legal order? Intoxication, for example, differs from colour or liquidity because of what it does to cognition, self-government and conduct. That explanation can make a proposed ground intelligible; it cannot by itself tell us whether a prohibition concerns a drink's kind, the intoxicating quantity, every smaller quantity, or a particular penalty. Those are additional legal questions.

The primary intoxicants discussion prevents a simplistic example. At Arabic I473, Ibn Rushd reports the Iraqi argument from the Qurʾānic ends of avoiding hostility and obstruction of remembrance to the intoxicating amount; he then weighs it against the scope of the transmitted prohibition. He finds reference to the intoxicating kind more probable, invokes blocking the means and deterrent strictness even when the immediate injury lies in much consumption, and notes that acceptance of the more explicit report about small and large quantities would alter the dispute. This is interpretation, practical causal assessment, evidential comparison and prevention operating together. It is not the single inference “wine harms reason, therefore all legal details follow.” Nor does his report that others infer the correctness of every mujtahid make that his own unqualified conclusion. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF p.473; image checked

The penalty comparison must remain separate. Arabic II444 reports the argument attributed to ʿAlī that drinking leads to intoxication, disordered speech and false accusation, supporting eighty lashes, alongside the rival forty-lash account and its reports. A predicted sequence supplies the resemblance, but it does not itself reveal a textual universal prescribing the same numerical punishment. This is precisely why the introduction and Ḍarūrī use it as a difficult example of genuine transfer. Describing its inferential weakness does not settle every evidentiary argument about the penalty in the later chapter. The penalty chapter is not certified complete by this targeted check. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF p.444 Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF p.4 al-Ḍarūrī §273, PDF pp.308–309

2.5.2 Aristotelian differentiation and the place of virtue in reasoning

Ibn Rushd's restraint is intelligible through his differentiation of sciences, objects and epistemic methods. Practical inquiry normally works with contingent facts and probable indications; particular rulings can nevertheless have decisive grounds. The generality of a proposition, the formal validity of an inference, the truth of its premises and the certainty of its conclusion are different matters. Neither a universal legal formulation nor an Aristotelian vocabulary makes jurisprudence demonstrative throughout.

Virtue and political goods can inform the identification and assessment of a juridically relevant feature during reasoning. They are not reserved for a moral commentary written after derivation. Ibn Rushd's ribā discussion actually assesses the rival grounds through justice, commensuration and the uses of exchange. But final explanation—why an order is good—and proximate juridical warrant—why this act bears this ruling under these conditions—remain distinct. A general end can help discriminate between interpretations without mechanically generating a number, threshold, sequence or remedy. The conclusion of Bidāya makes virtue and social order explicit; it does not dispense with the intervening work of legal determination. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.131–133,475–476

The methodological sequence “reconstruct the argument before proposing our interpretation” is therefore a rule for the researcher, not a theory that Ibn Rushd reasons without ethical understanding until the last stage. We must discover where the primary jurist uses purposes, where he does not, and where he rejects a proposed extension despite its attractive end. His criticism of generic interest in §266 remains in force as a demanding countertext to his situational reasoning about illness-marriage; neither passage should silence the other. al-Ḍarūrī §§265–266, PDF pp.304–305 Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.46–47

The earlier emphasis on marriage and transactions had a precise primary point of contact; it never justified excluding worship from detailed inquiry. In §268 necessary affairs such as sales and marriage make the relevant indicators more evident; the contrast names fixed penalties and expiations. It is not a declaration that every social rule is transparent or that worship excludes intelligible benefit.

2.6 Identifying, refining and applying the operative ground

Al-Mustaṣfā supplies a particularly concrete bridge between general practical knowledge and the singular decision. Ghazālī distinguishes taḥqīq al-manāṭ, determining a known criterion in an instance; tanqīḥ al-manāṭ, removing irrelevant accompanying features from an event to which a ruling is attached; and takhrīj al-manāṭ, inferring a ground not explicitly supplied. These are not three interchangeable words for applying a rule. In his account the first is indispensable even for those who contest legal analogy, while the third is a principal site of controversy.

His maintenance example concerns relatives: that sufficiency is owed can be established, while whether a given quantity suffices for this person is a probable practical assessment. His other examples include valuation of destroyed property, appointments, the direction of prayer and judging through witnesses whose reliability must be assessed. These examples show why legal knowing cannot be exhausted by an inventory of transmitted sentences. Unbounded particulars require qualified assessment. They do not show that a jurist may substitute an arbitrary preference for an adopted legal standard.

This distinction changes the architecture of several existing cases. In spousal maintenance, M003, choosing between a fixed measure and adequacy is prior to measuring adequacy in a household; Ghazālī’s example illuminates the second operation but does not settle the first. In Z008, accepting debt as an exemption differs from accepting a particular person’s assertion that a debt exists. In the found-property proof sequence, L015–L021, the kind of legally sufficient proof differs from the assessment of a claimant’s imperfect description under that standard. In C004, the scope of rushd differs from evidence that a person possesses it. In J001, identifying impairment as the relevant ground differs from finding impairment in the judge before us. These mappings are ours and are identified as analytical comparisons in the notes.

The distinction also sharpens the upward connection to virtue. A judge’s patient observation and fairness may be required for accurate assessment; their exercise can in turn train those qualities. But good character does not itself decide a disputed evidentiary rule. Nor does a correct standard ensure that an official has the knowledge, time, resources or independence needed to apply it. The conceptual relation to prudence and the Khaldunian conditions of professional competence belongs precisely at that juncture.

2.7 Four kinds of “principle,” with different authority

The word “principle” must not cover every general sentence indiscriminately. The annotations distinguish the following uses. Kızılkaya’s historical analysis supports the distinction while documenting variation in medieval terminology; this is a modern control, not a definition retroactively assigned to Ibn Rushd.

Kind What it organizes What it cannot do alone
Uṣūl principle or disputed methodological position Sources, language, indication, extension and conditions of warranted inference Determine an individual’s facts or prove that a particular social effect occurred
Cross-chapter fiqh maxim, qāʿida fiqhiyya A recurring legal relation across domains, such as intention, harm or continuity Override all exceptions or replace the specific evidence governing a contested case
Chapter-specific criterion or ḍābiṭ A local class of acts or relationships, such as the sufficient knowledge required in the unseen-sale dispute Automatically govern other contracts or be presented as a verbatim historical maxim when the label is ours
Philosophical or historical proposition Formation of virtue, cooperation, authority, vocation or conditions of civilizational development Serve unannounced as a juristic proof or an author’s explicit sabab

There is now a directly checked primary location for the well-known maxims. At the end of Book V, Jamʿ al-Jawāmiʿ attributes to al-Qāḍī Ḥusayn four foundations: certainty is not removed by doubt; harm is removed; hardship brings facilitation; and custom has determining authority. It then introduces “matters are according to their purposes” separately with qīla, “it is said.” The printed wording and that asymmetry of attribution matter. The editor’s examples below the matn must not be silently attributed to al-Subkī.

These maxims now function as controlled questions within the cases. What exactly was certain before the alleged change? Whose harm would an intervention remove, and whose might it introduce? Is the hardship legally relevant, and what relief is authorized? Does custom help determine an open measure or conflict with a fixed requirement? Does intention constitute this legal undertaking, and how could a court know it? They are productive precisely when they direct inquiry instead of terminating it. A statement that every rule embodies all five would conceal the legal differences the project is meant to explain.

The supplied translated qawāʿid compilation now provides a wider working catalogue: all 91 numbered entries of its index are recorded, with repetitions and mixed types preserved. Twenty-four additional typed notes distinguish such matters as initial liability, unproved changes, remote conjecture, evidence-supported doubt, necessity, the measure and duration of relief, surviving rights, prevention, lesser harm, contractual substance and public office. The catalogue’s apparent completeness is not mistaken for doctrinal uniformity. Some entries are questions; some are uṣūl rules; some occur only in the index. Its internal page column does not reliably locate this 168-page file, so the apparatus uses actual PDF pages.

This expansion matters to the philosophy of formation. Requiring proof before imposing a debt trains one kind of justice; requiring proof of discharge after an established debt trains another. Emergency permission can preserve a life while leaving a claim to compensation. Care can require intervention, restraint or an authorized substitute. Public benefit can limit an office without creating that office’s power. The alchemical interpretation must follow these differentiated relations, rather than beginning with a single unrestricted maxim of benefit.

The guardianship sequence adds a constraint on the move from general good to practical determination. A duty to prevent an unlawful act is not the same legal relation as an exclusive power to authorize another person’s act. The relevant competence is also domain-specific: Ibn Rushd distinguishes financial rushd from sound judgment about matrimonial suitability. A rank among guardians can govern precedence without deciding validity; a witness can announce an event without qualifying to prove it judicially. The architecture therefore asks four further questions at each institutional step: which duty, whose power, competence for what, and what kind of public evidence? These are source-grounded distinctions; their integration into one methodological test is our reconstruction. Bidāya Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.10–14,17–18

The Ḍarūrī’s account of bayān also sharpens the temporal relation between general and particular knowledge. Further specification can in certain cases await the time of need, but clarification cannot be postponed beyond it. The distinction does not eliminate probable knowledge: §§198–199 retain the authority of apparent indications. Bidāya’s appeal to the public need for a clear guardian institution is therefore a qualified evidentiary argument, not a demand that every legal rule be unambiguous or an independently verified history of early practice. al-Ḍarūrī §§188–194, PDF pp.252–259; §§198–199, PDF pp.260–263

2.8 How to read the new short references

The abbreviations identify both a source and a type of operation: Ḍ for al-Ḍarūrī, M for al-Mustaṣfā, J for Jamʿ al-Jawāmiʿ, Q for a fiqh maxim or its historical classification, and B for a local Bidāya criterion. The full register gives the proposition, its limits, the precise witness and page or paragraph. In the HTML reader each abbreviation opens that explanation on hover, keyboard focus or click. In Markdown it links to the complete register entry.

“Rushdian primary” identifies an argument in Ibn Rushd’s text. A note applying it to a Bidāya discussion still states whether that connection is explicit or reconstructed. “Ghazālian comparison” can support a distinction or register disagreement. “Later control” never means that Ibn Rushd used al-Subkī’s terminology. The notes are intentionally absent where a principle would be merely decorative. Coverage of the current dossiers is not completion of the unprocessed books.

2.9 Three universalities and two directions of inquiry

The following distinction is our analytical reconstruction, tested against the preceding passages. It does not translate three technical divisions expressly listed by Ibn Rushd.

Level What is general How it is established What it cannot supply alone
Semantic universality The wider normative meaning intended by a revealed expression Wording, implication, tanbīh and authorized contextual indications, with their varying strength The truth of every empirical premise or the applicability of the criterion to this object
Practical-causal universality Recurring relations among acts, faculties, means, consequences and institutions Relevant experience, competent observation and discipline-specific reasoning A sharʿī status or judicial power merely because a causal relation is plausible
Teleological universality Goods such as justice, ʿiffa, generosity and cooperative order, and their higher orientation Explicit legal ends and a controlled reading across particulars; comparative philosophy where identified The determinate morphology of every positive requirement

The three can interact within one argument without appearing in every case. In ribā the proposed food or measurement predicate is semantic, the economic function of goods and valuation supplies practical intelligibility, and justice supplies final explanation. None makes the others self-validating. In illness-marriage the concrete evidence of injurious intent is central, but Ibn Rushd does not furnish a new textual expression whose generalization settles the issue. In found property, the survival of an animal and the trustworthiness of custodians may change while the protected owner's claim remains. It would be an error to relabel every one of those judgments “semantic extension.” Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.46–47,129–135,304–309

The upward movement is from particulars to a defensible understanding of an order; the downward movement asks what that understanding can illuminate in another case. Both are corrected by contrary particulars. “Universal” must not conceal the difference between a generally worded norm, a recurrent causal tendency and an ultimate end. A social generalization may be probabilistic; a proposed textual meaning may be contested; a final good may be established while its proximate means remain disputed. The evidence for each receives a separate entry in the case record.

2.10 Sadd al-dharāʾiʿ and maṣlaḥa: foreseeable ends and the limits of discretion

Sadd al-dharāʾiʿ, blocking means to a prohibited or injurious end, has a distinctive direction: present act or arrangement → probable causal trajectory → legally significant future end. Semantic interpretation may establish the norm governing that end; it does not itself establish the probability that these means produce it. This operation therefore needs knowledge of incentives, circumstances, motives, institutions and circumvention. It is also different from assimilating one particular to another merely because they resemble one another.

Ibn Rushd explicitly attributes the illness-divorce dispute to whether sadd al-dharāʾiʿ is to be followed: a husband may use divorce to remove a wife's inheritance. He records different limits upon her continuing claim, then criticizes both the alleged consensus and especially expansive consequences of the Mālikī account. In commerce he attributes Mālik's restriction of deferred exchanges with identical benefits to closing a route to a benefit-bearing loan, but also considers whether a report establishes an independent substantive prohibition instead. These are competing explanations in the primary text. We must not use the Mālikī label to predetermine which explanation wins. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.82–83,134–135

Maṣlaḥa, benefit or welfare considered under its claimed legal warrant, is not identical to one inference form. It may help interpret an indicated meaning, assess consequences, rank competing claims, or support a contested proposed rule. In illness-marriage Ibn Rushd rejects a defective gift analogy and describes two dangers: adding law through remote benefit reasoning, and allowing adherence to outward forms to facilitate injustice. He directs qualified, morally trustworthy scholars knowledgeable in the wisdom of the laws to examine shawāhid al-ḥāl, evidence of the circumstances. The medical/craft analogy concerns trained discrimination where a fixed technical formula cannot anticipate opposed demands. It neither eliminates the law nor makes a virtuous reputation sufficient evidence of another person's intention. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.46–47

This is a substantive complication of the Ḍarūrī's rejection of generic interest. A bounded reconciliation is possible: unsupported general legislation differs from situated prevention of evidenced injury. Yet the two texts do not themselves provide a complete criterion for when one becomes the other, or a full procedural law for the inquiry. Chronological development is another hypothesis, not a conclusion established simply by placing the books side by side. Our case analysis must retain this unresolved boundary. Khidr cannot resolve it: a jurist's investigation concerns communicable evidence, not providential knowledge unavailable to the parties.

2.11 Later Mālikī systematization: comparison without retrospective attribution

A useful structural comparison distinguishes micro-hermeneutics—a revealed particular, its indicated general meaning and further application—from macro-hermeneutics—many transmitted particulars, induction and a universal principle used in further interpretation. These are our labels, not exclusive authorial methods. Ibn Rushd can reason across the law, and al-Shāṭibī can interpret individual expressions. The contrast concerns explanatory emphasis, not the discovery of induction by one author or proof that the later author borrowed this structure from the earlier one.

In the supplied Muwāfaqāt I, al-Shāṭibī argues that cumulative evidences can yield certainty unavailable from an isolated report; he grounds the necessities through a convergence of particulars and argues for subsequent reasoning through the resulting universals. He also insists on the primacy of transmitted authorization when reason and transmission work together. Thus particulars are evidence for knowing universals, and universals can discipline interpretation and further extension. His certainty thesis must remain his argued doctrine, not our certification that every modern list of purposes meets its demands. The present primary check uses Nyazee's translation, authorial preliminary concepts rather than its separately marked editorial notes. al-Shāṭibī, Muwāfaqāt I, PDF pp.36–43,76–78; printed pp.1–8,41–43

Opwis reconstructs the further relation: universals are realized through particulars, and the weight of a universal does not automatically defeat every particular indicant. Some of her fuller examples come from later Muwāfaqāt volumes not independently collated here. Her distinction between singular permissible acts and a repeated pattern also bears on our account of habit, but legal classification of a pattern is not proof that moral virtue has been acquired. Opwis, Maṣlaḥa and the Purpose of the Law, PDF pp.269–270,337; printed pp.255–256,323

For al-Qarāfī, Opwis documents a more articulated means–ends apparatus: blocking harmful means, enabling means to good ends, legal licenses, and weighing competing principles. Her examples include agreement to prohibit some risks, agreement against overbroad prevention, and contested deferred-sale cases. That variation is essential: the mere possibility that grapes become wine cannot justify prohibiting cultivation. This development helps formulate questions for Ibn Rushd but cannot be projected backward as his completed theory. These particular al-Qarāfī claims are secondary-mediated through Opwis's citations to al-Dhakhīra, al-Furūq and his commentary. The locally supplied Criterion has been used directly for institutional distinctions; it must not be cited as though it were the primary witness for all these different passages. Opwis, PDF pp.165–168, printed pp.151–154

The resulting historical comparison is a series of differently organized problems of meaning, benefit and authority. It is not a demonstrated linear genealogy from Ibn Rushd through al-Qarāfī to al-Shāṭibī, nor a claim that later maqāṣid retrospectively supplies the warrant for every earlier rule.

2.12 Scripture, transmitted explanation and the ethical field of judgment

The project's goal is now to reconstruct the rule within its scriptural and ethical field, as well as its technical derivation. For each detailed social-law question, identify the Qurʾānic passages and reports actually invoked in the Bidāya, restore their relevant textual setting, trace the reports through collections, and read selected commentaries for what they say about purposes, affections, responsibilities, relations and formation. Related evidence introduced by the researcher must be marked separately. The aim is to recover the wider human address that a narrowly extracted legal proposition can leave implicit.

The disciplines have distinct objects. Hadith criticism assesses attribution and transmission, with different routes and wordings retained. Hadith commentary interprets language, reconciles versions, reconstructs the narrated situation and draws legal, ethical or spiritual implications. Tafsīr interprets Qurʾānic discourse through transmitted reports, language, context and other author-specific methods. Prophetic explanation within tafsīr is distinguished from Companion and Successor interpretation and from a commentator's reasoning. Ishārī exegesis develops spiritual allusions through its own interpretive moves; some amplify an overt ethical exhortation, while others transpose a textual relation into a spiritual analogy. Uṣūl al-fiqh evaluates the normative force of these materials and the legitimacy of inference. These are intersecting sciences, not interchangeable names for one body of explanation.

Ethical wisdom is therefore a governing research priority, without requiring that every report have the same primary purpose. A narrative can teach by the Prophet's manner of attending, asking, withholding, correcting or facilitating, as well as through an explicit injunction. Conversely, an attractive moral interpretation does not establish a report's authenticity or convert a recommendation into an enforceable claim. A commentator's ḥikma must also be distinguished from an operative ʿilla: the former may illuminate an act's end without defining the legal extension of its rule.

The new unit is a linked dossier, not a quotation appended to each ruling:

Bidāya position and explicit reason ↔ identified verse/report and its variants ↔ full relevant discourse or encounter ↔ attributed commentarial interpretations ↔ disciplined account of goods, dispositions and institutions.

A report family can serve several legal questions. Its common textual history should be maintained once, with each question recording the wording and feature on which it depends. Qurʾānic records likewise preserve the exact verse, neighbouring discourse and competing readings, rather than reusing an isolated phrase as if every school gave it the same construction. An aḥkām anthology helps find material, but its omissions cannot define the limits of the inquiry. The six major collections are central witnesses; Mālik's Muwaṭṭaʾ, Aḥmad's Musnad, the muṣannaf collections and al-Bayhaqī may be necessary when the actual argument leads there.

Commentaries must be read for counterevidence as well as enrichment. Record the author's preferred reading separately from opinions and reports merely transmitted. Distinguish the circumstances supplied by a narrative from an independently attested date or occasion; reported asbāb al-nuzūl or al-wurūd require their own transmission assessment. Chapter titles are evidence of a compiler's arrangement, not additional prophetic speech. Numbering is edition-dependent: retain narrator, Arabic opening, collection, book/chapter, number as used and actual page locator. Online text is a provisional witness until collated with a specified edition.

The dower pilot implements this method in K053, K055, K057, K064 and K067. Its controls are , , and the Sahl marriage narrative; appears as the context of Ibn ʿAjība's combined exposition. These cases distinguish an obligatory gift, attentive facilitation, provision through time, enforceable entitlement, free relinquishment, cultivated moral perception and symbolic spiritual transposition. Each source interpretation is cited at the point of use. The remaining dower reports, all earlier cases and the rest of the book still need this layer. The acquired scripture and commentary library supplies the working texts for that expansion; acquisition status and edition defects are kept separate from interpretive completion. See the source acquisition and task plan and pilot evidence register.

3. A map of fields, objects and warrants

Field or function Principal object in this project What it can establish What it does not establish by itself
Theology and metaphysics God, creation, human powers, final ends Ontological and theological commitments of an author The detailed ruling on every transaction or ritual
Historical uṣūl al-fiqh Sources, indications, inference, qualifications Conditions of warranted legal judgment Actual compliance or achieved sanctity
Fiqh Determinate classifications, rights, obligations, conditions and remedies A juristic account of what an act or situation requires The historical frequency of that act or automatic moral transformation
Legal maxims Generalizations across legal particulars Cross-case coherence and recurring relations An unrestricted license to override particular evidence
Maqāṣid / maṣlaḥa discourse Purposes, benefits, harms and their ordering An author’s account of legal goods and the authority of considering them A single timeless theory shared by all jurists
Virtue ethics Excellent dispositions, choice, feeling and practical judgment How an agent becomes and acts well Whether a claimed legal proof is authentic
Spiritual discipline Purification, attention, sincerity, realization A tradition’s account of inward formation and its practices Judicial proof of another person’s hidden state
Political philosophy Cooperative order and common ends Norms for evaluating a city and its offices A causal history of how actual dynasties rise or decline
ʿIlm al-ʿumrān Conditions and regularities of human association Explanations of possibility, durability, change and breakdown The validity of every legal or theological claim
Fatwā Advice about a legal question A qualified jurist’s answer within its conditions A binding judicial determination of disputed facts merely by being issued
Qaḍāʾ Disputes, proof, jurisdiction, enforceable resolution The authorized settlement of a case within competence Knowledge of every inward or providential truth
Historical legal practice Documents, cases, offices, institutions and conduct What people actually did in particular settings, with evidentiary limits Transparent access to an ideal legal system from a handbook alone

The last three rows are particularly important. Al-Qarāfī distinguishes legal opinions from judicial rulings and administrative acts. His account of judicial action concerns disputable worldly matters within limits; it cannot simply be transferred to ritual validity or all inward duties. The categories are normative distinctions, and the historical allocation of offices can vary. al-Qarāfī, Criterion, PDF pp.79–82, printed pp.62–65, first question.

Masud, Messick and David Powers’ collection offers a complementary historical method: identify the question, doctrine, factual construction, intended audience, rhetorical strategy and institutional setting of a fatwā. Its introduction describes both private advice and official or semi-official service, as well as differences among Andalusian, Mamluk and Ottoman arrangements. This corrects any blanket equation of “mufti” with either a fully autonomous sage or a uniform state official. The Ibn Rushd whose fatwās are mentioned there as those of the scholar who died in 1126 is the grandfather, not the author of the Bidāya. Masud, Messick and Powers, Islamic Legal Interpretation, PDF pp.7–8, preface; pp.16–21, printed pp.8–13.

The intelligible background of positive law must itself be differentiated. The following map names tasks in this reconstruction; “economics” and “philosophy of language” are convenient analytical labels, not a claim that Ibn Rushd institutionalized modern disciplines under these names.

Field Contribution to interpretation and judgment Limit of that contribution
Logic Distinguishes inference forms, valid transitions and kinds of premise. Formal validity does not authenticate a report or supply an absent legal premise.
Rhetoric Explains probable assent and transfer through exemplum. Persuasive force is not demonstration or independently sufficient legal warrant.
Language and interpretation Discloses scope, implication, metaphor, context and intended meaning. Words do not establish all facts about the things they signify.
Psychology Clarifies cognition, appetite, intention, agency and acquired habit. A proposed psychology does not establish hidden intention in court.
Natural philosophy and medicine Investigates relevant bodies, illness, capacities and effects. Technical knowledge informs the case without itself creating jurisdiction.
Economic inquiry Clarifies use, valuation, property, scarcity, incentives and circumvention. A predicted gain or loss does not by itself authorize a sharʿī ruling.
Ethics Interprets dispositions, practical excellence and flourishing. A final good cannot manufacture every threshold or condition.
Politics Examines common goods, cooperation, office and allocation of power. An efficient institution may serve unjust ends.
Metaphysics Clarifies final causality and the hierarchy of ends. Ontological rank does not prove the legal powers of an officeholder.

The primary legal anchors are sense-perception and ijtihād in applying a meaning, the economic explanation of ribā, and trained situational judgment in illness-marriage. The fuller distribution among sciences is our reconstruction. The relation is assistance in understanding the realities implicated by revelation, not nine independent sharʿī sources. When such assistance changes the interpretation, the relevant factual premise and the source of its normative force must both be stated. al-Ḍarūrī §260, PDF pp.300–301 Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.46–47,131–133

3.1 The jurist, mufti and judge: generality is relative to the task

A later, unusually precise control is al-Subkī’s classification as translated and examined by Norman Calder. Al-Subkī distinguishes the writing and teaching jurist’s consideration of general legal matters, the mufti’s application to the particular situation and its circumstances, and the judge’s additional ascertainment of grounds, response to opposition and binding decision. The same person may perform all three functions. Calder stresses that the ideal classification must not be confused with every officeholder’s actual competence. We have read the translated passages in this modern study; their Arabic Fatāwā source remains to be collated independently. Calder, Islamic Jurisprudence, PDF pp.127–131, printed pp.119–123; pp.135–137, printed pp.127–129.

This is not a contradiction of Ibn Rushd’s classification of fiqh as comparatively particular practical knowledge. It demonstrates that generality is relative: a rule of ablution is particular relative to general rules of legal inference, yet general relative to this person’s ablution under these conditions. Al-Subkī’s distinction also warns that a particular fatwā may include circumstances preventing its unqualified incorporation into a general school rule. Upward movement from case to principle therefore requires scrutiny, not copying a response into a universal proposition. Calder, Islamic Jurisprudence, PDF pp.129–131.

There are consequently at least four transitions to trace: a source or general inference to a legal rule; a legal rule to a situation as described; a described situation to facts established through an authorized procedure; and a warranted determination to action and compliance. Neither uṣūl, a handbook nor an exemplary judge eliminates the need for the other transitions. Juristic knowing is civilizational because it depends on training, transmission, trustworthy descriptions, offices, records and the practical ability to enact a decision.

Calder’s argument is itself an object of criticism. His treatment emphasizes the juristic significance of preserved fatwās and the different status of judgments; this should not be enlarged into a claim that judicial records have no historical value or that muftis were always independent of appointment. His own discussion notes changing Ottoman institutional arrangements. Period, place, genre and function need independent entries in the social map. Calder, Islamic Jurisprudence, PDF p.137, including notes 25–26; Masud, Messick and Powers, Islamic Legal Interpretation, PDF pp.16–21, introductory discussion.

The found-property and zakāt commentaries make these transitions concrete. Proof of ownership differs from the substantive owner’s right; evidence of debt differs from the legal debt exemption; judicially authorized expense differs from a voluntary undertaking; and the collector’s arrival can itself enter a condition of obligation. These are legal operations through which the city continually constitutes and corrects its relations, not merely examples of a theory developed elsewhere.

Jamʿ provides a later primary formulation for the jurist’s formation itself: al-Subkī reports his father’s description of someone for whom the relevant sciences have become malaka through knowledge and practice, producing a capacity to understand the Lawgiver’s intent. This is a normative account of acquired legal competence. It supports inquiry into teaching, repeated judgment and professional formation without identifying intellectual malaka with moral virtue, spiritual realization or the actual competence of every historical officeholder.

Representative route: worship and public practice

Revision 14 · 4 October 2026. Selected studies across every editorial division; exact source spans below delimit the selection. These are representative interpretations, not chapter-completion or elementary-rule counts.

Quoted scriptural clauses below are selected working translations from the cited Arabic. Exegetical views are named; the paragraph labelled “Its ethical argument” is the manuscript’s close reading of the passage and its surrounding clauses. The purple note gives the full explanation and exact sources. A related passage does not become the direct evidence for a ruling merely by being placed beside it.

The representative route begins with the formation of the jurist, then follows the ritual and public books through food. It does not reduce worship to civic utility. A practice can order the body, school attention, provide for another person and orient the practitioner toward God; these effects differ in bearer and in the evidence needed to establish them. The existing detailed prayer and purification chapters remain alongside this route.

The cases distinguish changes from their conditions. Digestio concerns assimilation over time; cohobatio a return to the same action with renewed understanding; temperamentum the correction of one legitimate tendency by another. Athanor and balneum name enabling surroundings. The terms do not form one obligatory sequence. The chapters on voluntary fasting and funerals test the framework precisely where greater severity or greater haste can defeat the good sought.

REP-02. Ablution: repeated washing and renewed attention

Follow the argument RulingLegal reasoningScripture

Division 2: Ablution.

Ibn Rushd: summary of the ruling and disagreement. Ibn Rushd reports that Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, Aḥmad, Abū Thawr and Dāwūd make intention a condition of valid ablution; Abū Ḥanīfa and al-Thawrī do not. His stated reason is ablution’s double character: it combines worship with cleanliness. Its closer resemblance to worship whose purpose is not rationally intelligible, or to cleansing whose purpose is understood, changes whether intention is required for validity. Ethical force of the passage. The concession belongs to the gift described by the verse. Gratitude answers a form of access to worship that accommodates illness, travel and scarcity; it is not appreciation for an ordeal as such. Purification and gratitude therefore belong together, while the precise acts remain matters of juristic interpretation.

REP-03. Bathing: completeness of the act and the body as a whole

Follow the argument RulingLegal reasoningScripture

Division 3: Bathing.

Ruling and reason for disagreement. Most jurists in this passage require water to reach the body; Mālik and most of his followers also require rubbing, with al-Muzanī reported alongside them. Ibn Rushd considers the meaning of washing and the relation between descriptive reports and an answer giving sufficient performance. He treats the latter evidentiary issue as more important than an unsupported appeal to ordinary washing. Intention and rinsing the mouth and nose produce further, distinct disagreements. Bidāya Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.43–45

How the legal argument works. · . These notes identify the relevant mechanism or comparative control; later maxims do not establish Ibn Rushd’s historical vocabulary.

Bathing, bodily completeness and an unnecessary burden

Text and setting. Umm Salama asks whether tightly braided hair must be undone for the major bath. The reply directs water to the head and body without requiring the braids to be undone in the reported case. This is a woman’s practical question about her own washing. A variant adds menstruation to the question about janāba; the variant is relevant to competing distinctions between kinds of bathing.

The ethical argument. Completeness concerns the required reach of water, not an independently meritorious dismantling of every bodily arrangement. The difference is between removing an obstruction to the act and multiplying the act’s burdens.

How the commentators read it. Al-Nawawī makes the answer conditional on water reaching the hair as required in his school: when braiding prevents that, undoing is necessary; when it does not, undoing is unnecessary. He reports contrary views requiring undoing generally or specifically after menstruation. The same reasoning applies to a man with braided hair. His reading of Ibn ʿUmar’s stricter instruction offers alternatives—different hair, a different doctrine, or precaution—rather than declaring one historical motive certain.

Scope of this reading. This directly explains the braids report. The contemporary inference about proportionate burden remains distinct from Ibn Rushd’s school attributions and from inward interpretations of washing.

REP-05. Removing impurity without humiliating the learner

Follow the argument RulingLegal reasoningScripture

Division 5: Removal of impurity.

Ruling and reason for disagreement. Ibn Rushd records obligation, emphatic recommendation, and obligation conditional on remembrance among the positions on removing impurity. His three explanations are the literal or figurative meaning of , apparently conflicting reports, and whether an intelligible ethical purpose changes the force of an imperative. This is unusually direct evidence that the relation between practical benefit and legal modality is itself disputed. Bidāya Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.74–75

How the legal argument works. · · . These notes identify the relevant mechanism or comparative control; later maxims do not establish Ibn Rushd’s historical vocabulary.

Text and reported setting. In Muslim284–285, bystanders move to interrupt a Bedouin urinating in the mosque. The Prophet restrains them, explains the mosque’s purpose and has water poured over the place.

Ethical force of the passage. The shared sacred space is protected through repair and instruction that do not turn the ignorant person into an enemy. Attention to the sequence matters: an immediate display of indignation could worsen the bodily and spatial harm it seeks to stop.

How the commentators read it. Nawawī explains that interruption could harm the man and spread contamination to his clothes or more of the mosque. Gentle instruction is appropriate to someone ignorant of the rule. Thus compassion, practical causal knowledge and preservation of the place cooperate; none requires pretending that the conduct was already acceptable.

·

The surrounding Qurʾānic argument. belongs to the opening summons to warn, magnify the Lord, purify, leave defilement and endure for the Lord. Ibn ʿĀshūr distinguishes literal clothing from the person it can signify, and physical cleansing from ethical purification; he considers the combinations jointly possible. This preserves a genuine interpretive plurality behind Ibn Rushd’s question about the verse’s indication. Physical and inward readings need not compete, but their coexistence does not settle the precise legal degree of removing impurity.

REP-06. Prayer: humility expressed through deliberate movement

Follow the argument RulingLegal reasoningScripture

Division 6: Prayer and its ordinary requirements.

Ruling and reason for disagreement. R001–R015 already distinguish the disputed movements, their transmitted variants and their legal force. The representative question is how a received bodily form expresses humility without making every variant a separate metaphysical doctrine. Ibn Rushd's local argument and his identification of expressed humility remain the starting point. Bidāya Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.133–140

How the legal argument works. · · · . These notes identify the relevant mechanism or comparative control; later maxims do not establish Ibn Rushd’s historical vocabulary.

Text and reported setting. begins with the success of believers whose prayer is marked by khushūʿ, reverent attentiveness. The passage continues through avoidance of empty activity, giving, sexual restraint, fidelity to trusts and preservation of prayer, ending with inheritance of Paradise (23:3–11).

Ethical force of the passage. The opening promise concerns a whole form of life: attentive prayer stands alongside the keeping of promises and the restraint of appetite. The connection is not that a single gesture mechanically produces salvation. Prayer belongs to a pattern of sustained fidelity whose promised good exceeds civic success. This is a reading of the passage’s sequence, not a claim that all the listed qualities are legal conditions of prayer.

How the commentators read it. Ibn ʿĀshūr reads the listed qualities as manifestations of faith rooted in the person; the list is not an exhaustive inventory of virtue. Qurṭubī’s and Wāḥidī’s reports about correcting the direction of the gaze give one bodily setting for attention. Their different transmissions are retained rather than converted into one certain event.

· · · · · ·

Text and reported setting. The man in Bukhārī757 repeatedly prays and is told to repeat it, then asks to be taught. The instruction describes the movements together with coming to rest in them.

Ethical force of the passage. The encounter connects correction with teachability. Repetition alone had not corrected the action; the learner needed to acknowledge a limit and receive an intelligible account. Its formative possibility lies in attentive correction, not humiliation or the sheer multiplication of attempts.

How the commentators read it. Ibn Ḥajar discusses teaching without harshness and the learner’s acknowledgment of error. He records different explanations for delaying the full instruction, including making the deficiency apparent, with objections retained. These are explanations of the teaching encounter, not additional words spoken in the report.

REP-07. Additional prayer: varied nightly forms and durable devotion

Follow the argument RulingLegal reasoningScripture

Division 7: Further prayers and congregational occasions.

Ruling and reason for disagreement. For witr, Ibn Rushd reports Mālik's preference for three units with a separating salutation, Abū Ḥanīfa's three without that separation, and al-Shāfiʿī's one-unit form. He begins with the diversity of reports, including ʿĀʾisha's descriptions and Ibn ʿUmar's report about making the night prayer odd. The evidence does not warrant reading the three schools as three spiritual temperaments. Bidāya Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.200

How the legal argument works. · . These notes identify the relevant mechanism or comparative control; later maxims do not establish Ibn Rushd’s historical vocabulary.

Durable worship: attention, capacity and the quality of repetition

Text and setting. The reports commend works a person can sustain and describe the household’s persistence in an adopted practice. A neighbouring report concerns a rope used to continue praying after fatigue. Al-Nawawī’s chapter brings habitual night prayer together with moderation. The rope is removed; exhaustion is not made a measure of the practice’s excellence.

The ethical argument. Repetition matters because it repeatedly renews an attentive relation. The number of movements alone does not measure this renewal. A manageable practice can become more formative than an impressive effort followed by abandonment.

How the commentators read it. Al-Nawawī glosses capacity as capacity to continue without harm. He explicitly extends the principle beyond prayer to acts of good generally. His reason is precise: modest continuity sustains obedience, remembrance, watchfulness, intention, sincerity and turning toward the Creator. Excessive strain can produce abandonment or performance without the heart’s openness. He also excludes literal weariness from God and explains the report’s language through the continuance of reward, while recording alternative interpretations.

Scope of this reading. This supports an account of attentive habituation; it does not decide the disputed number of units in a night prayer. Increased effort in the final nights of Ramadan remains a separately attested practice, not a contradiction to be erased.

·

Text and reported setting. gives fasting’s orientation as “so that you may acquire taqwā.” sets it within the month of revelation and joins completion of the prescribed days with ease, magnifying God for guidance and gratitude.

Ethical force of the passage. The passage binds self-restraint to guidance received, not to the amount of deprivation one can endure. Its concessions make faithful completion possible. In the related Salman narrative, care for wife, body and guest limits the pursuit of additional fasting and night prayer: greater intensity is not automatically greater fidelity.

How the commentators read it. Ibn ʿĀshūr situates the prescribed fast among already known practices of fasting. Ibn Ḥajar’s explanation of Salman’s intervention is more pointed than a generic appeal to moderation: a recommended act may be discouraged when exhaustion or neglect of a weightier claim follows. The wife’s circumstances and the body’s needs are part of the practical judgment.

· · ·

REP-08. Funeral care: duty, grief and the need to establish death

Follow the argument RulingLegal reasoningScripture

Division 8: Funerals.

Ruling and reason for disagreement. Ibn Rushd introduces funerals as the rights of the dead upon the living. Washing is treated as a communal obligation or communal sunna; the disagreement concerns transmitted practice and whether instructions to wash teach the manner alone or also command the act. He also qualifies prompt burial where apparent death may be mistaken, extending a caution about drowning to conditions discussed by physicians. Bidāya Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.225–226

How the legal argument works. · . These notes identify the relevant mechanism or comparative control; later maxims do not establish Ibn Rushd’s historical vocabulary.

Text and reported setting. Muslim939 records women washing the Prophet’s daughter under instructions to wash three or five times, or more if needed, with the final treatment and a garment provided for her shroud.

Ethical force of the passage. The person receiving care can no longer reciprocate or complain. Need and honour therefore guide a practice performed entirely by others. The number is not an invitation to maximize ritual labour regardless of the body’s condition.

How the commentators read it. Nawawī distinguishes the minimum communal obligation from recommended repetitions and explains “if you consider it” by the need for cleansing. He treats the final care as honouring the dead. The conduct can cultivate tenderness and responsible judgment in the living while serving the deceased without any claim that the deceased undergoes a new acquired habit.

·

The whole funeral sequence and the missing English leaves

The funeral book is present in the Arabic witness. Its sequence is: attendance at dying and certainty of death; washing; shrouding; carrying and following; funeral prayer, including its agents, times, place and form; and burial, with the connected acts around the grave. Washing is the representative developed here. The primary book inventory exposes the other chapters and their source pages without pretending that this one study supplies their complete analysis.

The supplied English Volume I moves from PDF p.264, printed p.258, to the zakāt book at PDF p.265; its next numbered page is284. Printed pp.259–282, including the funeral book, are absent from this file. The two sides of the jump have been checked as images. This is a defect in the supplied witness, not an omission from Ibn Rushd’s work. Arabic I225–244 supplies the missing route.

REP-09. Zakāt: provision and the transformation of attachment

Follow the argument RulingLegal reasoningScripture

Division 9: Zakat.

Ibn Rushd: summary of the ruling and disagreement. Ibn Rushd reports disagreement over zakāt on a minor’s wealth. Mālik and al-Shāfiʿī are among those who require it; other jurists deny it, while Abū Ḥanīfa distinguishes agricultural produce from other assets. The central reason is whether zakāt is understood as worship, which requires maturity, or as an obligatory right of the poor in the wealth of the rich. The same transfer can therefore be considered from the giver’s responsibility and the recipient’s claim. Bidāya Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.244–246

al-Ḍarūrī · method · Arabic / Englishal-Ḍarūrī: maturity and personal obligation

Bidāya Arabic II, printed/PDF p.476

How the legal argument works. · . These notes identify the relevant mechanism or comparative control; later maxims do not establish Ibn Rushd’s historical vocabulary.

Text and reported setting. asks for respite to the distressed debtor and commends remission. recalls return to God, full recompense and absence of wrong. then requires truthful dictation, an impartial writer, reliable testimony and protection against harm to writer or witness; it explicitly names greater justice, stronger evidence and reduced doubt.

Ethical force of the passage. The sequence places the creditor, debtor and record-maker under different responsibilities. Mercy does not erase truthful accounting; a documented claim does not justify impossible exaction. Return to God relativizes the advantage obtained by manipulating a record: no party’s worldly success determines the final accounting. The call to taqwā addresses, among other things, the debtor’s temptation to understate what is due.

How the commentators read it. Ibn ʿĀshūr explains that ending ribā does not end credit. A trader, craft worker or farmer may have ability but lack capital; reliable documentation supports confidence and useful activity. His treatment of distinguishes genuine distress from the burden of immediate payment and records disagreement about the provision’s scope. The Study Quran carries the discussion beyond the record to : one reported reading concerns the witness’s concealed knowledge, while another concerns inward accountability more generally. This continuation prevents documentation from being treated as an exhaustive account of truthfulness. The editors’ synthesis is cited as such, rather than assigned wholesale to one classical commentator.

· · · · ·

Direct context and explanation. addresses people who acknowledge mixed conduct. Ibn ʿĀshūr relates the offering to repentance after failure to join the Tabūk expedition and its common expenses. The Study Quran records both an expiatory reading tied to that episode and a reading of as obligatory zakāt. Ibn ʿĀshūr explains cleansing as removing the blameworthy condition (takhliya) and tazkiya as acquiring virtues (taḥliya). He connects reassurance to the repentant person’s unsettled heart. The Study Quran preserves the dispute between the specific expiatory offering and obligatory alms, then explains how the Prophet’s prayer brings gladness, peace and mercy. This prevents an undifferentiated use of the occasion to settle all later fiscal questions. Its mediated report of al-Rāzī on purification remains an attribution through that editorial work.

· · · · · ·

Direct context and explanation. Muslim19 places the instruction at Muʿādh’s dispatch to Yemen: teaching, prayer and alms are presented in sequence to the community he is to encounter. Nawawī derives a duty for the ruler to warn governors against injustice. He explains that the collector should take neither the owner’s choicest property nor accept the worst: the middle quality protects both sides. He also preserves differing readings of “their poor,” so the phrase cannot by itself establish an uncontested prohibition of transferring alms elsewhere. These distinctions belong inside an account of zakāt’s formative and civic effects.

REP-10. Zakāt al-fiṭr: dependence within the household

Follow the argument RulingLegal reasoningScripture

Division 10: Zakat al fitr.

Ruling and reason for disagreement. The majority classify zakāt al-fiṭr as obligatory; Ibn Rushd records contrary accounts and relates them to the reports and the interpretation of Ibn ʿUmar's statement that the Prophet prescribed it. A further disagreement asks whether responsibility for another person's payment follows guardianship or maintenance. The text calls it a zakāt of the person rather than of accumulated wealth. Bidāya Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.278–279

How the legal argument works. · . These notes identify the relevant mechanism or comparative control; later maxims do not establish Ibn Rushd’s historical vocabulary.

Festival provision: a purpose does not exhaust a rule

Text and setting. Ibn ʿUmar’s report prescribes a measured food contribution for the community, including young and old, male and female, free and enslaved persons. Abū Saʿīd’s account records both earlier food practice and his refusal to replace it with Muʿāwiya’s proposed wheat equivalent. The narrated administrative setting is a public address about the equivalent amount of Syrian wheat; it is not a newly authenticated occasion for the original obligation. Payment before the festival prayer situates the contribution within a shared public day.

The ethical argument. The text joins individual inclusion to provision for others. A theory that the payment only repairs the giver’s fasting faults cannot explain its application to children. Nor does finding a distributive benefit resolve whether the owed object is a received measure of food or its assessed equivalent.

How the commentators read it. Al-Nawawī reports al-Māzarī’s explanation of the contribution as repairing shortcomings in a prolonged worship. He then answers the inference that children should be exempt: purification describes the predominant situation, not an indispensable condition in each payer. He also points to a sinless person and a person entering Islam just before the due time. On food, he argues that the same measure is prescribed across goods of different values, and therefore rejects reducing the obligation to value alone. He identifies Muʿāwiya’s proposal as an expressed judgment, opposed by another Companion, rather than a Prophetic statement. His Shāfiʿī position is part of the disagreement, not its neutral settlement.

Scope of this reading. The distinction between an explanatory wisdom and the rule’s operative conditions is verified in the commentary. Whether money satisfies the duty remains disputed. This dossier does not independently authenticate every report used by either school.

REP-12. Voluntary fasting: the claims that limit zeal

Follow the argument RulingLegal reasoningScripture

Division 12: Voluntary fasting.

Ruling and reason for disagreement. Ibn Rushd juxtaposes recommended days, disagreements about their specification, and reports restraining excessive fasting. He presents more than one possible explanation for Mālik's dislike of the six days of Shawwāl; his hypothesis about non-reception or non-validation of the report must remain a hypothesis.
