REP-13. Retreat: concentration and the boundary of service

Follow the argument RulingLegal reasoningScripture

Division 13: Retreat.

Ruling and reason for disagreement. Ibn Rushd reports a narrow understanding of iʿtikāf confined to prayer, remembrance and recitation, and Ibn Wahb's wider admission of other acts directed to the hereafter, such as attending funerals, visiting the sick and studying. He identifies the absence of an explicit verbal definition and disagreement about what being held to retreat means; differing reports also enter the argument. Bidāya Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.312–313

How the legal argument works. · . These notes identify the relevant mechanism or comparative control; later maxims do not establish Ibn Rushd’s historical vocabulary.

Retreat: a bounded place and the possibility of mixed motives

Text and setting. The Prophet sees the tents erected for his wives’ retreat, questions the purpose, and has his own tent removed. The report occurs alongside the account of entering the place of retreat after morning prayer. Permission had been given to some of the wives. The later intervention therefore requires explanation; it cannot simply mean that women’s retreat is invalid.

The ethical argument. A secluded space can help concentration while also becoming an object of competition or an intrusion into shared space. The practical boundary serves withdrawal only when the conduct within it serves that end.

How the commentators read it. Al-Nawawī permits a place within the mosque for solitude provided it does not crowd others. Relaying Qāḍī ʿIyāḍ, he gives several explanations of the intervention: concern about competitive proximity, the circumstances of exposure in a public mosque, reproducing domestic life inside the retreat, or crowding. These are competing explanations, not certain knowledge of the wives’ hearts. He explicitly treats the report as evidence that women’s retreat is valid and then records disagreement about withdrawing an earlier permission.

Scope of this reading. The narrator’s sequence is distinguished from proposed motives. Neither the presence of rivalry nor its absence can be diagnosed from the outward form of another person’s retreat alone. The local Muslim file repeats1172 for the tents report, generally referenced as1173; the narrator, chapter and exact file line identify the passage without silently correcting that witness.

·

Text and reported setting. calls spouses garments for one another, permits eating, drinking and intimacy during the fasting night, then excludes intimacy during mosque retreat. It closes with divine limits and their explanation “so that they may acquire taqwā.”

Ethical force of the passage. The same passage acknowledges bodily need and sets apart a time of concentrated worship. Its limits do not declare marital intimacy intrinsically impure. Taqwā here includes recognizing the right time and relation for a good, rather than pursuing either appetite or austerity without measure.

How the commentators read it. Ibn ʿĀshūr distinguishes competing accounts of the night restriction. Against the prevalent abrogation reading, he favours clarification of a permission obscured by people’s own restrictive understanding. That is his exegetical choice, not a settled chronology that cancels the other reports.

·

REP-14. Pilgrimage: capacity, substitution and who actually travels

Follow the argument RulingLegal reasoningScripture

Division 14: Pilgrimage.

Ruling and reason for disagreement. All agree that ability matters, but they differ over its specification through provisions, transport and bodily capacity. Ibn Rushd relates the difference to a report explaining ability and the general wording of . Proxy pilgrimage raises a different opposition: the usual non-substitutability of personal worship and the reports concerning an aged father and a deceased mother's vow. Bidāya Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.319–320

How the legal argument works. · · . These notes identify the relevant mechanism or comparative control; later maxims do not establish Ibn Rushd’s historical vocabulary.

Text and reported setting. commands completion of pilgrimage “for God,” addresses obstruction, illness and inability to afford an offering, then enjoins taqwā and warns of accountability. Muslim1334–1335 places the daughter’s question about an incapacitated father within the pilgrimage setting.

Ethical force of the passage. The passage asks for faithful completion under real limits, not a display of independence from bodily or financial need. The daughter’s question adds filial responsibility: her capacity may serve her father’s incapacity. Whether a particular act admits representation remains a separate legal question.

How the commentators read it. Ibn ʿĀshūr relates to obstruction and distinguishes completing an act already begun from performing it fully. Nawawī explicitly treats the daughter’s act as filial devotion, alongside service, maintenance and repayment of a parent’s debts. He records the disagreement over proxy pilgrimage; the ethical good of service does not erase it.

· · ·

The surrounding Qurʾānic argument. joins the sanctuary and pilgrimage with ability, then declares God independent of the worlds. The obligation cannot be understood as supplying a lack in God. Ibn ʿĀshūr connects ability with such conditions as bodily capacity, resources and safe access, and preserves disagreement over proxy performance. He treats the concluding language about disbelief through several readings, including ingratitude and rejection of the obligation; those alternatives should not be flattened into a judgment that every failure to travel is unbelief.

REP-15. War: protection, restraint and the force of a promise

Follow the argument RulingLegal reasoningScripture

Division 15: Jihad and its public rules.

Ruling and reason for disagreement. The representative problem is amān, a pledge of safety. Ibn Rushd relates disputes about a woman's or an enslaved person's pledge to general wording, status-based analogy, and the interpretation of the Prophet's acceptance of Umm Hāniʾ's protection. Was he recognizing an already effective act or making it effective by approval? The adjacent discussion disputes the scope of protection for noncombatant groups and the relation between and . Bidāya Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.383–384

How the legal argument works. · . These notes identify the relevant mechanism or comparative control; later maxims do not establish Ibn Rushd’s historical vocabulary.

Text and reported setting. In Bukhārī357, Umm Hāniʾ reports that ʿAlī threatens a person she has protected; the Prophet upholds her protection. The related addresses believers before commanding fulfilment of commitments.

Ethical force of the passage. The encounter makes a promise of safety consequential even amid conquest. The ethical question is whether a person who has relied on protection can depend on it when another participant has power to disregard it. The report does not make all grants of protection equally authoritative.

How the commentators read it. Ibn Ḥajar collates versions identifying those protected and the circumstances of the encounter; the identities cannot be made certain by merging the variants. The legal extension of a woman’s protection must still be assessed in the relevant juristic discussion.

· ·

The surrounding Qurʾānic argument. ’s command to fight is followed by the prohibition of transgression and the statement that God does not love transgressors. Ibn ʿĀshūr relates it to anticipated fighting around access to Mecca, while preserving differing accounts of scope and abrogation; his chronology is an exegetical reconstruction. His reading of is broader than a modern exclusively defensive interpretation and must not be silently softened. Yet the local sequence retains treaties in and grants protection to a person seeking it in . On the latter verse he insists that even membership in a treaty-breaking group does not authorize treachery towards someone admitted under protection. Security continues until the person can reach a place of safety. This gives amān a specific ethical demand: hostility towards a group must not dissolve an undertaken obligation towards this individual.

· ·

The surrounding Qurʾānic argument. connects the specified share with belief in God and what was sent down on the day the two forces met. Ibn ʿĀshūr reads its opening demand to know as also demanding action upon that knowledge, and places it in the sūra’s dispute over spoils. The allocation challenges a fighter’s assumption that acquisition by force is sufficient title to the whole gain. The verse concerns booty; that setting is precisely why Ibn Rushd requires an argument before transferring its distribution to fayʾ or conquered land.

Public authority: land, revenue and the claims of future people

Where this belongs in Bidāya. The state is not absent, but it is not represented by one comprehensive chapter of constitutional government. The jihād book proceeds from warfare to a second major division on acquisition and distribution: the fifth, the combatants’ shares, discretionary awards, recovered property, conquered land, fayʾ and jizya (Arabic I390–407). Zakāt concerns another form of public collection and distribution; the final book treats judgment and ends with the civic sunan. The earlier amān study represented only one small part of that political material. Bidāya Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.390–403, division headings and fiscal questions Bidāya Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.460,474–476, judgment and civic conclusion

Land retained for continuing public use. At I401 Ibn Rushd reports Mālik’s position that conquered land ordinarily remains undivided, its revenue supporting Muslim public interests such as fighters’ provision, bridges and mosques, while allowing division when the ruler judges that interest requires it. Al-Shāfiʿī treats it as divisible booty. Abū Ḥanīfa gives the ruler a choice between division and leaving land with its occupants subject to kharāj. These are the reported alternatives of this passage, not a complete doctrine of taxation or a justification of every conquest. Bidāya Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.401–402; page images checked

The explicit reason for disagreement. Ibn Rushd begins with the apparent relation between on booty and Q59 on fayʾ. One reading brings those who come later into the community of claimants and supports reserving land for continuing revenue; another distinguishes the property categories and appeals to the Prophet’s division of Khaybar. At I402 Ibn Rushd sharply questions making one verse specify or abrogate the other without first establishing that they address the same object. Treating both as general texts and selectively restricting each requires evidence. A persuasive picture of intergenerational provision does not repair that evidentiary gap. Bidāya Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.401–402; Arabic checked

An intended list or an indication of wider need? At I403 the dispute about fayʾ asks whether the named recipients exhaust its beneficiaries or indicate a wider class. On the wider reading, funds can support judges, administrators, defence and common works; a restrictive reading gives the enumeration a different force. Ibn Rushd also questions al-Shāfiʿī’s argument for taking a fifth of fayʾ. This is a particularly clear link between uṣūl and government: a semantic and classificatory difference changes who can claim, what a ruler may allocate, and which public activities can be maintained. Bidāya Arabic I, printed/PDF p.403; page image checked

Setting. concerns fayʾ, property acquired without the combat described in the verse. The commentaries relate its immediate setting to Banū al-Naḍīr. This property category must be distinguished from war booty and from ordinary privately owned wealth.

Text and reported setting. lists recipients and says the wealth must not circulate only among the rich. recalls emigrants expelled from homes and property; praises hosts who prefer others despite their own need and are protected from avarice; gives later believers a prayer free from rancour towards predecessors.

Ethical force of the passage. Distribution is set within displacement, welcome and continuity between generations. The passage addresses both the institutional direction of resources and the desires that make redistribution difficult. The later community must not inherit wealth and institutions while treating earlier or poorer members as morally absent.

How the commentators read it. Ibn ʿĀshūr contrasts circulation beyond the wealthy with pre-Islamic commanders’ privileged shares and draws a wider purpose of circulation across several institutions. That is his teleological extension, not a license to ignore their distinct rules. The Study Quran recounts distribution to emigrants in straitened circumstances and selected helpers, and reads the following verses through preference for others and freedom from avarice. Nawawī, on Muslim1757, explains the provision set aside for the Prophet’s family and the remainder for collective defence. He distinguishes foresight from a failure of trust in God and records limits on stockpiling purchased food during scarcity. He also preserves the Shāfiʿī disagreement over a fifth of fayʾ. Responsible public provision, private security and spiritual reliance therefore need not oppose one another.

· · · · · · · · ·

Peace, revenue and the limits of public discretion

Ruling and reason for disagreement. Ibn Rushd’s treaty discussion asks whether truce is allowed whenever the relevant interest calls for it or only under necessity, whether payment by Muslims is permissible in an extreme situation, and whether a fixed maximum term applies. His explanation begins with the relation between the fighting passages and , together with the Hudaybiya agreement: are the apparent conflicts resolved by abrogation, by specification, or by situational judgment? A general desire for peace cannot decide the historical reach of those texts. Conversely, a general fighting command cannot simply erase the received agreement without an argument about its force. Bidāya Arabic I, PDF pp.387–388, truce and its reasons for disagreement

Peace, warranted trust and the things expenditure cannot buy

Text and setting. moves from accepting a genuine inclination toward peace to reliance on God amid possible deception, and then to the joining of believers’ hearts which all earthly wealth could not itself accomplish. Ibn ʿĀshūr reads these verses in sequence with preparation for war and the earlier rule for openly ending a treaty when evidence of treachery appears. Hidden possible deceit and visible indications are not the same condition.

The ethical argument. The passage places a limit on preventive suspicion and on political purchasing power. A treaty needs public fidelity and practical preparation; trust is not certainty about another’s hidden motives. Expenditure can support cooperation without producing love by purchase.

How the commentators read it. Ibn ʿĀshūr distinguishes taking available precautions from entrusting what lies beyond human power to God. He contrasts , where deceit is merely concealed, with , where signs warrant action. He records different identifications of the addressees and readings through abrogation or specification, retaining broad warfare assumptions about some groups. His account therefore supports fidelity and epistemic restraint without becoming an unrestricted pacifist theory.

Scope of this reading. No single definitive occasion is established here. The rival accounts of addressees and the legal reach of peace remain visible. This is directly relevant to Ibn Rushd’s truce disagreement, not evidence that every truce has produced inward reconciliation.

· · ·

The six fiscal questions. At I403–407 Ibn Rushd asks from whom jizya may be accepted, which persons owe it, its amount, when it is due and ceases, its kinds, and where the proceeds go. His opening does not describe a uniform service charge. It connects the standard male, adult and free qualifications to the historical relation between fighting and the payment; then it records disputes concerning old age, disability, poverty and monastic life. Eligibility of religious communities is a further question. These classifications belong to the historical doctrine and cannot be replaced by a modern account of equal fiscal citizenship.

The rates disclose several different ways of treating precedent. Mālik takes the reported assessment of ʿUmar as fixed; al-Shāfiʿī specifies a minimum and leaves a higher amount to agreement; Abū Ḥanīfa’s reported scheme differentiates means; another position leaves assessment to the ruler. Ibn Rushd identifies the disagreement of reports and their relative force. At I405 he observes that if the reports specify no securely agreed fixed amount, the general scriptural term may leave more discretion. This is a legal argument about the strength and scope of evidence, not an inference that whatever raises the most revenue is just. Bidāya Arabic I, PDF pp.403–405; pp.404–405 checked as images

Conversion, accrued duty and negotiated payment. A person’s entry into Islam before the annual condition is met and entry after the liability has accrued generate different questions. Ibn Rushd gives rival accounts of whether the prior obligation survives: does the new status remove the ground before the debt arises, or does it cancel a debt already due? His classification then distinguishes conquest assessment from a treaty settlement. Commercial duties form a further disputed case: are they owed by entry for trade itself, or only by a condition accepted in the agreement? He links the dispute to the interpretation of ʿUmar’s practice, its possible Prophetic basis and reciprocity. The same payment cannot be moved freely between tax, contract and voluntary giving. Bidāya Arabic I, PDF pp.405–407; pp.405–406 checked as images

Public revenue and unequal political standing

Text and setting. couples fighting with the stated endpoint of payment and subjection. Its language concerning belief, the true religion and public authority belongs to the verse’s actual argument, not merely to an administrative tax schedule. Ibn ʿĀshūr places it in the transition from Arabian conflicts toward relations with Byzantine-backed groups and records the attribution to Tabūk. He notices a chronology difficulty in that attribution. His historical account is an exegetical reconstruction, not independent archival verification.

The ethical argument. This text and its commentary cannot honestly be presented only as reciprocal funding for protection. They articulate a hierarchy of religious and political standing. The project must ask whose security is obtained, who bears the payment and subjection, and what kind of inward change can or cannot follow from them.

How the commentators read it. Ibn ʿĀshūr rejects a strained reading that would simply deny that Jews and Christians affirm God and a final judgment; he analyzes how the verse groups its addressees and descriptions. He nevertheless retains the superiority of Islamic rule and explicitly interprets ṣaghār through subordination and an intended inducement to leave the prior religion. His reading of payment by hand also concerns unresisting submission. This is genuine counterevidence to an account of the law as nothing but civic reciprocity or uncoerced ethical education.

Scope of this reading. The interpretation is attributed rather than adopted as the project’s normative conclusion. It is not a report of how every government collected the levy. Ibn Rushd’s disputes about payers, rates, treaties and fiscal practice still require their own separate reconstruction.

· ·

Office as an entrusted capacity

A commander’s instructions: governing without claiming divine omniscience

Text and setting. Burayda’s report places a commander’s personal taqwā and care for those accompanying him before military instructions. It forbids treachery and misappropriation and concludes by distinguishing the commander’s own undertaking and judgment from God’s. This is a reported pattern of commissioning commanders, not a single dated siege. It also distinguishes migration, military participation, revenues and the offer of jizya.

The ethical argument. Public power has an inward discipline and a public limit. The person commanding must care for subordinates and honour undertakings; that responsibility does not make his judgment identical with divine knowledge. His office remains answerable precisely where its decisions are consequential.

How the commentators read it. Al-Nawawī explains the need to teach commanders what is obligatory, permitted and forbidden, together with care for their followers. On taking a fortress under one’s own judgment, he says the warning supports those who hold that an investigator can miss the true ruling; he preserves the opposing answer that revelation could still correct the judgment during the Prophet’s life. On an undertaking in God’s name, he explains the danger of subordinates breaking a pledge whose gravity they do not understand. He also records incompatible school allocations of revenue and the scope of jizya, rather than extracting a uniformly benign administrative doctrine.

Scope of this reading. The words concern warfare within a premodern religious polity. Their epistemic distinction is relevant to the framework, but is not a modern constitutional doctrine attributed to Muslim. The warning’s classification as precautionary is al-Nawawī’s.

·

Fitness for office and justice across the household and city

Text and setting. Abū Dharr requests office and is warned of his weakness for its demands. Neighbouring reports praise those who judge justly in government, family and what they administer, and censure rulers who impose hardship. Personal esteem and affection accompany the refusal of office. The report does not infer incapacity from lack of piety.

The ethical argument. Different functions require different capacities. A spiritually serious person may be unfit for administration; a technically capable officer still has to exercise justice. Household care, guardianship and public office share responsibility without becoming interchangeable authorities.

How the commentators read it. Al-Nawawī says the warning particularly concerns inability to perform the office’s tasks. He distinguishes the incapable appointee from the capable but unjust one, and both from the competent person who governs justly. His explanation of the neighbouring praise expressly includes rule, judgment, market supervision, orphan property, alms, endowments and family rights. The description of responsibility concerns preserving and advancing the good of what is entrusted, in religious and worldly matters.

Scope of this reading. These reports supply an ethical control for the project’s functional map. They do not by themselves establish the appointment procedure or jurisdiction of every historical office.

·

REP-16. Oaths: expiation cannot purchase another person’s loss

Follow the argument RulingLegal reasoningScripture

Division 16: Oaths.

Ruling and reason for disagreement. The majority reported here deny a prescribed expiation for a deliberately false oath about the past; al-Shāfiʿī and others require one. Ibn Rushd relates the disagreement to general scriptural wording and a report threatening grave consequences for appropriating another's right. He then asks whether expiation can address the oath while the injustice persists, and links complete repentance to restoration of the wrong. Bidāya Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.409–410

How the legal argument works. · . These notes identify the relevant mechanism or comparative control; later maxims do not establish Ibn Rushd’s historical vocabulary.

An oath, a hidden reservation and another person’s right

Text and setting. The report locates the oath’s meaning in what the person requiring it can accept as truthful. A variant speaks of the intention of the person administering the oath. Al-Nawawī’s principal application is a judicial oath in a claim, where a litigant privately intends a meaning different from the judge’s. He separately discusses nonjudicial oaths.

The ethical argument. An inward intention is morally significant without becoming a private power to dissolve a publicly owed truth. The question is whose practical reliance the words have engaged.

How the commentators read it. Al-Nawawī gives his school’s detailed distinction: in an authorized judicial oath the judge’s intended matter controls, so equivocation does not avoid the oath. Outside that setting, a reservation can affect whether the oath is broken; nevertheless it is impermissible to use it to cancel someone’s rightful claim. He then reports more differentiated Mālikī accounts, including whether the oath was demanded or volunteered and whether deceit was intended. His account preserves the difference between the oath’s technical effect and the wrong of depriving another.

Scope of this reading. This is commentary on Muslim1653, not a general instruction to distrust every ambiguous statement. Reported consensus claims and the competing school detail remain attributed to the commentator.

·

Text and reported setting. forbids making an oath by God an obstacle to doing good, exercising taqwā and reconciling people; God is hearing and knowing. contrasts inadvertent speech with what hearts acquire, ending with forgiveness and forbearance.

Ethical force of the passage. The divine name must not turn a person’s earlier words into an excuse to perpetuate estrangement or refuse a good. Hearing and knowing place the utterance and its inward purpose together; forgiveness and forbearance prevent inadvertence from being equated with a settled malicious resolve.

How the commentators read it. Ibn ʿĀshūr reads the oath passage as preparing the treatment of marital abstention. Its concern with reconciliation therefore has a concrete domestic continuation. He preserves more than one proposed occasion; none is adopted here as the single established cause.

· ·

REP-17. Vows: giving without manufacturing dependence

Follow the argument RulingLegal reasoningScripture

Division 17: Vows.

Ruling and reason for disagreement. When a person commits all his property, Ibn Rushd tests the general duty to fulfil the vow against the Abū Lubāba report limiting the gift to a third and a report criticizing a person who gives everything and then begs. He also criticizes the consistency of a Mālikī distinction between specified property and an unspecified total. The interpretation turns on the actual reports, not on a universal maxim that greater giving is better. Bidāya Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.428

How the legal argument works. · . These notes identify the relevant mechanism or comparative control; later maxims do not establish Ibn Rushd’s historical vocabulary.

Vows: fulfilling an undertaking without bargaining with providence

Text and setting. The reports reject the belief that a vow changes what is decreed and say that it extracts giving from someone reluctant to give. A neighbouring narrative concerns an escaped captive who vows to sacrifice the very camel that carried her to safety. The general warning about vows and the particular escape narrative are separate reports. In the latter, the camel is not the woman’s property; her intended gratitude would dispose of another’s good.

The ethical argument. Giving can acknowledge a good already received, or become an attempted price for securing a desired event. The law may bind a valid undertaking without endorsing the motive that produced it. Gratitude cannot appropriate another person’s means of life.

How the commentators read it. Al-Nawawī transmits al-Māzarī’s two explanations: the self-imposed obligation may be performed grudgingly, and a conditional devotion can take the form of exchange for the desired benefit. Qāḍī ʿIyāḍ adds the risk of believing that a vow controls decree. Al-Nawawī distinguishes a vow disposing of a specified thing one does not own from a valid undertaking in one’s own liability to acquire and give something later. The escape report therefore limits the object of the vow, not all future commitments.

Scope of this reading. The commentary’s hadith assessments are attributed assessments. Its disapproval of bargaining is not a ruling that every vow is void, nor does it remove another person’s claim.

· · ·

Repentant giving: leave a cause of wrongdoing without destroying provision

Text and setting. The Muwaṭṭaʾ’s report has Abū Lubāba propose leaving the place of his offence, living near the Prophet and divesting himself of his property in charity. The reply says a third suffices. Mālik transmits the story through a balāgh, a report introduced as having reached a transmitter. The displayed chain must not be represented as fully connected. The report itself gives the repentance setting without establishing every familiar biographical detail.

The ethical argument. Repentance concerns the practical setting that sustained a wrong and the renewed company that may correct it. But renouncing a cause of attachment differs from making oneself dependent through indiscriminate disposal.

How the commentators read it. Al-Bājī proposes that place, property or distance from corrective instruction may have contributed to the offence; he labels these as possibilities. He reads the word “suffices” as indicating an undertaking already made and uses it to defend the Mālikī third. He also preserves the opposing interpretation: the man was still proposing the gift, so the reply advises a proportion rather than reducing an established obligation. His account then differentiates rich, modest and poor givers through attributed opinions. Repentant purpose therefore does not remove the linguistic and factual question of whether a duty had already arisen.

Scope of this reading. The moral interpretation and the rival readings of the report remain distinct. The cause of Abū Lubāba’s offence and the exact status of his undertaking are not settled by the wish to make the episode fit a theory of purification.

·

Related scriptural comparison. The following passage illuminates a neighbouring good; the direct report or legal tradition is treated above.

Text and reported setting. Muslim1628 places Saʿd’s wish to dispose of wealth within grave illness. The answer limits disposal to a third, calls even that much, prefers leaving heirs adequately provided for, and includes ordinary household expenditure undertaken for God within rewarded action.

Ethical force of the passage. The encounter corrects an opposition between lofty giving and ordinary responsibility. Care for dependants is itself capable of being devotion. The religious quality of renunciation cannot be measured by the amount removed from one’s estate while ignoring those left exposed to need.

How the commentators read it. Nawawī makes intention decisive in explaining how habitual acts such as providing food for one’s wife become obedience. He also reads the passage through the needs of relatives. Ibn ʿĀshūr’s discussion of describes reform of existing bequest practices that could exclude relatives or deepen hostility; the later relation of bequest and inheritance remains a distinct legal question.

· · ·

REP-18. Sacrifice: prescribed offering and the reach of an example

Follow the argument RulingLegal reasoningScripture

Division 18: Sacrificial offerings.

Ruling and reason for disagreement. Mālik and al-Shāfiʿī regard the sacrifice as an emphatic sunna; Abū Ḥanīfa requires it of specified resident persons with means, while his two principal companions differ. Ibn Rushd identifies the legal force of repeated prophetic practice and the implications of reports directed to other questions. His warning is precise: a report not delivered for the point under argument is a weak basis for that inference. Bidāya Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.429

How the legal argument works. · . These notes identify the relevant mechanism or comparative control; later maxims do not establish Ibn Rushd’s historical vocabulary.

Text and reported setting. directs that sacrificial animals provide food for the offerer and people in need. says that neither flesh nor blood reaches God; what reaches Him is taqwā. It links the animals’ availability to magnifying God for guidance and gives good news to those who act with excellence.

Ethical force of the passage. The distinction is ontological as well as ethical: God is not nourished by the gift. Human beings receive its material benefit, while the offerer’s acknowledgment answers the guidance and provision already received. This is why more blood or a more costly display is not, by itself, a greater return to God.

How the commentators read it. Ibn ʿĀshūr explains that slaughter serves human benefit, including the offerer’s household and the poor; bloodshed is not an end in itself. His account of earlier blood-smearing is a transmitted historical explanation, not an independently established occasion for every sacrifice rule. The Study Quran connects 22:37 with the earlier reference to taqwā in 22:32 and treats the statement as disclosure of sacrifice’s inward reality. Its preceding discussion includes feeding those who ask and those who do not. The story about smearing blood is an attributed occasion report, not an independently checked event. Al-Rāzī denies that anything literally reaches God in a spatial or material sense; the language concerns acceptance and the recording of an act. In a dispute with Muʿtazilī arguments, he maintains that someone guilty of a grave sin may nevertheless exercise taqwā in a particular sincerely performed obedience. Acceptance of this act is therefore not proof of the agent’s comprehensive virtue. The distinction strengthens the project’s separation of particular acknowledgment from an accomplished state of character.

· · · ·

REP-19. Slaughter: a permitted act whose manner still matters

Follow the argument RulingLegal reasoningScripture

Division 19: Slaughter.

Ruling and reason for disagreement. The selected discussion concerns injured animals and whether slaughter can still make their meat lawful. Ibn Rushd examines the exception in , its grammatical relation to the preceding categories, and the animal's remaining life. He argues that the result cannot simply be obtained by attaching the label “connected” or “disconnected” exception without attending to what the prohibition concerns. Bidāya Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.440

How the legal argument works. · . These notes identify the relevant mechanism or comparative control; later maxims do not establish Ibn Rushd’s historical vocabulary.

Text and reported setting. Muslim1955 states that God has prescribed iḥsān in all things, then requires good conduct in killing and slaughter: sharpen the blade and relieve the animal.

Ethical force of the passage. The instruction reaches the exercise of permitted lethal power itself. Permission to kill for the relevant purpose does not make avoidable fear or suffering morally irrelevant. Here excellence is an exacting limit on how appetite or authority uses a vulnerable living being.

How the commentators read it. Nawawī makes the implications concrete: do not sharpen the blade before the animal, drag it to slaughter or kill another before it. The following discussion rejects using living creatures as targets. These are his developed practical explanations; they should not all be placed inside quotation marks as the wording of Muslim1955.

·

The surrounding Qurʾānic argument. sets the exception for an animal properly slaughtered within a longer account of permitted nourishment, prohibited deaths and cultic dedication, religious fidelity and necessity. Its permission in severe hunger is qualified by not inclining towards sin and ends with forgiveness and mercy. Ibn ʿĀshūr explains the slaughter exception by distinguishing the animal’s substance, the condition affecting it, and whether life remains; he preserves disagreement about the decisive condition of life. Later in the same verse he reads the displacement of fear of opponents by fear of God as a reorientation of allegiance. Neither hunger nor a pleasing symbolic reading makes every damaged animal lawful; neither does the prohibition erase the verse’s accommodation of real necessity.

·

REP-20. Hunting: taking responsibility for the means of acquisition

Follow the argument RulingLegal reasoningScripture

Division 20: Hunting.

Ruling and reason for disagreement. Ibn Rushd makes the ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim and Abū Thaʿlaba reports principal controls. The dispute over an object that strikes by weight rather than piercing turns on the relation between the prohibited beaten animal, the distinctive means of hunting, and the report's discrimination between kinds of impact. He prefers the reported distinction over blanket permission or prohibition. Bidāya Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.455

How the legal argument works. · . These notes identify the relevant mechanism or comparative control; later maxims do not establish Ibn Rushd’s historical vocabulary.

Text and reported setting. The hunting reports ask about trained animals, invocation, another dog’s participation and whether an instrument pierces or merely strikes. The narrated questions concern how the animal actually died.

Ethical force of the passage. Responsibility includes knowing enough about one’s use of power to distinguish permitted provision from a doubtful killing. The person’s wish to eat cannot decide a causal fact. A further ethical distinction separates hunting for a useful end from destroying animals without benefit.

How the commentators read it. Nawawī explicitly distinguishes useful hunting from wanton destruction. He examines the additional dog because one cannot simply ascribe the kill to the trained animal over which the invocation was made. He retains the disagreement over invocation’s legal force. The commentary’s restraint of appetite begins with these concrete uncertainties and purposes, not a free-floating symbol of conquest.

REP-21. ʿAqīqa: welcoming a child through a shared act

Follow the argument RulingLegal reasoningScripture

Division 21: Aqiqa.

Ruling and reason for disagreement. Ibn Rushd records an obligation according to a group including the Ẓāhirīs, a sunna according to the majority, and a non-obligatory voluntary act in his account of Abū Ḥanīfa. The disagreement arises from the differing implications of reports, including the description of the child as pledged to its ʿaqīqa and the wording about a person wishing to offer. Bidāya Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.463

How the legal argument works. · . These notes identify the relevant mechanism or comparative control; later maxims do not establish Ibn Rushd’s historical vocabulary.

Text and reported setting. The report from Salmān ibn ʿĀmir connects ʿaqīqa with the newborn and removal of harm. Other reports used in the discussion distinguish numbers of animals.

Ethical force of the passage. The child is received through acts performed by others. The useful ethical question is how provision, care and acknowledgment surround that arrival. The differing numbers cannot by themselves prove a corresponding difference in the worth of children.

How the commentators read it. Ibn Ḥajar compares reports concerning girls as well as boys, distinguishes recommended number from validity, and transmits proposed explanations rather than one demonstrated rationale. Al-Ḥalīmī’s analogy with blood money and the possibility that a reported number reflected available means remain different kinds of explanation. Neither is adopted here as a verified metaphysics of sex.

·

REP-22. Food and transformation: the product and the action differ

Follow the argument RulingLegal reasoningScripture

Division 22: Food drink transformation and necessity.

Ruling and reason for disagreement. Ibn Rushd distinguishes wine becoming vinegar on its own, which he reports as accepted, from deliberately making it vinegar, where prohibition, dislike and permission are reported. The Abū Ṭalḥa report concerning wine inherited by orphans confronts reasoning from the transformed substance. He also distinguishes a prohibition interpreted as blocking a means from one not assigned that cause, and asks whether forbidding an act invalidates its result. Bidāya Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.476

How the legal argument works. · . These notes identify the relevant mechanism or comparative control; later maxims do not establish Ibn Rushd’s historical vocabulary.

Text and reported setting. Muslim1983 gives a negative answer to making wine into vinegar. The short wording supplies no developed story about the questioner or the occasion.

Ethical force of the passage. A desirable material result does not alone justify every means of producing it. This is especially important for an alchemical interpretation: transformation of the substance, the agent’s permission to intervene and a subsequent judgment of purity are distinct questions.

How the commentators read it. Nawawī separates spontaneous change from adding substances or moving the vessel, and records different accounts of whether a prohibited intervention nevertheless yields a pure result. The commentary therefore prevents “transformation” from becoming an indiscriminate moral approval of whatever successfully changes matter.

Part II.B. Ablution and footwear

Main worship commentary, under reconstruction. Restored in revision 9 under the expanded whole-work brief. The existing arguments and source problems are retained. Their verse, hadith and spiritual-commentary audits remain incomplete; the new standard is explained in the worship introduction.

Continuous reading of Arabic volume I, printed/PDF pp.7–23, stopping immediately before the substantive discussion of water. This is the first sequential installment of the whole-work commentary, not a claim that all purification or the entire Bidāya has been interpreted. Rule IDs distinguish subsidiary questions that the first atlas compressed. The final register records the boundaries and unresolved textual points.

The verse’s ending governs the account of purification

Setting. Wāḥidī places the necklace journey under : the travelling party lacks water, and a purification concession is revealed. His report names al-Bayḍāʾ or Dhāt al-Jaysh; the necklace is eventually found beneath the camel.

The passage. gives washing and wiping requirements and the concession of earth when water is unavailable. It ends: God does not intend hardship, but purification and the completion of His favour, “so that you may give thanks.”

Its ethical argument. The concession belongs to the gift described by the verse. Gratitude answers a form of access to worship that accommodates illness, travel and scarcity; it is not appreciation for an ordeal as such. Purification and gratitude therefore belong together, while the precise acts remain matters of juristic interpretation.

What the commentary explains. Wāḥidī retains the necklace journey under . Ibn ʿĀshūr discusses the difficulty of assigning all the purification provisions to one first occasion: he treats as confirming an already practised purification and its concession. His chronological reconstruction and the reported event are not identical evidence.

· ·

P001–P004. What purification is, who owes it, and when

Text and rules. Ibn Rushd distinguishes purification from ḥadath and purification from khabath, then divides purification from ḥadath into ablution, bathing and the substitute, tayammum. He presents ablution through five questions: evidence for obligation, persons and times; its acts; its material; its nullifiers; and the acts for which it is required. The opening grounds obligation in Qurʾān, Sunna and agreement. It identifies maturity and reason as qualifications, reports a dispute about Islam as a condition of obligation, and relates performance to prayer time or intending another act for which ablution is a condition. He calls the Islam-condition dispute of little practical yield here because it returns to otherworldly judgment. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.7–8.

These statements already constitute a philosophy of a practical object. Purification is neither merely a substance removed nor an undifferentiated moral quality. Its analysis includes a normative state, physical operations, an eligible material, a temporally situated agent and another act for which it functions as a condition. Its place in practical science comes from that relation to possible action. The general classification does not itself perform ablution or settle every material case; it makes further determinations intelligible.

P001: the two kinds and three forms. The primary distinction prevents the inference that every legal state of impurity is bodily dirt or moral blame. It also prevents the opposite inference that material conditions do not matter. Tayammum’s place as a substitute already means that a purely hygienic account will be inadequate. The detailed scope of substitution must await its own chapter. The formative question is how a person learns distinctions among bodily condition, moral responsibility and ritual eligibility, rather than experiencing all three as a single vague state of unworthiness.

P002: obligation and capacity. Maturity and reason locate the demand within an account of responsible agency. They do not imply that children have no place in religious education or that an incapacitated person lacks human worth. Those are separate questions. The difference between present obligation and preparatory formation becomes decisive later in zakāt and guardianship. Here the juridical subject is not an interchangeable unit of population.

P003: Islam as a condition. Ibn Rushd’s assessment of limited practical yield is an important methodological restraint. A classification can concern ultimate accountability without supplying a different immediate civic procedure. The vertical dimension is real within the question, but it does not automatically generate another administrative task for the ruler. This is a particularly clear case where “linking upward” must not be confused with inventing a worldly institutional consequence.

P004: time and the intended conditioned act. The rule joins the body’s preparation to a socially and religiously structured time. Our reconstruction is that repeated thresholds can interrupt an otherwise continuous pursuit of private business and make readiness for worship a learned part of ordinary life. Avicenna explicitly argues that repeated acts at proximate intervals renew remembrance across generations; his explanation provides a comparison for this temporal morphology, not the source of Ibn Rushd’s ruling. Avicenna, Metaphysics of the Healing, PDF pp.382–383, printed pp.367–368.

What this changes in the larger argument. Before the first famous disagreement, the text has already required distinctions among person, capacity, material, state, time, means and end. The “alchemy” begins by making action intelligible and possible; it does not begin with a hidden symbolic interpretation of water.

P005. Intention in ablution: what makes the act the act?

The question and its evidence. Ibn Rushd asks whether niyya is a condition of validity. He attributes the requirement to al-Shāfiʿī, Mālik, Aḥmad, Abū Thawr and Dāwūd, and the absence of that validity condition to Abū Ḥanīfa and al-Thawrī. The shared starting point is the requirement of intention in worship. His explicit explanation is the hesitation between classifying ablution as pure worship, sought for nearness, and as worship with an intelligible meaning, such as washing away impurity. Ablution combines worship and cleanliness. Fiqh must examine which resemblance is stronger and attach it accordingly. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.8–9.

The issue is therefore not whether water can wash someone who has no religious motive. It is what is needed for that washing to constitute the legally relevant preparation. Nor does the permissive validity position say that insincerity is a virtue, that devotion is unnecessary in life, or that worship has become secular hygiene. The object’s dominant juridical resemblance governs a specific inference about validity.

The general-to-particular movement. At the universal practical level there are sources, types of rulings and an account of worship. At the instrumental level there is a comparison between relevant kinds and the extension of a requirement through the stronger resemblance. At the particular practical level there is the rule governing an actual ablution. At the level of the agent there remains the decision and act. These levels explain why knowledge of a general maxim about intention does not, by itself, settle the case: the maxim’s field of application is precisely what is disputed.

Paul Powers’ treatment of niyya as helping constitute and differentiate acts clarifies why “inner versus outer” is too crude. The same visible sequence can instantiate different practical descriptions. His discussion of purification also distinguishes removing a state from obtaining permission to perform a conditioned act in exceptional cases. This is a useful comparative account of legal intentionality, subject to checking his terminology against primary sources. Paul Powers, Intent in Islamic Law, PDF pp.30–33, printed pp.48–55.

Dynastic condition Specific question for this rule
Shared founding solidarity Do exemplary performers communicate intention as an intelligible undertaking within common worship?
Concentration of power Are officials or teachers claiming access to inward states beyond what public evidence warrants?
Prosperity and specialization Do developed schools distinguish validity, reward and spiritual excellence carefully enough to teach without confusion?
Inherited routine Does an intention formula remain while its practical meaning becomes opaque?
Breakdown Can basic instruction survive displacement and interrupted transmission without imposing inaccessible expertise on ordinary worshippers?

These are questions of realization, not evidence for relaxing or tightening the ruling at will. No particular dynasty is documented by this passage.

What would defeat an over-reading? A school text showing reward depends on intention even where validity does not would refute an “anti-intentional Ḥanafī” thesis. A ritual performed with correct intention but used to cultivate superiority would refute an automatic virtue claim. The absence of evidence for a political effect prevents a causal assertion about the rule’s historical success. These are productive limits: they tell us exactly how much the case establishes.

P006. Washing the hands before entering the vessel: the act or its shared material?

Positions and cause. Ibn Rushd lists four principal arrangements: an unrestricted sunna, the well-known attribution to Mālik and al-Shāfiʿī; recommendation for someone doubtful about the hand’s purity, also reported from Mālik; obligation upon waking from sleep, attributed to Dāwūd and followers; and obligation after night sleep rather than daytime sleep, attributed to Aḥmad. Their interpretation concerns a command to wash before putting the hand into the vessel and the explanation that the sleeper does not know where the hand has been. Variant wording includes three washes. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.9–10.

Several mechanisms interact. Does the Qurʾānic list delimit obligatory ablution acts so that an additional imperative is read as recommendation? Does “spent the night” restrict the rule to night sleep? Is sleep itself the relevant condition, or is uncertainty the reason allowing extension to other doubtful cases? Does persistent prophetic performance support an emphasized practice? These mechanisms cannot be reduced to one disagreement over cleanliness.

Ibn Rushd then makes the decisive object-level observation: the report appears to concern the water’s status rather than the hand as an independent ablution act. Reports of beginning with handwashing can nonetheless be read in either way. The same movement can therefore be classified as a ritual component or as preservation of the material needed for the ritual. This anticipates the larger distinction between the person’s act and the ecology of its performance. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF p.10.

A later Shāfiʿī handbook further differentiates doubt, known purity and known impurity in relation to a limited quantity of water. This is an example of downstream legal morphology becoming more articulated; it is not proof that the Bidāya’s brief account intended every later detail. Reliance of the Traveller, PDF p.80, e5.6, printed p.62.

What this changes in the larger argument. Not every formative law works directly on an inward state. Some preserve a material condition that makes a whole sequence of meaningful action possible. The theory needs indirect and relational causation.

P007. Mouth and nose: embodied completeness and differentiated authority

The positions are: both actions are sunna, attributed to Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī and Abū Ḥanīfa; both are obligatory, attributed to Ibn Abī Laylā and a group of Dāwūd’s followers; or nasal rinsing is obligatory while mouth rinsing is sunna, attributed to Abū Thawr, Abū ʿUbayda as printed, and a group of literalists. The explicit cause again concerns additions to the Qurʾānic prescription, but another distinction now matters: a reported action and an explicit command need not have the same evidentiary force. Mouth rinsing is described through action; nasal rinsing through command and action. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF p.10.

This is an important corrective to a generic “more purification means more spirituality” account. The third position divides two bodily acts commonly experienced as one preparatory sequence because their proofs differ in form. The practical object is thus constituted by both bodily differentiation and the history of address. A complete interpretation must retain both.

The formative reconstruction differs correspondingly. Making both obligatory establishes them as necessary elements; making both recommended preserves an obligatory core with a fuller exemplary performance; differentiating them teaches that not all imitated acts carry an identical demand. In each case the citizen can learn reverent imitation. The distinct lesson concerns how imitation is governed by evidence, not whether the nose represents one metaphysical faculty and the mouth another. No such symbolism is supplied here.

The later Reliance treats both as recommended and adjusts the intensity of performance in relation to fasting. That illustrates how ritual goods must be coordinated rather than independently maximized. It is a later control and does not add a fasting exception to this Bidāya paragraph as though it were printed there. Reliance of the Traveller, PDF p.80, e5.7.

For virtue, the nearest mechanism is disciplined completeness without confusing obligation and excellence. Ghazālī’s criticism of outward purification detached from character is directly relevant: elaboration of bodily acts can support attention, but it can also become an avenue of pride. .

What this changes in the larger argument. A philosophy of embodied law needs a theory of differentiated authority. Otherwise it turns every exemplary performance into a compulsory instrument of moral engineering.

P008–P010. The face and beard: specifying a bodily universal

P008: the area between beard-line and ear. The obligation to wash the face is agreed; what the name includes is disputed. The well-known Mālikī report excludes this area, another includes it, and a further report distinguishes bearded and unbearded persons. Abū Ḥanīfa and al-Shāfiʿī include it. This is intra-school plurality as well as disagreement among schools. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF p.11.

The practical object is a named bodily region whose boundary is not fully self-interpreting. The reference to differing bodily conditions makes application more than a geometrical diagram. The formative good is careful, achievable performance of a received act; the juristic virtue is precision without inventing certainty. It would be an over-reading to interpret the excluded strip as an area of spiritually inferior concern. The legal issue is the extension of the name.

P009: the hanging length of the beard. Mālik requires water over it; Abū Ḥanīfa and one reported Shāfiʿī position do not. Ibn Rushd again identifies uncertainty about the scope of “face.” A later Shāfiʿī handbook requires washing the outer hanging beard. This is exactly why “the Shāfiʿī view” must not be treated as timeless and singular: the Bidāya itself marks one of two positions, while the later handbook presents a practical school determination. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF p.11; Reliance of the Traveller, PDF p.81, e5.9, printed p.63.

The difference concerns how an acquired bodily feature relates to the normative part. An individual learns not merely to copy a diagram of someone else’s body but to understand how a general instruction reaches his own. The alchemical operation, if that language is used, is specification: a universal address becomes responsible treatment of this body. Neither inclusion nor non-inclusion entails a distinct doctrine of the soul.

P010: passing fingers through the beard. Mālik, Abū Ḥanīfa and al-Shāfiʿī do not make it obligatory in ablution, while Ibn ʿAbd al-Ḥakam does. The cause is the reliability of reports commanding it; Ibn Rushd also notes its absence from the sound descriptions at issue. This is an authentication problem, not simply another question of the word “face.” The three disputes must therefore remain separate even though they occur in one numbered issue. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF p.11.

What this changes in the larger argument. “Upward meaning” sometimes consists in understanding how universal speech becomes an exact, repeatable bodily practice. That is philosophically substantial even where no separate spiritual meaning for the bodily boundary can be established.

P011. Elbows: why a stronger semantic argument need not settle the whole case

The majority, including Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī and Abū Ḥanīfa, include the elbows in obligatory washing. Some literalists, some later Mālikīs and al-Ṭabarī do not. Ibn Rushd identifies two ambiguities: the extent of the word yad and the use of ilā as limit or accompaniment. A report of washing toward the upper arm supplies additional evidence. He considers the non-inclusion reading stronger on the linguistic side, and the inclusion reading clearer on the report side, with the further possibility that the reported extension is recommended. His conclusion leaves the matter open to consideration. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.11–12.

This is a compact demonstration of integrated legal rationality. The philologist’s preferred reading does not automatically conclude the legal inquiry; the report must be weighed too. Conversely, a physical performance extending beyond the elbow does not settle its obligatory status without a theory of what a prophetic act establishes. The inferential path contains more than one type of evidence and more than one question.

In small communities, embodied imitation can communicate the boundary; concentrated offices may standardize a teaching; learned prosperity enables preservation of conflicting reports; inherited routine can turn a defensible position into an unwarranted claim that no alternative ever existed; breakdown increases dependence on abbreviated manuals. The civic risk is not the elbow itself but the social handling of warranted disagreement. The passage supplies no evidence that one anatomical interpretation produces a superior political order.

What this changes in the larger argument. The atlas must record Ibn Rushd’s differentiated evaluation of arguments, not just his alleged preferred verdict. “All positions are perspectives” would be too weak: he actually weighs their strengths. “One strongest argument settles everything” would also be too weak: strength differs by evidentiary dimension.

P012. How much of the head: totality, minimum reference and measured participation

Mālik requires wiping the entire head. Al-Shāfiʿī, Abū Ḥanīfa and some Mālikīs require part. Some Mālikī reports determine that part as a third or two-thirds; Abū Ḥanīfa specifies a quarter and a wiping instrument of at least three fingers; al-Shāfiʿī specifies no such quantum for either the wiped extent or wiping instrument in this passage. The explicit cause is the force of bāʾ in the expression, together with a report about the forelock and turban and a further question about the least or fullest extension of a name. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF p.12.

The legal morphology is richer than strictness versus ease. Whole-head wiping makes totality constitutive. Minimum-reference wiping makes a sufficient instance of the named act constitutive. Intermediate measures make an amount decisive. The instrument requirement adds a second variable: how the act is done as well as how much is covered. These variables must not be collapsed into an ordinal scale of piety.

A later Shāfiʿī manual is particularly useful: it permits a minimal wiping that falls under the name while recommending the fuller performance. The opposition between a small obligatory minimum and the whole ritual’s proper completion is therefore not an opposition between indifferent and serious worship. It is a differentiation within one legal account. Reliance of the Traveller, PDF pp.81–82, e5.11, printed pp.63–64.

Shaʿrānī’s second-order interpretation. The Mīzān discusses whole and partial wiping in connection with differing conditions, including heat, cold and vulnerability. Its editor notes that some jurists permit partial wiping generally, including for those without excuse. Consequently the climatic explanation cannot replace Ibn Rushd’s semantic and report-based explanation. It can propose an additional appropriateness relation, but its historical attribution is a separate question. al-Shaʿrānī, Mīzān I, PDF/printed pp.96–97, especially p.97 note 3.

The deeper contribution of the Mīzān is therefore not “we have discovered why Mālik and al-Shāfiʿī really differed.” It is “a later spiritual interpreter asks how a plurality of authorized forms can be inhabited by differently situated persons.” The distinction makes room for the user’s proposed alchemical differences without falsifying the original dispute.

What this changes in the larger argument. The theory must distinguish quantitative morphology, legal rank and intensity of realization. Treating them as one variable would misread the evidence.

P013–P016. Repetition, fresh water and direction: the grammar of completion

P013: one wash and recommended repetition. Ibn Rushd reports agreement that one complete washing of the washable members satisfies the obligation, while two and three are recommended. He invokes reported performances and the point that the command requires the act once. The adjective “complete” matters: three incomplete attempts are not simply equivalent to one achieved act. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF p.13.

The formative distinction is between sufficiency and enrichment. A stable minimum makes obligation accessible; repetition can reinforce deliberateness and exemplary practice. The same repetition can become thoughtless or ostentatious. Ghazālī’s criticism of external purification without inner reform prevents assuming that repeated wetting accumulates virtue like a measurable substance. .

P014: repeating the head wipe. Al-Shāfiʿī commends three wipes with a triply performed ablution; most jurists do not find additional excellence in repetition of wiping. Ibn Rushd’s explicit cause concerns an additional detail in a report transmitted by one route but not the others, and the interpretation of a general description of triple performance. He says that if the additional report is sound, it should be followed: silence about a detail is not by itself evidence against someone who relates it. The conditional “if sound” must remain conditional. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF p.13.

This dispute reverses a simplistic reading of the previous case. A jurist can require little of the head for validity yet commend repeated wiping. That is a concrete reason not to classify a school as generally minimalist. The alchemical difference concerns how completion and repetition are distributed among legal ranks and bodily acts, not a global intensity of religion.

P015: renewed water for wiping. The text attributes renewed water to the majority by analogy with other members, then reports the use of moisture remaining on the beard when water is exhausted, with several named endorsements. This is a distinct material-condition question and cannot disappear inside “repeat three times.” The adjacent wording should receive another-edition collation before a definitive account of the named attributions is published. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF p.13; B1E, PDF p.11, printed p.9.

Its philosophical object is the fitness and continuity of the means. Under scarcity, the material residue of one act may sustain another; under plentiful provision, fresh material can be used. The interpretation concerns practical dependency, not the spiritual inferiority of poor people’s ritual. The historical prevalence of either arrangement remains unestablished.

P016: direction of wiping. The text recommends beginning at the front, proceeding toward the nape and returning, on a report from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Zayd; another preference begins at the back, linked to a report from al-Rubayyiʿ bint Muʿawwidh whose canonical status is noted differently. Direction is therefore part of transmitted morphology. No source here warrants interpreting front-to-back as a journey through cosmic levels. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF p.13.

What this changes in the larger argument. Repetition is not one homogeneous mechanism. Repeating an obligatory constituent, repeating a recommended completion, renewing a material and traversing a bodily region in a prescribed direction are four different operations.

P017–P019. Wiping the turban: mediation, substitution and received practice

The Bidāya reports disagreement over wiping the turban, with rejection attributed to Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī and Abū Ḥanīfa, and permission to a group. The discussion turns on the report of wiping forelock and turban; its reliability; the Qurʾānic command to wipe the head; the place of widespread practice, particularly in the Mālikī account; and analogy with footwear. Many permissive jurists require putting it on in purity. Some do not require wiping the forelock together with it, reasoning from a report variant and the relation between an original and its substitute. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.13–14.

P017 is permission itself; P018 is the purity condition for putting it on; P019 is whether some direct wiping of the head remains required. They must be recorded independently. The later Reliance permits completing a wipe over a difficult-to-remove turban after the minimum head wipe. This helps identify the scope problem: a rejection of substitution must not be misreported as an absolute prohibition of any contact with a turban during the ritual. Reliance of the Traveller, PDF p.82, e5.11.

The ontology of the object is the central matter. Can the required action be mediated through a covering? Is that covering a locus of a substitute, or is direct performance on the original still necessary? If analogy to footwear is used, what relevant similarity licenses it? The question is neither simple convenience nor mere symbolic identification of garment and body.

What this changes in the larger argument. Law does not only measure the amount of an act; it can determine what counts as performing it through another material locus. This becomes a cross-book comparison with agency through guardians and proxies, but material substitution and personal agency must not be equated.

P020–P023. Ears: part, independent member, or supplemented practice?

The question divides into the obligatory status of wiping, the renewal of water, the treatment of inner and outer surfaces, and repetition. Some Mālikīs require wiping and fresh water, reasoning from an attribution that the ears are part of the head. Al-Shāfiʿī and other Mālikīs treat wiping as sunna and renew the water; the latter Mālikīs appeal to a different transmitted comparison with mouth rinsing. The printed main text also attributes obligatory wiping to Abū Ḥanīfa and his followers, with the head’s water. The edition’s footnote explicitly disputes this attribution, stating that the established Ḥanafī position is sunna, not obligation. The English translation repeats the main-text attribution. This is a textual-control issue, not permission to choose whichever version suits our theory. An independent Ḥanafī primary control is now available: al-Qudūrī explicitly lists wiping the ears among the sunan in his opening purification passage (printed p.11, PDF p.14), checked on the page image. This supports the school-doctrine correction, while leaving the textual history of the Bidāya attribution unresolved. QUDURI, PDF p.14, printed p.11. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF p.14, main text and note 1; p.15; B1E, PDF pp.12–13.

The explicit mechanisms are two. First, are reports of wiping an addition to the Qurʾānic prescription or an explanation of what “head” already contains? Second, are the ears an independent ablution member for purposes of water, or part of another member? The text also records outlying treatments by washing with the face or splitting treatment between head and face, then appeals to reports and established practice. Al-Shāfiʿī’s repetition is connected to his treatment of the head. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.14–15.

This is a legal mereology: how parts belong to wholes for the purposes of an act. Anatomical proximity alone does not resolve normative membership. It also demonstrates why two claims need separate proof: “part of the head” does not transparently tell us whether fresh water is needed without specifying the rule’s purpose.

The formative analysis concerns learning distinctions without fragmenting the act into unrelated gestures. At the personal level, a stable sequence can organize attention. At the intellectual level, the jurist must resist letting one familiar analogy settle every subquestion. A symbolic reading of the ears as obedient hearing might be spiritually suggestive, but no text examined here establishes it as the reason for these competing rules. It therefore cannot be the dossier’s conclusion.

A later Shāfiʿī control gives fresh water and repeated wiping within the recommended acts. It confirms one later practical configuration; it does not resolve the disputed Ḥanafī attribution. A primary Ḥanafī manual and another Bidāya witness are still required. Reliance of the Traveller, PDF pp.78 and 82, e5.1 and e5.12.

What this changes in the larger argument. The atlas must keep an unresolved evidence state. A disputed reading is not a philosophically fruitful disagreement until we know whether it is the jurists’ disagreement at all.

The reported warning about incomplete washing

Setting. Muslim241 locates the warning during a journey, when people hurried to perform ablution and some heels remained untouched by water.

The passage. The warning concerns the omitted part of the act, not a demand to multiply water without limit.

Its ethical argument. Attentiveness must survive hurry. The possible habit is completion of what is due even at a bodily extremity that can escape notice; neither waste nor self-conscious display follows from that purpose.

What the commentary explains. Nawawī reads the report as evidence for washing the feet and against interpretations making wiping alone sufficient for bare feet. This is his legal use of the narrative, not neutral proof that every reading of disappears. Ibn Rushd’s account of washing, wiping and the conjunction of sensible cleanliness with purification of the soul remains the primary analysis in P024–P026.

·

P024–P026. Feet and ankles: the decisive conjunction of sensible good and purification of the soul

P024: the mode of purification. The majority require washing; another group requires wiping; a further view permits either as an obligation with a choice, attributed to al-Ṭabarī and Dāwūd. Ibn Rushd begins with the two readings of the Qurʾānic expression and their syntactic relations to washed or wiped members. The positions then depend on preference, interpretation of the other reading, or acceptance of their equal apparent force. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.15–16.

The report warning about heels is not accepted by Ibn Rushd as a decisive proof of the mode rather than completeness. He asks what the warning actually establishes. A warning against incomplete coverage can bear on the act’s extent without proving that washing, rather than wiping, is its only valid species. This is a remarkably useful distinction for the whole project: a source supporting one property of an act must not be made to establish every other property of it. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.15–16.

A translation correction that changes the theoretical argument. On Arabic p.16 the text says that intelligible benefits are not precluded from being causes of prescribed acts of worship, so that the law may consider two meanings, maṣlaḥī and ʿibādī. The English printed p.12/PDF p.14 instead reads as though rational interests are “probably not applicable” as causes. Both page images were inspected. The Arabic is the controlling witness for our interpretation; the English wording reverses or seriously obscures the relevant proposition. A publication should collate the Arabic with another edition, but it should not build the thesis upon that English sentence. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF p.16; B1E, PDF p.14, printed p.12.

What the Arabic does and does not warrant. Ibn Rushd finds washing more fitting for feet and wiping more fitting for the head in relation to ordinary bodily conditions. He then distinguishes the sensible-benefit meaning from that concerning purification of the soul. He is not saying that the soul is a dirty physical surface, that the hygiene argument independently determines every divine prescription, or that every ritual detail has an evident utility. He expressly opens the possibility of a conjunction. This is a strong basis for the master framework because it comes from within a particular disagreement rather than from a modern external classification.

The operative unity. The body becomes the place where an intelligible material good and a devotional end are coordinated. Water’s sensible effect is neither the whole meaning nor an obstacle to spiritual meaning. The act can train the person to perform a bodily task as service while actually attending to the condition of the body. The “alchemy” is this coordination: material action is taken into an acknowledged order without ceasing to be material action.

The conjunction is not yet a demonstrated causal chain to every virtue. The passage names purification of the soul generally. We can compare temperance as orderly bodily conduct, attentiveness as careful completion, and humility as acceptance of a received form; we cannot report that Ibn Rushd expressly assigns each here. The closing virtue passage strengthens the general connection while leaving the exact pathways to be argued. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.475–476.

Avicenna and Ghazālī as distinct controls. Avicenna expressly treats bodily preparation and comportment in prayer as means of maintaining remembrance among ordinary people, with benefits in this world and the next. Ghazālī distinguishes levels of purification and criticizes fixation on the outermost level. Together they explain how the material and spiritual can be joined without being identical. They also expose a failure: an elaborate ritual can preserve its public form while its inward intention weakens. Neither author’s explanation is an alternate reading of the Qurʾānic case-ending. Avicenna, Metaphysics of the Healing, PDF pp.382–383; .

This analysis does not say that a city's plumbing determines the truth of a Qurʾānic reading. It says that legal validity and the conditions of enactment are different explanatory levels. The city supplies materials and instruction; the practice can in turn form temporal regularity, attention and shared recognition. Whether it actually does so requires evidence.

P025: whether the ankles enter the act. Ibn Rushd relates the disagreement over inclusion to ilā, as with elbows, but notes that the earlier issue had also involved the extent of yad. Thus a cross-reference is not proof that the mechanisms are wholly identical. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF p.16.

P026: what kaʿb names. The term can designate different anatomical locations in the linguistic discussion. The text records the bones near the fastening of the sandal and the projecting bones at the lower leg, with a qualified statement about agreement in the former interpretation. It also reports the principle that a boundary of the same genus may enter the bounded object, contrasted with night as the limit of fasting. The exact anatomical identifications and attributions need lexical and edition controls before further symbolic interpretation. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF p.16.

Their formative contribution is accurate delimitation and intelligible completion, not a new independent cosmology of the ankle. Their civilizational contribution is mediated through teaching and common practice. Their uncertainty belongs to language and attribution, not automatically to the reality of the religious end.

What this changes in the larger argument. This dossier gives the whole project a primary hinge: one legal act can bear bodily and spiritual meanings, while the warranted determination of its mode still depends on precise textual and evidentiary work.

P027–P028. Sequence: can the right parts make the wrong whole?

For the sequence of obligatory acts, Ibn Rushd reports recommendation from later Mālikī presentations and from Abū Ḥanīfa, al-Thawrī and Dāwūd; obligation from al-Shāfiʿī, Aḥmad and Abū ʿUbayd. He separately mentions ordering obligatory with recommended acts, described as mustaḥabb in Mālik’s account and sunna in Abū Ḥanīfa’s. The causes are the force of the conjunction wāw and what persistent prophetic performance establishes. The discussion also raises whether obligatory conditions can attach in relation to acts that are themselves not obligatory. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.16–17.

P027 is the order among obligatory constituents; P028 is the relation of that order to recommended constituents. These cannot be flattened into “order is required” without specifying the domain.

The object is a temporally structured whole. One position allows completion of the requisite constituents to suffice despite a changed order; another makes their relation part of the act’s valid identity. The distinction is not unlike a broader philosophical difference between a collection and an organized whole, but the legal conclusion is grounded in syntax and transmitted performance, not derived from an abstract doctrine that every whole must have this sequence.

Formation can proceed through a stable bodily sequence that reduces distraction and sustains memory.
