Making sequence constitutive can discipline faithful enactment; leaving it non-constitutive can distinguish the act’s core from the exemplary order. Both can teach order in practice. The second does not commend disorder, and the first does not prove superior inward concentration.

What this changes in the larger argument. Law forms relations among actions as well as actions themselves. The master framework must therefore include temporal composition, not only individual commands.

P029. Continuity: the difference between willing neglect, forgetting and inability

Mālik makes continuity obligatory when remembered and possible, while accounting for forgetting and excuse, with a qualification about excessive separation in the reported formulation. Al-Shāfiʿī and Abū Ḥanīfa do not make continuity one of ablution’s obligations. Ibn Rushd again discusses what wāw establishes, adduces delayed washing of the feet in the setting of bathing, and considers the force of prophetic acts. He explains Mālik’s differentiation through the law’s treatment of forgetting and the effect of excuse in mitigation. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.17–18.

The legal object is now not ordered succession but temporal connectedness. A person can preserve order yet introduce a long interval; one can also act continuously in an altered order. A whole-work atlas must keep those properties distinct because later substitutions and repairs depend on them.

The strongest formative reading is responsibility adjusted to agency. A deliberate interruption and an interruption through incapacity need not signify the same practical relation to the obligation. The distinction can educate a person to take an act seriously without treating every involuntary failure as culpable neglect. It is also a control on a false asceticism: difficulty does not by itself prove greater fidelity.

Attas’ acknowledgement requires acting according to the true place of things; forgetting, capacity and excuse are among the things whose place must be recognized. Al-Shaʿrānī’s discussion of varied prophetic practices and concessions is relevant, but his organization does not replace the specific grammar and evidence given here. Attas, Concept of Education, PDF pp.10–12; al-Shaʿrānī, Mīzān I, PDF/printed pp.95–97.

For the city, a workable practice must be teachable to people whose lives contain interruptions and unequal resources. That does not mean reducing law to convenience. It means distinguishing what the law itself treats as a failure, what it excuses and what it leaves valid. The later Reliance makes successive washing recommended and expressly preserves validity after a long pause without renewal of intention. This is a precise later Shāfiʿī control. Reliance of the Traveller, PDF p.83, e5.17.

Founding solidarity may supply immediate help with interruptions; concentrated official oversight can misclassify incapacity as disobedience; urban specialization may make water, assistance and instruction more available while introducing fragmented schedules; inherited routine can erase the distinction between excuse and indifference; breakdown increases interruptions and makes legally sound guidance important. None of these conditions alone chooses the correct legal position.

What this changes in the larger argument. A formative law is not merely a form imposed on passive matter. It addresses differently situated responsible persons, and its morphology can include the distinction between intention, memory and capacity.

P030. Naming God: devotion does not authenticate a proof

After the twelve principal issues, Ibn Rushd mentions a view making the naming of God obligatory and its supporting report. He states that the report has not been established as sound by the transmitters in the account before him; he also mentions readings in terms of intention and recommendation, the latter qualified by “as I think.” Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF p.18.

This apparently brief addition carries a fundamental safeguard. The manifestly devotional character of an act does not by itself establish its obligatory legal rank, nor does the beauty of its meaning repair a weakness in a report. The atlas must preserve Ibn Rushd’s epistemic wording and not turn a tentative attribution into a settled doctrinal statement.

The proposed formative meaning is explicit recollection of the divine orientation of the act. That meaning can be real while its place in validity remains disputed. The later Reliance recommends naming God at the beginning and permits making up an omission during the act, within its own school presentation. Reliance of the Traveller, PDF pp.79–80, e5.5.

At the civic level, this teaches a community that love of a devotional form and accurate classification are compatible. A concentrated authority or forceful teacher may be tempted to promote recommendation into obligation; inherited routine may do the same without conscious intent. Prosperous scholarship can preserve gradation; disrupted teaching can flatten it. These are institutional possibilities requiring evidence, not historical verdicts on particular schools.

P031–P040. Wiping footwear: concession, material integrity, time and repair

This connected group follows immediately after the ablution acts. The continuity is important: substitution is not an unrelated exception outside the order of worship. It is another mode whose permission, object, manner, duration, conditions and termination need determination. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.18–23.

P031. Permission in residence and travel

Ibn Rushd reports unrestricted permission, permission in travel alone, and general rejection; he notes transmission of all three from early authorities and from Mālik. The cause is the apparent relation between the Qurʾānic washing prescription and reports of wiping, including the chronology raised by the report of Jarīr. Later permissive interpreters distinguish the bare-footed addressee from the person wearing footwear; travel-only permission attends to the circumstances of the reports and the hardship of removal. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.18–19.

The legal operation can be abrogation, reconciliation by differentiated subjects, or limitation by circumstance. Calling the result “ease” does not tell us which operation established it. The person is not excused from relation to the ritual order; the order itself can specify a different performance.

Al-Shaʿrānī’s discussion sharpens the inward meaning. Someone who recoils from accepting an authenticated concession may need to perform it as a discipline of the self. That is a direct challenge to the idea that outwardly harder action is always spiritually superior. His account concerns the appropriate appropriation of a permission, not permission to invent one. al-Shaʿrānī, Mīzān I, PDF/printed pp.95–96.

P032. The surface to wipe

The text distinguishes upper surface obligatory with lower surface recommended, associated with Mālik and al-Shāfiʿī; both surfaces obligatory, associated with Nāfiʿ among Mālik’s followers; upper surface only without recommendation below, associated with Abū Ḥanīfa, Dāwūd and Sufyān; and an outlying either-surface position associated with Ashhab, with a variant recorded in the edition. The page image was checked because OCR had omitted a substantial portion of this list. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF p.19, including footnote.

The causes include differing reports and analogy to washing. Ibn Rushd commends reconciliation assigning different legal ranks and criticizes the bottom-only result as lacking a basis known to him. That criticism must remain visible within a study of meaningful plurality.

The formative lesson is restraint of private plausibility: the underside may seem the obvious place to clean, but wiping here is not merely a convenient version of scrubbing dirt. At the same time, the passage includes reasoned comparison and reconciliation; it is not a blanket rejection of reasoning. The case differentiates obedience, analogy and surface utility.

For communities, teaching the exact distinction prevents practical intuition from silently rewriting the received act. Prosperous scholarship supplies report comparison; routine or collapse may retain a gesture without its reason. An imposed official uniformity is not justified merely by a theory of bodily order. The higher meaning is disciplined integration of evidence and action, not a symbolism of “upper” as heaven and “lower” as earth.

P033. Socks and leather-covered socks

Ibn Rushd reports disagreement over extending wiping to socks: rejection from Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī and Abū Ḥanīfa in this presentation; permission from Abū Yūsuf, Muḥammad and Sufyān al-Thawrī. The causes are the reliability of reports and whether the permission can be extended by analogy or must remain confined to its received object. Leather-covered socks are intermediate objects yielding two reports from Mālik. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.19–20.

The ontology is a graded material resemblance. This is not a mere change of product name: the question is which features make the object eligible for a transmitted substitute. The personal good is continuity of worship in actual embodied circumstances; the juristic task is controlled extension. A qualified extension is different from letting convenience erase the object’s definition.

P034. Torn footwear

Mālik permits a slight tear; Abū Ḥanīfa specifies a threshold less than the exposed area of three toes/fingers in the printed expression; a position associated with al-Thawrī allows substantial damage while the object retains the name khuff; one Shāfiʿī report rejects a front opening exposing the foot even if small. The explicit cause is whether substitution depends on covering the foot or on the hardship of removal. Ibn Rushd characterizes the slight/large distinction through istiḥsān and removal of hardship. He also reports an argument from the familiar condition of early footwear and the absence of a transmitted prohibition; his own comment stresses that an obligatory boundary in this unaddressed case would have needed clarification. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF p.20.

The formative stakes are unusually concrete. A rule interpreted through intact covering can preserve the legal identity of substitution; a rule interpreted through removal hardship can preserve accommodation despite ordinary wear. A threshold mediates between them. Clothing condition also distributes burdens unequally: a poor wearer may confront a tear much more often. That is a plausible social implication, not a demonstrated origin of the opinions.

In an austere or mobile group, wear may be ordinary; prosperous crafts can facilitate repair or replacement; dynastic extraction can reduce disposable resources; inherited elite standards can mistake expensive equipment for religious excellence; breakdown can increase material hardship. Each scenario makes the adopted legal distinction consequential. The vertical question is whether fidelity includes recognition of lawful ease and finite resources. It does not authorize us to decide the legal threshold by our preferred social theory.

P035. Duration of the permission

Mālik’s reported view leaves wiping unbounded by a fixed period until removal or major impurity; Abū Ḥanīfa and al-Shāfiʿī specify a period. The passage contrasts the reports associated with ʿAlī, Ubayy ibn ʿUmāra and Ṣafwān ibn ʿAssāl. It records three days and nights for the traveller and one day and night for the resident in the timed account. Ibn Rushd finds the untimed report unestablished in the discussion before him, prefers working with the stronger reports, and still notes a conceptual difficulty: time itself is not ordinarily one of the events that nullify purification. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.20–21.

This is a collision between transmitted temporal form and an account of what changes a legal state. The difference is not between caring and not caring about purity. A fixed interval can provide a teachable reset; an event-based rule ties persistence to a change in condition. The formative descriptions are possible consequences, not the evidence that creates either rule.

P036–P038. Purity before putting footwear on; one foot; an additional covering

The general condition is prior ritual purity, with an exceptional dissent interpreting the report’s purity linguistically. P036 concerns putting footwear on after washing the feet but before completing the whole ablution. Abū Ḥanīfa permits in the reported account; al-Shāfiʿī and Mālik do not, for distinguishable reasons. Sequence matters for al-Shāfiʿī, while Mālik’s account concerns whether a member possesses legal purity before completion of the entire act. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.21–22.

P037 concerns putting on one item after washing that foot but before washing the other. The text reports rejection from Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, Aḥmad and Isḥāq; permission from Abū Ḥanīfa, al-Thawrī, al-Muzanī, al-Ṭabarī, Dāwūd and some Mālikīs including Muṭarrif. It reports agreement that removing and replacing the first item after washing the other foot permits wiping. The OCR of one name is uncertain; the list should be collated again before a critical edition of this dossier. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF p.22.

P038 concerns one covering over another, with two Mālikī reports. Can the first transfer of the prescribed treatment from foot to covering license a second transfer? The cause is analogy between the two transfers or recognition of a relevant difference. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF p.22.

These are three distinct compositions of legal state and physical sequence. They show why “same school, same philosophy” is insufficient: agreement in outcome can follow from different premises. The rule about removing and replacing also demonstrates that a material act can alter the legally relevant description without improving cleanliness. The object is the relation between a completed state and a permitted substitute.

The civilizational effect on ordinary people depends on pedagogy: competent teaching can make a practical sequence manageable; unexplained complication can create dependence. The latter is a hypothesis to test against adab and teaching literature, not a criticism derived from complexity alone. No independently supported metaphysical meaning for two layers of leather has been established.

P039–P040. Nullification and removal: what survives the disappearance of a substitute?

P039 records agreement that the ordinary nullifiers of ablution apply to this purification. P040 asks what removal itself does. One position requires washing the feet while retaining the rest, associated with Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī and Abū Ḥanīfa, with Mālik’s continuity qualification; another retains purity until an ordinary nullifier, associated with Dāwūd and Ibn Abī Laylā; a third, associated with al-Ḥasan ibn Ḥayy, treats removal as invalidating purity. Ibn Rushd calls the matter unaddressed by an explicit text and explains it through whether wiping is an independent basis or a substitute for washing while the feet are covered, together with continuity. He criticizes the demand for immediate action simply from the instant of removal as weak. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.22–23.

The practical ontology is persistence. Does a validly attained state survive the disappearance of the means by which it was attained? If it does, removal is not a new impurity. If it does not, what repair is sufficient: the missing member or the whole? This question has analogues elsewhere in law, but each analogy requires proof of relevant likeness.

In a stable city, accurate advice can prevent unnecessary repetition or invalid reliance. In periods of mobility and scarcity, the burden of whole renewal may be more significant. Concentration of power matters if institutional actors turn contested private validity into coerced uniformity. Inherited routine can conceal the distinction between an event that creates impurity and a condition whose disappearance changes permission. Breakdown can make clear manuals and capable teachers especially valuable. The primary passage does not measure any of these effects.

Upward result of the footwear sequence. Permission, matter, extent, time, sequence, state and repair are distinct dimensions. A theory that labels this whole chapter merely “takhfīf” misses most of its intellectual content. A theory that treats its distinctions as empty formalism misses how precisely they regulate finite persons’ access to worship. The deeper synthesis must preserve both conclusions.

What this installment establishes and leaves open

The opening sequence supplies substantive support for an account of legal formation, but it also disciplines that account. It demonstrates composite practical objects, degrees of obligation, interpretation of bodily universals, temporal wholes, mediated acts, ordinary uncertainty, concessions, and persistence or repair of legal states. It repeatedly distinguishes strong and weak arguments. It provides direct primary language connecting sensible benefit and purification of the soul.

The comparative readings here are sustained interpretations of those mechanisms. They do not establish historical outcomes without records of actual teaching and practice. The main unresolved textual controls concern the textual history of the ears attribution (the school doctrine is now controlled against al-Qudūrī), some named subsidiary positions and variant readings, and collation against another Arabic edition. The next continuous boundary is the water chapter beginning on p.23. It is not yet included in this installment’s interpreted coverage.

Part II.C. Water and purification

Main worship commentary, under reconstruction. Restored in revision 9 under the expanded whole-work brief. The existing arguments and source problems are retained. Their verse, hadith and spiritual-commentary audits remain incomplete; the new standard is explained in the worship introduction.

This installment continues the Arabic base from volume I, printed/PDF p.23, at al-bāb al-thālith fī al-miyāh, through p.33, stopping before the chapter on nullifiers of ablution. It treats the preliminary rules and all six principal questions in that chapter, with subsidiary propositions distributed across W001–W031. These are working analytical units, not a final count of elementary rules. Printed Arabic pages23,26,27,30–33 have been inspected visually; the chapter has also been compared with the supplied English, printed pp.20–31/PDF22–33. Several school attributions still require an independent primary control.

The chapter is unusually important for the master argument. Ibn Rushd moves from revealed designation through ordinary naming, physical relations, sensory judgments, competing reports and juristic reconciliation into determinate permissions and restrictions. He occasionally states his own preference and explains it at length. We can therefore examine how a rule is made intelligible without pretending that everything in its material object is exhausted by that explanation.

“Transformation” below has three distinct senses: the text’s account of a material process, the constitution or alteration of a legal status, and our reconstruction of a person’s formation through practice. They must be connected by an argument. The same word does not prove that they are the same event.

Purification as an accessible form of gratitude

ends by connecting purification, relief from hardship, completion of divine favour and gratitude. This is the shared orientation of the act; it does not independently decide each dispute about water or bodily states below. Ibn ʿĀshūr treats the verse as confirming an existing practice and its concession, and discusses why its provisions should not all be assigned to one first occasion. Qushayrī’s related reading preserves outward duties when inward attainment is absent: lack of spiritual intensity is not a reason to abandon the available form of worship.

· ·

W001–W005. Ordinary water, the sea, unavoidable change and impurity

The chapter begins with Qurʾānic warrant for water as a means of purification and for clean earth where water is unavailable. It then establishes a field of agreement, qualified by early outlying disagreements, before examining six questions functioning as principles of the chapter. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF p.23

W001: the required material. Water is introduced through its prescribed use, not simply through its ability to dissolve dirt. Its place is that of an authorized means in a practical relation: a person prepares for an act by a specified operation upon the body. This explains why a liquid can be clean and useful yet fail to be an eligible means of ritual purification. The universal practical science classifies sources and rulings; instrumental reasoning determines what falls under the relevant designation; particular fiqh specifies the material that can be used. Neither a theory of substances alone nor an undifferentiated “general hermeneutics” can replace that sequence.

W002: seawater. Ibn Rushd reports an early anomalous disagreement, then rejects the exclusion of seawater by the ordinary unqualified name of water and the report transmitted by Mālik. He notes disagreement over the report’s soundness while observing that the apparent sense of the revealed law supports it. This is not a free-standing empirical inference from saltwater’s usefulness. It is convergent textual and semantic reasoning. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF p.23

The Muwaṭṭaʾ’s fuller report makes the practical setting explicit: seafarers carry limited fresh water and fear thirst if they use it for ablution. The answer recognizes seawater’s purifying capacity and also addresses sea carrion. The latter clause belongs to the report but requires its own food-law analysis; its presence does not make this water commentary a completed treatment of marine food. Here the primary setting joins travel, bodily need, available resources and worship.

W003: unavoidable ordinary alteration. Water altered by things from which it is ordinarily inseparable retains purity and purifying capacity. Ibn Rushd mentions an anomalous report from Ibn Sīrīn concerning stagnant or altered standing water and again appeals to the unqualified name. The rule does not demand that ordinary people find a substance isolated from all environmental conditions. Its ontology is ordinary natural water as encountered, with distinctions among kinds of change. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF p.23

The developmental significance is not indifference to cleanliness. It is learning to distinguish an operative alteration from the unavoidable conditions of ordinary existence. For personal formation, that can support composure and discrimination rather than a futile search for material impeccability. Whether it actually reduces anxiety in a population is a historical or psychological question, not a fact established by the rule. For civic life, the rule prevents the conceptual baseline from excluding the kinds of water on which actual settlements depend; separate judgments about drinking, illness, ownership and access remain necessary.

W004: alteration by impurity. The agreed prohibition concerns impurity changing taste, colour, smell or more than one of these. The causal description matters: the same sensory alteration produced by a pure additive belongs to another question. Sensation supplies evidence, but juridical significance depends on what caused the change. The practical habit to be cultivated is therefore attentive discrimination, not disgust indiscriminately attached to every unfamiliar colour or smell. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF p.23

W005: abundant water without such alteration. Very large water is not rendered impure by a small impurity that changes none of its relevant qualities. This is the agreed starting point from which the next dispute develops. The relation between quantities is already important, even before a school fixes a threshold. A body of water is not treated simply as a collection whose every part receives an identical status from the bare presence of an impurity. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.23–24

Upward and downward connections. Together W001–W005 establish authorized material, environmental toleration, relevant transformation and scale. Downward, these distinctions affect what people must obtain, inspect, avoid or replace. Upward, they show that a legal ontology can be relational without becoming arbitrary: the material is considered under a particular action and end. The virtue connection is mediated through the agent’s use of these distinctions—practical discernment, restraint in suspicion and care for the conditions of worship. It would be inaccurate to say that each water category directly corresponds to one cardinal virtue.

W006–W011. Small impurities, quantities, washing and aversion

W006. The positions and the explicit conflict

When impurity enters water without changing an attribute, one position permits it regardless of quantity; Ibn Rushd attributes this to a report from Mālik and to the literalists. A second distinguishes small from large quantities. A third report from Mālik makes the small affected quantity disliked, rather than invalidating its use. The Mālikī reports therefore contain prohibition through impurity, permission absent alteration, and disapproval. They cannot be collapsed into a single school disposition. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF p.24

Ibn Rushd’s explicit cause is conflict among the apparent meanings of reports. The waking hand and stagnant-water reports seem to imply that a little impurity affects a little water. The report of pouring water over the Bedouin’s urine in the mosque and the report concerning the well of Buḍāʿa support a different reading. The jurists attempt reconciliation; different reconciliations yield different rules. The primary disagreement is not initially a contest between “ecological” and “ritual” philosophies. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.24–25

One reconciliation treats the prohibitions as prescriptions whose meaning is not explained by water becoming impure. Ibn Rushd criticizes an extreme consequence he attributes to the literalists: distinguishing direct urination from urine poured from a vessel. That criticism belongs in the record. Perspectival differentiation must not convert his criticism into praise for an equally adequate higher truth. The position may illuminate the problem of extending an addressed act beyond its form, but illumination of the problem is not vindication of the solution. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF p.25

The material circumstances can be identical while the described action differs. Conversely, the legal status can be different while no sensory change is detected. That is the problem requiring uṣūl: deciding which difference the evidence makes operative. To classify all restrictions as “vertical” and all permissions as “horizontal” would conceal the inferential work.

W007–W009. Three ways to determine the boundary

W007: movement as an indicator. Abū Ḥanīfa is presented as determining abundance by whether movement produced at one end reaches the other. Ibn Rushd explains this as an analogical indication of whether impurity could spread through the whole. The measure relates a perceivable event to an inferred material condition. This is a historical physical model employed in legal reasoning, not a claim about modern fluid mechanics. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.24–25

Its formative demand upon a competent practitioner is observational judgment. It leaves work to be done in recognizing the actual body of water. Its possible institutional advantage is that it can be applied without standardized vessels; its possible difficulty is variability in the conditions of observation. Those are our functional deductions from the criterion, not Abū Ḥanīfa’s stated reasons. The deeper axis is an inferred causal reach assessed through an indicator, not permission opposed to precaution.

W008: the two-qulla threshold. Al-Shāfiʿī’s boundary is tied to the report specifying two qullas; the passage relates this to approximately five hundred raṭls. The primary reason for choosing it is the report’s role in reconciling the evidence. It is not derived here from the number’s symbolism. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.24–25

A fixed measure can coordinate practice among people unable to reproduce the full reasoning behind the rule. It can be taught, embodied in vessels or recognized in a reservoir. Its application still requires reliable measures and knowledge of what is being measured. A later Shāfiʿī handbook uses a metric equivalent and adds details about used water, contact and changes; those are later operational specifications, not proof that Ibn Rushd used that modern volume. Reliance of the Traveller, PDF pp.70–74, e1.1–e1.17

The apparent alternative between “formality” and “reality” is misleading. A formal threshold can serve an actual social and epistemic purpose while resting on a revealed report. At the same time, the report’s authority must not be replaced by an invented utilitarian derivation. The virtue of the jurist is to know why the threshold binds in the argument; the competence required of a household user is different.

W009: distinguishing small and large without a fixed limit. Ibn Rushd records a Mālikī report that impurity affects a small quantity without assigning the specific boundary adopted by the preceding positions. This must remain distinct both from the alteration-only report and from the disliked-use report. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF p.24

Here application depends more heavily on competent recognition of scale. It may avoid false precision, but it may also produce inconsistent judgments where shared practical understanding is weak. Simon’s distinction between practical science and judgment about the singular helps identify the remaining task; it does not itself decide how indeterminate a legal threshold ought to be. Simon, Critique of Moral Knowledge, PDF pp.28–31, printed pp.8–11.

The common good of shared water is present as a possible field of application, but none of these three criteria is automatically a theory of municipal water regulation. We must still ask who owns, supplies and supervises the water, whose judgment people rely upon, and which other legal rules govern injury or deprivation.

W010. Why pouring water over impurity is not simply impurity falling into water

Ibn Rushd considers the Shāfiʿī distinction between water arriving upon impurity and impurity arriving in water. Although he reports that many jurists regard the distinction as arbitrary, he explains a possible rational basis. In successive washing, the impurity diminishes before the water is exhausted; the final portion of water stands to the remaining impurity as abundant water to a little impurity. The process, its direction and successive proportions matter. He invokes the agreed ability of an ablution-sized quantity to wash a drop from a garment or body while its receiving the drop remains disputed. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.25–26, p.26 visually checked

This is a particularly strong example of the practical particular requiring more than static classification. “The same water and the same impurity” can name materially related situations whose operations differ. To understand the rule one must grasp what the person does, in what order, to what remaining object. The relevant whole is an action through time.

At the material level the passage speaks of the disappearance or alteration of the impurity’s substance. At the legal level this supports the intelligibility of purification. At the personal level, learning the operation develops competent attention to an endpoint rather than mere repetition of gestures. These are connected levels, but they are not identical. The passage does not prove that washing away impurity mechanically washes away a vice.

The social mechanism is equally concrete. A teacher who can explain the operation can train others to recognize completion. A population taught only that impurity contaminates whatever it touches might conclude that purification is impossible; one taught only that water cleans might ignore the conditions under dispute. Juristic reasoning mediates between these errors. The transmitted practice is a civilizational accomplishment because it makes a complex judgment reproducible in ordinary life.

Ibn Rushd rejects an argument that water could never purify if a little impurity invalidated a little water. He thinks it wrongly transfers an agreed proposition about one situation to a disputed different situation. His own explanation shows why good effects attributed to a conclusion cannot repair a defective analogy. The alchemical interpretation must obey that same discipline.

W011. Legal validity, aversion and nearness to God

Ibn Rushd states his preference: understand the relevant prohibitions as disapproval and the other reports as establishing permissibility. He then gives a criterion of disapproval involving what the soul recoils from as foul. He relates avoiding water one recoils from drinking to avoiding its use upon the body in seeking nearness to God. The passage explicitly links affect, bodily use and devotional orientation. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF p.26, visually checked

This is stronger evidence for the project than a symbolic gloss invented by the commentator. Yet it requires careful boundaries. It occurs within the discussion of small impurity in unchanged water; it does not revoke his recognition of seawater merely because people do not ordinarily drink it. Nor does it make every private disgust a universal legislator. The argument distinguishes valid use from fitting use and seeks to preserve the force of all the reports.

The alchemical operation is education of affect within an intelligible legal order. A person is not asked simply to perform what is minimally valid while ignoring the disposition in which it is offered. Neither is the person authorized to declare invalid whatever feels unpleasant. The will learns to choose a fitting material in accordance with evidence; affect is admitted but bounded. This is a meeting of discernment and concentration: discerning the status of the water, and bringing bodily feeling and intention into the act of approach.

Attas clarifies the structure of acknowledgement: recognizing what is fitting becomes one’s own ordering of action. Ghazālī supplies an essential counterpressure. His criticism of excessive external cleanliness, pride and contempt for others shows how refined aversion can become a vice when treated as spiritual superiority. The synthesis must therefore distinguish cultivated propriety from status-conscious fastidiousness. Attas, Concept of Education, PDF pp.10–12; .

For political life, the rule raises a question about the distribution of material options. Someone with abundant alternative water can avoid a disliked use easily; a traveler or poor household may not. That difference does not itself authorize us to alter the ruling, but it changes the burden of realizing its fuller performance. A common-good inquiry asks whether provision can remove that obstacle. It must also ask whether privileged tastes are being imposed on people whose resources differ. These are hypotheses for the social history of practice, not facts about an identified society established by this passage.

Feedback from W006–W011. A single dispute has yielded several axes: report reconciliation, quantitative threshold, causally relevant operation, validity versus propriety, and disciplined affect. Severity/alleviation is only one possible description of the outcomes. The richest evidence is often in the reasoning connecting them.

W012–W016. Pure admixtures, naming and water already used

W012–W014. When something clean ceases to be the prescribed means

W012: pure additives changing an attribute. Water mixed with saffron or another ordinarily separable pure substance remains pure, but Mālik and al-Shāfiʿī are initially presented as denying its purifying capacity, while Abū Ḥanīfa permits it provided the alteration is not through cooking. Ibn Rushd identifies uncertainty about the extension of the unqualified name “water” as the cause. What counts as water simpliciter, and what counts only as water of a specified kind? Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF p.27

Personal formation here is less about suppressing appetite than about accepting a specified form whose integrity is not interchangeable with personal enhancement. Making the water fragrant or luxurious does not necessarily improve its suitability. The user’s motif of giving back in fullness must therefore mean fulfilling what is due, not always adding more elaborate material. This is our reconstruction from the rule’s structure, not a motive attributed to every jurist.

W013: degree, smell and a further Mālikī report. Ibn Rushd immediately qualifies a binary presentation. Mixture varies in quantity; it may or may not remove the unqualified name. Change of smell alone is treated differently by some jurists. He cites the washing of the Prophet’s daughter with water and sidr, with camphor in the final washing, and reports from Mālik a distinction between slight and abundant admixture even where qualities appear. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF p.27, visually checked

A completed record must preserve this qualification. “Mālik forbids all changed water” would erase the text’s own internal differentiation. The emergent axis is degree of presence of what changes the object’s name, rather than an absolute opposition between received form and purpose. Ordinary linguistic competence, recognition of the mixture and interpretation of the report cooperate.

The later Reliance likewise distinguishes substantial from slight change and unavoidable from avoidable alteration, while separating use that lifts ritual impurity from other uses. This shows how a handbook makes action possible by teaching intermediate distinctions. It is a later Shāfiʿī control, not a retroactive explanation of every early report. Reliance of the Traveller, PDF pp.71–72, e1.5–e1.9.

W014: cooking, expressed plant liquids and the rosewater exception. Ibn Rushd records agreement against purification with water cooked with a pure substance where the designation ceases to apply, and against liquids extracted from plants, while noting Ibn Shaʿbān’s permission for the Friday purification with rosewater. The exception is specifically reported in that setting. It must not be generalized to obligatory ablution without another source. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF p.27

W015–W016. Use, exhaustion and reuse

W015: used water. Ibn Rushd reports prohibition of renewed purification with used water from al-Shāfiʿī and Abū Ḥanīfa; disapproval without permission to substitute tayammum while it is available from Mālik and his followers; no difference from unqualified water from Abū Thawr, Dāwūd and followers; and an anomalous impurity attribution to Abū Yūsuf. His explanation again concerns whether the unqualified name still applies, including a claim that “washings” is a more appropriate name. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.27–28

The Mālikī position requires particular attention: disliked does not mean dispensable. A person cannot infer from a less fitting means that the legally available means is absent. This is a direct case of ordered alternatives. Al-Shaʿrānī’s later account of capacity can illuminate it: the appropriate available level remains binding; concession is not abandonment. But his general terminology must not be confused with the uṣūl manuals’ technical ʿazīma/rukhṣa distinction, which he expressly disclaims. al-Shaʿrānī, Mīzān I, PDF/printed p.98.

The differing operations are these. The prohibition treats prior legally significant use as altering eligibility even where ordinary cleanliness may remain. The disapproval preserves eligibility while registering a reason to prefer another supply. The unrestricted permission refuses to infer a loss of eligibility from use alone. The impurity position makes a stronger claim about status, which Ibn Rushd rejects for lack of evidence. A perspectival account must record that rejection; it cannot equalize the positions by supplying each with an attractive spiritual metaphor.

W016: drops, actual alteration and the author’s assessment. Ibn Rushd invokes the Companions’ desire for the Prophet’s remaining ablution water and infers that drops of used water would fall into the remaining supply. He regards used water generally as unqualified water where washing has not altered its attributes; if alteration does occur through clean bodily dirt, it falls under the preceding admixture question. He recognizes greater aversion as relevant to disapproval. The report, the inference about drops, the ordinary material assessment and the evaluative conclusion are distinct steps. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF p.28

The inference is not an express prophetic statement authorizing every conceivable reuse. Nor does the report establish that used water is medically safe. The legal chapter concerns the conditions of ritual purification; practical safety is another inquiry. The commentary must resist converting either devotional blessing or ordinary appearance into a universal empirical guarantee.

The formative potential is an ability to avoid confusing physical dirt, a legal state and imagined moral contamination. Water has touched a person performing a purificatory act; it does not follow that the person’s spiritual defect has become a material substance deposited in it. Ghazālī’s distinct levels of purification offer a comparison precisely because they prevent collapsing body, conduct, character and inward orientation into one process. .

In a water-rich city, reuse may be an occasional question. In travel or scarcity, its classification can determine whether people must obtain another supply or proceed with what is present. The legal difference thus has material consequences even though scarcity is not Ibn Rushd’s stated cause of disagreement. A theory of law’s alchemy should follow those consequences through labor, access, bodily preparation and attention while keeping the evidentiary basis of the rule intact.

W017–W025. Shared water, living beings and the grounds of exclusion

W017–W020. Life, food, contact and religious difference

W017: the baseline and competing classifications. Ibn Rushd reports agreement concerning the remnants of Muslims and livestock, then several classifications of other animals: all living animals; all except pigs; all except dogs and pigs; exclusion of predators; and a scheme relating remnants to the legal status of meat. The first two are reported from Mālik, the dog-and-pig exception from al-Shāfiʿī, and the predator exception from Ibn al-Qāsim. The meat-based scheme is subsequently explained in connection with Abū Ḥanīfa. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.28–30

The explicit causes are three: analogy against the apparent sense of the Qurʾān, analogy against reports, and reports against one another. The analogy links the impurity of an animal dying without prescribed slaughter to the purity of life, then the purity of the living animal to its remnant. This is a juristic argument, not a self-evident biological theorem. The exceptions test which part of that chain remains warranted.

The practical ontology is a relation among a living being, its mouth, the material it touches and the next user. It is neither simply an isolated substance nor an abstract list of species. Accordingly, the personal good is not exhausted by hygienic caution, and the social good is not exhausted by a prohibition. The rules define the extent to which life in shared environments can proceed without recurrent exclusion of available water.

W018: pigs and the interpretation of rijs. One route treats the Qurʾānic designation as establishing physical impurity; another reads it as censure without the same material conclusion. The debate concerns the kind of predication being made. A moral or religiously evaluative predicate does not automatically operate as a material one; whether it does so here must be argued. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.28–29

W019: the remnant of the mushrik. Ibn Rushd similarly distinguishes taking the Qurʾānic designation as bodily impurity from reading it as censure, and records a view of disapproval connected with wine drinking. Later he tentatively prefers exceptions including the dog, pig and mushrik, while saying that preference in this purely juristic question is difficult. His evaluative position must be reported even where it creates tension with the proposed account of civic cooperation. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.28–31

A responsible civic interpretation does not erase this tension by calling every boundary beneficial. If a rule restricts shared material use across a religious boundary, it may structure everyday interaction and dependency. It does not by itself establish the full legal standing, dignity, property rights or political membership of the person concerned. Conversely, identifying other rights does not make the material restriction disappear. We need the relevant chapters on food, persons, transactions and governance before claiming the integrated legal position.

The formative possibilities also cut in more than one direction. A bounded rule can train fidelity to an adopted norm; it can also be taught in a way that cultivates contempt beyond its legal scope. Which outcome occurs depends on the wider education of affect and the institutional handling of difference. Maritain’s person/common-good distinction poses a comparative question about irreducible personal good, but cannot be used as evidence that the medieval text already answers in modern terms. Maritain, Person and Common Good, PDF pp.14–17, printed pp.16–19.

W020: actual or customary exposure to filth. Ibn al-Qāsim’s disapproval extends to animals ordinarily not avoiding impurity, with examples such as roaming poultry and filth-feeding camels or dogs. The explanation is not identical with essential species impurity. The Muwaṭṭaʾ provides a sharply delimited control: Mālik allows the cat to drink from the vessel unless impurity is actually seen on its mouth. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF p.28; .

A rule keyed to observed contamination and a rule keyed to typical exposure impose different epistemic burdens. The former asks for a relevant fact; the latter permits a qualified inference from a pattern of behavior. Neither is a license for limitless suspicion. This distinction belongs in every future case concerning testimony, trust or custom: what is directly known, what is presumed from a recurrent condition, and how far the presumption reaches.

W021–W024. Dogs, cats, predators and different kinds of legal reason

W021: the Mālikī reading of the dog-vessel report. Ibn Rushd presents the command to discard the water and wash the vessel as worship whose reason is not the water’s impurity. The usual Mālikī view does not extend discarding to every non-water substance the dog touches. He supplies the conflicts motivating this reading: the analogy from life, the Qurʾānic permission to eat game caught by trained animals, and the specified number of washings, which ordinary removal of impurity does not require. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.29–30

The morphological result combines ordinary purity with a prescribed operation. The act is not vacuous merely because the water is not legally impure. Nor does calling the operation devotional mean there is no possible intelligible benefit. It means that this juristic explanation does not derive its legal requirements from the impurity category. Our framework must distinguish an unknown ratio, a nonexclusive ratio and the absence of any divine wisdom; those are not equivalent claims.

W022: al-Shāfiʿī, the remnant and the animal. Ibn Rushd takes the command as evidence of impurity and reports washing the caught game. He qualifies his attribution that the impurity is in the saliva rather than the animal with fīmā aḥsabu, “as I think.” That reservation is present in the Arabic and must survive our summary. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF p.30, visually checked

The later Reliance classifies dogs and pigs themselves among filth and states that living animals are otherwise pure. It therefore does not permit Ibn Rushd’s tentative saliva-only statement to become an unqualified account of settled Shāfiʿī doctrine. This is an attribution problem to collate, not an opportunity to fabricate a developmental history from two passages alone. Reliance of the Traveller, PDF pp.113–114, e14.1(8), e14.1(14) and commentary.

The rule’s immediate formative demand is accurate recognition of contact and the prescribed remedy. Its virtue cannot be identified simply with aversion to an animal. Care in complying with a material restriction must be distinguished from cruelty or generalized contempt, neither of which this passage licenses. A complete political account would ask how the restriction affects hunting, domestic space and provision; the water chapter alone does not answer all three.

W023: Abū Ḥanīfa and the relation to meat. Ibn Rushd reconstructs the remnant rule through the prohibition or disapproval of the animal’s flesh, treating the particular examples as intended generally. Concerning the dog, Abū Ḥanīfa accepts impurity but does not make the specified number of washings a condition; the general principle is removal of the impurity itself. Ibn Rushd explicitly observes the acceptance of one part of a report and nonuse of another where it conflicts with the principles, reinforced by the reported practice of its transmitter. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF p.30

Here “universal versus particular” has a concrete legal content: which general rule governs the particular report, and what force remains to a specification in that report? The philosophical issue is not a simple choice between rational thought and revelation, since both the general principle and the report function within legal reasoning. The jurist’s intellectual virtue is consistency that still accounts for the evidence resisting the system.

W024: cats and predators. The reports include a washing prescription concerning a cat and the Abū Qatāda report grounding its non-impurity in its circulating among people. Ibn al-Qāsim’s reconstruction, as Ibn Rushd presents it, can extend the familiar-circulation reason to the dog while distinguishing predators by an implied opposite. Other positions adhere to other report combinations. Thus the same cat report can support a direct rule, an extension and a delimiting implication. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.29–30

The Muwaṭṭaʾ preserves a small but revealing performance: Abū Qatāda tilts the vessel so a cat can drink, then explains the rule to a surprised observer. Juristic knowing is embodied as an action, witnessed, questioned and verbally transmitted. It is not merely a proposition stored in a book. Another report has ʿUmar stop a question about predators visiting a cistern, observing that humans and animals use the water in turn. These reports support an inquiry into restraint in inquiry and practical coexistence; they do not prove a modern ecological theory or an unrestricted rule against asking relevant questions. .

W025. Medical explanation and the scope of a water rule

Ibn Rushd recounts his grandfather’s explanation in the Muqaddimāt: the dog-vessel prescription is intelligible through a feared harmful condition of the dog rather than ritual impurity. He regards this as a good account on Mālikī premises and considers an objection about the dog’s relation to water at different stages of the condition. He also distinguishes the vessel from water alone. The English adds “[viral]” to its rendering; that term must not be attributed to the Arabic author. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF p.31, visually checked; B1E, printed p.29/PDF p.31.

This is a historical explanatory proposal, not medical guidance or a verified scientific derivation of the number seven. The text’s use of examples from treatment does not establish that the precise procedure has the claimed effect. Its value for this project is methodological: a rule interpreted as non-rationally specified by one account can receive a proposed intelligible rationale within the same school, and Ibn Rushd prefers offering a reason on those premises to simply declaring the rule inexplicable.

Nor should that preference erase his preceding tentative preference for an impurity interpretation. He is testing explanatory possibilities at more than one level. “The author’s position” therefore needs a record of local argument, conditional approval and final preference, where any final preference is actually supplied. An isolated sentence about his grandfather cannot settle the entire problem.

The distinction between a rule’s force and the certainty of its explanation is decisive. A legal prescription can be supported while a proposed medical rationale remains contestable. If that rationale were defeated, one would have to reassess the explanatory claim; it would not follow without further argument that every textual basis of the rule disappeared. Conversely, attaching a traditional name to the rationale does not exempt it from scrutiny.

Ibn Rushd also rejects restricting the dog to a prohibited or stray kind as remote from that explanation, while acknowledging a possible deterrent reading aimed at keeping such an animal. Again, therapeutic protection, ritual impurity, specified worship and behavioral deterrence are distinct possible accounts of a superficially identical act. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF p.31.

Feedback from W017–W025. The chapter already defeats any fixed table assigning Mālik to intelligible purpose and another school to received form. Mālikī material contains a non-explanatory devotional account and a proposed medical account; the Shāfiʿī discussion combines transmission with intelligible impurity; the Ḥanafī account accepts one component and subjects another to a general principle. The emerging unit of analysis is the argument and operation, not a school personality.

W026–W030. Men, women and water remaining in the vessel

This question concerns remaining water, and must be distinguished from water that has already run over a body. Conflating it with W015 would erase the object under dispute. Ibn Rushd gives five arrangements and explains their relation to reports of the Prophet’s shared bathing with his wives, use of Maymūna’s remaining water, a prohibition addressed to a man’s use of a woman’s remainder, and a report allowing simultaneous use while restricting successive use. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.31–33.

W026: unrestricted permission. The position attributed to Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī and Abū Ḥanīfa permits the remnants generally. One argument prefers the well-established joint-bathing report, reasons that each participant is necessarily using water remaining after the other, and accepts the Maymūna report. This is both evidentiary preference and an analysis of the action’s structure. It does not depend only upon an independently asserted ideal of domestic equality. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF p.32.

The formative interpretation concerns ordinary cooperation in bodily preparation. Water remains a shared means; the fact that another person has begun purification need not create a barrier to the next person. The household can embody order through coordinated access. This is a real social good even though the immediate act is worship. The public/private distinction therefore does not coincide with trans-individual/individual: a household ritual arrangement is already relational.

W027: asymmetric sequential permission. Ibn Ḥazm’s reconstruction allows joint use and a woman’s use after a man, but not a man’s use after a woman. Ibn Rushd explains preference for the prohibiting report over Maymūna’s and reconciliation with the joint-bathing report by distinguishing simultaneous from sequential use. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF p.32.

A rigorous commentary must neither suppress the asymmetry nor invent an account of women’s inferior spiritual substance to justify it. The explicit argument concerns the directional wording and comparison of reports. The possible effects include differentiated ordering of household access, but the text does not tell us how often that ordering was enacted or contested. Political and virtue analysis must ask whether faithful compliance is being taught with restraint about its scope or supplemented by unsupported social judgments.

W028: mutual prohibition of successive use, with joint use permitted. This reconciliation retains a distinction between sharing an ongoing act and using the other person’s remainder afterward, extending the restriction in both directions through the Ibn Sarjis report. Ibn Rushd notes the contrary Maymūna report and a criticism based on a transmitter’s qualified recollection. The confidence attached to a narration helps constitute the rule’s practical shape. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.32–33.

Its operation differs from W027: reciprocal separation of successive use rather than one-sided restriction. Shared bodily preparation remains possible through beginning together. The social meaning is therefore not blanket segregation. A source-based analysis can identify the temporal morphology without claiming that contemporaneous action possesses an independently revealed metaphysical superiority.

W029: prohibition even of simultaneous use. The supplied Arabic attributes this to Aḥmad b. Ḥanbal; the supplied English repeats it. Ibn Rushd offers only a conjectural explanation: perhaps only the prohibiting report reached its holder, with analogy extending the restriction. Both the attribution and the conjectural status need to be preserved. An independent Ḥanbalī primary-source check is outstanding; this entry must not be presented as an audited description of the entire school. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.32–33, p.32 visually checked; B1E, printed pp.29,31/PDF pp.31,33.

The possible household burden is greater separation of the means of purification. Whether it requires an additional vessel or merely a different sequence depends on further details not given here. Those missing details are material to any proposed civilizational effect. The commentator must not move from a compressed ruling to a grand theory of domestic organization without them.

W030: a restriction associated with janāba or menstruation. Ibn Rushd records a position allowing the man’s use except where the woman is in one of these conditions, then expressly says he does not know its proof, apart from a report from an early authority whom he thinks is Ibn ʿUmar. That admission is a positive evidentiary result. We should not fill the gap with an invented theory of bodily or spiritual contagion. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.31–33.

A further primary control identifies the early attribution more firmly: the Muwaṭṭaʾ transmits through Nāfiʿ precisely this permission from Ibn ʿUmar, excluding the remainder of a menstruating woman or one in janāba. This confirms a transmitted Ibn ʿUmar position in this witness; it does not supply a prophetic proof or resolve why that distinction should control. The adjacent reports also distinguish a person’s ritual state from impurity on fingers or clothing. Thus a new source can resolve one evidentiary question while leaving the reason of the rule open. .

The ontology of legal state is the key comparative issue. A person’s need for purification does not by itself tell us whether unused water touched or left by that person changes status. The point must be proved within the relevant doctrine. Ghazālī’s distinctions among kinds of purity and Powers’ analysis of intentional and legal states help keep the questions apart; neither supplies the unknown report’s rationale. ; Paul Powers, Intent in Islamic Law, PDF pp.30–33.

What this changes in the larger argument. A coherent alchemy of law needs a theory of socially mediated agency. Even an individual’s ritual preparation has prior users, shared material, temporal coordination and relationships of teaching and authority. The law works through those relations; it can also be misused within them. Legal validity, good character and a just household must be evaluated distinctly before they can be integrated.

W031. Date nabīdh during travel: substitution and the integrity of proof

Ibn Rushd reports Abū Ḥanīfa’s permission to perform ablution with date nabīdh during travel, against most of his associates and the regional jurists. The cited report concerns Ibn Masʿūd and the night of the jinn; a further claim invokes Companions’ positions with no known contrary Companion opinion. The traditionists reject the report because of weak transmitters and a stronger contrary account of Ibn Masʿūd’s presence. The majority also argues from the revealed alternative of earth when water is unavailable. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF p.33, visually checked.

The object must be described accurately as the date preparation under discussion. The passage does not justify replacing the term with “wine” or extending the permission to intoxicants generally. Nor does it supply every condition later Ḥanafī manuals might attach to the case. Those require separate primary control.

Ibn Rushd reconstructs a possible reply: the report itself calls it water, and an addition need not amount to abrogation. He immediately notes a tension with the principle attributed to the school that addition is abrogation. The commentary must record the tension rather than excuse it because the practical result appears convenient. This is a particularly useful test of the proposed relation between universal and particular science: a particular conclusion can put pressure on the school’s general account of how sources interact.

At the level of practical life, the alternatives allocate a traveler’s available material differently: retain an aqueous preparation as an eligible means, or move to the prescribed substitute when eligible water is absent. Both are intelligible arrangements for continuing worship under constrained conditions. Their shared practical attractiveness does not decide which has the stronger warrant. The user’s demand to understand “real meaning” therefore includes the authority question itself; it is not satisfied by a functional story about travel.

The alchemical interpretation is continuity of acknowledged obligation through a change of means, constrained by legitimate authorization. Bodily action, intention and the journey remain integrated with worship. Yet it matters whether the means is recognized through sound evidence, analogy, ordinary naming or an unsupported report. “The same higher end” cannot make these epistemic routes interchangeable.

Material provision, teaching and civic practice

What the chapter changes in the master theory

First, the object of legal knowing includes processes, not just named things. The direction and sequence of washing can matter as much as quantities or categories. The full case database therefore needs an operation through time field, not only a rule and its purpose.

Second, the normative vocabulary must preserve pure, purifying, valid, disliked, fitting and harmful as potentially different judgments. The same material can occupy different places under them. The project should not collapse these into one scale of spiritual intensity.

Third, an inward orientation can enter the jurist’s reasoning explicitly, as in Ibn Rushd’s relation between aversion and nearness to God, while remaining bounded by legal distinctions. This is a more precise bridge between law and affect than saying that all bodily washing symbolizes purification of the soul.

Fourth, the chapter demonstrates recurring movement between universal principles and particular applications. General claims about names, reports, impurity and abrogation are tested by particular operations and counterexamples. The upward movement can correct a principle’s scope; it is not merely a process of gathering illustrations for an already completed philosophy.

Fifth, the epistemic limit remains. A spiritual account can explain how a person inhabits a received operation more fully. It cannot invent a missing proof, turn an uncertain attribution into a verified one, or allow claimed inward knowledge to override another person’s publicly warranted position. In the Mūsā–Khiḍr image, awareness that deeper wisdom may exist is a reason to limit interpretive presumption, not to license it.

Coverage and checks still required

The entire water chapter in this witness has received a continuous interpretive draft. This does not certify that every elementary proposition has been independently collated across editions and school texts. The following concrete items remain open: the Aḥmad attribution concerning simultaneous bathing; the exact history of al-Shāfiʿī’s saliva-only attribution; the scope of Abū Yūsuf’s used-water report; primary Ḥanafī conditions concerning date nabīdh; and the textual and doctrinal history of the sea-water and stagnant-water outliers. The status of each cited report here is what Ibn Rushd reports, unless a separate control is expressly supplied.

The next continuous boundary is Arabic I p.33, al-bāb al-rābiʿ fī nawāqiḍ al-wuḍūʾ. The water commentary neither covers those nullifiers nor fills the other substantial gaps in the two volumes.

Part II.D. Bodily states and required acts

Main worship commentary, under reconstruction. Restored in revision 9 under the expanded whole-work brief. The existing arguments and source problems are retained. Their verse, hadith and spiritual-commentary audits remain incomplete; the new standard is explained in the worship introduction.

Continuous reading of Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.33–43, beginning with nullifiers of ablution and ending before the Book of Ghusl. U001–U035 are working analytical units, often containing several attributed positions or conditions. Arabic pages35,39,42–43 have been visually checked, with the English parallel used for comparison. This installment continues the previous two purification commentaries; it does not cover the bathing book introduced at the bottom of43.

The principal question changes. The water chapter asked what material could perform a prescribed operation. These chapters ask what changes the person’s ritual eligibility and for which acts that eligibility is required. The distinction is foundational for the project: an event can alter legal eligibility without being a vice, and an act can be morally objectionable without being a nullifier of ablution. To understand the formative meaning, we must first preserve that differentiated practical ontology.

The most direct upward link is to Ibn Rushd’s analysis of practical generality. A known particular—an agreed nullifier—does not reveal, without further argument, the general feature under which it was prescribed. The most direct downward link is to a person living through bodily events, illness, sleep, intimacy, work and worship. Legal knowledge must coordinate those circumstances without turning ordinary embodiment into undifferentiated moral contamination.

Purification as an accessible form of gratitude

ends by connecting purification, relief from hardship, completion of divine favour and gratitude. This is the shared orientation of the act; it does not independently decide each dispute about water or bodily states below. Ibn ʿĀshūr treats the verse as confirming an existing practice and its concession, and discusses why its provisions should not all be assigned to one first occasion. Qushayrī’s related reading preserves outward duties when inward attainment is absent: lack of spiritual intensity is not a reason to abandon the available form of worship.

· ·

Bathing, bodily completeness and an unnecessary burden

The major bath is a neighbouring continuation of these bodily-state questions. The braids report gives a concrete limit on the identification of completeness with added difficulty.

Text and situation. Umm Salama asks whether tightly braided hair must be undone for the major bath. The reply directs water to the head and body without requiring the braids to be undone in the reported case. This is a woman’s practical question about her own washing. A variant adds menstruation to the question about janāba; the variant is relevant to competing distinctions between kinds of bathing.

What the commentary explains. Al-Nawawī makes the answer conditional on water reaching the hair as required in his school: when braiding prevents that, undoing is necessary; when it does not, undoing is unnecessary. He reports contrary views requiring undoing generally or specifically after menstruation. The same reasoning applies to a man with braided hair. His reading of Ibn ʿUmar’s stricter instruction offers alternatives—different hair, a different doctrine, or precaution—rather than declaring one historical motive certain.

The practical meaning. Completeness concerns the required reach of water, not an independently meritorious dismantling of every bodily arrangement. The difference is between removing an obstruction to the act and multiplying the act’s burdens.

·

U001–U005. Substance, outlet and the manner of emergence

U001: the agreed baseline. Ibn Rushd grounds the chapter in the Qurʾānic passage and the report that prayer after ḥadath requires ablution. He reports agreement concerning urine, feces, wind, madhī and wadī when their emergence is in the normal manner. The qualification concerning normality belongs to the proposition; it must not disappear from a summary. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.33–34.

U002: impurity emerging from the body. The first major account focuses on what emerges, regardless of the place of emergence. Ibn Rushd associates it with Abū Ḥanīfa and followers, al-Thawrī, Aḥmad and others, and gives blood, nosebleeding, bloodletting, cupping and vomiting as examples. The passage also differentiates slight blood, which these holders generally do not count apart from the report concerning Mujāhid, and phlegm, excluded by Abū Ḥanīfa but counted by Abū Yūsuf when it fills the mouth. These are subsidiary scope rules, not dispensable illustrations. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF p.34.

The operative generalization is that the agreed cases matter as impure things leaving the body. Ibn Rushd notes that this purification is ḥukmiyya, a legal or normative purification, yet resembles cleansing impurity. The same passage explains the sense of the comparison; its use of maʿnawiyya must not be translated into an unargued claim about mystical inward purification. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF p.35, visually checked.

The formative task under this account is recognizing relevant substances and degrees, including consequences of care for a wound or bodily treatment. It can create a stable practice of re-preparation following a recognized event. It does not classify receiving treatment as a moral failure. The broader social question is whether teachers, attendants and patients have usable instructions, resources and privacy. The rule’s realization can depend on caring work that remains invisible in an exclusively inward interpretation.

U003: the outlet. Al-Shāfiʿī and followers, and Muḥammad b. ʿAbd al-Ḥakam among Mālik’s followers, are reported as taking emergence from the two passages as decisive, including uncommon things such as blood, stones or worms and emergence in health or illness. Ibn Rushd reconstructs an argument from the different legal treatment of wind through different outlets, then criticizes the inference because the two winds also differ in characteristics. The attempted isolation of a cause is not accepted merely because it is elegant. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.34–35.

The ontology here is bodily location rather than only substance. The performer learns a comparatively determinate boundary, while the jurist must explain why that boundary, rather than an associated feature, is operative. The later Reliance gives an elaborated Shāfiʿī account, including exceptions and relations to major impurity not developed in this Bidāya paragraph. It confirms the importance of the outlet but must not be treated as a verbatim explanation of the early position. Reliance of the Traveller, PDF p.89, e7.1.

U004: the usual substance, usual outlet and normal occurrence together. Mālik and most followers are presented as retaining all three: the normally emerging named substances, through their ordinary passages, in health. Blood, stones, worms and incontinence are accordingly not simply assimilated. The reasoning keeps the particular address in its particular scope until evidence supports extension. The treatment of persistent discharge also involves illness as a basis of alleviation and the disputed addition commanding ablution for every prayer in the report of irregular bleeding. Ibn Rushd records Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr’s acceptance of that addition and the comparison with an continuously bleeding wound. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.34–35.

The Muwaṭṭaʾ directly records Mālik’s refusal to require ablution for bleeding, nosebleeding or pus as such. It is an independent primary control on that part of the classification, not a substitute for the whole discussion of chronic conditions. .

U005: the structure of the disagreement. Ibn Rushd says that al-Shāfiʿī and Abū Ḥanīfa agree that a particular wording is intended generally but disagree about which general is intended. Mālik’s reconstruction retains the particular scope. This is a precise case of universal practical reasoning operating inside a science of particulars. The philosophical work is to identify the relevant universal, not merely to announce that all parties apply general principles. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF p.35.

The “alchemical differences” should therefore be stated concretely. One pattern trains attention to material impurity wherever it emerges; another to a bodily boundary; another to the conjunction of named event, place and normal condition. Each establishes a different relationship between bodily awareness and renewal. None is yet an entire anthropology or madhhab character.

For virtue ethics, the immediate excellence is discriminating response within an adopted practice. Justice becomes relevant through the treatment of persons whose bodies cannot conform to an ordinary pattern: do institutions preserve access, or add humiliation to illness? The latter question is ours, but it arises from a primary legal differentiation of illness and normal occurrence. Al-Shaʿrānī’s account of acting at the available level clarifies why an accommodated practice can remain full obedience, while the actual form of accommodation must be derived from the school’s law. al-Shaʿrānī, Mīzān I, PDF/printed pp.98–100.

U006–U011. Sleep: event, probable cause and the conditions of attention

Ibn Rushd first distinguishes three general positions: sleep itself requires ablution whether little or much; sleep does not itself do so, with actual ḥadath or relevant doubt treated under its own rule; and a distinction between light and deep or prolonged sleep. He then relates the disagreement to conflicting reports and the choice between preference and reconciliation. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.35–37.

U006: sleep as nullifier in itself. This reading treats the reported inclusion of sleep with other nullifiers as operative. Its practical advantage is a simple recurrent boundary, but simplicity is not the stated proof. The performer learns to renew after an ordinary interruption of waking life. The virtue claim must remain modest: a reliable routine can sustain readiness, while its mere occurrence does not prove attention or moral improvement.

U007: sleep as non-nullifying unless another ground is present. On this reading, the reports of sleeping followed by prayer support the absence of a requirement from sleep alone. Ibn Rushd distinguishes those who require certainty of the actual event from those who count doubt, and mentions an early practice of having another person observe the sleeper. This is an unusually direct indication that the question can concern access to evidence rather than a substance called sleep. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.35–36.

The observer’s role shows legal cognition distributed across people. The self is not always in a position to know its own bodily history. That does not authorize intrusive supervision as a general institution. It does show why the agent’s responsible knowledge may depend on another’s observation, and why trust belongs within even apparently private worship. The fact of sleep is morally neutral; the epistemic problem is how to know what occurred during it.

U008: light versus deep or prolonged sleep. Reconciliation reads the requiring reports in relation to substantial sleep and the permissive reports in relation to light sleep. Ibn Rushd says reconciliation is generally preferable where possible among the uṣūl scholars. This is a principle stated within the primary text, but its application depends on whether the distinction is warranted. It is not an instruction to reconcile every conflict at any interpretive cost. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.36–37.

The embodied competence required is recognition of a relevant quality of one’s own sleep. This lies between an externally fixed event and an unbounded investigation of hidden bodily happenings. The person learns a practical threshold through experience and instruction. Simon’s singular practical judgment helps describe that remaining task; Klubertanz’s account of attentive learning explains why repeated exposure alone is not equivalent to mastery. Simon, Critique of Moral Knowledge, PDF pp.28–31; KLUBERTANZ, PDF pp.177–179.

U009: Mālik’s relation among depth, duration and posture. The reported positions require ablution after lying or prostrated sleep whether short or long, and after seated sleep when prolonged, with variant treatment of the bowing posture. Ibn Rushd explains this by the likelihood of the underlying event: in postures where it is normally expected, depth or duration need not also be required; in other postures those features matter. The rule is multivariable. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.36–37.

Its general meaning is proportionate attention to evidence of a cause, not a simple ranking of postures by holiness. The practical object is a bodily configuration through time. The text supports an inquiry into ordinary probabilities; it does not supply numerical risk estimates or establish the physiological correctness of every criterion.

U010: the Shāfiʿī seated exception. Ibn Rushd presents seated sleep as the exception and connects it to the transmitted practice of Companions. The later Reliance specifies firm seating and distinguishes drowsiness, awareness and uncertainty. Those later details are useful controls on how a concise early formulation becomes teachable practice, without erasing their chronological and textual distance. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.36–37; Reliance of the Traveller, PDF pp.89–90, e7.2.

U011: the Ḥanafī reclining criterion. The requirement is presented as attaching to lying sleep, connected to a reported saying and a firmly transmitted report from ʿUmar. The Muwaṭṭaʾ independently transmits ʿUmar’s reclining-sleep rule and Ibn ʿUmar’s seated-sleep practice, while its separate report of Zayd b.
