Aslam interprets arising for prayer as arising from sleep. These sources make clear that practice, report and interpretation interact. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.36–37; .

The strongest link to concentration is also in Ibn Rushd’s evidence: he cites the instruction that a drowsy worshipper should sleep until capable of knowing what is being said, lest an intended request for forgiveness become something else. This report is part of the legal evidentiary discussion; it also directly resists an alchemy based on maximizing strain. A body unable to sustain attention cannot be made spiritually whole by pretending that fatigue is irrelevant. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF p.36.

Al-Shaʿrānī later uses overpowering sleep to connect permitted practice with willing, receptive worship. Ghazālī’s account of presence in prayer distinguishes verbal motion from attentive address. Together they support a specific formative sequence: adequate bodily readiness, awareness of the act, willing performance and sustained orientation. They do not make inner attention a newly invented legal condition of validity in every school. al-Shaʿrānī, Mīzān I, PDF/printed p.100; .

What this changes in the larger argument. Here the law can form vigilance by limiting vigilance: it supplies warranted conditions under which a person renews or continues, and recognizes the need to sleep. Spiritual concentration is supported by embodied measure, not by treating every interruption as moral defeat.

U012–U014. Touching women: language, desire and the kind of event

U012: direct bodily touch. The position associated with al-Shāfiʿī and followers treats direct unmediated touch as nullifying, including kissing and without requiring pleasure. Ibn Rushd also reports differences concerning the active and passive party, and maḥram relatives as opposed to a wife. These intra-school reports must remain visible. A later handbook’s resolved formulation must not retroactively eliminate them. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.37–38.

The later Reliance excludes unmarriageable kin and identifies relevant skin contact, intention, uncertainty and other scope details. Its function here is a dated doctrinal control: it shows which distinctions a later practical text teaches, not that Ibn Rushd’s multiple reports were imaginary. Reliance of the Traveller, PDF p.90, e7.3.

U013: pleasure or intending pleasure. Mālik and most followers connect the rule to pleasure or its intention, whether contact occurs through a barrier or directly, while treating the kiss differently in the report as presented. Ibn Rushd remarks that he does not recall a Companion making the pleasure condition. That is his stated limit of recall, not a proof that no earlier evidence ever existed. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.37–38.

The practical ontology joins bodily contact, intention and affect. Its formative demand includes knowing the character of one’s own action. Yet pleasure is not automatically vice: the example can concern a lawful relation. Temperance cannot be equated with preventing every experience of attraction. The legal result concerns renewed eligibility for a further act, not a comprehensive moral verdict on the preceding contact.

This is one of the clearest places to reject a crude “lower body versus higher spirit” account. The law coordinates bodily relationships with worship through determinate transitions. A transition can be meaningful without portraying the body as an enemy. Attas’s proper placement clarifies the relational structure: an affection or bodily power is acknowledged through fitting exercise and through recognizing the conditions of another activity. It does not authorize us to create a nullifier because a feeling seems insufficiently elevated. Attas, Concept of Education, PDF pp.10–12.

U014: the non-nullifying touch account and Ibn Rushd’s semantic judgment. Abū Ḥanīfa’s position does not require ablution for ordinary touching. The explicit cause is the Arabic word’s use for bodily touch and as a reference to intercourse. Within the bodily-touch reading, a general wording may be understood generally or with the pleasure qualification. Reports of contact with ʿĀʾisha and of kissing create evidentiary pressures, including disputed authentication. Ibn Rushd records al-Shāfiʿī’s conditional willingness to change his view if the relevant report is established. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF p.38.

The interpretive issue is not solved simply by saying that literal meaning always wins. Ibn Rushd observes that a frequently used figurative sense can become more evident in ordinary discourse than an original sense, giving ghāʾiṭ as an example. He prefers the intercourse reading in this context, connecting it with other Qurʾānic expressions and with the possibility of tayammum for janāba. He rejects treating one use as simultaneously intending every meaning of the shared word. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.38–39.

The vertical/horizontal vocabulary is of little use until this reasoning is preserved. All three readings address a revealed instruction. The difference is which practical event it designates and how other reports specify it. A hermeneutical choice here has consequences elsewhere in purification, demonstrating why the commentary needs cross-references across chapters, not isolated entries.

The social implications concern bodily proximity, domestic affection and the distribution of required renewals. A rule resting on contact can be taught through a relatively public criterion; one resting on pleasure requires self-knowledge; one locating the verse in intercourse leaves ordinary touching outside this particular requirement. These are different forms of practical attention. Their actual effects on daily interaction require historical evidence. No one of them proves that a school values marital life, civic interaction or inwardness more highly as a whole.

U015–U019. Touching the genital organ: ordinary body and prescribed renewal

Ibn Rushd organizes the dispute around two opposed reports: Busra’s command to perform ablution and Ṭalq’s response treating the organ as part of the person’s body. He records different assessments of the reports and three broad methods: preference, abrogation, or reconciliation through differing circumstances or degrees of demand. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.39–40.

U015: requiring ablution. The initial list associates obligation with al-Shāfiʿī, Aḥmad and Dāwūd. U016: no requirement. Abū Ḥanīfa and followers are associated with the opposing report. Both are said to have earlier authorities. The formal dispute is not whether the organ is physically part of the body; it is whether the transmitted prescription creates a distinctive consequence for touching it. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF p.39.

U017: circumstance, pleasure and the inner palm. Ibn Rushd records distinctions between touches with and without pleasure, and between the inner palm and another surface, associated with Mālikī reports. He suggests the palm criterion may relate to the cause of pleasure. That suggestion is explanatory, not an express cause supplied by every holder. U018: deliberate and forgetful touch. Another report distinguishes intentional from forgetful contact, attributed to Mālik and to Dāwūd and followers. The latter qualification must be retained alongside the initial unqualified list. U019: recommendation rather than obligation. Ibn Rushd cites Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr’s description of the position settled among western Mālikīs, while noting unstable transmission from Mālik. It cannot be made a statement about every Mālikī everywhere and at every time. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.39–40, p.39 visually checked.

The Muwaṭṭaʾ supplies a revealing sequence of reports: a conversation in which ʿUrwa learns the Busra report through Marwān; a person holding Qurʾānic pages being directed to renew after touching; Ibn ʿUmar’s explanation of renewing after bathing because he may have touched; and recollection leading to repeated prayer. These are different forms of learning—discussion, correction in practice, explanation of a routine and retrospective repair. They support a social morphology of legal knowledge without requiring us to infer that every narrated practice was uniformly observed throughout the city. .

The virtue analysis must begin from bodily modesty and appropriate self-command without declaring ordinary contact inherently culpable. Depending on the account, a touch occasions renewal, is irrelevant to ritual state, is assessed through its manner or intention, or recommends a fuller practice without invalidating what follows. These differences have consequences for self-monitoring and for how a teacher corrects a student. A recommended renewal should not be presented as proof of invalid prayer; a binding renewal should not be ignored merely because another position would have been easier.

At the civilizational level, these questions require channels for private, competent consultation. The city’s juristic function is not merely to issue public prohibitions. It also makes delicate practical knowledge available without making every bodily circumstance a matter for political surveillance. Al-Qarāfī’s differentiation of advice, judgment and administration helps prevent the leap from a personal ritual question to a ruler’s unrestricted jurisdiction. al-Qarāfī, Criterion, PDF pp.79–82.

The upward result is a distinction between the event, its legal consequence, the agent’s responsibility for it and the teacher’s mode of response. An adequate philosophy of law must explain all four. Spiritual language that collapses them would make the analysis less exact than the legal text.

U020–U024. Food, laughter, care for the dead and loss of awareness

U020: food touched by fire. Ibn Rushd reports early disagreement arising from conflicting reports, followed by the regional majority’s abandonment of the requirement, supported by the practice of the four caliphs and a report concerning the later practice of the Prophet. The temporal relation among reports therefore matters. A philosophy based only on the supposed symbolism of fire would miss the explicit source of the rule. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF p.40.

The practical relation is between nourishment and return to worship. The final majority position as reported removes a recurrent renewal from ordinary cooked eating. This can reduce the work required to coordinate meals and prayer, but ease is not the stated evidentiary foundation. The formative lesson is that fidelity may involve ceasing to impose a requirement where the stronger account of the tradition no longer imposes it. More repetition is not necessarily more obedience.

U021: camel meat. Aḥmad, Isḥāq and a group of traditionists retain a specific requirement because of the report concerning camel meat. The exception concerns a named object, not every food transformed by fire. We should not invent a causal explanation concerning the animal’s temperament or a hidden bodily property; Ibn Rushd does not supply one here. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF p.40.

U022: laughter in prayer. Ibn Rushd describes Abū Ḥanīfa’s requirement of renewed ablution, grounded in a mursal report of people laughing and being commanded to repeat both ablution and prayer. The majority objects to the report’s transmission form and to a consequence apparently restricted to prayer though absent outside it. Ibn Rushd nevertheless calls it a sound mursal. “Sound” and “mursal” must both be retained; neither term automatically eliminates the controversy over using it as proof. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF p.40; B1E, PDF p.42, printed p.40.

This case is a counterexample to simplistic school portraits. The account of Abū Ḥanīfa here accepts a particular report despite a general-principle objection; the dog-vessel discussion presented him limiting one part of a report by general principles. A school’s handling of evidence must be reconstructed across the actual hierarchy and classification of proofs, not inferred from the preferred outcome of one case.

The virtue connection is attention and reverence in common worship. Yet we must distinguish a disruption of prayer from a nullification of ablution. The majority’s objection concerns that second consequence; it is not approval of heedless worship. The Ḥanafī morphology adds bodily renewal to resumption of the act, which can be interpreted as a more extensive reset, but Ibn Rushd gives the report as its warrant rather than that pedagogical hypothesis. The amount of formative work assigned by a rule cannot validate a weak inference on its own.

U023: carrying and washing the dead. Ibn Rushd reports an outlying obligation of ablution after carrying the deceased, supported by a report he calls weak; the quoted report also commands bathing after washing the dead. Both clauses must be preserved, although the present discussion centers on carrying. The bathing clause is a cross-reference for later analysis, not a completed treatment of funeral washing. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF p.40.

The social function is care for a person who cannot care for himself or herself, together with the community’s responsibility for burial. A requirement imposed upon that work affects those who perform it, while an unsupported requirement can increase their burden. The philosophical question is not whether care for the dead is noble—it is how the legally warranted preparation, service and subsequent return to other acts are related. We cannot turn the weak report into a reliable proof by attaching a compelling symbolism of death and rebirth.

U024: loss of awareness. The majority requires ablution following fainting, insanity or intoxication by an a fortiori comparison with sleep understood as ordinarily occasioning the underlying event. The criterion thus concerns loss of awareness and its relation to the body, not a single moral evaluation of all its causes. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.40–41.

This grouping is especially important. A blameless loss of consciousness and a culpable act may share a ritual consequence without sharing moral status. A humane account of formation must not blame an incapacitated person because the legal taxonomy places the event beside another kind of event. The relevant virtues of others may instead be care, patience and truthful assessment. The person’s own obligation must be related to restored capacity and the appropriate further act; those details require the relevant chapters rather than inference from this short paragraph alone.

The alchemical meaning of U020–U024 is the reconstitution of readiness across a varied life. Nourishment, distraction, service and interrupted awareness are not one moral category. The law differentiates their consequences and creates routes of continuation or renewal. The city supports those routes through instruction, material provision and competent care; it can frustrate them through neglect or indiscriminate coercion.

U025–U029. Prayer, the written Qurʾān and preparation for learning

U025: purification and prayer. Ibn Rushd reports agreement that purification is a condition for prayer, while distinguishing disagreement over whether it is a condition of validity or of obligation. The difference matters especially for exceptional cases of inability, but the present passage does not resolve all their consequences. A complete database needs the relation between conditions, capacities and performance rather than simply a yes/no “required” field. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF p.41.

The rule’s formative effect is to constitute a bodily threshold to a specified act of address. Its social function includes a widely transmissible form of readiness for shared worship. Its vertical orientation is explicit in the act’s religious end. None of this implies that legal eligibility is identical with inward presence; Ghazālī’s prayer discussion supplies that further question. .

U026: funeral prayer. The majority extends the condition because funeral prayer falls under ṣalāt; the outlying contrary account focuses on the absence of bowing and prostration. U027: prostration of recitation. The same classification question arises where standing and bowing are absent. These are two distinct practical objects, not a single omitted exception. Their underlying issue is the extension of a legal name to a form whose components differ. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF p.41.

The first concerns communal intercession for the deceased; the second a bodily response within recitation. A name can unite forms without making all their components identical. The intellectual operation is classification by the relevant whole rather than mechanical counting of visible parts. The formative operation is continuity of reverence across different acts. But the contrary position is not thereby deficient in reverence: it disputes the legal entailment of the name. The later Reliance’s placement of prayer and prostration among acts restricted without purification is a control on one school’s practical formulation. Reliance of the Traveller, PDF p.92, e8.1.

U028: touching the muṣḥaf. Mālik, Abū Ḥanīfa and al-Shāfiʿī require purification; the literalists do not. Ibn Rushd identifies two questions in the verse: whether “the purified” refers to humans or angels, and whether a statement is functioning as prohibition or as report. The majority also invokes the letter associated with ʿAmr b. Ḥazm; its authority is contested. The nonrequiring argument returns to original nonliability or permission where no adequate proof imposes the condition. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.41–42.

The construction of the norm therefore depends on referent, speech act and transmission—not on “literalness” alone. It is possible to read a description as a norm, but the shift requires grounds. This case should become a methodological cross-reference for every later movement from descriptive order to obligation. Attas’s recognition/acknowledgement architecture does not remove the need to establish which action is in fact due.

The Arabic’s description of the disputed ʿAmr b. Ḥazm reports and the English’s explanation in terms of a writing error require a further textual control. The present secure finding is that authority and transmission of the reports are disputed and that Ibn Rushd cites acceptance under trustworthy transmission. We do not settle the disputed technical expression merely by choosing the English gloss. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF p.42, visually checked; B1E, PDF p.43, printed p.41.

The formative connection to adab is especially concrete: a material object bearing revelation is handled under a learned mode of preparation. The physical book participates in a relation of address, transmission and study. Yet the position not imposing ablution does not reduce the Qurʾān to an ordinary commodity or deny respect; its argument is that this particular condition has not been established by sufficient proof. Reverence and legal condition must be kept distinct so that neither side is misrepresented.

U029: children’s access. Mālik’s exemption for children is explicitly explained by their not being legally accountable. That reason is primary. Its educational significance can then be reconstructed: access to the object through which one learns is not simply made contingent upon already possessing adult legal discipline. This creates space for formation before full obligation without denying the object’s reverence. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF p.42.

A later Shāfiʿī control is particularly useful: the Reliance’s commentary explicitly discusses learning needs and the hardship of maintaining ablution for discerning children, with further qualifications. That pedagogical rationale belongs to the later control; it must not be silently substituted for Ibn Rushd’s explanation of the Mālikī exemption. Reliance of the Traveller, PDF p.93, continuation of e8.2.

The emerging alchemical operation is graduated incorporation into a practice. It differs from both unrestricted access without formation and demanding completed excellence as a prerequisite to beginning. The child is a developing person, not merely a deficient adult. That reconstruction must be tested further against the actual teaching and guardianship literature.

U030–U035. Ordinary activity, circumambulation and remembrance

U030: sleep while in janāba. The majority recommends minor ablution before sleep; the literalists require it on the basis of the command. Ibn Rushd reports the majority’s argument from the lack of a legally fitting relation between sleep and obligatory purification. He also criticizes an inference from a report linking ablution with intended prayer as a weak implication, and identifies another supporting report as weak. The position and the quality of each argument must be recorded separately. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF p.42.

The Muwaṭṭaʾ transmits the command, ʿĀʾisha’s instruction and Ibn ʿUmar’s practice before eating or sleeping. This gives primary material against which the Bidāya’s interpretive discussion can be read, but the presence of an imperative in a report does not itself settle the very question of obligation versus recommendation. .

The ontological distinction is that minor preparation can be prescribed while the state requiring the major bath has not yet been removed. Purification is not an indivisible substance present or absent in the person. Different acts stand in different legal relations to different preparations. This alone is enough to defeat a theory that treats all degrees of bodily ritual state as a scale of personal moral worth.

U031: eating and drinking. Ibn Rushd reports disagreement over ablution before these activities in janāba and the majority’s nonobligatory account, invoking both the purpose of purification in occasions of reverence and conflicting reports. U032: renewed intercourse. The same field includes commands to perform ablution before returning to intercourse and reports of repetition without it. These are distinct activities even where the majority’s evaluative reasoning is shared. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.42–43.

The explicit concept of munāsaba sharʿiyya, a legally appropriate relation, is vital. The jurist asks what sort of act the law makes purification obligatory for. This is not permission for every interpreter to choose requirements by personal taste. It is an argument about the coherence of transmitted prescriptions and their relevant fields. The “real meaning” of the rule includes this question about form and occasion.

A formative interpretation can distinguish an obligatory sacred threshold from a recommended integration of preparation into ordinary life. Recommended acts may help unite everyday bodily activity with recollection without converting every moment into a new compulsory ritual. Al-Shaʿrānī’s distinction between the available appropriate performance and self-imposed strain supplies a comparison. Attas’s giving due helps explain why fullness is fittingness, not undifferentiated maximization. al-Shaʿrānī, Mīzān I, PDF/printed pp.98–100; Attas, Concept of Education, PDF pp.10–12.

The household and its material resources are central conditions here. Privacy, water, timing and mutual regard affect performance. The legal question cannot be adequately interpreted through a solitary will alone. At the same time, this passage does not establish the full ethics of sexual relations or the rights within a household; those require the family-law commentary.

U033: circumambulation. Mālik and al-Shāfiʿī require purification; Abū Ḥanīfa is presented as rejecting the condition. The explicit problem is whether ṭawāf receives the ruling of prayer. Its exclusion during menstruation and reports calling it prayer support association; the counterargument notes that fasting too is prohibited during menstruation, yet ablution is not made its condition afterward. A shared exclusion does not prove identity of every further condition. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF p.43, visually checked.

The case therefore teaches a limit upon the project itself: shared symbolism or a shared spiritual end is not sufficient to transfer every legal condition between acts. The exact form of the act and the legitimate route of inference remain decisive.

U034: reciting the Qurʾān. The majority permits recitation without minor ablution; another group does not. The relevant conflict concerns a report of delayed response to a greeting until purification and another saying that only janāba prevented recitation. Ibn Rushd reports abrogation as the majority’s reconciliation and preference for the former report among those requiring ablution. U035: remembrance of God. Dhikr is included alongside recitation, but it must remain distinct from physically touching the muṣḥaf. The legal acts are not interchangeable merely because all concern sacred language. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF p.43.

The formative difference is the range of life in which verbal recollection can continue without a renewed bodily threshold. Under the majority account, ordinary minor ritual events do not close that possibility. This is a direct structural opening of daily activity toward remembrance, even though its full realization depends on attention and intention. Under the restrictive account, preparation is more tightly joined to sacred utterance; its legitimacy rests on the report argument, not simply on its apparent solemnity.

The social relation includes a greeting and its return, not only a solitary devotional exercise. The chapter therefore connects the legal conditions of sacred speech with ordinary encounters. An urban account should attend to how worship, learning, work and interpersonal recognition coexist through a day. It should not identify all sacred activity with the institution of congregational prayer or all public activity with temporal power.

Conditions of realization and the stages of civilization

A primary control on differentiated fullness

A passage in the Muwaṭṭaʾ gives unusually direct support for a disciplined account of differentiated performance. Mālik explains that the person using authorized tayammum in the absence of water has obeyed the command appropriate to that condition; the person using water is not thereby purer, nor the prayer better. Both act according to what is required of them. This belongs to the tayammum discussion and does not certify that every disputed opinion is equally right, but it decisively prevents a general equation of materially fuller performance with superior obedience. .

This is an early primary control for our engagement with al-Shaʿrānī. The common structure is not “everyone chooses what suits them”; it is different warranted requirements under different conditions. The agent gives back in fullness by faithfully inhabiting the requirement, including its recognition of actual capacity. The link to Attas is acknowledgement of one’s proper act and limit. The link to virtue is willing, intelligent performance; the link to civilization is preserving the material and learned conditions under which that performance remains available.

Results and remaining textual work

The case sequence has generated five corrections to the master theory. Legal state is not moral character. An agreed instance does not uniquely determine its general cause. More bodily work is not always more adequate acknowledgement. Public and private relations enter even personal worship. And shared symbolic orientation does not justify transferring a legal condition between different acts.

The most important outstanding checks are the multiple Mālikī reports on touching, the relationship of later school formulations to Ibn Rushd’s compressed attributions, the technical description of the ʿAmr b. Ḥazm reports, and a detailed source control for each authentication or abrogation claim. The text has been read continuously and interpreted; a completed independent critical audit is not claimed.

The next continuous boundary is the Book of Ghusl beginning at Arabic I43. Its opening, acts, causes and further rulings remain to be analyzed in their own right.

Part II.E. Prayer in movement

Revision 10. The study covers eight numbered masāʾil at Arabic I133–140, from raising the hands to iqʿāʾ, ending before congregational prayer. Their subsidiary disagreements are organized into fifteen working groups, not an elementary-rule census. The Arabic page images have been checked. The restored purification and fasting studies retain their outstanding source checks. This revision tightens the legal summaries and commentary without extending coverage.

The inquiry follows a received bodily form into understanding and acknowledgment. Ibn Rushd supplies the disputed rulings and their reasons; Ghazālī distinguishes the powers engaged in their practice. Ibn ʿArabī treats many of the same ritual differences before developing their iʿtibār, or inward interpretation. Similar sequence and wording warrant investigating textual dependence, but do not establish its route or extent. His interpretations retain their own authorship. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.133–140;

Attention and the conditions of practice

Reported setting of . Qurṭubī transmits an account through Ibn Sīrīn linking the verse to the Prophet's upward gaze in prayer, followed by looking toward the place of prostration. A second version concerns Muslims looking around before attending to prayer. Wāḥidī gives a version through Ibn Sīrīn from Abū Hurayra. The witnesses differ in chain and focus; recording them does not complete their transmission audit. As reported occasions, they locate khushūʿ in a correction of attention and comportment. They do not establish the occasion of each disputed hand movement. ; .

The qualities of prayer within a whole life

Setting. Qurṭubī relates to an upward gaze in prayer, and preserves another version about Muslims looking around. Wāḥidī transmits a version through Ibn Sīrīn from Abū Hurayra. The reports concern the correction of gaze and attention.

The passage. begins with the success of believers whose prayer is marked by khushūʿ, reverent attentiveness. The passage continues through avoidance of empty activity, giving, sexual restraint, fidelity to trusts and preservation of prayer, ending with inheritance of Paradise (23:3–11).

Its ethical argument. The opening promise concerns a whole form of life: attentive prayer stands alongside the keeping of promises and the restraint of appetite. The connection is not that a single gesture mechanically produces salvation. Prayer belongs to a pattern of sustained fidelity whose promised good exceeds civic success. This is a reading of the passage’s sequence, not a claim that all the listed qualities are legal conditions of prayer.

What the commentary explains. Ibn ʿĀshūr reads the listed qualities as manifestations of faith rooted in the person; the list is not an exhaustive inventory of virtue. Qurṭubī’s and Wāḥidī’s reports about correcting the direction of the gaze give one bodily setting for attention. Their different transmissions are retained rather than converted into one certain event.

· · · · · ·

Setting. The command to establish prayer occurs within the divine address to Moses. Qushayrī develops an inward interpretation of dependence, remembrance and intimacy from that address.

The passage. Within the address to Moses, moves from “I am God; there is no god but Me” to worship and prayer “for My remembrance.” The next verse announces the Hour and recompense for each person’s striving.

Its ethical argument. Here prayer’s ground is the identity of the One addressed; its orientation is remembrance, and its horizon is accountable action. The person does not first manufacture a sacred achievement and then offer it as self-owned merit. That last formulation is the project’s synthesis, sharpened by Qushayrī’s warning about self-admiration.

What the commentary explains. Ibn ʿĀshūr connects the disclosure of divine identity with the ensuing command. He treats worship as involving heart, speech and action, with prayer gathering these into a maintained practice.

· ·

Durable worship: attention, capacity and the quality of repetition

Text and situation. The reports commend works a person can sustain and describe the household’s persistence in an adopted practice. A neighbouring report concerns a rope used to continue praying after fatigue. Al-Nawawī’s chapter brings habitual night prayer together with moderation. The rope is removed; exhaustion is not made a measure of the practice’s excellence.

What the commentary explains. Al-Nawawī glosses capacity as capacity to continue without harm. He explicitly extends the principle beyond prayer to acts of good generally. His reason is precise: modest continuity sustains obedience, remembrance, watchfulness, intention, sincerity and turning toward the Creator. Excessive strain can produce abandonment or performance without the heart’s openness. He also excludes literal weariness from God and explains the report’s language through the continuance of reward, while recording alternative interpretations.

·

R001. Raising the hands: obligation and relinquishment

Ruling. Raising the hands is sunna according to the majority; Dāwūd and some followers require it, while differing over its occasions. The dispute concerns normative force, not the gesture's value. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.133–134.

Sabab al-ikhtilāf. Reports of prophetic performance are read against the instructional report commanding the opening takbīr without commanding raised hands. The issue is whether performance establishes obligation and whether instructional omission distinguishes the requisite from the supplementary. The omission has force because the report teaches prayer. Its narrative setting—correction after repeated unsuccessful attempts—also grounds an ethical reading centered on teachability. ; .

Encounter and teaching. Abū Hurayra's report places the instruction in a mosque encounter: the man prays, exchanges greetings, repeats the deficient performance and finally asks to be taught. Ibn Ḥajar draws out teaching without harshness, clarification and the learner's acknowledgment of error. He also records different explanations for delayed instruction—allowing self-correction, making the deficiency evident, and increasing receptivity—and an objection to one explanation of the delay. The formative reading thus belongs to a narrated pedagogy with interpretive questions of its own. ; .

Nawawī records several proposed wisdoms: magnification and imitation of the Prophet, surrender, recognition of entry into prayer, and setting worldly affairs aside so that body and takbīr agree. He questions most of these explanations. They document interpretations, not a prophetic declaration of the gesture's hidden cause. His consensus language must also be read alongside Dāwūd's reported dissent. .

For Ibn ʿArabī, raised hands signify coming before God without possessions or an independent claim to power. Renewal of the gesture relinquishes even the gifts just received in prayer. The movement is from grasping to receptivity, and from receptivity to gratitude without appropriation. Setting concerns aside thus extends to attachment to one's own spiritual attainments.

Spiritual importance and legal obligation remain distinct. Relinquishing possessiveness also differs from neglecting debts or dependents: empty-handedness before God can deepen acknowledgment of what is owed to others. This connects the gesture to trusts and family maintenance. Teaching can join form to intention, but cannot use visible performance to rank inward realization. Legal warrant, report reliability and the fruit of practice require separate judgments.

Uṣūl. The Ḍarūrī asks what a prophetic act establishes and how an explanatory act relates to an utterance. Here that question meets a report specifically teaching prayer. Ibn ʿArabī supplies an inward reading of the resulting practice; he does not replace the argument that determines whether it is required.

R002. Repeated raising and renewed acknowledgment

Positions. Opening only: Abū Ḥanīfa, al-Thawrī and the Kufan line, with Ibn al-Qāsim's transmission from Mālik. Opening, before bowing and on rising: al-Shāfiʿī, Aḥmad, Abū ʿUbayd, Abū Thawr, many traditionists and the Ẓāhirīs; also a transmission from Mālik recommending these occasions. Some traditionists add prostration. The Mālikī transmissions must remain distinct. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.133–134.

Sabab. Divergent reports and their relation to Medinan practice. Ibn Masʿūd and al-Barāʾ support opening only; Ibn ʿUmar supports three occasions and excludes prostration; Wāʾil's report adds occasions. Ibn Rushd distinguishes tarjīḥ, evidential preference, from jamʿ, reconciliation. He calls Ibn ʿUmar's report sound and gives weight to its wide transmission, without equally authenticating its rivals. Bukhārī 735 confirms the three occasions and exclusion of prostration. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.134; .

Ibn ʿArabī interprets repetition as renewed need: each stage gives something, and each raising relinquishes possession of the received state. His legal discussion also reports a dream prescribing the opening, bowing and rising, while separately arguing from public reports and reliable additions for the transmitted occasions more broadly. The dream is his experiential claim; the report arguments remain available to other jurists.

An initial gesture can establish an orientation; repetition can recall it when attention disperses. This is our formative comparison, not an attribution of motive to the schools or a measure of realization by frequency. Teaching a definite practice while accurately representing alternatives can cultivate proportion. Its failure reverses the gesture's meaning: relinquishment becomes a claim to superiority. Several practices may have serious transmitted arguments without those arguments being equally strong.

Uṣūl. Report comparison must precede the interpretation of repetition. Jamʿ supplies a later control on treating inspiration as public proof; it is not evidence that Ibn ʿArabī used this later taxonomy. A possible formative benefit does not make every report or conclusion correct.

R003. The height of the hands and coordination of form

Positions and assessment. Shoulders: Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī and others; ears: Abū Ḥanīfa; chest: some jurists. Each rests on a report. Ibn Rushd ranks the shoulder report above the ear report, and the latter above the chest report. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.134.

The teaching problem is how reported descriptions become a reproducible movement. Nawawī reconciles them by aligning fingertips with the upper ears, thumbs with the earlobes and palms with the shoulders. Ibn ʿArabī proposes movement through chest and shoulders toward the ears. One coordinates bodily parts at a single position; the other coordinates successive positions. They remain distinct reconciliations. ;

Ibn ʿArabī relates chest level to facing the divine presence and ear level to divine elevation, citing God's being above His servants. These interpret orientation, not a causal relation between physical height and spiritual attainment. Our formative reading concerns coordination: intention, movement and magnification can become one deliberate act. Instruction can refine this coordination, though bodily accuracy alone does not establish attention.

Uṣūl. The evidential ranking here belongs to the actual reports in Bidāya. The Ḍarūrī is a methodological comparison about unequal indications, not a substitute grading of these reports. Reconciliation must specify exactly what each description describes.

R004. Settling in bowing and standing

Positions. Ibn Rushd attributes non-obligation of the disputed settling or straightening to Abū Ḥanīfa, obligation to al-Shāfiʿī, and uncertainty to Mālik's followers in the absence of an explicit transmitted position. The Ḥanafī attribution requires control against the later distinctions among farḍ, wājib and deficiency before generalization to school doctrine. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.135.

Sabab and assessment. Does partial fulfillment of the act's named content suffice, or is its fuller content required? Ibn Rushd resolves the issue through the instructional report commanding settled bowing and an upright return, affirming obligation. He also requires consistency from those who use this report to distinguish obligatory from supplementary acts. The case tests an inferential policy as well as the scope of an act-name. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.135; .

Ibn ʿArabī understands stillness as allowing reception of the knowledge disclosed in a state. Hastening to good and remaining within it are complementary: readiness brings one into the act; abiding allows its fulfillment. Ghazālī joins bowing to humility, magnification and repeated attention, then rising to hope and gratitude. The first account emphasizes receptivity to disclosure; the second develops understanding and affect. .

Uṣūl. The command in the teaching report limits the appeal to minimal naming. The comparative account explains why remaining can matter for formation; it does not derive the legal requirement from a psychological preference for slowness.

R005. Seated postures and permissible alternatives

Positions and sabab. Mālik: buttocks on the ground, right foot upright and left leg bent, for men and women. Abū Ḥanīfa: sitting on the left foot, right foot upright. Al-Shāfiʿī: the latter posture for the intermediate sitting, the former for the final sitting. Divergent reports include those of Abū Ḥumayd, Wāʾil and Ibn ʿUmar. Mālik and Abū Ḥanīfa prefer different reports; al-Shāfiʿī reconciles them by distinguishing occasions. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.135–136.

Assessment. Al-Ṭabarī accepts the transmitted forms as alternatives; Ibn Rushd approves. Different acts more readily admit choice than contradiction, which arises especially between statements or between a statement and an act. This is a specific criterion for plurality, not a general dissolution of conflicting legal judgments. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.136.

Ibn ʿArabī begins with the servant permitted to sit before the master. The intermediate seat retains readiness to stand; the final seat turns reflection toward one's dependent being. The sequence relates movement and rest to knowledge. It does not establish why the jurists selected their reports.

The formative possibility is responsive stillness: rest without withdrawal from duty, readiness without restless anticipation. Recognized alternatives also require proportion in teaching; difference from the teacher's practice need not be error. This bears on common worship and transmission in a diverse city, although any historical reduction of conflict remains to be demonstrated. Several ways of fulfilling an act must still be distinguished from rival judgments about what is true.

Uṣūl. Ibn Rushd himself offers the choice-versus-contradiction distinction. The inward interpretation may illuminate the alternatives, but the permission rests on the transmitted acts and the way their indications are read.

R006. The sittings: status, omission and repair

Positions and sabab. Most regard the intermediate sitting as sunna and the final sitting as obligatory. Others require both or treat both as sunna. The disagreement concerns the instructional report, prophetic performance and analogy between the sittings. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.136–137.

Assessment. In Ibn Buḥayna's report the omitted middle sitting is compensated by prostrations; an omitted rakʿa is elsewhere supplied. One argument infers different status from different remedies; another treats compensation as a special rule compatible with obligation. The view requiring both sittings follows a general presumption about prophetic acts. Ibn Rushd considers the view making both sunna weakest. The remedy's significance is itself disputed. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.136–137.

Ghazālī reads sitting and testimony through adab: praise, good conduct and sovereignty are acknowledged as God's; the Prophet is greeted, righteous servants remembered, testimony renewed and others included in supplication. Collected attention thus opens into relationship. .

Ibn ʿArabī treats the intermediate seat as an interruption within unfinished movement. His account of pairs, servant and Lord distinguishes the divine essence's independence from relations implied by willing and power toward a world. The numbers belong to that argument and cannot be reduced to a generic symbolism of balance. This comparison preserves the distinction; a full reconstruction of its ontology and any derivation of prayer's numbers remain beyond the present reading.

Repair does not always require repetition. Learning to continue after an omission, while taking its remedy seriously, may cultivate steadiness and teachable humility. That formative possibility neither selects the proper remedy without the reports nor establishes its historical effect on a community.

Uṣūl. The analogy between the two seats is contested, and the different treatment of omission supplies counterevidence. No general maxim of repair can erase the distinction between supplying an omitted component and compensating for an omission.

R007. Pointing and the coordination of attention

Ruling and sabab. Ibn Rushd reports approval of placing the hands on the knees and pointing with the finger. Movement is disputed because the reports differ; he considers pointing alone established. Independent comparison of the movement reports remains open. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.137.

Ghazālī's account locates the gesture within renewed acknowledgment of divine unity and Muhammad's messengership. It provides a setting in which speech, attention and gesture can agree, but does not assign a metaphysical operation to each speed, direction or frequency of movement. The Futūḥāt pages checked here provide no separate interpretation of finger motion. .

Uṣūl. The public evidence concerns reported acts and their reliability. The testimony’s meaning can illuminate the gesture’s setting, but cannot decide the contested movement report.

R008. Folded hands: support and expressed humility

Positions and sabab. Ibn Rushd reports that Mālik dislikes folded hands in obligatory prayer and permits them in voluntary prayer; the majority counts the gesture among the sunan. This is the passage's transmission, not a complete account of Mālikī practice. Reports mentioning the gesture compete with descriptions omitting it, raising the question of accepting an addition. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.137.

Interpretation and assessment. The act may be understood as support during prolonged standing or as devotional expression. The former helps explain different treatment in obligatory and voluntary prayer. Ibn Rushd prefers khudūʿ, humility or submission. Ethical meaning thus enters the identification of the practical act within juristic reasoning, alongside the reports. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.137.

Ibn ʿArabī relates posture to the address received: a verse calls for asking, magnification, joy or humility. He extends this responsiveness to folding or releasing the hands and favors latitude. Meaning, affect and body are joined, but his position can stand in tension with settled school instruction. It does not confer a general authority to reshape prescribed acts according to feeling.

The formative aim is agreement between recognition, speech and posture. Its failure is performed submission that leaves pride intact. A visible gesture may also become a group badge, turning a form of humility into self-assertion; this is a historical hypothesis to test. The case returns a precise lesson to the framework: identifying an act's meaning may be necessary to identifying the legal dispute itself.

Uṣūl. Ibn Rushd explicitly compares two understandings of the act. Ibn ʿArabī then provides a distinct account of responsive comportment. Keeping those stages separate allows ethical meaning to matter without turning private feeling into a new public rule.

R009. The resting seat and collected transition

Positions and sabab. Al-Shāfiʿī and a group favor a brief sitting after an odd-numbered rakʿa; Mālik and a group favor rising directly. Mālik ibn al-Ḥuwayrith reports settling before rising, whereas Abū Ḥumayd describes a direct rise from the second prostration. The dispute concerns the implications of these descriptions. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.137–138.

Ibn ʿArabī connects sitting and rising to the invitation received in prayer. His nearby interpretation of the seat between prostrations concerns a different sitting and must remain distinct. The associated discussion of divine descent and the names al-Raḥmān and al-Rabb belongs to his theology of disclosure, rather than bodily change in God.

Our comparison concerns continuity and a collected transition. A pause may gather attention or become empty delay; prompt rising may express readiness or impatience. Teaching must transmit the form and cultivate attention within it. Bodily capacity and comfort matter to application, but the passages establish neither a complete doctrine of disability concessions nor an explanation of the original report by the Prophet's age.

The proposed alchemical operation is gathering before renewed action. It cannot decide between reports by declaring one movement more integrated. Its civic relevance lies in competent instruction and shared rhythm; a separate contribution to state formation remains unestablished.

Uṣūl. Different descriptions of an act invite comparison or reconciliation. Capacity is a separate inquiry, not an assumed historical explanation of why the Prophet paused. A proposed spiritual meaning does not fill that evidential gap.

R010. Order of descent: trust and generosity

Positions and sabab. The supplied Arabic Bidāya attributes knees-first to Mālik. Wāʾil's report gives knees before hands; Abū Hurayra's warns against camel-like descent and directs hands before knees; Ibn ʿUmar is also reported to put hands first. Some traditionists prefer Wāʾil. The stated cause is divergent reports. The Mālik attribution is verified on the scan, not merely OCR, but requires another edition and Mālikī controls before generalization. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.138.

Ibn ʿArabī interprets knees through reliance and hands through power and giving. One person begins with trust while retaining the capacity to act; another gives despite attachment, anxiety and fear of poverty. He compares the latter with charity before private consultation in . The verse supports his inward comparison, not Ibn Rushd's legal argument about limb order.

The consultation verse used in the inward comparison

Setting. The Study Quran records the explanation that wealthy visitors monopolized private conversation with the Prophet, excluding poorer members. It retains reports about ʿAlī’s application and differing accounts of the duration before the command was lifted.

The passage. joins private consultation to prior charity, calls this better and purer, and exempts those unable to give under divine forgiveness and mercy. relaxes the command, calls attention to reluctance to give, and redirects the community to prayer, zakāt and obedience under divine knowledge.

Its ethical argument. A claim on the Prophet’s time is placed in relation to another person’s need. Cost exposes whether access is being pursued casually or for prestige, while inability is not treated as exclusion from mercy. The relaxation preserves the larger demand for acknowledged obedience.

What the commentary explains. The Study Quran presents the social problem as unequal access to counsel and explains the subsequent command through continuing prayer and giving. Its chronology and personal occasion reports remain mediated. In the prayer chapter Ibn ʿArabī uses the verse as a comparison for giving before intimate address; that spiritual application must remain distinct from the verse’s reported consultation setting. The text is not a direct proof of an order for placing hands and knees on the ground.

· ·

These beginnings can converge: trust enables generosity, and giving despite fear teaches trust. Ibn ʿArabī says that the second state is acquired in prostration whichever comes first. This is his spiritual claim, not a guarantee about every performance. He also prefers hands-first on legal grounds; recognition of two fruitful paths does not suspend that judgment.

The alchemical account identifies a starting condition—fearful attachment or claimed self-sufficiency—an action, a developing disposition and its relation to another virtue. Formation is reciprocal: trust enables giving, while giving changes the capacity to trust. Ghazālī's tongue that first teaches and later expresses the heart supplies a parallel in another practice. .

Generosity under material uncertainty is explicit in Ibn ʿArabī's comparison. It does not establish greater generosity among communities following one posture. A historical inquiry would instead examine teaching, economic security and actual giving as conditions of formation. The inward path, the ritual evidence and the social effect remain distinct claims.

Uṣūl. Report evaluation determines the legal argument; the intention maxim is a later comparative aid for distinguishing what an action means to its agent. Ibn ʿArabī supplies an explicit two-way relation between giving and trust, not evidence for a stable spiritual personality of each school.

R011. Seven points and the integrity of the act

Ruling and sabab. Face, hands, knees and toe-ends together fulfill the agreed form. Omission of a point other than the face is disputed: does the act-name suffice, or must all seven points in the report be present? Ibn Rushd identifies a part–whole problem concerning fulfillment of the command's named content. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.138–139.

A practical act has an organized whole. In the adjacent face discussion, Ibn Rushd refuses to infer from partial sufficiency that contact as small as a mustard seed must suffice. The relevant kind of part must be identified. The same analytical demand applies to social acts with several conditions. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.139.

Ibn ʿArabī interprets the seven through life, knowledge, will, power, speech, hearing and sight. Their relation matters: treating hearing and sight as particular relations of knowledge changes the account of completeness. The face's indispensability is compared with life as a condition of the other attributes. He further distinguishes the divine essence from relations under which God is called creator and cause. These comparisons concern attributes and relations, not a bodily composition of the divine.

Our formative reading concerns gathering the powers into one dependent activity: knowing, willing and acting are offered without claiming them as autonomous possessions. The possible virtue is integrity; its failure is confusing visible completeness with integrated intention. Instruction coordinates complex action, and distinguishing essentials from further completion matters across learned crafts. Historical effects on civic character remain hypothetical. Legal fulfillment and metaphysical wholeness illuminate one another without the numerical comparison deciding the ruling.

Uṣūl. The report specifies the bodily form, while the juristic dispute concerns the force and scope of that specification. The seven-attribute interpretation is Ibn ʿArabī’s comparison; it cannot resolve the part–whole question by numerical correspondence.

R012. Forehead and nose: honor and humility

Positions and sabab. Forehead and nose together suffice by agreement. Mālik accepts forehead without nose, not nose without forehead; Abū Ḥanīfa accepts either; al-Shāfiʿī requires both. The dispute concerns the content of “face,” its required extent and reports explaining the instruction. Ibn Rushd takes Muslim's forehead-only wording, among variant wordings, to support Mālik. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.138–139.

Ghazālī begins with the honored face touching earth. He reads this as humility and the branch's return to its origin: the human being comes from earth and returns to it. Speech and repetition deepen the acknowledgment. His preference for direct contact where possible concerns cultivation of humility; it does not alone decide validity through a barrier. .

Ibn ʿArabī continues the comparison of face with life and the divine attributes, relating the nose to dignity and breath. His anatomical explanation belongs to the premodern account and is not independently verified as contemporary anatomy. Different aspects of one form support different readings; the passage does not establish a universal symbolic code.

The proposed transformation reorders honor through acknowledgment of dependence, preserving human dignity and responsibility. Devotional humility therefore differs from submission to arbitrary human power. The posture gives humility a bodily exercise, but cannot establish social justice or furnish a complete judgment of character. Bodily exactness and moral interpretation each disclose something the other alone cannot measure.

Uṣūl. The question is which bodily performance fulfills the report. Ghazālī explains a possible meaning and exercise of humility, while Ibn ʿArabī interprets the face through a separate metaphysical vocabulary. Neither makes the disputed legal minimum disappear.

R013. Uncovered hands and the conditions of completion

Positions. Ibn Rushd reports from Mālik a condition that the hands be uncovered and placed on the face's surface of prostration, adding that he thinks it concerns completion. A group does not require it. His qualification leaves the distinction between full performance and validity unresolved; it must not be hardened into a condition of validity. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.139.

Argument. Against the requirement stand the report of seven points and the prohibition on gathering clothing or hair, with analogies to covered knees and prayer in footwear. The relevant question is which contacts require directness and what warrants the comparison. General reverence does not decide among these analogies. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.139.

Bodily immediacy may have formative value, but the passages collated here establish no author-specific inward meaning for bare palms. Ghazālī's preference for facial contact with earth cannot simply be extended to every limb. Clothing's mediation has different meanings within the same practice; material covering alone does not establish spiritual obstruction.

Teaching, climate and clothing belong to the conditions of practice, though their effect on a ruling requires further evidence. Here proportion and intellectual honesty chiefly govern the interpreter: retain the qualified judgment and resist converting symbolic plausibility into obligation. Fullness must be specified for the act; it does not invariably mean greater exposure, effort or sensory immediacy.

Uṣūl. The analogy must explain why a covered knee or footwear is relevant to the hand. Ibn Rushd’s own hesitation over “condition” remains part of the finding; the later framework must not harden it into a certainty.

R014. Turban layers, mediation and direct contact

Positions. The passage announces three positions on prostrating through a turban but lists four: prohibition, permission, few versus many layers, and some forehead contact versus none. It places the differences within the school and among regional jurists. All four formulations and the numerical mismatch are retained. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.139.

Argument. Reported practice with head coverings is considered alongside a possible extension of the prohibition on gathering clothing or hair. Ibn Rushd offers the latter as an available argument, not necessarily his verdict or every position's rationale. The distinctions differ in kind: thickness concerns degree of mediation; partial contact concerns the presence of direct contact. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.139.

Ghazālī's preference for earth contact gives it a place in spiritual training without making every mediated form invalid. Personal discipline and a community's sufficient form can differ: what assists one learner need not be universally requisite. Legal permission still needs its own evidence. .

The alchemical question is what obstructs the act. Fabric, pride and distraction are different objects, though each may be called a veil in its own discourse. Clothing and material resources condition practice without establishing a class hierarchy of worshippers. The case develops distinctions of degree, threshold and partial presence; it does not divide schools into material and spiritual types.

Uṣūl. The possible extension of general wording must retain its stated uncertainty. The variants distinguish degree of mediation from the presence of direct contact. A spiritual preference for earth contact is not itself the specifying evidence for a prohibition.

R015. Iqʿāʾ: identifying the object of judgment

Positions and object. Ibn Rushd reports disapproval of iqʿāʾ, then distinguishes its referents: sitting on the buttocks with raised legs, as in the animal comparison; or sitting on the heels between prostrations. The latter reading of the prohibition is associated with Mālik and Ibn ʿUmar's reported discomfort, while Ibn ʿAbbās calls heel-sitting sunna. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.139–140.

Sabab and assessment. Ordinary linguistic meaning conflicts with an alleged prescribed technical meaning. Ibn Rushd retains ordinary usage until the technical usage is established; once established, the latter takes priority absent contrary evidence. Ibn ʿAbbās's report is substantive counterevidence. Disapproval of the name cannot settle which posture receives the ruling. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.140.

Nawawī distinguishes the postures and judges the particular prohibition reports he enumerates weak. He defends heel-sitting as Ibn ʿAbbās's intended practice. His Shāfiʿī account recognizes both heel-sitting and sitting on the left foot, while discussing preference. These later assessments do not authenticate all the reports in Bidāya. .

Ibn ʿArabī states a similar principle of ordinary and prescribed usage. His inward reading distinguishes the transmitted posture from the animal resemblance and develops alertness to the next call. Poised readiness joins receptivity to prompt action. It complements stillness: remaining with the present act and becoming ready for the next are different, compatible skills.

The civic implication concerns judgment itself. Teachers and jurists must identify the actual posture before applying an inherited name and ruling. This intellectual justice can prevent misplaced correction, humiliation and conflict. Institutions may amplify careful teaching or standardized misdescription; the need belongs to no single urban stage. Knowing a rule's name, identifying its object and mastering its performance remain distinct attainments.

Uṣūl. Clarify the word’s established meaning before assessing the actual posture. Ghazālī’s account of applying a known criterion is a later analytical comparison here: it follows the semantic inquiry and cannot replace it.

Practical meaning, plurality and formation

The eight masāʾil make at least four demands on the philosophy of law. First, a bodily act has several kinds of meaning: what counts as performing it, what the evidence requires, what its agent intends, and what a spiritual commentator sees in it. Second, plurality takes several forms: uncertain reports, alternative acts, differing rules of inference, and distinct inward paths are not interchangeable. Third, formation can move in both directions: trust can lead to giving, and giving can cultivate trust; speech can teach the heart before it expresses the heart. Fourth, humility is sometimes part of the jurist's interpretation of the practical object itself, as Ibn Rushd's folded-hands discussion shows. Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF pp.135–140; .

In this chapter “alchemy” therefore names changes that can actually be described: loosening possessiveness, collecting dispersed attention, remaining with a received meaning, joining feeling and action, learning one virtue through another, and returning from prayer with a clearer sense of what is owed. The word should not conceal the conditions: instruction, effort, repetition, correction and grace as these authors understand it. The same forms can become occasions for display, rivalry or distraction. Nor does their beneficial use exhaust their orientation toward God.

Evidence and outstanding checks

The source boundary and all eight numbered questions have been read on Arabic I133–140. The fifteen groups preserve the subsidiary discussions identified here, including finger motion, exposed hands and turban layers. This is a completed first interpretive pass through that bounded chapter, not an independently audited census of every attributed proposition. The Mālik attribution for knees-first, the three/four turban mismatch, the scope of the settling attribution to Abū Ḥanīfa, and the competing movement and prostration reports remain explicit tasks.

The Futūḥāt extract preserves Maymaniyya I437–442. Its page numbers differ from the complete acquired text's edition; the two witnesses are linked by wording, not by an assumed page offset. The raised-hands, sitting, folded-hands, descent and seven-point passages have been collated to their images; the iqʿāʾ continuation also has a saved text locator. Nawawī, Ghazālī and the two tafsīrs are cited to exact local text lines and their electronic markers. Their selected Arabic passages have been read, but those editions have not all received page-image collation. A quoted narrative or report inside a commentary retains its own authentication question.

Next come the earlier prayer sections on times, conditions and recitation, the congregational questions beginning on I140, and a systematic reconstruction of bathing, tayammum, fasting and pilgrimage. Existing purification and expiation notes remain main-text working studies and will receive this same scripture/commentary audit. Full worship coverage remains a research obligation, not an achievement inferred from restoring those notes.

Part II.F. Fasting and expiation

Main worship commentary, under reconstruction. Restored in revision 9 under the expanded whole-work brief. The existing arguments and source problems are retained. Their verse, hadith and spiritual-commentary audits remain incomplete; the new standard is explained in the worship introduction.

Detailed commentary on Bidāya I, printed/PDF pp.301–307, from intentional violation through the conclusion of obligatory fasting. The opening discussion of pregnancy, nursing and old age on p.301 belongs to the preceding section and is not claimed as covered here. The commentary identifies F001–F018 as working question-units; agreements and subsidiary positions within each remain separately described. It does not replace the still-needed commentary on the earlier fasting chapters.

Why this passage changes the master argument

This passage supplies an unusually direct link between particular fiqh, practical psychology, virtue and the purpose of the law. In explaining why some analogical jurists confine a severe expiation to intercourse, Ibn Rushd reports an argument about the unequal strength of desire: more severe restraint may attach to an especially compelling appetite even when different violations are comparable in another respect. The purpose stated in the discussion is that people adhere to the laws and become akhyār ʿudūl, good and upright or just. He then invokes the Qurʾānic purpose of fasting, taqwā. This is primary evidence of a formative account within the explanation of a disagreement. It does not establish that Ibn Rushd endorses every step of that particular argument or that deterrence exhausts the meaning of fasting. Bidāya, Arabic I, p.303; B1E, PDF pp.336–337, printed pp.354–355.

The following pages also prevent “alchemy” from becoming a single theory of punishment. Expiation is compared with deterrent penalties, but an opposing argument insists that it also contains a kind of qurbah, an act of drawing near. The same legal object is therefore analyzed through corrective restraint, renewed worship, material provision for others, temporal repair and responsibility before God. These aspects can lead to different conclusions about how many expiations are owed. Bidāya, Arabic I, p.306.

The movement upward is consequently exact: what expiation is helps determine how liability is individuated; the particular rulings then test whether the proposed account of expiation was adequate. This is a working example of universal practical knowledge, instrumental inference and particular practical science interacting. It is not a metaphysical image attached after the legal reasoning has finished.

What the fast trains before we ask how a violation is repaired

Ghazālī's three degrees distinguish abstention from intake and intercourse, the restraint of the senses and limbs from wrongdoing, and the heart's collected orientation. The first is not meaningless; it provides a definite practice within which deeper restraint can be learned. The second reaches into speech, hearing, sight and conduct, making fasting a discipline of relations as well as appetite. His criticism of unlawful food and compensatory overeating gives two concrete failure mechanisms: a person may withhold what is permitted while continuing what is harmful, or merely postpone excess until night. .

His language about inwardly breaking a fast should not be transferred without argument to the jurists' rules about replacement and expiation. He distinguishes their inquiry into sufficiency from acceptance as reaching the intended end, and develops non-spatial nearness through transformed qualities. This makes the later repair cases more demanding to interpret: legal discharge can be complete while appetite remains untrained; inward remorse does not by itself tell us which outward remedy is owed. His vivid subsidiary reports retain separate transmission questions. .

The resulting alchemical account distinguishes restraint, exposure of attachment, re-education of desire, repair of a violated duty and assistance to others. The sequence can turn back on itself: outward repair may become self-satisfaction, severity may become pride, and relief may be accepted without renewed obedience. These are possible failures to test, not hidden accusations about a person using a lawful concession. Al-Mustaṣfā's treatment of the Ramadan report remains decisive for the legal extension: obvious incidental details can be removed, but extending intercourse to other violations is disputed. Spiritual resemblance alone does not perform that legal work. .

The reported encounter and the argument about relief

Setting. addresses fasting and concessions. In the Salman–Abū al-Dardāʾ encounter discussed by Ibn Ḥajar, a wife’s neglected circumstances, hospitality, food, sleep and night prayer are brought into one deliberation.

The passage. gives fasting’s orientation as “so that you may acquire taqwā.” sets it within the month of revelation and joins completion of the prescribed days with ease, magnifying God for guidance and gratitude.

Its ethical argument. The passage binds self-restraint to guidance received, not to the amount of deprivation one can endure. Its concessions make faithful completion possible. In the related Salman narrative, care for wife, body and guest limits the pursuit of additional fasting and night prayer: greater intensity is not automatically greater fidelity.

What the commentary explains. Ibn ʿĀshūr situates the prescribed fast among already known practices of fasting. Ibn Ḥajar’s explanation of Salman’s intervention is more pointed than a generic appeal to moderation: a recommended act may be discouraged when exhaustion or neglect of a weightier claim follows. The wife’s circumstances and the body’s needs are part of the practical judgment.

· · ·

Setting. In Muslim1111 a man reports intercourse during the Ramadan fast. He cannot undertake the successive remedies; when dates are provided, he explains that his household is itself exceptionally poor, and he is told to feed it.

The passage. The encounter moves from acknowledged wrongdoing through questions about actual capacity to immediate provision for dependants. The narrated relief does not by itself answer every later question about continuing liability.

Its ethical argument. Correction must encounter the person and those dependent on him. The family’s hunger is not erased by his violation. A humane response can preserve responsibility while giving urgent need priority; whether it also extinguishes the expiation is precisely what remains disputed.

What the commentary explains. Nawawī records two Shāfiʿī positions on inability and prefers continuing liability: feeding the family addresses an immediate necessity, while the expiation remains a deferred obligation. He argues that the provision of dates itself supports the obligation’s persistence. The opposing reading treats the absence of an explicit renewed demand as significant. His discussion also preserves the relation between ordered remedies and textual variants. This account must stand beside Ibn Rushd’s school differences, especially Mālik’s preference for feeding, rather than be presented as a universally agreed meaning of mercy.

·

F001. The basic liability: replacement, expiation, or both?

What happens, and what the sources require. For intentional intercourse during Ramadan, Ibn Rushd reports the majority’s combination of qaḍāʾ and kaffārah. He sets out the report in which a man acknowledges his act, is questioned about manumission, two consecutive months of fasting and feeding sixty needy persons, and ultimately receives food that he is allowed to give his own needy household. He also records two outlying positions: replacement alone and expiation alone. For the first, he proposes possible explanations, including lack of access to the report or reading its direction as not categorically binding. For the second, he identifies the absence of qaḍāʾ from this report and the problem of extending scriptural replacement provisions for excused persons to deliberate violators. His conjectures about why an unnamed group held a view must remain conjectures. Bidāya, Arabic I, pp.301–302; B1E, PDF pp.335–336, printed pp.353–354.

What kind of act is this? Qaḍāʾ answers the question of an unperformed or spoiled duty; kaffārah answers a further question arising from violation. Treating them as separate obligations refuses to reduce repair either to repeating the original act or to paying a penalty. Conversely, the outlying positions expose the need for a warrant for each obligation. A desirable moral result cannot supply a missing command by itself. The word “debt” is therefore illuminating only if we specify what is owed, why, by whom and through which recognized form of discharge.

Attas’s recognition/acknowledgement distinction is particularly apt here: recognizing the norm is not yet giving it its due in one’s own conduct. “Giving back in fullness” can mean the finite person’s actual undertaking of what is due, rather than claiming to repay the source of existence as an equal creditor. This is a comparison with Attas, not an explanation Ibn Rushd supplies in this paragraph. Attas, Prolegomena, PDF pp.27–29, printed pp.41–46; Attas, Concept of Education, PDF pp.10–12.

Persons other than the offender. The household at the end of the report is indispensable. Need is not erased by culpability. The report’s movement from admission to an allocation of food makes it impossible to describe the entire encounter as maximizing pain. The legal question of continuing liability is still disputed later; compassion in the narrative must not be silently converted into a universal rule cancelling every poor person’s obligation.

What this changes in the larger argument. Legal repair has plural objects. The master framework must distinguish discharge of duty, response to culpability, restoration of practice and assistance to others before calling all of them “purification.”

F002. Extending expiation to intentional eating and drinking

Positions and sabab. Mālik and his followers, Abū Ḥanīfa and his followers, al-Thawrī and others extend qaḍāʾ and this expiation to intentional eating and drinking. Al-Shāfiʿī, Aḥmad and the literalists restrict this expiation to intercourse. The explicit cause is whether the first cases can be assimilated to the reported case. One reasoning identifies the shared violation of the fast’s sanctity. Another recognizes that shared feature but treats the stronger attraction of intercourse as relevant to the severity of the remedy. Rejection of analogy supplies a third route to restriction. The same restrictive result therefore has at least two different inferential explanations. Bidāya, Arabic I, pp.302–303.

What the competing rules make salient. Extension foregrounds the common normative object: a sacred fast deliberately violated. Restriction by practical psychology foregrounds the relation between a specific appetite and an appropriately forceful response. Literalist restriction foregrounds the authorized reach of the transmitted determination. These are not three degrees of devotion. Nor is the restrictive position necessarily “lenient” in its account of intercourse: it can assign that act distinctive gravity or distinctive remedial need.

Juristic craft. Ibn Rushd then rejects a simple argument from a report saying merely that a man “broke his fast.” Its unelaborated description is not automatically a universal proposition embracing every mode of violation. He nevertheless notes that the narrator’s choice of description may indicate how the narrator understood the event. This discriminates the report’s legal generality from an inference about its transmitter’s understanding. The Muwaṭṭaʾ’s report 818 allows this wording to be checked directly in the supplied translation. Bidāya, Arabic I, p.303; .

F003–F004. Forgetfulness and mistaken sunset

F003: positions. For intercourse while forgetting the fast, Abū Ḥanīfa and al-Shāfiʿī are reported as requiring neither qaḍāʾ nor expiation; Mālik requires qaḍāʾ without expiation; Aḥmad and the literalists require both. Ibn Rushd separates the arguments about replacement from those about punitive liability. The first dispute opposes analogy with forgotten prayer to reports excusing forgotten eating and drinking and the broader removal of liability for error, forgetfulness and coercion. Bidāya, Arabic I, pp.303–304.

The ontology is the relation between an objective interruption and the agent’s awareness. A rule can recognize that an act did not instantiate the prescribed performance while denying culpability; that is the conceptual space occupied by replacement without expiation. Another can treat the relevant excuse as preserving the fast’s legal sufficiency. A third can attach both consequences, but Ibn Rushd expressly criticizes punitive liability in forgetfulness and challenges the use of an unelaborated narrative to establish it. An exhaustive account must preserve his adverse judgment. Perspectival differentiation is not a ban on calling an argument weak.
