F004: a mistaken belief that the sun has set. Ibn Rushd relates this to the category of error and therefore to the forgetting problem. The brief comparison does not provide an independently exhaustive list of school positions on sunset; it must be linked to the earlier fasting discussion before that list is certified. The example distinguishes sincere factual judgment from deliberate disregard. Bidāya, Arabic I, pp.303–304.

The important methodological passage. Ibn Rushd argues that the lack of detail is ours, not a defect in the Lawgiver’s concrete judgment. He contests the principle that failure to distinguish circumstances in a report should always be treated as generality. He also argues that a new obligation of replacement requires its own warrant and criticizes inconsistency across analogically related cases. This is a direct limit on inference from finite access to a singular event. It parallels our use of Mūsā–Khiḍr as an epistemic boundary without turning the story into a legal proof for these rulings. Bidāya, Arabic I, p.304.

What this changes in the larger argument. Normative formation must include a theory of excusable failure. An “alchemy” that interprets every burden as beneficial simply because it is heavier cannot accommodate Ibn Rushd’s criticism here.

F005. The woman’s separate liability when she participates voluntarily

The Arabic asks about the woman who ṭāwaʿathu, voluntarily participates; its earlier list distinguishes her from one coerced. Abū Ḥanīfa and Mālik and their followers impose expiation; al-Shāfiʿī and Dāwūd do not. The explicit cause is conflict between the report’s not commanding her to expiate and analogy from both persons being legally accountable. The English phrase “coaxed into” should not obscure the operative distinction between voluntary participation and coercion. Bidāya, Arabic I, pp.302, 304; B1E, PDF p.339, printed p.357.

The extension position treats her as a distinct responsible agent, not merely part of the man’s transgression. The restrictive position cannot on this evidence be interpreted as denying her moral agency; it contests the proof of this additional obligation. Moral responsibility, the existence of a specific expiation, and the transmission of an instruction to a named questioner remain different matters.

For virtue, the issue concerns the first-person appropriation of responsibility within an intimate relation. For justice, it concerns whether each participant bears an independently warranted burden. For social development, it prevents the household from being treated as a single undifferentiated moral person. It also exposes the need to keep coercion separate: a theory of marital or civic unity must not erase the agency and vulnerability of an individual member.

The institutional task is therefore qualified personal advice and a faithful account of the actual circumstances. Nothing in the passage makes a ruler the arbiter of another person’s unexpressed intention. Across dynastic conditions, the relevant risks are household coercion, elite impunity and inaccessible counsel, rather than a unique “stage” to which this rule belongs. The vertical relation is each person’s accountability before God; it is not evidence that a jurist knows the inward acceptance of either participant’s act.

F006–F007. Ordered remedies, choice and Mālik’s preference for feeding

F006: the legal alternatives. Ibn Rushd defines order as inability to move to a later remedy until unable to perform the preceding one; choice permits an alternative from the outset. Al-Shāfiʿī, Abū Ḥanīfa, al-Thawrī and the Kufans are presented as requiring manumission, then fasting if unable, then feeding if unable. Mālik permits choice. The explicit causes are differently worded reports and analogies with expiation for ẓihār or for an oath. The sequential questions in one narrative support order; the connective aw in the other supports choice. The competent narrator’s understanding of circumstances and expressions is itself relevant evidence. Bidāya, Arabic I, pp.304–305; B1E, PDF p.339, printed p.357; .

Textual correction requiring disclosure. The supplied Arabic p.305 actually prints ghayr murattabah, “not ordered,” immediately before giving an ordered sequence for the first group. This is visible on the page image, not merely an OCR artifact. Its own explanation and the English translation support reading the intended proposition as ordered. We therefore report the order with this explicit qualification rather than silently correcting the source. Another Arabic edition or manuscript collation is still required to determine the history of the erroneous negation.

F007: preference within permission. Ibn al-Qāsim reports Mālik’s preference for feeding over the other forms. Ibn Rushd says this runs against the apparent direction of the reports and reconstructs its support through the recurrent substitution of food for fasting elsewhere in the law. He describes the move as something like preferring analogy supported by legal foundations over a report not similarly supported. Preference and obligatory sequence are different normative forms. Bidāya, Arabic I, p.305.

An ordered account binds the agent to the prescribed relation among forms and capacities. A choice account permits agency among authorized forms. The preference for feeding adds an evaluation within that latitude. Shaʿrānī’s insight into differentiated human states is useful here, but it must work within the actual permission structure. It cannot turn a jurist’s therapeutic preference into a condition omitted by the school. His own discussion recognizes cases of genuine choice. al-Shaʿrānī, Mīzān I, pp.95–97.

F008. How much food is due to each recipient?

Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī and their followers require a Prophetic mudd per needy person; Abū Ḥanīfa and his followers require two mudds, half a ṣāʿ. Ibn Rushd identifies conflict between analogy with the fidyah for harm and an inference from a report that the basket contained fifteen ṣāʿ. He cautions that the basket’s quantity indicates the obligation per recipient only weakly. The Muwaṭṭaʾ’s adjacent report gives a range of fifteen to twenty ṣāʿ, which further requires attention to recension and report rather than an assumed single exact basket. Bidāya, Arabic I, pp.305–306; .

The practical object is a measured obligation, not simply generosity. A determinate minimum permits discharge to be known; a different minimum changes the recipient’s provision and the offender’s burden. Voluntary giving beyond the minimum is a separate question. Calling the larger amount “more generous” does not settle whether it is legally owed, just as calling the smaller amount “easier” does not settle its proof.

At the civic level, a rule about a small measure depends on a larger ecology of standard measures, food supply, identification of need, reliable agents and ordinary trust. Growing specialization can improve distribution; monopolized supply, fraud and fiscal extraction can defeat it. The rule is therefore linked downward to material practices and upward to fair dealing. Its exact quantity remains grounded in juristic evidence, not a symbolic numerology.

F009–F011. One violation, one day, several days: what counts as a unit?

Ibn Rushd records three distinguishable rules. F009: intercourse on a day, expiation, and a later violation on another day entail a new expiation. F010: repeated intercourse within one day entails one expiation in the agreement as he reports it. F011: when violations occur on different days before any expiation, Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī and others require an expiation for each day; Abū Ḥanīfa and his followers require one until the first has been expiated. The scope of an agreement is the formulation reported here; later school qualifications must be collated before treating it as exhaustive across all imaginable sequences. Bidāya, Arabic I, p.306.

The explicit sabab is analogy with ḥudūd, where repeated acts before enforcement can fall under a single punishment. The opposing argument gives each fasting day its own inviolability and distinguishes expiation’s element of qurbah from pure deterrence. This is not an abstract “individual versus community” dispute. It concerns the ontology of the remedial act and the individuation of sacred time.

If deterrence predominates in the analogy, one corrective act can answer a series before that correction has occurred. If each day’s worship has an independently reparable violation, multiple days generate multiple obligations. The distinction provides two possible accounts of self-development: interrupting an established pattern, and faithfully acknowledging the irreducibility of repeated failures. Neither should be psychologized beyond its evidence; Ibn Rushd reports a legal comparison, not a clinical theory of addiction.

For the public, the common calendar makes days shareable and mutually recognizable; it does not eliminate each person’s particular liability. In inherited routine, a standard answer can conceal a mistaken classification of recurrence. In political or educational breakdown, abbreviated instruction may lose exactly these distinctions. The higher orientation remains renewal of a relation to God, but this passage gives positive reason to resist reducing kaffārah to a secular fine.

F012. Poverty now, resources later: continuing debt or a completed encounter?

Al-Awzāʿī is reported as holding that nothing remains owed when the person was unable at the time; al-Shāfiʿī hesitates. The text does not authorize inventing a neat four-school distribution. The explicit cause is silence about the later condition. One can compare the obligation to a debt that becomes payable when resources return; alternatively, if continuing liability were obligatory, the Prophet would have explained it in the reported encounter. Bidāya, Arabic I, p.306; B1E, PDF p.341, printed p.359.

This is a decisive limit on the Attasian analogy of repayment. An existential account of indebtedness cannot decide whether this particular legal debt persists. Historical uṣūl must determine the extent of obligation; metaphysical indebtedness does not manufacture liabilities in the absence of a warrant.

The continuing-debt interpretation can sustain memory of an unfinished responsibility across changing fortune. The other interpretation can make inability a legally effective boundary rather than a permanent moral arrear. Both have consequences for the poor person’s relation to future prosperity, and neither can be evaluated simply by counting burdens. The moral difference between present incapacity, culpable evasion and later ability must be preserved.

F013–F014. Disputed invalidators and the departure-day traveller

The passage next treats acts whose invalidating effect is itself disputed, giving cupping, induced vomiting, swallowing a stone and breaking the fast on the first departure day as examples. These examples must remain distinct from intentional intercourse, whose invalidating effect is agreed in the opening case. F013 is the general problem: does one who deems the fast invalid also impose expiation, or replacement alone? Ibn Rushd explains the dispute through resemblance both to a genuine invalidator and to an act that does not invalidate. Most exclude expiation where the violation is doubtful. Bidāya, Arabic I, pp.306–307.

He names Abū Thawr and al-Awzāʿī for replacement plus expiation after induced vomiting, against others who regard it as invalidating but require replacement alone; ʿAṭāʾ alone is identified among the relevant jurists as imposing both for cupping. Swallowing a stone is listed as an example without a full attribution matrix here. Exhaustive research must link this entry to the earlier invalidator discussion rather than fabricate missing positions. Bidāya, Arabic I, p.306.

F014 distinguishes the departure-day traveller. Mālik requires replacement and expiation in the reported case; Ibn Rushd states that other provincial jurists and most of Mālik’s own followers disagree. This is another direct obstacle to a unitary “Mālikī style.” The underlying question about whether travel permits breaking the fast that day precedes the question of additional liability. Bidāya, Arabic I, p.306.

For formation, these rules teach a disciplined relation to uncertainty. Acting on a disputed classification does not necessarily warrant the same sanction as violating an undisputed obligation. But recognition of dispute is not a general right to choose whatever is easiest. The passage assesses consequences within specified arguments and classifications.

The Muwaṭṭaʾ supplies a useful control for cupping: Mālik’s concern in its report 824 is possible weakness preventing completion, while cupping without that concern is not discouraged in that account. A material act can therefore be evaluated by its effect on the ability to finish worship without being classified as an intrinsic invalidator. This is a concrete primary instance of condition-sensitive practical judgment. .

F015. An excuse arising later: the act’s known circumstances or the completed day?

Abū Ḥanīfa is reported as removing expiation when a deliberate violation is followed that day by a condition permitting non-fasting. The examples are menstruation, illness and travel. Mālik and al-Shāfiʿī are presented on the other side of the governing distinction: at the moment of violation the actor did not know of a permission. These reports must be read within each school’s already different account of which acts generate this expiation; they do not make al-Shāfiʿī impose it for every deliberate act of eating. Bidāya, Arabic I, p.307.

The practical ontology is temporal. Does later disclosure that the day was one on which non-fasting became permitted affect liability for the earlier act? Or is the earlier intentional disregard sufficient? One perspective gives weight to the day as ultimately constituted by its circumstances; the other to the actor’s relation to the norm at the time of choice. The contrast links objective situation, practical knowledge and culpable will without equating any two.

Ibn Rushd’s phrase about what the unseen disclosed to the actor must not be read as a claim to mystical kashf. Here a later ordinary event makes something known that was previously unknown. The example is especially valuable for the Mūsā–Khiḍr boundary: later knowledge can alter the description of a situation, but it does not follow that a person may act now on an imagined future excuse. The passage concerns the legal consequences after the event, not prophetic foreknowledge or permission to violate a norm in anticipation of illness.

The formative issue is whether responsibility attaches chiefly to the act’s realized circumstances or the agent’s acknowledged reasons at the time. Prudence requires attention to what can legitimately be known when acting. Simon’s distinction between practical science and singular practical judgment helps formulate this, while his account cannot settle the classical attribution. Simon, Critique of Moral Knowledge, PDF pp.28–31, printed pp.8–11.

In social life, hindsight can excuse everything or condemn everything unless the order of knowledge is preserved. Judges and muftis must distinguish evidence later obtained from the actor’s earlier knowledge. Public records and stable institutions can assist that reconstruction; coercive or partisan institutions can manipulate it. The vertical limit remains: finite adjudication proceeds through available evidence, not an assumed view from providence.

F016. Doubt at dawn and doubt at sunset

Ibn Rushd relates Mālik’s replacement-only rule for eating in doubt about dawn to replacement plus expiation for eating in doubt about sunset, referring to the distinction already discussed earlier. The asymmetry must not be reduced to arbitrary severity. It concerns entry into and exit from the bounded fast and the different presumptions at those boundaries. The earlier passage still needs separate collation before its whole evidentiary argument is marked complete. Bidāya, Arabic I, p.307.

The formative interpretation is calibrated caution: practical uncertainty is structured by the situation, not a single demand always to choose the harder act. This is a small but important legal education of attention. The institution’s part may include trustworthy timekeeping and teaching; the individual’s part remains acting responsibly upon what is available. Fasting among the many consequently joins shared temporal coordination with differentiated personal responsibility.

This case must be kept next to the recommendation to hasten breaking the fast once its time has arrived. A discipline that teaches precaution under unresolved uncertainty can also teach prompt acceptance of permission once the boundary is known. More delay is not inherently more devotion.

F017. Violating a replacement fast: the irreplaceable quality of Ramadan time

The majority do not impose this expiation for deliberately breaking a replacement fast for Ramadan, because the replacement day does not possess the sanctity of the original Ramadan time. Qatādah imposes replacement and expiation. A report from Ibn al-Qāsim and Ibn Wahb requires two days by analogy with spoiled pilgrimage. These are separate positions, not a single minority category. The Muwaṭṭaʾ’s report 820 provides a relevant Mālikī control concerning violation of a replacement fast and the absence of a second expiation. Bidāya, Arabic I, p.307; .

The difference between original and replacement time limits an accounting model of worship. A later day can discharge an obligation without reproducing every property of the original day. The calendar is therefore constitutive, not merely a convenient scheduling device. The relation to Attas’s “giving due” is that acknowledgement must respect the kind of due; it does not make all temporal occasions interchangeable.

For the city, the common month joins otherwise differentiated households and occupations in one rhythm. Replacement acknowledges the individual’s disruption within that common order without making the entire community repeat the month. This is our civic reconstruction, supported comparatively by Avicenna’s account of recurrent ritual preserving common remembrance, not a claim that Ibn Rushd wrote a sociology of calendars in this paragraph. Avicenna, Metaphysics of the Healing, PDF pp.382–383, printed pp.367–368.

The two-day minority analogy also forces an evidentiary question: why should a rule from pilgrimage govern this temporal repair? The formative attractiveness of an extra day cannot replace that inquiry. The upward result is that legal time has qualitative differentiation grounded in received practice and its interpretation.

F018. The fast’s completion: meals, speech and the difference between validity and fruition

The closing paragraph reports agreement on delaying the predawn meal and hastening the breaking of the fast. It then gives the majority’s account of restraint from obscene or foolish speech among fasting’s recommended practices and reports the literalist view that such speech invalidates the fast, which Ibn Rushd calls outlying. This paragraph must not be read as making otherwise prohibited abuse lawful outside fasting, or as saying that moral discipline is irrelevant to a legally valid fast. Bidāya, Arabic I, p.307; B1E, PDF p.342, printed p.360.

The first rules establish a disciplined acceptance of nourishment as well as disciplined abstention. The law’s form measures appetite in time; it does not simply maximize deprivation. The speech rule moves the fast outward into relations. An insult becomes an occasion for refusing retaliatory escalation. That is a more specific formative operation than “fasting teaches self-control”: the agent learns to preserve an acknowledged commitment under provocation from another person.

Ghazālī’s fasting chapter deepens this analysis through its distinction among abstention from bodily satisfactions, guarding the faculties from wrongdoing, and the heart’s orientation toward God. He criticizes lawful fasting followed by unlawful consumption or conduct and overeating that reinstates the appetite’s domination. His bodily, ethical and contemplative dimensions are directly relevant to the user’s demand for upward and downward links. They are not all legal invalidators in every madhhab. The supplied English translation is used for the conceptual comparison; its awkward renderings and embedded reports need Arabic and hadith control before exact doctrinal quotation. .

The same result can have opposed reasons: three political fatwā narratives

Maribel Fierro’s study offers an unusually useful historical control because it distinguishes the literary transmission of legal advice from an actual fatwā document. Her three narratives survive in a later anti-innovation treatise and biographical materials; they are not contemporary transcripts of consultations. That distinction must govern every inference from them. Masud, Messick and Powers, Islamic Legal Interpretation, PDF pp.63–70, printed pp.55–62, Fierro, “Caliphal Legitimacy and Expiation in al-Andalus”.

In the first, al-Ḥakam II is advised to fast after intercourse in Ramadan because, according to Isḥāq ibn Ibrāhīm’s argument, the wealth he controls belongs to the public treasury rather than to him. In the second, Yaḥyā ibn Yaḥyā prescribes two consecutive months to ʿAbd al-Raḥmān II because financial remedies would be too easy for a wealthy ruler and would fail to restrain recurrence. In the third, attributed to Mālik concerning Hārūn al-Rashīd, three days of fasting concern a broken oath; the reason for preferring that remedy is not explicitly supplied. Masud, Messick and Powers, Islamic Legal Interpretation, PDF pp.63–67.

The first two yield a similar outward prescription through opposing descriptions of capacity: absence of private funds in the first, abundance making monetary remedies ineffective in the second. One is primarily an argument about rightful ownership; the other is about therapeutic deterrence. A research method that assigns every difficult remedy to “the spiritually strong” would miss both. The third cannot establish the first’s rationale merely by resemblance; Fierro explicitly allows the possibility of later projection. Masud, Messick and Powers, Islamic Legal Interpretation, PDF pp.66–68.

The second narrative tests the authority of a therapeutic jurist. If the governing school permits choice, what warrants a counsellor in excluding alternatives? Is the advice moral guidance, a claim about legal obligation, a contextual application, or a narrative ideal of scholarly courage? The story’s existence does not settle its legal justification. This is precisely where the mujtahid-physician model needs public epistemic limits. One cannot infer from the desirability of restraining a ruler that every means of restraint is authorized.

Fierro herself notes the stories’ idealizing features and uncertainty about historicity. Her suggestions concerning legitimacy, dynasty and personal motives vary in evidentiary strength. The claim that a caliph owns nothing must therefore remain part of the specific argument under analysis; it is not adopted here as a universal description of Sunni property law. A later narrative about exemplary counsel is evidence of a normative imagination even where it is weak evidence of what an individual ruler actually did. Masud, Messick and Powers, Islamic Legal Interpretation, PDF pp.68–70.

Spiritual capacity, legal remedies and the physician analogy

The dissertation at PDF p.291, printed p.269, says that a person unable to feed sixty poor people for deliberately breaking a fast must fast three days. This does not match the two-consecutive-months expiation in the Bidāya passage. Its note 109 at PDF p.322 cites a further one-day report; that does not establish the three-day claim. The three-day oath expiation in Fierro’s third narrative shows how different legal objects can be confused, but we have not established that this was the dissertation author’s actual source of error. Sahib dissertation, PDF p.291, printed p.269; PDF p.322, note 109; Bidāya, Arabic I, pp.301–305; Masud, Messick and Powers, Islamic Legal Interpretation, PDF p.64.

The dissertation’s general account of physical, financial and spiritual capacity remains a useful lead. Its particular illustration is not reliable enough to carry the theory. Primary Mīzān passages must control claims about Shaʿrānī, and independent fiqh sources must control the legal examples. His own recognition of authorized choice and of an inwardly useful concession gives a richer model than “harder for every stronger person.” al-Shaʿrānī, Mīzān I, pp.95–97.

Civilization-wide integration: what changes at each stage?

What this cluster adds to the general theory

First, deterrence is a genuine legal explanation here, but qurbah prevents it from exhausting expiation. Second, the unit of liability depends on an account of time and the act’s nature. Third, incapacity and uncertainty are constitutive legal considerations, not inconveniences to a universal severity scale. Fourth, social redistribution and private self-discipline are sometimes alternative authorized morphologies, not competing secular and religious ends. Fifth, the same legal result can embody distinct understandings of wealth, responsibility and political office. Sixth, a spiritually attractive explanation still needs a legitimate inferential route.

The resulting “alchemy” is a disciplined account of how norm, act, agent, recipient and institution can be reordered together. It is strengthened, rather than weakened, by identifying where the text supplies no warrant for a particular symbolic meaning, where a remedy can fail to form virtue, and where a jurist’s own explanatory claim remains open to criticism.

Coverage and remaining controls. F001–F018 cover the identified questions in the specified passage. Earlier fasting obligations, moon-sighting, intention, permissible excuses, the full invalidator taxonomy and voluntary fasting remain outside this installment. The Arabic negation on p.305 needs another-edition collation; the earlier dawn/sunset and traveller arguments need cross-linking; later school qualifications of reported agreements need primary controls; the relevant legal chapters of the Mīzān still need direct comparison. The political narratives require their cited Arabic sources before their wording or historicity can be certified.

Part III.A. Marriage formation, authority and practical judgment

Revision 8, 1 October 2026. Sequential commentary covers Arabic II2–31, from the opening of marriage through the dower conclusion, stopping before the impediments heading on p.31. English II PDF5–40 supplies the parallel. K001–K084 contain 279 attributed proposition records, not an elementary-rule census. The targeted illness passage II46–47 remains separately identified. All Arabic pages in the contiguous envelope have been inspected; independent school, transmission and historical audits remain open.

Read the inspected Arabic source pages, the , and the later Shāfiʿī control alongside the commentary.

What is being constituted

The first object of this commentary is not “the family” in the abstract. It is a relation brought into legal existence through differentiated powers: to choose, to express permission, to contract, to act for another, to oppose a rival proposal, and perhaps to withhold or later supply acceptance. These powers are not interchangeable. A person may possess an entitlement to be consulted without personally pronouncing the contractual formula; a guardian's power may be disputed independently of the form of permission; and a prohibition governing conduct need not invalidate a resulting marriage.

The governing distinction is between a person's responsible action and another person's power to create a binding relation for that person. Ijbār in these passages names the claimed authority to conclude a marriage without the subject's legally required acceptance, not necessarily proof of physical force in a particular event. That clarification does not make the power voluntary from the subject's standpoint. Bulūgh means puberty in this source, not a modern statutory age of adulthood. Bikr and thayyib are classifications whose legal significance is disputed; translating thayyib invariably as “widow” or “divorcée” would prejudge K015.

The Rushdian classification of sciences has work to do here. A general account of obligation, validity and authoritative evidence belongs to comparatively universal practical knowledge. Rules about this kind of matrimonial permission or formula are comparatively particular practical knowledge, even though they govern many instances. Determining what a command indicates, whether contrary implication is warranted, or whether an extension is textually indicated rather than a residual transfer exercises the instrumental discipline. Practical knowledge and the law’s goods can enter the assessment of the relevant feature; they do not independently supply its normative authority. Deciding whether this person's silence or this guardian's act satisfies the rule is a further situated judgment. The chapter must not collapse those four activities into the single word “application.”

The chapter's recurring formative mechanism is making desire answerable to another person's position. Its recurring danger is that the language of benefit authorizes somebody else to determine that position without adequate warrant. The legal disagreements decide different parts of this problem. Their historical effects remain hypotheses until tested against records of consultation, contracting, disputes and remedies.

Aquinas supplies a demanding comparative test: law can make a person good relative to a regime without making the person good without qualification; he also distinguishes how habitual acts relate to acquired and infused virtue. That is not a verdict on these matrimonial rulings, but a reason to test the ends served by the competence they cultivate. Simon adds that knowing another's due and being effectively moved to render it are different: practical philosophy aims at action while still needing further determination toward the singular. These comparisons sharpen the inquiry into the guardian and jurist. They do not identify Thomistic prudence with juristic skill, infused virtue with wilāya, or natural-law determination with every madhhab variant. Aquinas, Treatise on Law, PDF p.23, I–II q.92 a.1 Simon, Critique of Moral Knowledge, PDF pp.67–68, printed pp.47–48

Marriage under terminal illness: benefit, form and trained judgment

This later passage is integrated here because it changes how the opening cases should be understood. It is a targeted case reconstruction of Arabic II46–47, not a continuous treatment of the intervening impediment chapters. The heading itself says marriage of the sick person; its surrounding discussion of the third of an estate and interference with heirs identifies the death-illness setting. Precise school definitions of the legally operative illness remain a separate doctrinal check. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.46–47, illness impediment through the first two lines of p.47 Nyazee II, PDF pp.57–58, printed pp.53–54

The competing determinations and their stated reasons

Ibn Rushd reports permission for Abū Ḥanīfa and al-Shāfiʿī, and prohibition as Mālik's well-known position. He records deductions from Mālik's statements concerning separation even after recovery and a different construction under which separation is recommended rather than obligatory. These are reported interpretive variants, not a single unqualified Mālikī ban with a uniform remedy. He identifies two issues: marriage's vacillation between sale and gift, and suspicion that admitting an additional heir injures existing heirs. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF p.46

Question Primary argument or assessment What changes in practice
Is this transaction assimilated to sale or gift? The sick person's sale is allowed, while a gift is limited by the third. The classification affects the capacity to enter the transaction and the claim to undo it.
Does the gift comparison justify this marriage prohibition? Ibn Rushd objects that the permissibility of a gift within the third has no corresponding role in the proposed marriage rule. A shared concern for the estate fails to establish an equivalent legal form.
Does admitting another heir suffice for prohibition? He classifies the argument as a contested maṣlaḥa-based inference and warns about its remoteness. Protecting the expectations of current heirs does not automatically give them a veto over marriage.
Can refusal to consider consequences facilitate injustice? He says adherence to outward forms can become a route to oppression. Formal characterization cannot terminate all inquiry into the use of the act.
How should the qualified investigator proceed? Examine evidence of the circumstances: do the indications point to a good purpose or injury to heirs? Permission or prevention turns on a trained and accountable assessment, not suspicion alone.

Every row follows the local argument; the third column spells out its juridical implications. The source neither identifies every court procedure nor supplies a numerical probability threshold. It does not say that any new heir is an unjust heir. We cannot convert the accusation of injury into a finding merely because someone stands to lose an expected share. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.46–47

Why this is more than linguistic extension

No newly identified general expression settles this case. The primary problem is the use of a legally recognizable institution under particular conditions. The investigator needs to distinguish a genuine marital undertaking from an arrangement directed at injuring others, identify which interests are legally protected, and assess observable circumstances without pretending to know the heart. The object is therefore a combination of status, intended action, future succession, competing expectations and the authority to intervene. Benefit language alone underdescribes it.

This is the strongest local challenge to a thesis that philosophy merely explains a ruling after the derivation is over. Ibn Rushd calls on knowledge of the ḥikma of the laws, moral trustworthiness and situational evidence within the judgment itself. His medicine/crafts analogy explains why a learned disposition must select between opposed possible responses when a fixed formula is insufficient. It does not declare law identical to medicine: the physician's knowledge of bodily processes does not itself confer juridical authority, and neither professional can replace evidence with personal conviction. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.46–47

The relation to the Ḍarūrī is a tension to work through. Section 266 warns that variable, generic benefits can make the jurist a legislator. The present passage repeats that concern before proposing circumstance-sensitive judgment. We can reconstruct a distinction between manufacturing a standing rule from an indeterminate good and assessing a concrete abuse within acknowledged legal relations. The texts do not yet establish a universally applicable test separating them. Calling the passage “maqāṣid” would name the problem without solving it. al-Ḍarūrī §266, PDF pp.304–305

Persons, virtues and the possible deformation of judgment

The intending spouse's practical task is to undertake marriage responsibly rather than instrumentalize it. The heirs' task cannot simply be described as relinquishing greed: they may face actual injury, while they may also use protection language to obstruct a legitimate marriage. The other spouse must be treated as a person with an independent interest, not as a suspicious addition to an estate. The investigator's virtues include attentive discrimination, justice between parties and resistance to factional pressure. These are our formative implications, not additional conditions expressly enumerated in the passage.

The “alchemical” operation is exact only when stated as a possible transformation: an outwardly effective device becomes a responsible undertaking subject to scrutiny of its use; possessive expectations become claims whose grounds must be articulated; professional cleverness becomes judgment accountable to the law's purposes and evidence. Its inverse is equally possible: an officeholder can use the alleged wisdom of the law to ratify prejudice, protect a powerful family or substitute conjecture for proof. Therefore validity, beneficent intention, ascertainable intention and moral achievement remain four different questions.

Civilizational conditions and the upward correction

K001. The ruling on marriage and the condition of the person

Primary argument. Ibn Rushd reports recommendation as the majority position, obligation as the position of the Ẓāhirīs, and a differentiated account among later Mālikīs: obligatory for some, recommended for some and permitted for others, according to the feared danger of falling into wrongful conduct. The explicit disagreement concerns the force of commands to marry. He separately identifies the differentiated account as attention to maṣlaḥa and a kind of mursal reasoning without a particular supporting source; many scholars reject it, while acceptance is apparent in Mālik's school. This is a report of the method and dispute, not an unqualified endorsement of every personalized benefit assessment. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF p.2 Bidāya, English II, PDF p.5, printed p.1

Distinct consequences. A uniform obligation, a recommendation and a condition-sensitive obligation distribute responsibility differently. The recommendation allows nonperformance without the same legal blame. The uniform obligation gives the command a general binding force. The differentiated account requires identifying the individual's condition before the classification is settled. The present passage does not give a complete five-ruling taxonomy or authorize coercing somebody to marry merely because a third party considers marriage beneficial.

Upward result. The person-sensitive position resembles differentiated spiritual or pedagogical treatment only at the level of structure. Its warrant here is disputed legal reasoning, not kashf, and it does not fit a single strong/weak binary without further evidence. Al-Ḍarūrī's restrictions on benefit-based inference create a real intra-authorial question: the report in Bidāya must be compared with the kind and strength of indication required there. It cannot be cited as “Ibn Rushd approves free maṣlaḥa.”

K002. The marriage sermon and the normative force of an exemplary act

Primary argument. The object is khuṭbat al-nikāḥ, the transmitted marriage sermon. The majority do not make it obligatory; Dāwūd does. Ibn Rushd identifies the dispute as whether the Prophet's act signifies obligation or recommendation. The supplied English calls it a form of proposal, blurring it with the next problem of proposing over another's proposal. The Arabic distinguishes the two objects. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF p.3 Bidāya, English II, PDF p.6, printed p.2

Practical meaning. The sermon places an undertaking within a publicly articulated religious horizon. Its possible formative effect is recollection: participants hear the act situated among duties and accountability, rather than treating the ceremony as a merely private acquisition. But the legal question is the sermon's normative force, not whether it can have this benefit. Both positions can acknowledge its religious value while differing over whether omission violates an obligation.

Distinct operations. On the obligatory account, the exemplary form sets a mandatory component of conduct. On the non-obligatory account, its value can be cultivated without that same burden. The passage does not establish whether omission invalidates the contract; deriving invalidity would require an additional argument. That prevents the reconstruction from confusing spiritual importance, obligation and validity.

This case moves the vertical into the social-law sequence without making it an ornamental preface. The formative pathway is speech heard, meaning attended to, undertaking remembered and conduct corrected over time; recitation without attention can leave the pathway unrealized. Al-Ḍarūrī's account of prophetic acts requires determining their explanatory role and context. Its classification is the relevant control, rather than a maxim that every good ceremonial practice is mandatory.

K003. A prohibited competing proposal and the fate of the resulting marriage

Positions and reason. The prohibition of proposing over another's proposal is treated as established. Dāwūd calls for rescission; al-Shāfiʿī and Abū Ḥanīfa do not. Both positions are reported from Mālik, together with a third: rescind before consummation but not afterward. Ibn Rushd's express question is whether prohibition entails the invalidity of what is prohibited, and under which conditions. The result under discussion must not be reduced to cancellation of a spoken proposal: the distinction before and after consummation concerns the resulting marital relation. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF p.3 Bidāya, English II, PDF p.6, printed p.2

What changes between positions. Rescission gives the prohibition force against the legal result. Non-rescission preserves the marriage while leaving the conduct prohibited. The intermediate Mālikī report makes the stage reached by the relation decisive. These are different arrangements of deterrence, status stability and the burden of undoing a completed relation. The passage does not say that those consequential descriptions are the original proof of each position; they are our reconstruction of what the positions do.

The case decisively qualifies the alchemical thesis: wrongful conduct and a legally preserved status can coexist. A coherent legal order need not erase every effect of every wrong. The right uṣūl question is whether the prohibition attaches to the constitutive act, a necessary quality, or an external circumstance. That is a comparison to the Ḍarūrī distinction, not a claim that Ibn Rushd explicitly resolves this passage by assigning one of those categories.

K004. When protection of a prior proposal begins and when it is qualified

Scope of the prohibition. Ibn al-Qāsim restricts the relevant prohibition to a righteous second suitor proposing over a righteous first suitor; where the first is not righteous and the second is, he permits it. For the majority, the protected stage begins when the parties have inclined toward one another, not at the first approach. Ibn Rushd invokes the account of Fāṭima bint Qays and multiple suitors. The Arabic phrase rakina baʿḍuhum ilā baʿḍ concerns mutual inclination; English II's “referred to a third party” supplies an institution absent from that phrase. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF p.3 Bidāya, English II, PDF p.6, printed p.2

Legal object. A proposal is neither no relation at all nor an already completed marriage. The majority's temporal qualification identifies a stage at which disruption becomes prohibited. The Ibn al-Qāsim qualification asks whether protecting that developing relation should itself depend upon the quality of the proposed match. These are separate dimensions and must not be merged into one supposed universal rule of first-comer priority.

K005. Looking before marriage and the lawful acquisition of knowledge

Positions and explicit reason. Mālik permits looking at the face and hands; unnamed others permit more, excluding the private parts; unnamed jurists prohibit looking altogether; Abū Ḥanīfa includes the feet with face and hands. Ibn Rushd connects the dispute to unqualified commands to look, unqualified prohibitions, qualifying interpretation of the verse on displayed adornment, and an analogy with exposure of face and hands during pilgrimage. Those prohibiting it retain the prior prohibition of looking. The unnamed positions must remain unnamed. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF p.3

Practical ontology. The prospective spouse seeks knowledge relevant to a consequential undertaking, but the person observed is not a commodity whose complete inspection follows from the need to choose. The extent of permissible looking is precisely what must be established. “Better information” cannot supply an unlimited permission.

For institutional actualization, the relevant variables are the setting, opportunity for refusal, trust in intermediaries and misuse of ostensibly matrimonial inquiry. The cited passage does not settle all of these. The alchemical interpretation is disciplined sight ordered to a legitimate undertaking; its failure is using that undertaking as a pretext for appetite. The upward finding is that the acquisition of information is itself norm-governed. This anticipates sales questions about adequate knowledge while resisting a simple assimilation of person and merchandise.

K006. Silence as permission in a specified act of consultation

Primary structure. For men and thayyib women, permission is expressed verbally; for virgin women who are being consulted, silence is treated as permission, while refusal is verbal. Ibn Rushd reports the general pattern with an exception attributed to Shāfiʿī adherents: verbal permission is required when the marrying guardian is neither father nor grandfather. The report on consultation and silence is the stated basis. The phrase “who are being consulted” matters: this is not a rule that any woman's silence in any setting signifies consent. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF p.4 Bidāya, English II, PDF p.7, printed p.3

Independent control. The Muwaṭṭaʾ places the consultation report beside reports of marriages contracted without prior consultation and Mālik's statement about practice. This makes the relation between a transmitted verbal rule and a school's legal construction visible. The explanatory note about bashfulness in the modern translation is the translator's explanation, not part of the prophetic report.

Meaning and danger. Law here gives a communicative act a determinate evidentiary significance. An inner state is not inspected directly. The person consulting, the legal subject and the eventual witnesses occupy different epistemic positions. A rule assigning significance to silence can accommodate a recognized mode of expression; it can also be misused when fear or pressure is ignored. The present passage does not itself provide a complete doctrine for those situations, and silence cannot simply be redescribed as free inward acknowledgement.

K007. Intention, words and the constitution of a marriage contract

Positions and reason. There is agreement on efficacy of the expressions nikāḥ and tazwīj. Mālik and Abū Ḥanīfa are among those allowing other expressions such as gift, sale or ṣadaqa; al-Shāfiʿī restricts the formula to nikāḥ or tazwīj. Ibn Rushd explicitly asks whether this contract requires both intention and its particular wording, or whether a word conveying the legal meaning through an intelligible relation suffices. Ṣadaqa here is giving in charity or donation; the English “sacrifice” is not a sound guide to the category. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF p.4 Bidāya, English II, PDF p.7, printed p.3

The difference. The narrower formulation protects a determinate public form. The broader formulation recognizes a communicated legal meaning despite lexical variation. Neither makes a private intention alone sufficient: the permissive account still requires intelligibility of the legal meaning. Nor does using the vocabulary of sale establish that the whole relation is ordinary sale.

The speech establishes a status and duties. The alchemical inquiry follows their application: does repeatedly honouring the undertaking make speech more trustworthy and desire more responsible toward another person? That formation requires subsequent conduct; the valid utterance alone does not accomplish it. The later maxim about meanings rather than expressions can illuminate one orientation, but cannot cancel the explicitly reported Shāfiʿī restriction or prove Ibn Rushd derived the position from that maxim. This is a decisive example of why maxims must remain qualified controls.

K008. The baseline consent of free men responsible for their affairs

Agreement and scope. Ibn Rushd reports agreement that men who have reached puberty, are free and control their own affairs must consent and accept for a valid marriage. Each qualification belongs in the record. This proposition cannot be generalized at once to everyone, because the next cases contest the position of enslaved men and interdicted wards. No separate sabab al-ikhtilāf should be invented for the reported agreement. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF p.4 Bidāya, English II, PDF p.8, printed p.4

Meaning. A binding undertaking is related to the act of the legally qualified person. Consent is not just an interior virtue and not merely an adviser identifying a benefit. It has a constitutive legal role. That produces a possible relation between responsible freedom and subsequent duties: the subject enters a relation he must sustain.

The constitutional analogy is limited but useful: a norm of authority requires identifying its bearer and scope. It is not enough to prove that marriage is good. That conclusion prepares the next two cases, where benefit and ownership are invoked as possible sources of power over another.

K009. Enslavement and the claimed power to impose marriage

Positions and reason. Mālik and Abū Ḥanīfa allow the master to compel the enslaved man to marry; al-Shāfiʿī does not. Ibn Rushd states the disputed object directly: is marriage among the master's rights or not? The passage therefore concerns the extent of a power claimed within slavery, not simply two techniques for promoting family life. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.4–5 Bidāya, English II, PDF p.8, printed p.4

Who acts and who bears the result. On the permissive account, the master's legally recognized power reaches the marital relation; on the restrictive account, that power stops short of imposing it. The enslaved person's interests cannot be inferred from the master's decision. Calling the former “social integration” and the latter “individual autonomy” would conceal both the historical status and the exact contested legal reach.

A severe test for the thesis. There is no basis here for claiming that imposition perfects the subject's will through acknowledgement. Any formative claim would first need to distinguish the master's restraint or domination, the enslaved person's constrained action and the prospective spouse's position. The restrictive ruling can be interpreted as limiting proprietary power; the permissive ruling's place within a slave society can be described without justifying the institution or treating its operation as virtue.

K010. An interdicted ward and the difference between welfare and pleasure

Primary argument. Disagreement exists within Mālik's school over whether an executor or guardian may compel his ward who has reached puberty. The stated reason is whether marriage is a benefit belonging to the ward's interests, or belongs only to the pursuit of pleasure. Ibn Rushd adds that, on an account making marriage obligatory, hesitation over this should not arise. That is a conditional move inside the argument, not a universal authority to impose every act deemed useful. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF p.5 Bidāya, English II, PDF p.8, printed p.4

Practical object. The guardian's jurisdiction is purposive: identifying the class of interests entrusted to him helps determine whether the proposed act falls within it. The disputed classification of marriage changes the scope of his power. This is more exact than saying that the “common good” permits intervention.

The legal comparison with interdiction is structural: powers granted for one protective purpose do not automatically extend to another. The link to al-Ḍarūrī's comparatively intelligible domain of marriage supplies a research direction, not a finding that the desired benefit defeats every contrary proof. The upward result is that the ontology of the activity—benefit, pleasure, obligation or some combination—has jurisdictional consequences.

K011. The consent of a thayyib woman who has reached puberty

Reported baseline and dissent. Ibn Rushd states agreement on requiring her acceptance, supported by the report that the thayyib expresses herself, but immediately preserves a dissent attributed to al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī. The correct record is therefore reported agreement qualified by named dissent, not unqualified unanimity. Nor should the classification thayyib be settled by substituting “widow”: its scope becomes an explicit issue in K015. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF p.5 Bidāya, English II, PDF p.8, printed p.4

Meaning of the right. Her acceptance has legal significance against the substitution of a guardian's will. Recognition of that significance does not by itself establish every later question about who pronounces the contract or whether a guardian is required. The next main section of Bidāya treats guardianship separately, so its results must not be anticipated here.

The case also sets a baseline for the following analogies. That function is indispensable: a philosopher may applaud consultation, but the jurist needs to know which settled cases can supply the contrast by which a contested case is classified. Virtue interpretation follows that reasoning; it does not replace it.

K012. The adult virgin: authority and the assessment of evidence

Positions. Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī and Ibn Abī Laylā are here reported as allowing the father to compel; Abū Ḥanīfa, al-Thawrī, al-Awzāʿī, Abū Thawr and a group require her consent. A report from Mālik agrees with the latter for an older unmarried virgin. Preserve this internal variant rather than assigning one unchanging position to “the Mālikīs.” Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF p.5 Bidāya, English II, PDF pp.8–9

The inferential dispute. A report requiring consultation of an orphan is taken, by contrary implication, to distinguish the girl with a father. Against that stands the general report requiring consultation of the virgin. Ibn Rushd says the general wording is stronger; he then invokes a variant specifying that the father asks her permission, calling it explicit at the disputed point. This is comparative legal judgment, not neutral registration of complementary temperaments. The exact assessment must constrain any account of plurality.

Control and limit. Reliance m3.13 includes the paternal grandfather with the father in its later Shāfiʿī formulation. Bidāya's wording here says “the father only.” The mismatch may reflect compression, scope or a transmission issue, but it is not solved by silently expanding the primary statement. The record keeps it open. Reliance of the Traveller, PDF p.540, printed p.522, m3.13

K013. The thayyib minor and variants inside a school

Positions. Mālik and Abū Ḥanīfa are reported as allowing the father to compel a thayyib who has not reached puberty; al-Shāfiʿī does not. Ibn Rushd then records three later Mālikī formulations: Ashhab permits compulsion while she has not reached puberty after divorce; Saḥnūn permits it even if she has; Abū Tammām rejects it even if she has not. He identifies the earlier attribution to Mālik as what writers of disagreement, including Ibn al-Qaṣṣār, report. The opening qualification about misconduct in the surrounding discussion is retained as an unresolved scope qualification; this passage does not supply its complete legal definition. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.5–6 Bidāya, English II, PDF p.9

Reason and problem. The same conflict between contrary implication concerning the orphan and general language concerning the thayyib appears. But the cross-classification differs: minority points one way, prior sexual or marital status another. A model that assigns all protective rules to incapacity would erase precisely what is in dispute.

The theoretical result is that a madhhab is not a single answer or a timeless personality. Intra-school variation can change the criterion's reach after a change of status. That bears on institutional formation: the jurist must learn to discriminate reports and their scope, not merely memorize the school name. The next group makes the competing criteria explicit.

K014. Minority and virginity as rival causes of compulsory authority

Ibn Rushd's causal reconstruction. From the baseline of paternal power concerning the minor virgin and the absence of that power concerning the thayyib who has reached puberty—with the reported exceptional dissent retained—jurists infer different causes. Abū Ḥanīfa identifies minority; al-Shāfiʿī identifies virginity; Mālik treats either as sufficient. Ibn Rushd states that the uṣūl give greater support to Abū Ḥanīfa's explanation. This is an explicit assessment of the proposed cause. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF p.6 Bidāya, English II, PDF pp.9–10

Disputed situation Minority as cause Virginity as cause Either quality sufficient
Virgin who has reached puberty No compulsion on that cause Compulsion Compulsion
Thayyib minor Compulsion No compulsion on that cause Compulsion

This table reconstructs the local argument. It is not a full school law of marriage or a resolution of the variants in K013.

What the inference does. The cause selects the legally relevant aspect of a person from qualities that co-occur in an agreed example. General resemblance is insufficient. Ghazālī's distinction between identifying a cause and applying an already established criterion is useful here: the dispute is about the criterion itself, not merely whether a known individual satisfies it. The Ḍarūrī likewise directs attention to the strength of an indicator, rather than a freely invented purpose.

Anthropological and political consequence. Each criterion constructs a different boundary for personal authority and substituted decision-making. The first makes a maturation threshold decisive; the second gives a sexual-status classification legal force; the third widens the circumstances in which substitution remains possible. These descriptions disclose what needs ethical evaluation without converting an inferred legal cause into a complete theory of the human person.

The upward result is strong: the practical object of law is not given as uninterpreted biology. The legal significance of a quality is argued from evidence and comparison. An alchemical interpretation that presumes the proper operation before establishing that significance would beg the central question.

K015. Legal classification and the meaning of thayyib

Positions and explicit reason. Mālik and Abū Ḥanīfa are here said to attach the relevant thayyib status to a valid marriage, a doubtful marital relation or ownership, excluding zinā and coercive violation from that effect. Al-Shāfiʿī is reported as treating every loss of virginity as removing compulsory authority. Ibn Rushd formulates the dispute as legal versus linguistic thuyūba. These attributions are those of this passage; broader school qualifications require independent control. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF p.6 Bidāya, English II, PDF p.10

Practical ontology. A factual occurrence and a legal status are distinct. The disagreement decides which occurrence changes the allocation of matrimonial power and the mode of expressing permission. It cannot be explained simply as disagreement over whether a physical change happened.

Ethical cost. Treating an occurrence as legally irrelevant for one purpose can leave a person exposed to compulsory authority; treating it as relevant changes her control of the relation. In cases of violation, language about “restoring order” can obscure whose power is increased and whose agency is diminished. The commentator must name this consequence instead of converting a classification into a story of purification or blaming the affected person. A person's dignity or spiritual worth does not follow from the legal category assigned here.

This case supplies a counterweight to a purely vocational or organic picture of society. A person is not exhausted by the legal function a category assigns. The formative question becomes whether the legal order makes responsible agency possible or conditions it on a disputed status; the answer remains contested rather than alchemically reconciled.

K016. Paternal authority over minors and the reported exception

Primary baseline. Ibn Rushd reports agreement that a father may contract the marriage of his minor son and minor virgin daughter without seeking her permission, then records the contrary report from Ibn Shubruma. The report concerning ʿĀʾisha's marriage is invoked in the passage. Here it is evidence Ibn Rushd uses for a historical legal position; neither this commentary nor its philosophical framework turns that citation into a recommendation or a complete appraisal of the practice. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF p.6 Bidāya, English II, PDF p.10

The object of authority. The person whose relation is created cannot supply the kind of permission recognized for the qualified adult. The legal account substitutes a father's act and treats the father's position as relevant. Its function in the next arguments is to supply an alleged baseline for extending or withholding authority from others.

The shared civilizational analysis must therefore ask about dependence and conflict of interest as well as cooperation. Kin solidarity may provide care; it may also turn a child's relation into an instrument of alliance. No stage of a dynasty settles which occurs. The existence of the recorded dissent is methodologically important: even the baseline used for analogical reasoning is not an unqualified statement of universal agreement. Any cross-case model must retain that limit.

K017. Other guardians of a minor girl and the limits of extending a protective rationale

Positions and qualifications. Al-Shāfiʿī includes the paternal grandfather with the father. Mālik restricts the power to the father, or a person to whom he specifically entrusts it with the husband designated, with a qualification concerning feared loss or corruption. Abū Ḥanīfa permits guardians more broadly and the passage attaches an option on reaching puberty. The checked Ḥanafī control now supplies an essential qualification: Qudūrī grants the puberty option for contracting by guardians other than the father and grandfather; their contracting does not carry that option. The compressed Bidāya sentence must therefore not be expanded into a universal school rule. Mukhtaṣar al-Qudūrī, PDF p.149, printed p.146, main text Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.6–7 Bidāya, English II, PDF pp.10–11

Two stated reasons. General consultation language pulls against analogy from the father to other guardians. The analogy turns on whether the solicitude and benefit assumed in the father's case exist in others: in all guardians, in the grandfather as an ascendant father, or only in the father. Ibn Rushd regards Mālik's restriction as more apparent, absent necessity. A second argument turns on the scope of “orphan”: must it refer to one below puberty, or can it include a girl capable of permission? The passage records both inference and counter-inference.

Practical consequences. Broad extension increases the supply of people able to create a binding relation; narrow extension reduces that power but may leave needs unmet when the father is absent. Necessity is therefore a possible qualification, not a license to assert whatever outcome a guardian prefers. The later maxim limiting necessity to its measure is a comparative safeguard, not the source of Mālik's position.

K018. A minor boy, an executor and the remedial option at puberty

Positions. Mālik permits the executor to contract for the minor boy; Abū Ḥanīfa permits guardians and recognizes an option upon puberty; Mālik does not impose that option in this account. Al-Shāfiʿī is reported as disallowing contracting by someone other than the father. As with K012, the compressed attribution must remain visible pending a more detailed school-source comparison. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF p.7 Bidāya, English II, PDF pp.11–12

Control on the option. Qudūrī explicitly excludes the father and grandfather from the puberty-option rule and includes other guardians. This resolves the immediate scope warning in the earlier draft while preserving the Bidāya’s compressed attribution and leaving the procedure and timing of exercising the option for further study. Mukhtaṣar al-Qudūrī, PDF p.149, printed p.146, main text

Reason and remedy. Ibn Rushd again identifies analogy to the father's judgment and solicitude. He then explains a distinction between boy and girl through the male's later power of divorce, which the female lacks in that form, and relates the Ḥanafī option for both to this problem. The already existing distribution of exit powers therefore enters the reasoning about entry powers. The present passage is not a full account of all possible routes by which a woman may obtain dissolution.

The analysis must distinguish the effects of an arrangement made for a dependent person from the effects of later giving that person an effective opportunity to decide. Protection may supply care; exercised choice may develop agency. Binding or recognizing a status is not itself either formative effect. A generic claim that guardianship gradually produces autonomy would be false where the rule does not provide that transition. The case contributes a concrete principle for the rest of family and property law: evaluate powers together with their remedies, duration and avenues of release, not in isolation.

K019. A stipulated option and the resistance of marriage to a single commercial model

Positions and textual limit. The majority disallow contracting marriage with an option; Abū Thawr permits it. Ibn Rushd offers several ways of construing the disagreement: marriage's relation to sale types with or without options; an original absence of options unless warranted; and a discussion involving gharar and the difference between mukārama and mukāyasa. The supplied Arabic edition explicitly notes that a sentence about the original prohibition of options is unclear. The English wording “quality and not measure” does not adequately expose the contrast between honorable or generous dealing and bargaining for advantage. No silent emendation is adopted here. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.7–8, especially p.8 editorial note Bidāya, English II, PDF p.12, printed p.8

Safe interpretive core. The existence of the two positions and the use of contract comparison are clear. The permissive reasoning invokes a greater need for choice or examination in marriage. The exact argumentative transition in the damaged or difficult sentence is not secure enough to make “marriage has no gharar” a general doctrine governing all dower and formation questions. Later marriage passages can in any case qualify how commercial categories apply.

Different practical forms. Refusing a stipulated option favors immediate finality of this undertaking; allowing it grants a structured period or power of reconsideration, subject to conditions not given here. Finality can sustain responsibility but can also make a poorly understood decision difficult to undo. Reconsideration can protect judgment but can prolong uncertainty for another person. These consequences are interpretive comparisons, not substitutes for a settled reading of the source argument.

K020. Delayed acceptance and the time at which authority becomes effective

Positions and reason. Al-Shāfiʿī rejects delayed acceptance in this account; Abū Ḥanīfa and his adherents allow it; Mālik distinguishes a short from a long delay. Ibn Rushd's example is a guardian contracting without the woman's permission, followed by her learning of it and approving it. The reason is whether acceptance by both contracting parties must occur together for formation. He notes the analogous disagreement in sales. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF p.8 Bidāya, English II, PDF p.12, printed p.8

Ontology of the interval. Time here is constitutive rather than merely chronological. The disagreement concerns whether a later act can give efficacy to a prior undertaking. It is not the same as a stipulated option in an already concluded contract. The passage does not enumerate every effect during the intervening period, so neither full validity nor complete nullity at every moment should be presumed beyond the attributed positions.

The alchemical reading is the passage from another's proposed undertaking to an accountable assent that can have legal effect. Its inversion is announcing a fait accompli and using social pressure to obtain a later yes. Attas's acknowledgement cannot be presumed from the retrospective legal effect alone. This opening sequence reinforces the chapter's principal finding: lawful form must be analyzed through persons, powers, signs and time before its contribution to virtue can be assessed.

Guardianship and witnessing: how the next sequence tests formation

The following K021–K052 continue the Arabic text without skipping the guardianship controversy. Their primary unit is a legal relation: a power to act, a claim to resist, a qualification for office, an ordering among officeholders, or a condition making a marriage publicly recognizable. These are related to virtues but are not virtues themselves. A guardian’s rank, financial competence, probity, concern for reputation and actual solicitude can come apart; so can witnessing, public announcement and admissible judicial proof. The case analyses below keep these distinctions operative.

Attas, Concept of Education, PDF pp.10–12 Simon, Critique of Moral Knowledge, PDF pp.67–68

How to read the principle references. B notes identify local Bidāya arguments; Ḍ notes supply independently located Rushdian controls. M notes distinguish mechanisms such as determining a relevant circumstance, without claiming that Ibn Rushd cites Ghazālī in each case. J and Q notes are later comparisons. No reference upgrades a probable inference to certainty or gives a public office access to hidden providential ends. Every case’s formative and historical effects remain argued possibilities, while its legal positions are attributed reports in the inspected witness.

K021. Is a guardian constitutive, supplementary, or unnecessary?

Positions and qualifications.

Attribution Rule or argument Limit
Mālik through Ashhab; al-Shāfiʿī A guardian is required for validity Preserve the separate Mālikī report below
Abū Ḥanīfa, Zufar, al-Shaʿbī, al-Zuhrī A woman may contract without a guardian The spouse is suitable; further qualifications are not erased
Dāwūd A guardian is required for a virgin but not a thayyib The source differentiates sexual/marital classifications
Ibn Rushd’s extraction from Ibn al-Qāsim’s report of Mālik Guardianship is a sunna or completion, not a validity condition A reconstruction from several rulings, contested by Baghdad Mālikīs

Source and reason. No unambiguous text establishes the contested condition; competing apparent indications and disputed reports. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.8, 9 Bidāya, English II, PDF pp.12, 13

The source gives four constructions, not simply a permissive and a restrictive school. In the first, another person's authorized participation helps constitute the marriage. In the second, the woman's act can constitute it subject to suitability. Dāwūd divides the two statuses. The fourth is Ibn Rushd's extraction from transmitted Mālikī rulings, including inheritance following a marriage without a guardian, the appointment of any man by a woman of non-elite standing, and the preference for a thayyib to have a guardian present. Calling this fourth construction “Mālik's position” without its inferential provenance would suppress the dispute within the school.

Textual correction. Arabic ghayr al-sharīfa here identifies social standing; Nyazee's “unchaste woman” introduces a sexual judgment unsupported by this phrase. The later reference to al-daniyya on p.13 confirms the status contrast. The source's unequal treatment remains a problem for the framework, but it is a different problem from misconduct.

Meaning and formation. The disagreement distributes the powers of undertaking, representing and reviewing a relation. A voluntary act may exercise responsibility; a representative may exercise care; neither possibility establishes which legal condition revelation requires. Ibn Rushd emphasizes the texts' probability and disputes over report authenticity. Legal plurality here is structured uncertainty about authority, not proof that every structure realizes an equal spiritual operation. The first civilizational test is therefore who can make a binding marriage and who can contest it, before asking what household habits result.

Principles at this step.

K022. A duty not to obstruct does not establish exclusive authority

Positions and qualifications.

Attribution Rule or argument Limit
Advocates of the guardian condition The prohibition of obstruction supports guardianship Argument from Qurʾān 2:232
Ibn Rushd’s counterargument A prohibition of obstruction need not confer exclusive contracting power It may restrain a person who can obstruct in fact
Ibn Rushd’s alternative reading of Qurʾān 2:221 The address can concern rulers or Muslims generally The duty to prevent a prohibited marriage is not exclusive to relatives

Source and reason. Whether a prohibition addressed to relatives implies their exclusive power to constitute marriage. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.9, 10 Bidāya, English II, PDF pp.13, 14

A command to relatives not to obstruct marriage can limit interference without making their consent a constitutive condition. Likewise, a duty to prevent a prohibited interreligious union can bind a stranger, a ruler or the community without giving each the same matrimonial office. Ibn Rushd separates the addressee of a norm from the holder of an exclusive power. This is interpretation of the relation indicated by the text, not a free appeal to the usefulness of autonomy.

The philosophical consequence is substantial. “Acknowledgement” can require an authority to refrain, not only to supervise. Justice may be the relinquishment of a claimed veto. An alchemical account must therefore include the transformation of possessiveness into respect for another's legally recognized undertaking. Its contrary is protective language used to monopolize action.

Principles at this step.

K023. Public need, clarification and the burden of establishing a condition

Positions and qualifications.

Attribution Rule or argument Limit
Ibn Rushd The party omitting the additional condition does not bear its initial proof burden The argument invokes original freedom from liability
Ibn Rushd A generally necessary detailed guardian institution should have been clarified and widely transmitted An evidentiary argument, not an independently established history of Medina
Ibn Rushd in this passage The disputed authentication of the ʿĀʾisha report weakens reliance on it Do not universalize the local wording into rejection of every contested report

Source and reason. Initial non-liability; expected clarification and transmission of a generally needed condition. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.9, 10, 12 Bidāya, English II, PDF pp.13, 15, 17

The phrase al-aṣl barāʾat al-dhimma puts the initial burden on the assertion of an additional binding requirement. This is not proof that no authority can exist. It requires the claimant to establish this authority. Ibn Rushd adds a public-need argument: if exact kinds and ranks of guardians were conditions of validity in an institution used generally, their clarification and transmission should match that need. His reference to the absence of a reported special Medinan marriage office belongs to this argument; it is not a finding produced by an independent archive of practice.

The Ḍarūrī supplies a precise control. Sections 188–194 distinguish postponing clarification until need from postponing it beyond need; the latter is rejected. They do not authorize the blanket claim that every general text must immediately disclose every detail. General knowledge can prepare for a more particular determination. That temporal distinction fits the practical-general/particular architecture: knowing the end or class of action is not yet knowing every condition for performing it.

The Bidāya's locally severe wording about a report whose authenticity is disputed must also be read beside Ḍarūrī §§198–199, where probable apparent meanings and solitary reports remain operative. The commentary records a tension of scope, not a fabricated rule requiring unanimous authentication. The jurist's formative task is disciplined restraint in imposing a burden; public comprehensibility is a condition of accountable obedience, not a guarantee that all valid law is immediately obvious.

al-Ḍarūrī §§188–194, PDF pp.252–259; §§198–199, PDF pp.260–263

Principles at this step.

K024. Permission and personal pronouncement are different requirements

Positions and qualifications.

Attribution Rule or argument Limit
Ibn Rushd’s conditional reading A requirement of the guardian’s permission need not require him to pronounce the contract The authenticity premise is conceded for argument
Ibn Rushd’s possible specification The report may concern a woman under guardianship rather than every woman A possible interpretation, not a resolved universal exemption

Source and reason. What the report would establish even if its authenticity were conceded. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.10 Bidāya, English II, PDF pp.15

Ibn Rushd asks what follows even on accepting the report invoked for guardianship. “With the guardian's permission” need not mean “only through the guardian's own contracting words.” The woman might pronounce the contract with that permission. A further issue is whether the report concerns women generally or those under a particular form of guardianship. Authentication, scope and legal consequence are three separate inquiries.

This is a small verbal difference with a large practical effect. Consultation, approval, representation and execution can belong to different persons. A system that combines them in one office has to justify that combination; the existence of one required act does not establish the others. This distinction also stops the philosophical model from treating a represented person as either wholly autonomous or wholly passive.

The possible formative operation is the coordination of acknowledged commitments: one authorizes, another undertakes, and both remain answerable for the acts attributed to them. Its failure is fictitious authorization. Communication and a way to prove permission are thus concrete conditions of actualization. Neither a family's honor nor an official's confidence supplies the missing sign. The vertical limit is especially clear: an inwardly benevolent intention cannot stand in for the public permission the chosen legal construction actually requires.

Principles at this step.

K025. Women’s acts, customary rightness and the strength of apparent meaning

Positions and qualifications.

Attribution Rule or argument Limit
Opponents of the guardian validity condition Texts attributing marriage or action to women support their own contracting power Attribution is a presumptive indication, not exclusive logical proof
