Ibn Rushd’s composite reading Woman’s contracting power could coexist with guardian rescission where action is not maʿrūf He says no one holds this combined interpretation; it is not an established school position
Readers of the Ibn ʿAbbās report The thayyib’s greater right can support independent authority or a different mode of expressing consent Ibn Rushd calls the indication apparent, not unambiguously explicit

Source and reason. Attribution of acts to women; restriction by maʿrūf; competing readings of the Ibn ʿAbbās report. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.10, 11 Bidāya, English II, PDF pp.15, 16

The Qurʾānic attribution of action to women is evidence for their agency, but an attributed act need not exclude every other person's legally relevant participation. Ibn Rushd explores a combined reading of self-disposition and the qualification bi-l-maʿrūf: a woman contracts, while a guardian might challenge an act outside recognized rightness. He explicitly notes the absence of an adherent to that complete construction. It belongs in the argument map as a considered interpretation, not in the school map as settled doctrine.

The Ibn ʿAbbās report that the thayyib has greater right over herself also admits competing implications: independent decision, or a contrast between spoken permission and the virgin's silence. Arabic ẓāhir marks an apparent or preponderant indication; the English “explicit” overstates its force. Related reports and the remembered or disavowed transmission of the ʿĀʾisha report are themselves disputed in the passage. No new independent hadith grading is supplied here.

The practical good is a relation in which an undertaking can be attributed correctly and challenged on stated grounds. But maʿrūf must not become an unlimited appeal to whatever dominant relatives find respectable. Attas's justice requires identifying a due rather than baptizing every inherited expectation as due. The case therefore returns two demands to the framework: record the degree of semantic confidence, and distinguish an imaginable reconciliation from a historically attested legal position.

Principles at this step.

K026. Financial agency and the limits of protective oversight

Positions and qualifications.

Attribution Rule or argument Limit
Argument for independent contracting A woman competent in financial disposition can act in marriage Analogy of practical agency
Argument for continuing guardianship Alleged desire and risk of family shame justify special restriction An anthropological premise reported in the controversy, not an established empirical fact
Ibn Rushd’s response Corrective oversight or rescission may meet the alleged concern Hisba here does not prove a historical market-inspector office
Ibn Rushd’s probable conclusion Either guardianship is not a validity condition, or its exact qualifications and ranks are not validity conditions A disjunction; not an unconditional abolition of guardianship

Source and reason. Analogy with financial agency versus alleged special vulnerability; critique of strict ranks. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.11, 12 Bidāya, English II, PDF pp.16, 17

The argument from financial competence treats a woman's power to manage property as evidence of matrimonial agency. Its opponent alleges a special susceptibility in sexual desire and an injury to relatives' reputation. These claims about women are premises of the controversy, not facts the commentary should endorse or smooth into “natural differentiation.” Ibn Rushd replies that a corrective right could answer the concern without the stronger constitutive restriction.

His own conclusion remains disjunctive and probable: either guardianship is not a condition of validity and guardians have a corrective oversight, or—if it is a condition—its exact classes, qualifications and ranks are not all constitutive. He accordingly weakens the view invalidating a remote guardian's act simply because a nearer one exists. Translating ḥisba as corrective oversight here does not identify a particular officeholder or establish a historical procedure.

The comparative agency argument must itself be limited by K028: competence in property and competence in choosing a suitable marriage are not identical. That qualification applies to both women and guardians. An alchemy of law cannot assume one uniform substance called competence and transfer it wherever convenient. Its more exact task is to discern the relevant capacity, assign only warranted powers, and create corrective routes. Kin solidarity can supply information and care or reproduce suspicion and exclusion. Those are competing social trajectories requiring evidence; no dynastic stage or spiritual hierarchy settles the argument.

Principles at this step.

K027. Guardian qualifications and an unresolved Ḥanafī attribution

Attribution Rule or argument Limit

Abū Ḥanīfa as reported in Bidāya An enslaved person may serve Contradicts the general prohibition in the checked Qudūrī passage; unresolved

Source and reason. Reported agreement on core qualifications; dispute over enslavement. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.12 Bidāya, English II, PDF pp.17

The report of agreement concerns a particular office. It cannot mean that all non-Muslim families lack recognized guardians or that a woman can never perform contractual speech: both would collide with distinctions already present. Reliance m3.4 expressly recognizes a non-Muslim guardian for a non-Muslim bride. This later control helps delimit the question without silently rewriting Ibn Rushd's wording.

The slavery attribution needs stronger scrutiny. The inspected Bidāya p.12 says the majority prohibit the enslaved guardian and Abū Ḥanīfa permits him. The inspected Qudūrī, PDF p.149, says “no guardianship for an enslaved person,” alongside the minor and the insane person. The discrepancy is real in these witnesses; a scope distinction, variant report or textual problem remains to be established. Neither witness is silently corrected by the other.

K028. Financial rushd and matrimonial judgment are different competences

Positions and qualifications.

Attribution Rule or argument Limit

Al-Shāfiʿī, a report from Mālik, Ashhab and Abū Muṣʿab Financial rushd is required Assimilation to property guardianship
Ibn Rushd Sound judgment in wealth differs from sound judgment in choosing matrimonial suitability Assessment of the analogy’s relevant subject

Source and reason. Assimilation to property guardianship; Ibn Rushd distinguishes the two kinds of sound judgment. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.12 Bidāya, English II, PDF pp.17, 18

The dispute tests whether the guardian's qualification should be modeled on property guardianship. Ibn Rushd's answer identifies a disanalogy: sound financial judgment is not identical with sound judgment in choosing a suitable match. A person's successful action in one field cannot by itself certify another competence. The source does not thereby eliminate every connection between money, maintenance and marriage; it denies their simple equivalence.

Principles at this step.

K029. Probity and family reputation: motivation is not yet virtue

Positions and qualifications.

Attribution Rule or argument Limit
One argument reported without a complete list of adherents Probity is required because a corrupt guardian cannot be trusted to choose suitably Do not supply missing school names
Counterargument reported Concern about family shame may motivate a suitable choice without acquired probity A proposed causal mechanism, not proof of moral excellence

Source and reason. Protective function and distrust of the morally unreliable versus a natural motive to avoid family shame. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.12, 13 Bidāya, English II, PDF pp.18

One argument requires ʿadāla because the office aims at protective judgment and a morally unreliable person may fail it. The counterargument appeals to a different motive: relatives may avoid an unsuitable match because they fear shame. Ibn Rushd distinguishes that supposedly natural motive from acquired probity. The passage does not provide a complete attribution list, so the ledger does not invent one.

This is a direct counterexample to the equation “socially useful conduct equals virtue.” A person may conform through reputation, rivalry or fear while lacking the disposition that would make the act just. Conversely, the appeal to shame can preserve a hierarchy at the expense of the woman. To call it a reliable mechanism requires specifying what counts as suitability and whose injury is prevented.

Reliance m3.4 retains uprightness in the main qualification but its marked commentary reports acceptance of a corrupt guardian by most later scholars. That layered witness is evidence of a later doctrinal discussion, not proof that Ibn Rushd's unnamed parties correspond exactly to it. Civilizationally, reputation works only through an audience with power to sanction; it can stabilize trust or punish justified dissent. The alchemical task is to distinguish conformity from acknowledged justice. No legal presumption about a motive establishes the guardian's inward station.

Reliance, PDF p.537, printed p.519, m3.4 and the separately marked O commentary

Principles at this step.

K030. Kinds of guardianship and the unequal reach of mere religious membership

Positions and qualifications.

Attribution Rule or argument Limit
Ibn Rushd’s enumeration Lineage, the sultan and upper/lower mawlā relations are grounds of guardianship Clientage terminology requires its own legal context
Mālik as reported Mere Islam can ground guardianship for a woman of low social standing The text preserves a class distinction; do not translate it as unchastity

Source and reason. Enumeration of grounds; no separate reason is supplied for every status distinction. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.13 Bidāya, English II, PDF pp.18

The enumeration concerns different grounds of legal authority: descent, public office and mawlā relations, with a Mālikī residual permission tied to a woman's non-elite status. “Upper” and “lower” mawlā are retained as the passage's clientage terminology; they should not be expanded into spiritual ranks or an imported caste taxonomy. The source does not supply a separate derivation for every item in this short list.

The status distinction limits any easy claim that a religious civilization gives identical legal form to acknowledgement. Membership in Islam supplies a sufficient residual ground in one reported situation while socially prominent women are treated differently. The analysis must ask whether that differentiation protects a particular interest or entrenches unequal access to marriage. The passage alone does not answer the historical question.

For the political architecture, the sultan's appearance among legal grounds establishes neither a saintly rank nor unrestricted discretion. Q-PUBLICFUNCTION offers a later maxim about public benefit as a control on the purpose of office; it cannot independently create its jurisdiction. The civilizational task is to trace actual access to kin, clientage networks and public forums. Their coexistence is an institutional structure, not a necessary sequence from tribe to city. Responsible service could operate through any warranted role; social rank alone proves neither its competence nor its moral worth.

Principles at this step.

K031. Executor and agent: delegation with different temporal structures

Positions and qualifications.

Attribution Rule or argument Limit
Mālik An executor can exercise the stated matrimonial authority See separate scope limits in K017–K018
Al-Shāfiʿī An executor cannot exercise it merely as executor Do not infer rejection of ordinary agency
Majority Ordinary agency in marriage is allowed Authority depends on the relevant appointing party
Abū Thawr Ordinary agency is disallowed in this report The local dissent is retained

Source and reason. Whether matrimonial authority admits delegation; distinction between testamentary office and ordinary agency. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.13 Bidāya, English II, PDF pp.18

The text first disputes the executor's authority and then reports broad acceptance of agency, with Abū Thawr dissenting. These are not redundant questions. A waṣī acts under an entrusted office whose relevant operation can follow death; a wakīl acts through an authorization whose ordinary dependence on the principal differs. Al-Shāfiʿī's acceptance of agency therefore need not contradict his refusal to let an executor inherit matrimonial power simply by appointment.

The legal object is an authorized act, not the delegate's personal benevolence. An executor may know the household well yet lack this particular power; an agent may have narrower knowledge but act within a defined commission. The formative good is fidelity, including refusal to exceed instructions. Its inversion is converting an entrusted responsibility into personal dominion.

The city's need for delegated functions gives the issue a Coomaraswamian comparison: differentiated work depends on knowing the end and measure of one's task. But “vocation” cannot answer who validly appointed the person. Literacy, reliable communication and accepted proof of appointment are possible civilizational supports, not express conditions added by this passage. The next institutional research must establish how commissions and testamentary appointments were evidenced. Upward, the framework should distinguish role, source of authority, duration and scope before it assigns any formative operation to an office.

Principles at this step.

K032. The agnatic order and the grandfather–brother dispute

Positions and qualifications.

Attribution Rule or argument Limit

Al-Mughīra Grandfather and his father precede brother and brother’s son The edition flags a difficult explanatory phrase; do not import the English repair
Al-Shāfiʿī Grandfather precedes brother Further difference over the son is separated in K033
Mālikī order reported Upper mawlā precedes lower mawlā Clientage titles, not spiritual degrees

Source and reason. Different judgments of proximity and analogy to agnatic ordering. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.13 Bidāya, English II, PDF pp.18, 19

The reported Mālikī sequence moves through sons and their descendants, the category termed fathers (al-ābāʾ), full and paternal brothers, those brothers' sons, paternal grandfathers ascending, paternal uncles and their descendants in corresponding order, then mawlā and sultan. Upper mawlā has priority over lower in the local enumeration. Nyazee's “uncles” where the Arabic first says brothers corrupts this structure. The lineage diagram must follow the Arabic, not that translation.

The text names fathers and later separately places paternal grandfathers; that wording must not be silently regularized into an unambiguous ascendant ladder. Al-Mughīra puts the grandfather and his father before brother and nephew; al-Shāfiʿī also places grandfather before brother. The reason concerns proximity, but the supplied Arabic edition flags a problematic phrase in al-Mughīra's explanation. The English “not an outsider” should not be promoted into a securely established rationale. Rank and the validity consequence of violating rank remain separate questions, taken up in K035.

The possible good of ordering is coordination: avoiding rival undertakings and identifying who should act first. Its coordinating function can succeed even where the ranking does not track differences of wisdom. It is a contested legal ordering with sex and lineage consequences. Civilizational analysis asks when kin proximity supplies reliable knowledge and when it supplies factional control. The upward result is that a hierarchy may settle an administrative conflict without measuring virtue, and its exact order still needs its own warrant.

Principles at this step.

K033. Son, father and the mistaken conversion of walāʾ into guardianship

Positions and qualifications.

Attribution Rule or argument Limit
Mālikī order described Son precedes father Reasons include the disputed Umm Salama report and succession to walāʾ
Al-Shāfiʿī The son has no authority merely by being the son Other possible grounds are not excluded by this formulation
Another report from Mālik, preferred here by Ibn Rushd Father precedes son Ibn Rushd calls this better

Source and reason. Reported practice and inheritance of walāʾ invoked for the son; competing judgment of paternal priority. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.13 Bidāya, English II, PDF pp.19

The son's priority is supported by a report concerning Umm Salama and by his succession to his mother's walāʾ, a clientage relation. The latter is not ordinary custodial guardianship; the English phrase “obligatory guardianship” conceals the legal object being used for comparison. Al-Shāfiʿī rejects authority arising from filiation as son, while another Mālikī report puts the father first; Ibn Rushd prefers that ordering.

The report and the analogy must be evaluated separately. A reported action can fail to establish a general rule if its circumstances or authenticity are contested. Succession to one legal relation does not automatically confer authority in another. Jamʿ's later original/branch/cause taxonomy can ask what common ground is alleged, but it is not evidence that Ibn Rushd has demonstrated a single indicated universal here.

This case complicates a simple picture of paternal temporal power: the disputed office can run from son to mother. Calling this an organic function explains nothing unless it identifies the legal title and practical good. The formative possibility is service across generations; the contrary is dependency exploited as control. Demography, survival of relatives and access to a public substitute alter the consequences without deciding the normative ranking. The philosophical synthesis must remain responsive to Ibn Rushd's actual preference rather than distributing every rank as an equally valid alchemical temperament.

Principles at this step.

K034. Executor or relatives: entrusted continuity against kinship priority

Positions and qualifications.

Attribution Rule or argument Limit
Mālik through Ibn al-Qāsim The father’s executor precedes relatives The report concerns ordering of admitted authority
Ibn al-Mājishūn and Ibn ʿAbd al-Ḥakam Relatives precede the executor Do not collapse into the earlier dispute whether an executor has authority at all

Source and reason. Competing weight of the father’s appointment and kin-based authority. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.13 Bidāya, English II, PDF pp.19

The question now presupposes a possible executor and asks whether that person or relatives take precedence. It differs from K031's question whether executorship supplies authority at all. Ibn al-Qāsim's report from Mālik favors the executor; Ibn al-Mājishūn and Ibn ʿAbd al-Ḥakam favor relatives. The short passage gives less argument than the preceding major controversy; its explanation through entrusted continuity and kin proximity is our reconstruction, not an explicit sabab quotation.

An appointment can preserve a deceased parent's judgment and select someone competent beyond the nearest kin. It can also perpetuate an outdated choice. Kinship can supply current knowledge and accountability or undermine a chosen representative through faction. These are alternative causal pathways, not reasons to certify one opinion historically superior without evidence.

The alchemical issue is whether an inherited responsibility becomes attentive present service or merely a claim to precedence. A settled disposition of fidelity must answer to the actual object entrusted. The institutional issue is how competing titles are proved and resolved; the source does not here prescribe the hearing. Upward, the synthesis gains a temporal distinction: continuity of office is not continuity of correct judgment, and the persistence of a title cannot by itself prove the persistence of its expected benefit.

Principles at this step.

K035. A remote guardian’s act and the difference between private claim and constitutive right

Positions and qualifications.

Attribution Rule or argument Limit
Three reports from Mālik Remote guardian’s contract is rescinded; or valid; or subject to nearer guardian’s ratification/rescission Near guardian exists; preserve the exceptions below
Mālikī exception reported Father with virgin daughter, and executor with ward: another’s contract is rescinded The passage reports no internal variation for these exceptions
Al-Shāfiʿī Another guardian cannot act while the father is present Applies here to virgin and thayyib
Some Mālikīs Reject the interpretation making every breach void Intra-school legal characterization is contested

Source and reason. Whether ranking is legally obligatory, and whether its breach affects a guardian’s claim or a non-waivable divine right. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.14 Bidāya, English II, PDF pp.19, 20

Three Mālikī reports give different effects to acting out of rank: rescission, validity, or dependence on the nearer guardian's decision. Ibn Rushd identifies two levels in the disagreement. Is the order legally binding? If so, does it protect a guardian's claim that can be waived, or concern a divine right whose violation cannot be repaired by that person's approval? Those alternatives determine the remedy; they are not merely different degrees of strictness.

The exceptional cases of a father with his virgin daughter and an executor with his ward remain separate in the source. Al-Shāfiʿī's rule concerning the father's presence is broader with respect to virgin/thayyib status. A diagram showing a single family ladder and labeling every step “validity” would be false.

The possible formative good of ratification is accountable reconciliation after an irregular act. Its danger is leverage: a person with a veto may extract concessions. Immediate validity reduces that leverage but may bypass an interest the legal construction recognizes. Rescission enforces the order but can unsettle the couple. This is why virtue analysis must follow the allocated right and remedy, not praise regularity in the abstract. The later prohibition/effect taxonomy is a control; the case's explicit distinction between kinds of right supplies the closer warrant. No appeal to hidden spiritual hierarchy resolves a public question of who may ratify.

Principles at this step.

K036. An absent guardian: does authority pass to kin or public office?

Positions and qualifications.

Attribution Rule or argument Limit
Mālik Authority passes to the next eligible family guardian on the relevant absence Particular paternal cases follow separately
Al-Shāfiʿī Authority passes to the sultan Absence is not treated simply as death
Agreement reported Death transfers the authority onward The dispute concerns extending this effect to absence

Source and reason. Whether absence is assimilated to death for transferring authority. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.14 Bidāya, English II, PDF pp.20

The legal difference is who acts when the ordinary guardian is unavailable. Mālik's reported construction transfers within the kin order; al-Shāfiʿī's transfers to public authority. Ibn Rushd locates the disagreement in the analogy of absence to death. Both interrupt present action, but only one necessarily terminates the original holder's position. A practical similarity therefore does not settle the legal consequence.

Reliance m3.9 confirms a later Shāfiʿī route to the judge for the specified long absence, refusal or ritual state, rather than simply to the next relative. Qudūrī describes a remote absence under which a later guardian acts and gives a communication-related measure. These are controls with their own conditions, not interchangeable glosses on every use of “absence.”

The political stakes are concrete: kin substitution keeps decision within a relational network; judicial substitution makes a public forum responsible for the interruption. Each can protect against the other's abuse and each can fail. A consolidated administration may make judges accessible while distant communities rely on relatives; this is a hypothesis about conditions, not a derivation of school law from city stages. The alchemical operation is maintaining a due function under interruption without confusing need with unlimited authorization. The public substitute needs its own title, competence and limits.

K037. The absent father: distance, knowledge, maintenance and request

Positions and qualifications.

Attribution Rule or argument Limit
Reported baseline Far, unknown or captive father; daughter maintained and protected, not requesting marriage: she is not married in this account No request is not an express refusal
Reported rule She requests marriage and father is captive or whereabouts unknown: marriage may proceed The absent-father setting is retained
Mālik Where she requests and father is at a known distant location, marriage may proceed Disputed by ʿAbd al-Malik and Ibn Wahb
ʿAbd al-Malik and Ibn Wahb In that known-distant case marriage does not proceed Not a denial of all need-based substitution
Ibn Rushd’s qualified agreement report Known nearby father: marriage does not proceed through substitution He qualifies his report; communication remains possible

Source and reason. A differentiated situational matrix rather than distance alone. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.14 Bidāya, English II, PDF pp.20

The source does not offer a single distance rule. It crosses known or unknown whereabouts, captivity, remoteness, provision of maintenance and protection, and whether the daughter asks to marry. If maintained and protected without a request, marriage does not proceed in the described remote/unknown/captive circumstances. If she asks and the father is captive or unknown, it can proceed. If he is known but far away, Mālik permits while ʿAbd al-Malik and Ibn Wahb refuse. A known nearby father is treated differently because communication remains possible; Ibn Rushd qualifies the agreement he reports.

This is a practical object constituted by relations and time, not the natural property “distance” alone. Mustaṣfā's taḥqīq al-manāṭ helps identify the operation of establishing a relevant condition in a case; it does not prove that every listed condition is derived by that method or that the rule itself is settled.

Principles at this step.

K038. Unmet need and extension under urgency

Positions and qualifications.

Attribution Rule or argument Limit
Rule reported for the absent-father matrix Failure of maintenance, protection, or both permits marriage in the described cases The three absence situations remain the context
Further qualification reported Where protection is lacking, marriage may proceed even without her request Do not equate lack of request with express refusal or fully voluntary consent
Ibn Rushd’s proposed reasoning Urgency and the sultan’s fear of harmful consequences might justify proceeding even with a nearby absent father An extension he proposes from maṣlaḥa, not a uniform transmitted Mālikī rule

Source and reason. Maintenance/protection failures; Ibn Rushd’s own maṣlaḥa-based extension when delay threatens harm. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.14, 15 Bidāya, English II, PDF pp.20, 21

Failure of maintenance or protection changes the preceding matrix. Most troubling for a simple autonomy narrative, the text permits action without a request in the unprotected case. That is not the same as authorizing action against an express refusal, but neither is it evidence of affirmative consent. The commentary must preserve the gap rather than fill it with an ideal of benevolent guardianship.

Ibn Rushd then proposes that attention to benefit might justify proceeding even when the father is nearby if time presses and the sultan fears harmful consequences. This is his reasoned extension. It is not merely application of the already stated distance rule, nor a newly disclosed lexical universal. It belongs beside illness-marriage as a bounded instance of situational practical reasoning and beside Ḍarūrī §266 as a warning against making variable benefit an unrestricted source of legislation.

The alchemical possibility is rescue from neglected dependence into a supported relation; the contrary is using alleged danger to accelerate a marriage for someone else's purposes. The ruler's fear is therefore not self-validating evidence. The supplied passage does not spell out a review procedure, proportionality threshold or complete set of alternatives. Q-MEASURE and the public-office maxim can frame those missing checks as later controls, not certify that the historical rule already satisfies them. Upward, every claim of urgent benefit must record whose need, whose assessment, which power and which protections are actually established.

Principles at this step.

K039. Two authorized guardians and the known earlier marriage

Positions and qualifications.

Attribution Rule or argument Limit
Agreement reported When the earlier contract is known and neither marriage consummated, the first prevails Two guardians are assumed able to act; do not erase that premise

Source and reason. Temporal priority under the assumption that both guardians could act. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.15 Bidāya, English II, PDF pp.21

The example assumes two guardians could act. Where the earlier marriage is known and neither has been consummated, Ibn Rushd reports agreement favoring the first. The relevant object is a conflict between incompatible purported relations. It is not a competition to award a woman to the more powerful representative.

The rule makes timing legally significant, so the conditions of knowing the sequence become part of its civilizational actualization. Reliable communication between guardians, witnesses and parties can prevent the conflict; a recognized forum may be needed to settle it. The legal text does not establish that a particular registration system existed, and the commentary adds none.

Formation here is principally a demand on representatives: coordinate before acting and acknowledge an already constituted relation. The couple's status may be secured without anyone acquiring a virtuous disposition. That distinction matters for the alchemical model: stabilizing a public relation is an immediate institutional effect, while fidelity and truthful reporting are possible human achievements within it. The later certainty maxim is only a comparison; it does not by itself prove which contract was first. Upward, the framework must distinguish a rule of priority from the evidence of priority.

Principles at this step.

K040. Second consummation and the limits of commercial analogy

Positions and qualifications.

Attribution Rule or argument Limit
Mālik and Ibn al-Qāsim The second marriage prevails after its consummation in the described case Contrasts with K039 before consummation
Al-Shāfiʿī and Ibn ʿAbd al-Ḥakam The earlier marriage prevails Supported by the general report concerning the first guardian
Ibn Rushd The comparison with the disapproved sale is weak His assessment prevents neutral romanticization of both arguments

Source and reason. General transmitted priority rule versus comparison with a disapproved sale after the goods can no longer be restored in the relevant way. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.15 Bidāya, English II, PDF pp.21

The second marriage's consummation produces a new disagreement. Mālik and Ibn al-Qāsim give it effect; al-Shāfiʿī and Ibn ʿAbd al-Ḥakam retain the earlier marriage. The reason contrasts the general report favoring the first guardian's contract with an analogy to fawāt al-silʿa fī al-bayʿ al-makrūh. Nyazee's “coerced sale” misreads makrūh. The comparison concerns a disapproved sale whose goods have passed beyond the relevant form of restoration; it need not mean only literal consumption. Ibn Rushd calls the analogy weak.

The analogy seeks to give weight to an accomplished state of affairs. But resemblance at the level of irreversible consequences does not make marriage an exchange of a commodity. Nor does consummation establish consent, moral achievement or an indefeasible right without further argument. The commentary must not transform “what happened” into “what ought to bind.”

The possible social good is avoiding disruption after a relation has acquired further effects; the competing good is protection of prior entitlement and restraint of unauthorized supersession. A doctrine rewarding the later accomplished act could also encourage strategic acceleration. That causal hypothesis requires historical testing. The upward lesson is decisive for alchemical plurality: outcomes may embody different concerns, while the argument for one is still judged weak. Their shared concern with stability does not equalize their warrant.

Principles at this step.

K041. Simultaneous contracts and an unknown sequence

Positions and qualifications.

Attribution Rule or argument Limit
Agreement as far as Ibn Rushd knows Simultaneous contracts are both rescinded His epistemic qualification is retained
Majority If the earlier contract is unknown, both are rescinded Unknown order is not proven simultaneity
Mālik If order is unknown, rescind unless one marriage has been consummated Consummation changes the consequence
Shurayḥ; also reported from ʿUmar b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz The woman chooses when priority is unknown Ibn Rushd calls this anomalous; it is not majority law

Source and reason. No temporal priority, or failure to know it; differing remedial choices. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.15 Bidāya, English II, PDF pp.21

True simultaneity and ignorance of the earlier contract are different objects. Ibn Rushd qualifies his agreement report for the first; for the second he records rescission by the majority, a consummation exception for Mālik, and choice for the woman attributed to Shurayḥ and also ʿUmar b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz. His description of the choice opinion as anomalous belongs in the record. A modern preference for its apparent agency cannot erase that assessment or supply its missing rationale.

Rescission avoids declaring an unproved priority but dissolves both purported relations. A consummation exception attaches legal weight to a later ascertainable event. Choice assigns resolution to a person's act rather than recovering the missing temporal fact. These are different methods of managing uncertainty, not different claims about what the original chronology was.

The formative possibility is accepting the limits of knowledge instead of fabricating certainty. For witnesses and judges that means truthful testimony and an authorized remedy; for the parties it means understanding what remains undecided. Social pressure can distort all three. A developed city may provide more records yet also more opportunities to manipulate them. Q-CERT is therefore insufficient without a specified baseline and contrary proof. Upward, the master framework must distinguish ontic absence of priority, epistemic uncertainty, and remedial decision.

K042. Obstruction and recourse to public authority

Positions and qualifications.

Attribution Rule or argument Limit

Mālikī disagreement Whether the father has an exception is disputed Do not convert the reported baseline into an unlimited right against every paternal decision

Source and reason. Reported duty not to prevent a requested suitable marriage with appropriate dower; disputed paternal exception. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.15 Bidāya, English II, PDF pp.21, 22

The stated remedy moves a dispute from kin authority to the sultan when a suitable marriage at an appropriate dower is obstructed. The text also preserves disagreement about a paternal exception. “Suitable” and “appropriate” are not empty predicates; the next cases contest their content. Recourse cannot be understood without them.

The legal good is more specific than social harmony. It limits the use of a recognized office to prevent a relation the law allows under specified conditions. The guardian's formative task may be to surrender a personally desired outcome; the public official's is to distinguish a protected request from an unsupported complaint without reproducing family pressure. The woman's exercise of a remedy is a form of agency, not proof that the remedy is accessible in practice.

K043. Suitability limits compulsory power; it does not settle all questions of consent

Attribution Rule or argument Limit

The source recognizes resistance to an unsuitable spouse even when the guardian otherwise has compulsory authority. That is a limitation of the power, not a declaration that every marriage in the chapter requires the same mode of consent. For the minor case it is especially important not to turn this protection into a complete modern capacity doctrine.

Later Reliance m3.15 differentiates rival suitable choices: where compulsory authority exists the guardian's choice can prevail; where it does not, the woman's suitable choice does. This control shows why suitability, consent and the existence of ijbār have to be tracked separately. An unsuitable match may also be treated differently when the relevant parties agree, as m4.3 specifies. None of those later details silently fills the Bidāya's shorter formulation.

The possible alchemical operation is the disciplining of protective power by the actual good of its subject. Its contrary is defining “suitability” so that the guardian's preference is never challengeable. The institution needs a way to hear the affected person and judge the relevant facts; the text's recognition of a remedy does not establish that hearing's historical quality. Upward, beneficent authority must be analyzed together with its substantive limits, the standing to invoke them and the body empowered to enforce them.

K044. Religious conduct and the moral substance of suitability

Positions and qualifications.

Attribution Rule or argument Limit
General agreement with an exception reported Religion is considered in suitability A report from Muḥammad b. al-Ḥasan is excepted; do not claim unqualified unanimity
Mālikī examples Drinking, grave misconduct, unlawful wealth and frequent divorce oaths can ground refusal and judicial separation Examples concerning the father’s virgin daughter; their detailed thresholds remain to be checked

Source and reason. Religion as a suitability criterion; reported exception; concrete misconduct as a ground of refusal. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.16 Bidāya, English II, PDF pp.22

The text's consideration of religion has practical content. Its examples include a habitual drinker, a morally corrupt man, unlawful wealth and frequent use of divorce oaths. These can destabilize safety, maintenance, trust and the continuity of the relation. The school formulations identify defects relevant to matrimonial fitness; they do not prove every empirical allegation against a particular person.

This is one of the clearest places where virtue can enter legal reasoning before any subsequent habit is formed. The contemplated spouse's conduct matters in assessing whether a guardian has acted within the protective purpose recognized by the law. Yet the exact level of misconduct, proof and remedy needs further doctrinal work. Q-HARM cannot replace those thresholds with a general dislike of the match.

The formative mechanism is double: the suitor must make conduct answerable to the obligations he seeks, while guardian and judge must assess it without malice or faction. Reputation is useful evidence only under warranted conditions; accusation can become a weapon. A community rich in informal knowledge may detect habitual conduct but spread damaging rumor; an urban forum may formalize proof while missing private abuse. These are testable conditions, not a moral ranking of city stages. Vertical acknowledgement requires the person to embody obligations inwardly and outwardly; legal refusal or separation establishes only the public effect.

K046. Beauty, defects, provision and freedom are not one scale of worth

Positions and qualifications.

Attribution Rule or argument Limit

Mālik Freedom counts in suitability, with the emancipated woman’s option invoked A historical status rule, not a measure of spiritual worth

Source and reason. Different relevance of bodily defects, maintenance capacity and legal status; brief analogies rather than one uniform cause. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.16 Bidāya, English II, PDF pp.22, 23

The passage rejects beauty as a straightforward criterion while noting that defects giving an option of annulment can reintroduce a related consideration. It then treats inability to maintain and the status of freedom. These are heterogeneous: physical condition, performance of a continuing obligation, and a legal status produced by slavery cannot be placed on one metaphysical scale of human excellence.

The local contrast with Abū Ḥanīfa over the poor husband's consequence must be narrow. Qudūrī explicitly includes wealth in suitability, defining the relevant capacity through dower and maintenance; it also reports occupation as a consideration for Abū Yūsuf. Thus “Ḥanafīs ignore financial provision” would be false. Reliance m4.2, by contrast, excludes wealth as such while preserving other criteria. The distinct handbooks specify different legal objects and remedies.

The formative demand of provision concerns responsibility for an actual due, not display of affluence. Defect rules require attention to the affected parties and cannot license a general claim that disability reduces dignity. The freedom rule demands historical analysis of restricted agency, not a spiritual gloss on status. Civilizationally, material surplus may improve support or turn suitability into status competition. Upward, every proposed virtue interpretation must identify whether the predicate concerns capacity, obligation, preference or imposed status.

K047. Dower equivalence and a reversal of expected school styles

Positions and qualifications.

Attribution Rule or argument Limit

Ibn Rushd’s observation The alignment reverses what one might expect from the schools’ positions on guardianship A warning against fixed school temperaments

The same school labels now align differently. Mālik and al-Shāfiʿī allow the stated lower dower dispositions; Abū Ḥanīfa gives guardians a claim concerning an insufficient amount. Ibn Rushd notices the reversal: those granting the woman independent contracting power preserve family control over this financial term, while guardianship-requiring positions permit its reduction in the described cases. “Autonomy school” versus “authority school” cannot explain the sequence.

Qudūrī sharpens the Ḥanafī remedy: the guardians may object until the husband completes the appropriate dower or separation occurs. It separately permits a father or grandfather to set a lower dower for the minor daughter and restricts other guardians. Adult self-contracting and paternal contracting for a minor must therefore remain separate rows, not be averaged into one rule.

The good of protecting a financial due may compete with an adult's choice to accept less; family prestige may also enter the objection. Calling the reduction generosity would be premature where social pressure produces it. The alchemical question is whether an outward relinquishment expresses acknowledged freedom or concealed compulsion. Economic scarcity, alliance strategies and enforceability shape that outcome. Upward, recurring madhhab styles must emerge from a matrix of subject, power, term and remedy; a single permissive/restrictive axis fails even within these few pages.

K048. The guardian as prospective husband and the problem of self-dealing

Source and reason. Analogy with judge/witness acting in their own case versus prophetic marriage precedents and disputed generalizability. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.17 Bidāya, English II, PDF pp.23

The issue concerns an otherwise marriageable woman under the man's guardianship; it is not permission to marry a prohibited relative. The Shāfiʿī argument assimilates the conflict to a judge or witness acting in his own case. The Mālikī allowance is related to prophetic marriage examples concerning Umm Salama and Ṣafiyya. Their evidentiary force depends on circumstances and on whether a prophetic act is generalizable or specific. Ibn Rushd does not give an independent authentication of every reported circumstance.

Reliance m3.11 illustrates a guardian-cousin seeking marriage: another eligible representative or the judge acts on the woman's side. It also records a separate grandfather exception when representing both sides in a different configuration. This later control shows why “no person can ever act on both sides” would be too broad.

The virtue problem is conflict of interest. A person may sincerely intend a good marriage yet benefit from suppressing alternatives or construing consent favorably. Structural separation can protect both the woman and the officeholder; personal probity alone does not resolve the conflict. Civilizational specialization can supply an independent representative, but access and independence remain empirical questions. The Mūsā–Khiḍr limit applies directly: supposed inward knowledge of the match's goodness cannot replace the authority and permission the public rule requires.

K049. Witnesses: a condition at formation or before consummation?

The three principal authorities agree on some requirement of witnessing while differing over its time and legal characterization. Does witnessing form part of what constitutes the contract, or complete it before consummation? The question concerns the legal temporality of publicity, not simply whether publicity is useful. The later handbooks confirm witnesses at contracting for their respective Ḥanafī and Shāfiʿī formulations.

Witnesses turn a private undertaking into something others can attest. That can protect maintenance, succession and status against denial, but the passage does not enumerate every later consequence or equate witnessing with a modern register. K050. Two witnesses instructed to conceal: publicity as an end or a sufficient form

Positions and qualifications.

Attribution Rule or argument Limit
Three principal authorities Secret marriage is prohibited They disagree on what makes a marriage secret
Mālik Two witnesses instructed to conceal do not remove secrecy; the marriage is rescinded Witness presence alone does not secure the required publicity
Abū Ḥanīfa and al-Shāfiʿī The presence of the required witnesses removes the legal secrecy defect in this case Do not infer an endorsement of deceit or denial of every publicity good

Source and reason. Different definitions of secrecy; prescribed form versus prevention of denial and dispute. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.17 Bidāya, English II, PDF pp.24

The same event receives different legal characterizations: two people witness the contract but are instructed to conceal it. For Mālik this remains secret and is rescinded; for Abū Ḥanīfa and al-Shāfiʿī the witness requirement removes the specified secrecy defect. The claimed agreement against secrecy therefore does not settle the dispute. Its practical extension depends on the definition.

Ibn Rushd contrasts a prescribed form with prevention of the route to denial and dispute. This is a local sadd al-dharīʿa explanation: attestation or announcement blocks a foreseeable failure of public recognition. It is not the same operation as extending a word's general scope or comparing two objects by resemblance. The purposive construction also remains a legal construction, not an optional ethical improvement beyond law.

The alchemical difference concerns where accountability is secured: a determinate witnessed form, or a publicity condition not satisfied by deliberate concealment. Each needs scrutiny of actual operation. Two accessible trustworthy witnesses may secure claims with limited circulation; a public celebration may be remembered imprecisely. The source does not test those empirical alternatives. The upward result is that shared final goods underdetermine institutional means, while a legal definition can itself decide whether those goods are adequately represented.

For a Muslim marrying a protected non-Muslim woman it records a further disagreement over non-Muslim witnesses. Those control-source rules are not silently attributed to the shorter Bidāya passage.

Reliance m3.3 requires qualified witnesses but accepts apparent uprightness; its marked commentary explains the practical difficulty of requiring proof of inward rectitude for ordinary marriages. Thus the contrast is not “Ḥanafī practicality versus Shāfiʿī indifference to practicability.” Formal qualification can itself be determined through an administrable presumption.

Ibn Rushd does not let the dominant arrangement end the epistemic inquiry. He weakens an inference from the lack of a known opponent to the Ibn ʿAbbās report, records a transmitter problem in its raised prophetic form, and preserves Abū Thawr's dissent from witnesses as either validity or completion condition. The Muwaṭṭaʾ control is exact but narrower than a generic appeal to ʿUmar: report 1675 concerns one man and one woman as witnesses. That is not the same fact pattern as two qualifying male witnesses instructed to conceal. Its counterfactual threat and the Arabic law taqaddamtu fīhi require further textual control. Nyazee's “had they gone ahead” does not preserve the first-person expression. This commentary infers no general punishment from it. The separate announcement-and-drums report is attributed in the Bidāya; its hadith provenance has not been independently audited here.

The final lesson is methodological and civilizational. A public institution must both produce trustworthy acts and preserve trustworthy knowledge of its own warrants. Shared practice can become evidence, but absence of a known dissent is not automatically exhaustive consensus. The alchemical formation of the jurist includes resisting that shortcut. Our contiguous reading ends with this paragraph on Arabic p.18, before dower, not at the end of p.17.

Principles at this step.

Dower: obligation, generosity and the formation of a household

The dower sequence asks what must be given, when the claim becomes determinate, how it vests, who can relinquish it and how a court can know whether it has been discharged. These are different operations within one relation of owing. The chapter's scriptural language places that relation within a wider ethical field: a due is rendered; forgiveness has a possible object; affections need education; and adjudication must preserve claims that a person may freely surrender. K053, K055, K057, K064 and K067 now recover selected passages and commentaries before developing the comparative interpretation. This is a pilot across two verses and one hadith family, not a completed scriptural audit of dower.

Discernment, sustained will and affective conformity

From the ordered person to the household and public order

K053. An obligatory due can remain quantitatively undetermined

Bidāya, Arabic II, printed pages match PDF, PDF 18 Bidāya, English II, PDF 24, 25

Ibn Rushd’s stated reason or report: Reported agreement on the necessity of dower and impermissibility of contracting to omit it; Qurʾānic commands adduced.

Attribution Rule or argument Qualification
Agreement as reported Dower is necessary; parties cannot validly agree to omit its entitlement This does not prohibit a contract that leaves the amount unspecified
Qurʾānic warrants invoked Q4:4 and Q4:25 support the due The chapter later distinguishes naming, vesting, payment and waiver

The passage. commands that women receive their dowers as a gift due to them; taking any part back is permitted only where they freely relinquish it. The surrounding passage concerns orphans, marriage and the handling of vulnerable people’s property.

Its ethical argument. The moral issue is who can actually dispose of the wealth. A husband’s or guardian’s control of the transaction is not ownership of the woman’s dower. The qualification concerning her willing consent therefore matters as much as the initial command to pay: outward acquiescence obtained through shame or pressure would defeat the passage’s protection.

What the commentary explains. Ṭabarī preserves reports about guardians appropriating dowers, while preferring husbands as the immediate addressees. Ibn ʿĀshūr similarly places the verse within protection of weaker parties and warns against exploiting a woman’s shame or wish to please; even the difficulty of recovering a right can induce its apparent relinquishment. Thus the commentary concerns conditions of meaningful consent, not only a valid payment formula.

· ·

Operative principles: · ·

The chapter begins with a due, not a price list. Ibn Rushd cites the giving of women their marriage portions and the payment of their ujūr, then separately investigates amount, kind, postponement, full vesting, halving and disputes. This arrangement is conceptually important: existence of an obligation, determination of its object, maturity, discharge and evidentiary enforceability are different moments. A contract without a stated amount can preserve the entitlement; a stipulation eliminating it attempts something else. K070 returns to that difference through tafwīḍ.

The revealed address and its ethical texture. At , al-Ṭabarī explains niḥla as an obligatory gift and binding due. His treatment of a woman's remission distinguishes her willing disposition from injury or deception; the latter qualification appears in a report he transmits from Ibn ʿAbbās. This allows “giving” to name the manner and relational meaning of an obligation without making payment discretionary. (). The project’s inference is that formation begins by perceiving an obligation as another person's good, then giving it effect. A payment extracted by judgment still secures her entitlement; that outcome should not be confused with the payer's achieved generosity.

Reported social setting. Ṭabarī preserves accounts linking to guardians taking women's dower and to reciprocal marriage arrangements with little dower. He nevertheless prefers husbands as the addressees, arguing from the surrounding discourse. These reported settings sharpen the problem of appropriating another's due; they do not erase the exegetical disagreement or establish a single independently verified event. .

K054. Minimum dower and the relation between measure and worth

Bidāya, Arabic II, printed pages match PDF, PDF 18, 19 Bidāya, English II, PDF 25

Ibn Rushd’s stated reason or report: No maximum reported; minimum disputed through exchange and prescribed-worship characterizations.

Attribution Rule or argument Qualification

Al-Shāfiʿī, Aḥmad, Isḥāq, Abū Thawr, Medinan Successors and Ibn Wahb No prescribed minimum; something possessing value can suffice The scope and warrant of services are investigated separately
Mālik, well-known report One quarter gold dinar or three weighed silver dirhams; other goods valued by the three-dirham standard Another report permits valuation by either specified metal threshold
Abū Ḥanīfa Ten dirhams minimum The source links the amount to the disputed theft threshold
Other positions reported Five dirhams and forty dirhams Five is subsequently associated with Ibn Shubruma; forty is unnamed here

Operative principles: · ·

The first disagreement concerns whether a minimum should exist at all; the second concerns its amount. Ibn Rushd’s explanation gives dower a double aspect: exchange admits small and large amounts by consent, whereas a prescribed devotional element suggests a determined measure. The Arabic muwaqqat here concerns determination of quantity; the supplied English’s language of fixed time or duration confuses this dispute with the later question of postponement.

The spiritual issue cannot be settled by assuming that either more money means more honour or less money means greater detachment. A fixed minimum can mark an undertaking as consequential, yet it also places a monetary condition on entry. A consent-based amount can accommodate poverty and different circumstances, yet formal consent can coexist with pressure. These are rival institutional exposures, not evidence that one school cultivates generosity and the other avarice. No maximum in the reported rule likewise supplies no judgment that competitive display is virtuous.

K055. Timely clarification and the argument against a fixed minimum

Bidāya, Arabic II, printed pages match PDF, PDF 19, 20 Bidāya, English II, PDF 25, 26, 27

Ibn Rushd’s stated reason or report: Conflict between the Sahl report and the argument for quantitative determination; disputed premises about worship.

Attribution Rule or argument Qualification
No-minimum argument from Sahl b. Saʿd The request for even an iron ring would require clarification if a higher minimum were indispensable Ibn Rushd treats clarification at the time of need as decisive to the argument
Alternative constructions of the report The marriage is attributed to his Quranic knowledge or to teaching her A personal exception requires its own warrant; versions must be distinguished
Ibn Rushd’s criticism of the worship argument Both the devotional classification and the inference that every devotional obligation has a fixed quantity are contested Even accepting a devotional aspect does not settle a hybrid act’s quantum

Sandals report A small dower is adduced in support of the permissive amount Report authority and monetary value remain distinct questions

Operative principles: · · ·

This case directly activates the Ḍarūrī’s account of bayān: necessary clarification cannot be postponed beyond the occasion when the agent needs to act. The iron-ring instruction is therefore not merely an edifying story about simplicity. It bears on what an indispensable monetary requirement would have required the Prophet to disclose. The Muwaṭṭaʾ preserves the sequence of garment, iron ring and Quranic knowledge in report 1643; its wording should be compared with the teaching version rather than silently fused with it.

Ibn Rushd then tests the competing inference in stages. Even if dower has an aspect of worship, it does not follow that every such act requires a specified lower sum; some duties are satisfied by the least instance bearing the relevant name. Nor is this a purely devotional object. The evaluative power lies in the discriminations, not in a generalized preference for rationality over transmission: an authenticated explicit report fixing ten dirhams would change the evidentiary situation.

Aḥkām entry point. The downloaded Bulūgh al-marām places this narrative at report 979, PDF/printed pp.377–378, within marriage; the continuation records collection-specific wording. Its separate dower chapter begins on p.395. This demonstrates why searching only the anthology’s dower heading would miss a central source.

Recovering the prophetic encounter. Sahl's report links the attempted garment gift, the search for an iron ring, and Quranic knowledge within a single narrated encounter. Its circulation under different chapter headings makes it relevant to authority and contractual expression as well as dower. Compare al-Bukhārī 5135 and Muslim 1425a with Muwaṭṭaʾ 1643; the versions need separate wording records. (). (). Al-Nawawī reads the garment exchange as the leader's attention to people's welfare and gentle guidance: using the one garment for either person leaves the other without it. (). Here the ethical intelligence is attention to both parties' actual needs. Giving must be possible and useful to its recipient; the impulse to offer something does not settle that question. The iron ring then places effort and attainable provision within the encounter. This reading supplements Ibn Rushd's clarification argument with a pedagogy of responsible undertaking; it does not establish that every reported wording has identical legal implications.

Limits of the setting. The narrative concerns a woman presenting herself for marriage, another man's request, and his lack of material means. Its successive questions make the woman’s initiative, the suitor’s need and practicable provision visible before a rule is abstracted from the answer. The witnesses cited here do not fix an independent date or settle all differences between Quranic knowledge and teaching as the contractual consideration. The narrated encounter is established at the level of these reports; a fuller historical reconstruction remains open. .

K056. Why pleasure and affection defeat the theft-threshold analogy

Bidāya, Arabic II, printed pages match PDF, PDF 19, 20 Bidāya, English II, PDF 26, 27

Ibn Rushd’s stated reason or report: Equivocation in making-licit and absence of relevant meaning or indicated common ground.

Attribution Rule or argument Qualification
Analogy reported for minimum dower Money makes a bodily member licit in both marriage and theft punishment The proposed transfer imports the theft threshold
Ibn Rushd’s objection Punitive cutting involves injury and pain; marital intercourse involves pleasure and affection The word istibāḥa does not establish identity of practical meaning
Ibn Rushd’s methodological criterion Resemblance in meaning must be relevant to the ruling’s attachment; textual indication could supply a different route The passage denies the proposed analogy and does not supply such an indication here

Operative principles: · ·

This is one of the strongest passages for the project because the intended quality of a human relation enters Ibn Rushd’s assessment of the inference itself. The two acts share money and a language of permission. Yet cutting and intercourse differ precisely in the respect that matters: one inflicts loss and pain; the other concerns ladhdha and mawadda, pleasure and affection. The common wording conceals a disanalogy of practical meaning. A property cannot carry a rule simply because the commentator can name it in both objects.

The passage fits the Ḍarūrī’s criticism of a residual transfer lacking an indicated universal, but its own reasoning must remain visible: Ibn Rushd examines relevant likeness and the reason for the ruling’s attachment. Jamʿ’s original–branch–cause taxonomy can inventory the attempted analogy; it cannot vindicate the supposedly common cause. This is a concrete instance of ethical and anthropological understanding contributing to juristic criticism, not a moral commentary appended after the legal result.

The alchemical consequence is a reordering of measure. Money acquires its significance within a relation; it does not make qualitatively different relations equivalent. Applied inwardly, discernment resists the tendency to experience every due as a purchasable advantage. A marital transfer can acknowledge another person within a cooperative and affectionate life; a punitive threshold organizes a different action. This does not erase the exchange analogies that Ibn Rushd uses elsewhere in the chapter. It makes their pertinence a question to be answered each time.

For political philosophy the result is equally concrete. A city needs commensurable valuations to transact and adjudicate, but its institutions fail conceptually if monetary commensurability erases differences between punishment, kinship, labour and generosity. This case supplies an internal Rushdian reason to resist that flattening.

The practical object is temporally extended performance. The future service cannot be handed over like a coin: its duration, usefulness and completion must be recognized across time. The other concerns whether marriage may share hiring’s allowance of a benefit whose realization is future and therefore bears a kind of uncertainty. His notice of al-Aṣamm and Ibn ʿUlayya concerns opposition to hiring itself, not merely this dower variant.

Qudūrī controls the Ḥanafī attribution more closely: a free man’s own service or Quran teaching leads to mahr al-mithl, while a permitted marriage of an enslaved man on stipulated service retains that service. A commentary-based test of relational time. Ibn Ḥajar explains the advantage of naming dower in terms of reducing disputes and protecting the woman's claim, including the specified half upon pre-consummation divorce. Discussing teaching as dower, he proposes that uncertainty about its duration may be tolerated because continued companionship is normally envisaged. The latter is expressly a possible answer, not an uncontested ratio of marriage. (). This makes the proposed alchemical connection more precise. A household is an association through time: the beneficiary's good has to remain present to a skill-bearer's will across repeated acts. Legal specification can support that fidelity by making the promised benefit recognizable. Yet stable companionship is an anticipated condition, not a fact guaranteed by the contract; dissolution and failed performance are decisive tests. , which Ibn Rushd also invokes here, still requires its own contextual and tafsīr dossier.

Nyazee’s “frugality” does not convey the first term’s adversarial precision. The opposition concerns the normative character of dealings, not simply how economically one lives. It is explicit primary evidence that a relation’s ethos can influence its required legal morphology.

The contrast is nevertheless sharper when the rival protections are retained. Requiring full specification can protect the recipient against a disappointed expectation; allowing a middle standard can leave room for honourable performance without voiding the undertaking. Qudūrī permits a middle animal of a named species or its value, while an unspecified garment fails as a dower and yields mahr al-mithl. His editorial note distinguishes not knowing the species from merely omitting a description. Thus toleration is structured by what can still be recognized and valued. A deferred dower divides commitment from delivery. The debtor’s present resources and immediate desire no longer exhaust the relation: another person has a claim on his future conduct. A known date gives that claim a publicly anticipatable occasion; death or divorce ties it to the end of the relation or a person’s life. The distinction matters to planning, proof and recovery, even when both constructions permit delay. The source does not specify here every permissible length of delay, and the translation’s reference to an amount proportional to it should not supply a rule absent from the Arabic.

Civilizationally, deferment economizes present liquidity but requires durable memory, estate administration and enforceable priorities. Growing wealth can support those institutions; fiscal or political deterioration can impair them. The normative form therefore stores an obligation across time, while its actual protection depends on the city’s capacity to preserve and honour records. This is a precise feedback loop: fidelity sustains trustworthy credit relations, and trustworthy institutions make fidelity more practicable. Neither explains away the jurisprudential disagreement over which temporal forms are permissible.

The disagreement is about a legal threshold and its public representation. Qurʾānic mass and ifḍāʾ are read against Companion rulings on closing a door and lowering a curtain. The exceptions to valid seclusion show that the Ḥanafī construction is sensitive to the practical possibility of the relevant act; Ibn Abī Laylā’s broader rule gives seclusion a different legal reach.

The formative stakes cannot be described simply as inward intention versus outward form. Both accounts need outwardly workable criteria for a private relation. A broad proxy prevents later denial after an intimate setting has been established; requiring the act avoids treating opportunity as occurrence. The risks are opposed: evasion of a real due and imposition of a due whose event is denied. The wider arrangement protects marital privacy only if it can decide these consequences without demanding impossible public access to intimacy.

Muwaṭṭaʾ reports 1653–1655 preserve both the closed-curtain rulings and a distinction between his visiting her home and her coming to his. Qudūrī explicitly connects seclusion with the absence of impediments, then records Abū Ḥanīfa’s full-dower result for a castrated man’s seclusion. Those details resist a single physiological definition of the criterion. The civilizational question is which presumptions and accessible testimony permit private life and public justice to coexist. The passage. After specifying half the dower for divorce before consummation, adds: “To forgo is nearer to taqwā”; “Do not forget generosity between you”; and “God sees what you do.”

Its ethical argument. The half-share fixes what may be claimed. The ensuing appeal asks what each party will do with their own claim when the relationship ends. Taqwā here means resisting the reduction of a former partner to an adversary from whom the maximum must be extracted. Divine seeing reaches the intention and pressure behind an apparently generous settlement. This cannot authorize a guardian or judge to donate somebody else’s entitlement.

What the commentary explains. Ibn ʿĀshūr locates the verse within the sequence specifying the financial consequences of divorce before consummation. Ṭabarī’s report about Jubayr ibn Muṭʿim supplies an illustration of generosity through payment after divorce, not an independently established occasion of revelation. The ethical exhortation and the disputed identity of the person holding the marriage bond remain distinct questions. Al-Rāzī offers a formative explanation of why relinquishment is nearer to taqwā: someone who freely gives up a genuine right for God is further from wronging another by taking what is not theirs. He also understands generosity after separation as relieving the hurt each party may feel. This is a proposed mechanism linking practice to disposition, not proof that every waiver was free or beneficial. His separate appeal to male superiority in the same discussion is not a premise of this reconstruction.

· · ·

Operative principles: · ·

The source asks whether this prescribed division has an intelligible purpose of jabr, making good a disruption, or attaches to the named legal form. Under the first construction, who brings about the rupture helps explain who bears its cost. Under the second, determining that the act is divorce does more of the legal work. The disagreement over insolvency is especially revealing: the wife may initiate the demand, but the husband’s non-performance may occasion it. “Who acted?” and “whose conduct generated the predicament?” need not have the same answer.

Ibn Rushd employs a commercial comparison in discussing the woman’s affected situation. That vocabulary belongs in the record; it should neither be removed to modernize the source nor made a complete ontology of the person. The very next questions test where marriage resembles sale and where it does not. The compensatory rationale does not make the half-sum an exact measurement of emotional injury or erase the asymmetric legal powers involved.

The alchemical operation is rectification after failure. Desire for the original union may have ended, yet the agent remains responsible for consequences borne by another. Justice arrests the tendency to treat withdrawal of desire as disappearance of obligation. Generosity can qualify the manner of settlement, but the remedy first fixes an entitlement. Unlike habituation during an ongoing household, this operation orders the act of ending and preserves the possibility of subsequent social life.

Institutional classification matters because a party may gain financially by naming an event rescission rather than divorce, or by attributing its cause to the other. Competent judges, reliable procedural categories and evidence of the precipitating circumstances are therefore conditions of the remedy’s actualization. The upward lesson is that an alchemy of law must include repair, loss allocation and responsible termination, not only the consolidation of relations.

Half-dower within the whole verse. places the half-dower entitlement beside waiver, nearness to taqwā, remembrance of generosity and divine knowledge of acts. In his own exposition, al-Ṭabarī connects voluntary relinquishment with preferring what pleases God over appetite, and with readiness for obligatory obedience. He addresses both spouses and retains the half division when neither relinquishes a claim. (). The practical structure is therefore graduated: an enforceable allocation, an optional movement beyond it, and an inward orientation through which that movement may form the agent. The possibility of demanding one's due gives relinquishment a determinate object. A community that pressures only the vulnerable party to forgive destroys the symmetry of this ethical invitation. The formative question is not simply whether money moved, but whose will relinquished whose right, under what conditions, and toward what end.

Application distinguished from revelation. Ṭabarī illustrates generosity with report4199: Jubayr ibn Muṭʿim marries a daughter offered by Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ, divorces her and sends the dower, invoking generosity when questioned. In this passage the story illustrates conduct under the verse; it is not presented as the event that caused its revelation. The verse's legal situation—divorce before consummation after a specified dower—must likewise be distinguished from a separately authenticated occasion of revelation. .

An abstract instruction to return half cannot operate until law identifies what is being halved. Is it the thing as it now exists, its earlier value, or a claim whose subject has survived a change in the thing? Ibn Rushd’s account turns on the temporal structure of ownership. The same physical increase is shared under one construction and belongs to the woman under another because the original transfer is legally understood differently.

The formative difference is likewise determinate. Sharing change treats the period before final vesting as a relation of common exposure. Firm ownership assigns the woman the gain but also the relevant liability. Neither arrangement can be called generous merely because one party receives more in a selected example. A comparison must test both gain and loss, including wrongful damage as a separate case. Justice here is a proportionate relation between entitlement and exposure.

The verse can be read as permitting the husband to give what he could recover or as permitting a guardian to relinquish what the woman could claim. These are materially different acts even if both are called ʿafw. Ibn Rushd accordingly does more than list lexical alternatives: he notices that one construction introduces a new power over another’s right. The burden of establishing that power cannot be discharged merely by praising forgiveness.

The Muwaṭṭaʾ gives Mālik’s attribution directly in report 1650, associating the holder of the tie with the father of a virgin and the master of an enslaved woman. That control confirms the conflict rather than resolving it in favour of the interpretation preferred here.

The institutional issue is not marginal to that inward reading. Courts and witnesses determine whether the apparent act of generosity actually extinguishes a claim. Under concentrated kin power, a waiver may embody solicitude or silence the beneficiary. The legal alternatives distribute that exposure differently. The upward result is that the anthropology of giving requires a jurisprudence of giving powers: an alchemical interpretation becomes more exact, not less spiritual, when it attends to ownership and representation.

Generosity requires moral attention and a person entitled to give. Al-Qurṭubī reads the appeal against forgetting generosity with a reported variant emphasizing deliberate neglect; his commentary also retains the dispute about the holder of the marriage tie. (). The virtue term alone cannot settle that disputed subject. One person's generosity with another person's property is precisely what the jurisdictional disagreement requires us to investigate.

Ibn ʿAjība performs a different operation. After the outward commentary, his explicitly marked ishāra transposes separation into the disciple's detachment from self, distinguishes attraction before or after struggle, and discusses assigned devotions and contemplative orientation. (). That is a symbolic re-reading of the verse's relations. It does not explain why a spouse owes precisely half, and its discussion of devotions cannot be generalized into an exemption from prescribed duties. Its value here is comparative: the same verbal pattern can carry outward distribution and inward dispossession through distinct interpretive acts. The commentary must state which act it is making.

The institution must record the gift, its object, possession and the later separation. The distinction can matter disproportionately where property passes informally within kin households. Tafwīḍ shows how a legal undertaking can be sufficiently determinate for one effect while remaining open for another. This is a useful parallel to the Ḍarūrī’s distinction between general clarification and clarification at the point of practical need, although the analogy does not itself establish the marriage rule. Its formative possibility is trust in a continuing relation whose duties will receive appropriate specification. Its failure mode is the indefinite deferral of another’s claim under the appearance of trust. The subsequent rights to request fixation, receive a standard amount or separate are therefore part of the meaning of the permission. A civilization capable of flexible undertakings also needs procedures for bringing their open elements to a conclusion.

The source changes our understanding of form: determinacy is distributed across the life of an undertaking. It need not be exhausted at contracting, but it cannot remain arbitrary when performance or dissolution makes it consequential. ’s provision according to means also opens a distinct ethical question about honourable release, to be read with rather than collapsed into its half-dower rule.
