The exchange argument asks why payment should be owed where no counter-benefit was received. The report supplies a contrary determination for a marriage terminated by death. Ibn Masʿūd first gives a reasoned decision, after which a reported prophetic precedent confirms the result. Ibn Rushd endorses al-Muzanī’s methodological point about an established report’s priority. This is another reason not to read the chapter as progressively dissolving revealed form into an independently transparent account of benefit.

The supplied Arabic calls the reporting Companion Maʿqil b. Yasār al-Ashjaʿī; that naming needs collation rather than silent correction. It also prints mutʿa in the no-dower result, where further source checking is necessary. Muwaṭṭaʾ report 1646 gives Zayd b. Thābit’s no-dower decision and inheritance, without that additional payment; Qudūrī gives full comparable dower on death. Mukhtaṣar al-Qudūrī, printed p.147, PDF pp.150

The ethical issue is what a commitment generates beyond successfully received benefit. The school disagreement changes the widow’s share relative to the estate and other heirs. It therefore cannot be reduced to generosity toward a single beneficiary: an additional payment also affects others. The jurist’s virtue lies in recognizing all those relations while permitting a stronger warrant to overturn an initially plausible explanation. The civilizational requirements are estate administration, preservation of the marriage’s terms and reliable transmission of the governing report.

Operative principles: · ·

The same moral vocabulary—correcting a wrong—can conceal opposed operations. One rescinds the relation; another preserves it while replacing the defective financial specification. The latter treats the marriage as a composite whose good need not be destroyed by every defect in its dower. The former gives the invalid term a deeper constitutive reach. Consummation introduces a further question about whether an accomplished relation changes the appropriate remedy.

Ibn Rushd’s suggested distinction is a particularly important attribution test. It is his reconstruction from principles, not a recalled Mālikī ruling. The commentary must preserve that epistemic status. Qudūrī directly confirms the valid marriage/comparable-dower result for wine or pig; Reliance distinguishes a valid from an invalid specification in m8.5. Mukhtaṣar al-Qudūrī, printed p.147, PDF pp.150 Reliance m8.5, PDF pp.551–552

The alchemical difference is between removing an obstructive element while preserving an ordered relation and dissolving a relation whose form is judged vitiated. It is explanatory only when the legal ground of severability is specified. Spiritual language about purification cannot choose the remedy. Socially, replacing a term can preserve family stability and the woman’s claim, but it may also reduce incentives to avoid invalid terms; rescission may enforce care in contracting while imposing substantial collateral losses. The city’s judicial craft lies in executing the chosen remedy accurately and preserving the distinctions on which it depends.

The test case combines the purchase of an enslaved person from the woman with her dower in one sum. The monetary payment is physically one act but legally answers two purposes. Its uncertainty concerns allocation, not necessarily ignorance of the total. Treating every mixed payment as a simple exchange would therefore miss the practical object.

The intellectual operation is separation of the reasons for a transfer. The affective operation is willingness to let another’s entitlement be identified rather than buried within a bargain. That can serve both parties: a recipient knows what is hers by the marital undertaking, while the payer knows the consequences if the sale or marriage later fails. The permissive position instead requires confidence that the composite remains sufficiently intelligible under its adopted standards.

The operative suspicion is that the father’s benefit has been financed by reducing the daughter’s dower. The timing distinction therefore concerns the structure of bargaining and representation, not an assertion that fathers are invariably self-interested. Muwaṭṭaʾ reports 1647–1648 confirm the contract-time gift’s attribution to the daughter if she claims it.

The alchemical operation is disentanglement of care from possessiveness. Its public correlate is a rule assigning the benefit to the person whose relation supplied the occasion for it. The difference between that legal redirection and inward detachment matters: the woman can recover the gift even if the intermediary resents the result. At city level, the case anticipates a general institutional problem of conflicted mediation, while the exact rule remains local to its textual and doctrinal warrants.

A woman may have received a thing without acquiring the entitlement promised, because someone else owns it, or may receive an impaired thing. The defect lies in the transfer’s legal or practical adequacy. Preserving the marriage while correcting the payment recognizes that the existing relation may survive the failure of one performance.

The alchemical operation is the replacement of self-exculpation by responsibility for making the other whole under the adopted standard. It differs from generosity: restitution responds to an unfulfilled due. It also differs from reversing a transaction as if no time had passed. The available remedies select what counts as equivalence after failure, and Ibn Rushd preserves disagreements about that measure.

The sum is contingent on a fact that affects the anticipated household. The record’s difficult Abū Ḥanīfa sentence must not be silently regularized to fit an intuitively expected result. Institutionally, the pertinent condition is information about existing marriages and a forum able to establish it. The same financial form can protect a considered preference or merely price a concealed disadvantage after discovery. The civilizational analysis must therefore include access to knowledge as well as ability to pay. An ethical interpretation cannot repair a damaged source attribution by guessing which result would best serve that good.

K078. Mahr al-mithl: likeness, custom and social valuation

Al-Shāfiʿī Women among her agnatic relatives Reliance later supplies fallback groups and contextual qualities

Operative principles: · · ·

An objective comparison is not necessarily a universal quantity. It can depend on a socially maintained class of relevantly similar persons. The legal question is which similarities matter. The practical question is what those women’s dowers actually were. Ghazālī’s taḥqīq al-manāṭ illuminates the latter, while choosing the comparator is prior to it.

Qudūrī creates a real attribution problem: his main text specifies sisters, paternal aunts and paternal cousins, with age, beauty, wealth, intellect, religion, locality, period, virginity and nonvirginity among the comparative features. It excludes mother and maternal aunt unless of the pertinent tribal group. Reliance m8.8 begins with paternal female kin but gives maternal and local fallbacks and assesses additional characteristics. Neither handbook supports reading Bidāya’s short statements as exhaustive doctrine. Mukhtaṣar al-Qudūrī, printed p.149, PDF pp.152 Reliance m8.8, printed pp.534–535, PDF pp.552–553

The virtue at issue is equitable attention to likeness and difference. Its deformation is allowing inherited prestige or wealth to pass unexamined as a complete measure of persons. The relevant legal valuation measures an entitlement within an established practice; its social criteria still require criticism. Urban specialization can provide richer comparison data and also intensify positional competition. The upward lesson is that custom mediates determination through social valuation, so its formative effects must be tested rather than inferred from the word “custom.”

K079. Disputed amount: divergent procedures for a single claim

Bidāya, Arabic II, printed pages match PDF, PDF 29, 30 Bidāya, English II, PDF 38, 39

Attribution Rule or argument Qualification

Operative principles: · ·

Ibn Rushd’s example is a disagreement between one hundred and two hundred. The formulas do different work: an oath tests an accountable assertion; plausibility uses circumstantial knowledge; a standard dower supplies a substitute quantum; rescission terminates a relation whose terms cannot be established. A court cannot combine these casually without changing the rule.

The formative exercise for litigants is to state a claim they are prepared to own under oath and public consequence. For the judge it is to distinguish evidence from familiarity or preference. An oath can intensify responsibility before God within a public procedure without making the judge know whether the speaker is inwardly truthful. The vertical orientation is thus internal to the act’s seriousness, while its judicial function remains bounded.

Civilizational dependence is clear: the plausibility routes require trustworthy knowledge of local payments; an oath-based route still requires recognized authority and accepted consequences of refusal. The relational outcome also matters—one construction preserves the marriage by replacement, another permits its dissolution. The following two cases analyse the reasoning behind these differences rather than merely attaching “justice” to all of them.

Attribution Rule or argument Qualification

Operative principles: · ·

The general maxim assigning proof to a claimant and an oath to a denier does not automatically classify the parties. A person can acknowledge one relation and deny a further liability; both persons can deny the other’s account. The practical object of each assertion must therefore be analysed before the general rule is applied. This is a particularly clear instance of general practical science requiring determinate knowledge of a particular controversy.

The upward result is methodological: definitions and classifications are themselves practical operations. A legal science is general not because it avoids human circumstances but because it disciplines the kinds of circumstance that can affect a judgment. Scholarly malaka includes learning to perform this description accurately under pressure; the city depends on that acquired competence when private recollections conflict.

Bidāya, Arabic II, printed pages match PDF, PDF 30, 31 Bidāya, English II, PDF 39, 40

Operative principles: · ·

The remedial disagreement turns on the place of a financial term in the whole relation. If its failure undermines the undertaking in the manner assumed for sale, rescission follows. If marriage can remain valid without a named dower, a standard amount can repair the failure. The shared aim of ending controversy does not determine which route should be chosen.

Ibn Rushd then questions an additional prohibition on settlement. An analogy to liʿān cannot securely impose irreversible separation when the relevant consequence in the proposed original is itself disputed. This is a second kind of inferential criticism alongside K056: the problem is not only the likeness between objects but also the stability of the supposed original rule.

The formative stakes are the discipline of ending an argument and the capacity to repair cooperation. Legal finality can make resolution possible; excessive finality can prevent parties from reaching a later intelligible agreement. In civilizational terms, a forum needs both authoritative closure and a warranted account of when settlement remains open. The alchemical operation is reconstitution under a corrected measure, where the adopted law permits it, rather than an indefinite struggle for vindication.

A relationship’s duration can make performance plausible without proving it. The disciples’ customary explanation reveals a variable premise: entry into married life signifies prior payment only where the relevant sequence is normally followed. The source thus supplies an explicit point at which a legal presumption depends on social practice. Ibn Rushd nevertheless prefers the woman’s statement, retaining the distinction between a reason for the rival rule and endorsement of it.

The alchemical connection is fidelity made answerable. The debtor’s inward conviction that he is responsible is insufficient when the act of discharge is disputed. A receipt, credible witness or other accepted proof can preserve the truth of a generous or dutiful performance across time. Recordkeeping can therefore serve the relation rather than express mistrust of it. Conversely, using familiar custom to extinguish an unpaid claim converts the appearance of social order into a shelter for injustice.

A thing can matter to the recipient in ways not exhausted by its monetary value. The source’s example opposes an enslaved person to an animal as the alleged dower. The dispute is therefore about the identity of the promised object, not merely the amount of one agreed currency. Once agreement about that identity cannot be recovered, a standard dower may preserve the relation, or the failure may justify rescission under the relevant conditions.

Faithful performance requires attention to what was actually undertaken. The alchemical movement is from the giver’s unilateral estimation—“this should be enough”—to recognition of the other’s legally relevant expectation. A replacement rule then explains when law can resolve the impasse without recovering the original object. The city supplies the adjudicative craft and comparison standards that make such repair possible.

This is another limit on a uniform madhhab temperament. The Mālikī variants allocate priority differently, and the practical significance of consummation recurs without carrying one identical consequence in every case. School style must be inferred from a controlled series of differences, not from the philosophical attractiveness of one remedy.

Operative principles: · · ·

The final dower paragraph returns to time, now as a disputed term and as a question of payment’s proper occasion. A named amount, a vested claim and a presently enforceable demand are different legal relations. Disagreement about one cannot simply be treated as denial of all three.

The chapter ends before the heading al-rukn al-thālith: fī maʿrifat maḥall al-ʿaqd, the investigation of who may be married and the impediments to marriage. The dower sequence has traced a complete life of an obligation—from necessity and specification through performance, alteration, rupture, waiver and proof. That is the appropriate unit for its civilizational and alchemical interpretation: a relation sustained and transformed across time, not a sequence of unrelated moral labels.

What this sequence changes in the master framework

First, the passage provides a direct test of perspectival plurality. Ibn Rushd records positions, reconstructs arguments and sometimes prefers one. Differences can disclose aspects of a practical object without being equally true. Second, a legal cause is not a complete anthropology: minority, virginity, kinship and solicitude become criteria through contested argument. Third, authority to act for another requires its own warrant; neither a benevolent purpose nor a metaphysical hierarchy supplies it automatically.

Fourth, the routes from law to formation differ. K001 concerns the agent's condition; K002 a practice of religious recollection; K003 the relation between a wrong and a preserved legal result; K006–K007 legally significant signs; K009–K018 substituted decision-making and its limits; K019–K020 finality and temporally distributed assent. A single chain from command to habit to virtue cannot describe all these without intermediate branches.

Sixth, the guardianship and witness sequence separates duty from jurisdiction, domain competence from general prestige, priority from validity, publicity from proof, and remedy from historical accessibility. These distinctions correct the architecture itself: no general aspiration to care or public order supplies all those relations. K047 also directly defeats an unqualified permissive-versus-restrictive school typology.

Finally, inward realization remains a possible ultimate orientation of responsible action, not an effect established by a marriage's legal validity. The Mūsā–Khiḍr image fixes that boundary: a representative or judge cannot claim hidden providential knowledge to replace the evidence, permission or jurisdiction required for a public act.

The dower sequence adds three corrections. An obligation can exist before its amount is determined; payment, ownership, vesting and proof have different temporal structures; and generosity presupposes a person entitled to dispose of the good. Scriptural commentaries also establish an ethical field wider than the enforceable minimum. That field can educate perception and desire while leaving the technical inference answerable to its own evidence. The comparative framework now includes affective conformity and fidelity through time, alongside discernment and concentration.

Source checks still open in this bounded draft

The new source register preserves the unresolved dower attributions, variant names and editorial discrepancies. Qudūrī PDF148–151, Reliance PDF535–542 and Muwaṭṭaʾ PDF495 provide targeted new controls; earlier consultation controls remain. Qudūrī settles the immediate father/grandfather qualification of the puberty option, but a procedural school audit remains open. The paternal/grandpaternal compression in the Bidāya, K013’s scope qualification and K019’s unclear Arabic sentence remain unresolved. New priorities are the contradiction concerning an enslaved guardian (K027), the difficult explanation of al-Mughīra’s ranking (K032), and the precise scope of the financial suitability contrast (K046). Report authentication is recorded as Ibn Rushd presents it, not independently established here.

The philosophical interpretation has been argued case by case, but no historical practice archive has yet verified the proposed effects. Control-source propositions beyond the Bidāya boundary are labeled comparisons and are not counted as newly completed Bidāya rules. The next contiguous task is impediments beginning on Arabic II31, integrating the already targeted illness passage II46–47 without double counting. The scriptural pilot must first be expanded to the remaining dower evidence and then carried back to K001–K052; five enriched groups do not constitute a complete hadith/tafsīr audit.

Part III.B. Marital rights, dissolution and household justice

Detailed social-law draft, revision 6. The retained M001–M011 dossier has its bounded source at Arabic II 54–56, beginning at the heading on marital rights on p.54 and stopping before nursing on p.56. It corresponds to English II, printed pp.63–66, PDF pp.67–70. M001–M011 are working question groups. They retain the disagreements in this passage but are not a certified audit of every elementary proposition, nor a commentary on the whole marriage book. The Arabic images at pp.54–56 have been checked against the OCR and the principal English parallels. A targeted illness-divorce reconstruction at II82–83 is integrated below; it is separate from the M-group census and does not complete the divorce book.

The household as a practical and political object

The household is neither merely a site for training the husband nor a small state whose head owns its members. In this passage, it is a legally differentiated relation: a wife has claims; a husband has duties whose incidence and measure are disputed; provision can depend on capacity, absence, status and institutional determination; time can itself be apportioned justly. This interpretation begins with Ibn Rushd’s four inquiries concerning maintenance: when it begins, its amount, its recipient and its obligor. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.54–55

The horizontal good is not an unspecified increase in welfare. It is the lawful securing of food, clothing, housing and relational fairness for particular persons. The formative good is learning to give an enforceable due even when desire, convenience or household power pull elsewhere. These can diverge: payment can preserve a right without making the payer generous; inward benevolence can coexist with withholding the precise entitlement. The alchemical operation must therefore be described both personally and relationally—desire becomes responsibility, while dependency becomes a recognized claim rather than a mere appeal to favor.

The chapter also contains difficult historical institutions. Slavery, unequal marital authority and marriage involving minors form part of the juristic problem-space. Describing how a rule operates within them does not establish their justice. A virtue interpretation that makes those asymmetries disappear would fail precisely where the project needs moral and political scrutiny.

Dissolution and inheritance: testing prevention against legal coherence

The later illness-divorce passage is a necessary control on the household analysis, although the full divorce book remains unfinished. A husband gives an irrevocable divorce in the illness from which he dies. Ibn Rushd reports Mālik and others retaining the wife's inheritance, while al-Shāfiʿī and others deny it. Among those retaining it, Abū Ḥanīfa, his associates and al-Thawrī limit it to the waiting period; Aḥmad and Ibn Abī Laylā retain it until remarriage; Mālik and al-Layth retain it beyond both. These conditions materially change whose estate claim survives and for how long. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.82–83

Ibn Rushd expressly identifies disagreement over sadd al-dharāʾiʿ: divorce may be used to deprive the wife of inheritance. The preventive argument recognizes an incentive and blocks its intended benefit. The contrary argument demands coherence between the dissolution of marriage and its legal consequences: how can some effects of divorce coexist with selected effects of marriage? The question is not whether one party values justice and the other values words. They dispute the authority and structure of a remedy. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF p.83

The local distinctions remain sharper than a single “anti-evasion” label. Limitation to the waiting period connects the surviving claim to a continuing marital effect; limitation by remarriage invokes the concern about inheritance from two husbands. When she requests divorce or exercises delegated power, Abū Ḥanīfa's reported denial of inheritance responds differently to the suspicion; al-Awzāʿī distinguishes delegated exercise from the husband's divorce; Mālik's reported equivalence preserves her claim. Ibn Rushd rejects the claim of Companion consensus in view of Ibn al-Zubayr's opposition and calls the expansive asymmetry very contrary to the governing principles. We must preserve that judgment, not treat every variant as an equally successful realization of protective justice. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF p.83; Arabic image controls Nyazee II, PDF p.103, compressed and partly repetitive parallel

The practical-causal question is whether this conduct is a credible route to deprivation. The teleological issue is protection of lawful claims against manipulation, balanced against coherence and limits on imposed succession rights. A semantic universal determining the remedy is not supplied in this passage. Treating prevention as an inferred intention in every individual case would blur a general prophylactic arrangement with fact-specific proof. Conversely, preserving a claim does not show that every husband intended wrongdoing. The breadth of Mālik's reported rule is itself part of Ibn Rushd's criticism.

Hind’s complaint: what adequate support requires

The report belongs directly to the maintenance questions below. supplies a related Qurʾānic sequence: provision according to recognized right, no burden beyond capacity, and no harm to either parent through the child. The relationship between that nursing context and a particular maintenance rule must still be argued.

Setting. In Muslim1714, Hind complains that Abū Sufyān does not provide enough for her and her children, and asks about taking without his knowledge.

The passage. The answer permits taking what suffices for her and the children according to what is recognized as appropriate. Need and an intelligible measure constrain the permission.

Its ethical argument. The complaint makes an otherwise concealed household deprivation publicly speakable. The answer protects sustenance without licensing unlimited appropriation. Justice therefore needs both an enforceable claim and judgment about its adequate satisfaction; calling the husband generous would not supply what was missing.

What the commentary explains. Nawawī identifies maintenance of wife and dependent children, adequacy, recourse to custom where no amount is fixed, and the permissibility of stating another’s fault for a genuine complaint or legal question. He frankly notes that the wording challenges his school’s fixed allotments for wives. He then asks whether the Prophet acted as a mufti or judge, preferring fatwā: the answer is conditional on the questioner’s account being true. A competing judicial reading affects whether another woman needs a judge’s authorization. He rejects using the episode as proof of judgment against a legally absent defendant merely because Abū Sufyān did not attend the conversation.

·

M001. Maintenance and clothing are rights, not optional generosity

Primary legal structure. Ibn Rushd reports agreement that maintenance and clothing are among a wife’s rights over her husband. He cites the scriptural provision of food and clothing according to what is recognized as appropriate, the corresponding prophetic statement and the direction to Hind to take what suffices for her and her child. The passage then divides maintenance into its four inquiries. There is no supplied sabab for an agreement to invent. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF p.54; Bidāya, English II, PDF p.67, printed p.63

Discernment and object. The universal practical question is the nature of an obligation grounded in recognized evidence; the particular question is this spouse’s entitlement under its conditions. Sufficiency, appropriateness and a determinate allocation of duty belong to its morphology. The presence of a beneficiary changes the analysis: sincerity matters to the actor’s perfection, but a beneficiary’s food cannot await proof of that sincerity.

Principles in this argument. The maintenance obligation here is established by the reported substantive evidence. The Ḍarūrī classification locates that rule within particular practical knowledge; the later distinction between ruling, condition and impediment helps keep an owed right separate from optional generosity. Neither classification alone establishes this entitlement.

M002. When support begins: enjoyment or the restriction created by marriage?

Positions and explicit sabab. Mālik’s reported rule links the onset to consummation or being called to consummate, with the wife capable of intercourse and the husband mature. Abū Ḥanīfa and al-Shāfiʿī impose maintenance on a non-mature husband where the wife is mature. Where he is mature and she is a minor, Ibn Rushd gives two Shāfiʿī reports, one like Mālik’s and another granting maintenance without that qualification. The stated disagreement concerns whether maintenance is due because of istimtāʿ or because she is maḥbūsa ʿalā al-zawj, with the absent or sick husband supplying the comparison. These are the historical categories, not a recommendation concerning minors. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF p.54; Bidāya, English II, PDF p.67, printed p.63

What differs philosophically. On the first account, the juridically relevant relation is tied more closely to availability for marital enjoyment. On the second, the marriage’s restriction upon the wife supplies a basis that can persist without actual enjoyment. The distinction is between two accounts of why this duty attaches; it should not be embellished into an unsupported claim that one school defines marriage wholly as exchange and another wholly as companionship.

Operation, virtue and institutions. Each view disciplines an inference from relational benefit or restriction to a corresponding burden. For the husband or estate administrator, justice requires identifying whether the condition obtains; for the jurist, precision prevents a general call to care from obscuring the actual legal trigger. The principal risk of the enjoyment account is construing support as a reward at another’s discretion; the principal risk of the restriction account is naturalizing the restriction instead of examining it. These are critical questions for interpretation, not Ibn Rushd’s explicit verdicts.

The civilizational variable is the distribution of support where the person legally charged may lack ordinary agency or earning power. Kin, guardian and judge cannot be silently merged. Prosperity may make provision feasible; poverty exposes the gap between the existence of a claim and available means. The vertical interpretation is bounded by the same problem: language of acknowledged order cannot itself prove a contested status arrangement just. This case forces the master theory to account for whose freedom and vulnerability a formative rule presupposes.

Principles in this argument. The competing relations—enjoyment and restriction created by marriage—are candidates for the legally relevant ground. This is analytically closer to finding that ground than merely deciding whether an already agreed criterion occurs. The researcher must first recover the disputed grounds. Goods may already inform their assessment, but our preferred virtue story cannot substitute for the missing warrant. A comparison between legal relations is not proved to be semantic extension until an indicated universal is identified.

Subsidiary maxims. The contract-substance maxim adds a later question: what juridical relation has actually been undertaken? It cannot decide the enjoyment/restriction dispute by renaming marriage, and its purpose language must be kept distinct from an unexpressed private wish.

M003. Fixed quantity or contextual adequacy?

Positions and sabab. Mālik, followed here by Abū Ḥanīfa, does not regard the amount as a fixed legal quantity; the conditions of husband and wife, places, times and circumstances matter. Al-Shāfiʿī’s reported quantities are two mudds for the affluent, one and a half for the intermediate and one for the person in straitened circumstances. Ibn Rushd identifies competing assimilations: feeding in expiation is quantified, while clothing is not. The disagreement is not simply “reason against revelation”; it concerns which legally established comparison governs this obligation. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF p.54; Bidāya, English II, PDF p.67, printed p.63

Upward and downward links. Simon’s practical science/prudence distinction helps explain why the general obligation and its situated discharge are not identical. Aquinas’ distinction between conclusion and determination supplies a comparison for the need to make a general good actionable, but it does not decide which analogy is authoritative in Ibn Rushd’s dispute. Downward, the operative activities are assessing means and need, obtaining provisions and resolving disagreement; their success needs reliable information and institutions. Simon, Critique of Moral Knowledge, PDF pp.28–31, printed pp.8–11; Aquinas, Treatise on Law, PDF pp.37–38, I–II q.95 a.2

Principles in this argument. Two inquiries must be separated. The first chooses between fixed measure and adequacy; the second determines what is adequate after that rule is adopted. Ghazālī explicitly uses maintenance of relatives to explain the latter operation, taḥqīq al-manāṭ. This is a close comparison, not proof that his example settles spousal maintenance. The later custom maxim can organize contextual assessment; it cannot defeat a school’s contrary fixed-measure argument by itself.

M004. Service and housing: how far does provision extend?

Positions. Most jurists in the account require support for a servant where the wife is of a condition not to serve herself; another view assigns household service to the wife. Among those requiring provision, one servant and two are reported, the latter where her situation requires two, attributed to Mālik and Abū Thawr. Ibn Rushd says he knows no legal evidence for requiring this provision except analogy between ikhdām and iskān. Housing is supported through the text concerning the revocably divorced wife. Preserve his limited statement rather than presenting the analogy as an independently established demonstration. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.54–55; Bidāya, English II, PDF pp.67–68, printed pp.63–64

Object and formative operation. The object is assistance within a household and the cost assigned to it, not merely the wife's appetite for comfort. The rule can recognize material limits and a socially intelligible standard of provision. It can also preserve an inherited hierarchy of labor. The virtue analysis therefore needs the provider’s justice, the beneficiary’s practical needs and the position of the person doing the work. The source does not here supply a full law of that worker’s rights; that omission must lead to comparison with the relevant labor/status books rather than an imagined harmonious organism.

Under conditions of specialization and surplus, household support can involve additional workers; under deprivation the question becomes allocation of burdens and realistic means. The political danger is turning a status-sensitive duty into a universal sanctification of luxury. The vertical end requires ordering the whole relation toward justice, including the worker, rather than interpreting service to a privileged person as inherently sanctifying. This case limits the organic metaphor: cooperation must be assessed from each affected position.

Principles in this argument. The extension from provision to service or housing needs its particular legal warrant. The Ḍarūrī’s ranked indications prevent “both are useful to the household” from becoming a sufficient analogy. Once an entitlement and its measure are established, local conditions may enter the assessment of its fulfillment. No particular expression indicating a universal entitlement to every useful household service has been established here; the account must retain that gap.

M005. Nushūz and the continuity of a claim

Positions and explicit cause. Ibn Rushd reports agreement for the free wife who is not nāshiz, majority denial of maintenance in nushūz, and an opposing group retaining it. His cause is conflict between the general statement of support and an implication drawn from maintenance as corresponding to marital enjoyment. The general formulation includes both conditions; the inferential account excludes the disputed one. This passage does not give an exhaustive definition or proof procedure for nushūz. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF p.55; Bidāya, English II, PDF p.68, printed p.64

Practical object and stakes. The issue is whether a financial entitlement continues when a legally relevant relational condition fails. It must not be rewritten as permission to withhold food whenever a spouse is dissatisfied. Identifying the condition, who may establish it and what counts as sufficient evidence are separate legal tasks. Here the distinction between universal wording and inferred purpose protects the analysis from simply choosing the morally appealing description.

The family’s place within ʿumrān matters because access to alternate support and impartial adjudication changes exposure to coercion. Kin protection may help or align against the claimant; administrative concentration may supply a forum or strengthen the powerful spouse. Maritain’s refusal to absorb the person wholly into the polity supplies a comparative limit applicable also to household totalization. Divine accountability intensifies the obligation to distinguish a true due from an asserted prerogative; it supplies no private knowledge of guilt. Maritain, Person and Common Good, PDF pp.14–17

Principles in this argument. Generality of the support evidence and the proposed dependence of support on a marital relation are distinct routes of argument. Do not rename the latter automatically mafhūm al-mukhālafa: that technical inference concerns an exclusion from a textual qualification. Ghazālī’s rejection of a bare contrary inference is a control on classification, not an additional proof of either maintenance position.

M006. The enslaved wife: competing claims upon one person’s life

Reported variants and cause. Within the Mālikī discussion Ibn Rushd lists maintenance like that of the free wife, no maintenance, maintenance if she comes to the husband rather than he to her, maintenance during the time she comes, and maintenance where he is free rather than enslaved. The well-known view is the first. The conflict is between general entitlement and analogy with the master’s responsibility for the person whose service he uses; a divided allocation also follows because the two relationships involve different benefits. Ibn Ḥabīb requires the master of the married woman to allow her to come to her husband every four days. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF p.55; Bidāya, English II, PDF p.68, printed p.64

Multiple viewpoints. For the wife, the issue is subsistence and access to married life under constrained agency. For the husband, it is the incidence of a duty where access and household presence are divided. For the master, the legal account links use and support. For the judge, it is the allocation and enforcement of responsibilities without leaving the person unsupported between them. The variants must remain visible: time, movement and the husband’s status are actual legal differences, not incidental illustrations.

Principles in this argument. The general address competes with a restriction inferred from the wife’s divided obligations and availability. The analyst must identify the proposed specifying proof and the relation it preserves before interpreting the result as protection or exclusion. Neither the universality of human worth nor a historical status label supplies that legal specification by itself. This is a general-address/specification dispute; it need not be classified as a transfer from one case to another.

M007. The enslaved husband: duty and restricted property powers

Primary content. Ibn al-Mundhir is reported as finding agreement among those whose opinions he preserved that the enslaved husband owes maintenance. Ibn al-Muṣʿab, among Mālik’s followers, denies it. The cause is the general obligation in tension with the enslaved man’s restricted disposition of property. This is a qualified report of surveyed agreement alongside an explicit dissent, not an unqualified consensus that erases the dissent. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF p.55; Bidāya, English II, PDF pp.68–69, printed pp.64–65

Mechanism and good. The problem asks how a person can bear a marital obligation within a status limiting financial agency. It differs from M006: there the debate distributes provision among beneficiaries of service; here the conflict concerns the obligor’s capacity to act financially. The required goods are provision for the wife and intelligibility of the husband’s duty. Neither can be established by calling him responsible while omitting the powers and resources needed for performance.

In the larger theory, this is a downward test of universal obligation. Agency is not merely an inward intention; institutions can limit the means of discharging a duty. Teaching fidelity without addressing those limitations risks turning formation into an impossible demand. The comparison with al-Ḍarūrī’s rejection of impossible obligation is a question to investigate, not proof that Ibn Rushd resolves the doctrinal conflict through that principle here. Ibn Rushd / Akl edition, PDF pp.158–161, §§54–59

Its civilizational location concerns the constitution of property and dependency across household and public law. An expanded social commentary must connect the capacity books and actual administration to this rule. The vertical demand for acknowledgement cannot replace that work. The feedback is that the ordered person and ordered institution must be studied together: failure to perform may originate in constrained powers as well as defective will.

Principles in this argument. Generality of an address, capacity to act and legal powers over property require separate treatment. The Ḍarūrī’s rejection of impossible obligation informs the capacity question, but does not by itself establish which property powers an enslaved husband legally possessed or extinguish a wife’s claim.

M008. The absent husband and the need for public determination

Positions and limit. Most jurists impose maintenance on the absent husband; Abū Ḥanīfa’s reported position makes it depend upon imposition by the sulṭān. Ibn Rushd postpones the disagreement over whose statement prevails in a dispute about provision to the book of judgments. He does not supply a separate explicit sabab for the absent-husband disagreement here. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF p.55; Bidāya, English II, PDF p.69, printed p.65

Practical meaning. Absence creates a division between the person who bears the burden, the claimant who needs support and the institution able to recognize the claim. The verse or report establishing maintenance does not itself determine disputed payment. Conversely, the requirement of public imposition cannot be expanded without further evidence into a denial of every moral responsibility during absence. The present report is too compressed to settle all questions about accrued claims and procedure.

Principles in this argument. Where this short passage does not state a complete sabab, no borrowed principle should fill the gap as Ibn Rushd’s explanation. Ghazālī’s distinction between rule and instance supplies an analytical question for the public decision: which facts establish absence, resources and unfulfilled entitlement? The answer requires the relevant evidence doctrine as well as a substantive maintenance rule.

Subsidiary maxims. Initial non-liability and a wife’s already established entitlement must not be conflated. The question is whether a claim has been established, whether performance occurred and what authorized relief is available during absence—not whether the absence allows either party’s rights to be presumed away.

M009. Division of time as justice among wives

Agreed core. Ibn Rushd includes justice in division among wives among their rights. He invokes prophetic division, the warning concerning inclination toward one of two wives, and drawing lots when setting out on travel. The object is allocation of conduct and time within the given institution; the passage does not establish judicial access to every inward affection. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF p.55; Bidāya, English II, PDF p.69, printed p.65

This moves the analysis beyond wealth. Time and presence are finite goods. The formative act is accepting limits upon preference where another person’s recognized claim is involved. The right cannot be fulfilled merely by feeling affection; neither does equal allocation prove equality of feeling. The alchemical change is from unregulated inclination to accountable conduct.

Simon’s distinction between coordination and replacement for incapacity is pertinent: even willing participants need an arrangement where goods cannot be supplied simultaneously. That comparison does not justify polygyny or establish that a particular allocation secures the full good of everyone affected. Historical household power and the possibilities of complaint require independent investigation. Simon, Nature and Functions of Authority, PDF pp.27–29, printed pp.15–17

At the civilizational level, the point is the extension of justice into relations that can otherwise be governed by private preference. Prosperity, travel and status may complicate such households; none maps the rule to one dynastic stage. The eschatological warning is an explicit vertical dimension in the legal evidence itself. It intensifies accountability for conduct without making the court an examiner of hidden affection.

Principles in this argument. The evidential work concerns prophetic practice and its status as a guide to division. The Ḍarūrī requires inquiry into whether an act explains an established norm and what its context indicates. The later Jamʿ taxonomy helps name those possibilities; a repeated act is not by occurrence alone proof of every quantitative obligation attributed to it.

M010. Initial residence: equality over which interval?

Disagreement and evidence. Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī and their followers assign seven days to the newly married virgin and three to the previously married woman, without counting those initial days against the ordinary division where another wife exists. Abū Ḥanīfa gives equal initial residence in the two cases and counts it in the distribution. Ibn Rushd gives the conflict between the Anas and Umm Salama reports as the cause; he remarks that Medinan and Kufan jurists here adopt reports associated with the other regional transmission environment. This specifically resists a simple regional-practice stereotype. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF p.56; Bidāya, English II, PDF p.69, printed p.65

Comparative interpretation. The rules distinguish an entry period from an ongoing pattern in different ways. One can investigate adjustment to a new household as a possible good, but the supplied sabab is the relation of reports, not a psychological theory explaining seven and three. Neither the quantities nor the difference in marital history receives an invented metaphysical symbolism.

Principles in this argument. The rival transmitted practices must first be compared for their subject, occasion and normative bearing. The Ḍarūrī treats conflicting explanatory acts as an evidential problem comparable to conflicting statements. Our interpretation of equality over different intervals follows that comparison; it cannot select a report simply because one interval seems more symmetrical.

M011. Obligation or recommendation within the same form?

Ibn al-Qāsim makes the initial seven/three arrangement obligatory; Ibn ʿAbd al-Ḥakam recommends it. Ibn Rushd’s cause is whether the prophetic act indicates recommendation or obligation. The shared pattern of action does not settle its normative force. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF p.56; Bidāya, English II, PDF p.70, printed p.66

This is a compact but decisive example of the sciences’ relation. Universal practical knowledge distinguishes the ruling categories. Instrumental inquiry assesses the indication of a prophetic act. Particular fiqh specifies the force of this arrangement. An account of domestic harmony cannot bypass the second step and make all beneficial conduct obligatory.

The social effect must be tested in actual households rather than presumed from its label. Repeated recommendation can become a durable practice; compulsory form can be performed resentfully. The vertical difference between outward fulfillment, intention and reward remains beyond a mere schedule. This case prevents the alchemical model from treating one visible behavior as evidence of one identical legal or spiritual state.

Principles in this argument. This is a direct test of the passage on prophetic acts: explaining a commanded act and merely performing an act are different evidential situations. Ibn Rushd’s Ḍarūrī does not give an unrestricted “all such acts are recommended” rule. The Bidāya’s reported obligation/recommendation alternatives must retain their own warrants and their distinction from his methodological preference.

The chapter’s civilizational result and remaining boundary

Representative route: household and dissolution

Revision 14 · 4 October 2026. Selected studies across every editorial division; exact source spans below delimit the selection. These are representative interpretations, not chapter-completion or elementary-rule counts.

Quoted scriptural clauses below are selected working translations from the cited Arabic. Exegetical views are named; the paragraph labelled “Its ethical argument” is the manuscript’s close reading of the passage and its surrounding clauses. The purple note gives the full explanation and exact sources. A related passage does not become the direct evidence for a ruling merely by being placed beside it.

Household law concerns several persons whose goods can conflict. A rule may protect a child, give a spouse a remedy, or end a suspended relationship without improving the disposition of the person made to comply. The representative route therefore asks who receives a benefit, who must act, who may bind another and who bears the cost. The detailed formation and dower studies remain the control for questions not reopened here.

Compositio describes actual cooperation among distinct contributions; it is not absorption of one person into another. Temperamentum describes competing legitimate claims moderating conduct. Separatio describes several forms of effective disengagement, whose material and affective consequences must be studied separately. A divorce can end legal powers while leaving economic dependence and possessive resentment intact. Conversely, preserving a household can perpetuate injury. The alchemical comparison must explain which change occurred, rather than confer a positive meaning on togetherness or separation as such.

REP-23. Nursing: embodied dependence, kinship and parental cooperation

Follow the argument RulingLegal reasoningScripture

Division 23: Marriage formation rights and impediments.

Ibn Rushd: summary of the ruling and disagreement. Ibn Rushd separates the quantity, age, manner and proof of nursing from the duties of nursing within marriage. The first set determines a prohibited kinship relation; the second allocates care and its cost. Quantity disputes oppose the general wording of to differently delimited reports. On , interpreting a statement as a command, and the role of social custom, help explain divergent accounts of a wife's duty. A divorced woman's nursing and payment receive distinct treatment. Bidāya Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.35–39,56–57

al-Ḍarūrī · method · Arabic / Englishal-Ḍarūrī: when general wording is restricted

How the legal argument works. · · . These notes identify the relevant mechanism or comparative control; later maxims do not establish Ibn Rushd’s historical vocabulary.

Text and reported setting. joins nursing, customary provision, capacity, avoidance of injury, parental consultation and payment. It ends: “Be mindful of God, and know that God sees what you do.” addresses a distinct consequence of nursing: prohibited marriage relations.

Ethical force of the passage. The closing appeal directs attention to what happens inside a vulnerable relation of care. A parent may formally invoke a right while using the child to injure the other parent; consultation and provision counter that possibility. Divine seeing concerns the actual conduct behind the arrangement, including concealed pressure. This ethical setting cannot determine the number or age of feeds that establishes kinship.

How the commentators read it. Ibn ʿĀshūr reads within the divorce sequence and favours divorced mothers as its immediate addressees; other readings remain. Qurṭubī explains the prohibition on injuring either parent through nursing. Nawawī’s treatment of the Sālim case retains the disagreement over adult nursing; the suggestion of expressed milk is ʿIyāḍ’s explanation, not a detail supplied by the report.

· · · · · · ·

Text and reported setting. condemns marrying a father’s former wife as indecency, abhorrence and an evil way. enumerates prohibited relations and ends with divine forgiveness and mercy after its qualification concerning what has already occurred.

Ethical force of the passage. The passage locates sexual choice within enduring relations that the chooser did not simply invent. Its moral terms and treatment of the past matter alongside the categories. Yet identifying respect for kinship as a good does not prove why each boundary has exactly its revealed form.

How the commentators read it. Ibn ʿĀshūr explains that prohibition predicated of these persons concerns marriage to them; it is not a declaration that the persons themselves are bad or impure. This matters for the practical object of the ruling.

REP-24. Divorce: when severity defeats the opportunity to repair

Follow the argument RulingLegal reasoningScripture

Division 24: Divorce.

Ruling and reason for disagreement. For three divorces pronounced together, Ibn Rushd reports the majority's threefold effect and a onefold effect among the Ẓāhirīs and others. The dispute involves transmitted reports, whether a person can impose the third-divorce consequence through one utterance, and competing comparisons with regulated acts or self-binding vows. His own criticism is sharp: severity intended to block abuse can remove the concession and gentleness intended by the law. Bidāya Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.61–62

How the legal argument works. · . These notes identify the relevant mechanism or comparative control; later maxims do not establish Ibn Rushd’s historical vocabulary.

Text and reported setting. joins the counting of the waiting period, taqwā and protection against expulsion, then says: “You do not know; perhaps God will bring about something afterwards.” requires honourable retention or separation and testimony for God; 65:3 speaks of reliance on God and an appointed measure.

Ethical force of the passage. The passage interrupts the assumption that present anger knows the whole future. Counting time, preserving housing and giving truthful testimony make room for a future that neither spouse controls. Taqwā here concerns how separation is conducted; reliance on God is not a warrant to neglect provision or evidence.

How the commentators read it. Ibn ʿĀshūr connects proper timing with avoiding needless prolongation of a woman’s waiting. Nawawī calls the triple-divorce report difficult and preserves competing explanations. His preferred account distinguishes repetition intended as emphasis from repetition intended as fresh pronouncements, with a changed presumption about usage. He does not permit ʿUmar to abrogate prophetic law. This is a significant alternative to treating the report simply as an administrative change in the effect of identical words.

· · · · ·

REP-25. Īlāʾ: ending indefinite suspension

Follow the argument RulingLegal reasoningScripture

Division 25: Ila.

Ruling and reason for disagreement. Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī and others require a decision after four months: resumption or divorce. Abū Ḥanīfa and the Kūfan position reported here make the expiry itself effect divorce unless resumption occurred within the period. Ibn Rushd locates the disagreement in the temporal relation of return to the waiting period and in how “resolving divorce” in is understood. Bidāya Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.100

How the legal argument works. · . These notes identify the relevant mechanism or comparative control; later maxims do not establish Ibn Rushd’s historical vocabulary.

Text and reported setting. sets four months for sworn abstention, describing God as forgiving and merciful where the husband returns. speaks of a resolved divorce and ends with God as hearing and knowing.

Ethical force of the passage. The alternatives oppose indefinite suspension: the relationship must be resumed or brought towards release. Forgiveness addresses return after neglect; hearing and knowing deny that a man’s power over the outward decision makes his treatment of the wife invisible.

How the commentators read it. Wāḥidī’s accounts of prolonged pre-Islamic abstention are retained as attributed reports. Ibn ʿĀshūr explains the four months as an interval for reflection, with an earlier return possible, against a practice that could prevent a woman both enjoying marriage and remarrying.

· · ·

REP-26. Ẓihār: speech that damages a household and a remedy that restores a claim

Follow the argument RulingLegal reasoningScripture

Division 26: Zihar.

Ruling and reason for disagreement. All agree on the established formula comparing the wife to the mother's back; they differ over other body parts and other permanently prohibited relatives. Ibn Rushd identifies the opposition between the meaning of prohibition and the particular wording. He also reports the ambiguity of comparing the wife simply to one's mother: intended honour may differ from intended prohibition. Bidāya Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.105

How the legal argument works. · . These notes identify the relevant mechanism or comparative control; later maxims do not establish Ibn Rushd’s historical vocabulary.

Text and reported setting. opens by declaring that God has heard the woman disputing about her husband. rejects the identification of wives with mothers as objectionable and false speech, while naming divine pardon. makes expiation precede resumed intimacy and calls it an admonition under God’s knowledge of action.

Ethical force of the passage. The sequence moves from hearing an injured person to correcting a false speech act and placing a burden on the speaker before resumption. A husband’s utterance cannot make a wife ontologically his mother. Nor does rejection of that fiction make the injury costless. Hearing, truth and restorative obligation belong to one argument.

How the commentators read it. Ibn ʿĀshūr reads the passage as an answer bringing relief to the complainant and explains the older force of ẓihār. Wāḥidī’s versions preserve variations in names and circumstances; these should not become one seamless biography.

· · · ·

The surrounding Qurʾānic argument. continues from the emancipatory remedy to fasting and, when that is beyond capacity, feeding sixty poor people. It connects these forms with faith in God and the Messenger and the limits set by God. Ibn ʿĀshūr interprets their relationship through release, trained patience and relieving hunger: the offending speech’s interruption of marital life is answered by demanding acts whose beneficiaries are not confined to the speaker. This is his purposive explanation, not proof that the remedies are interchangeable or that their quantities can be deduced from a generic account of virtue.

REP-27. Liʿān: an exit from accusation without pretending to know the hidden

Follow the argument RulingLegal reasoningScripture

Division 27: Lian.

Ruling and reason for disagreement. The ʿUwaymir narrative begins with a question about finding another man with one's wife and the prospect of retaliatory killing. Ibn Rushd then distinguishes accusation from denial of a pregnancy. The majority allow liʿān following a general accusation; the predominant Mālikī position he reports requires a more specified claim, with another Mālikī report agreeing with the majority. General scriptural wording and the more particular narrated cases explain the disagreement. Bidāya Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.115–116

How the legal argument works. · . These notes identify the relevant mechanism or comparative control; later maxims do not establish Ibn Rushd’s historical vocabulary.

Text and reported setting. sets out opposed oaths when a husband accuses his wife without ordinary witnesses. then invokes God’s favour, mercy, acceptance of repentance and wisdom.

Ethical force of the passage. The concluding mercy does not mean that accusation has revealed the wife’s guilt. It points to a way out of a dangerous conflict where one party’s asserted certainty cannot simply determine the other’s fate. The parties answer before God for truthfulness while the public procedure works within its evidentiary limits.

How the commentators read it. Ibn ʿĀshūr insists that wives’ lives are not left to the differing temperaments of jealous husbands: the matter belongs to public authority, not private killing. His narrated ʿUwaymir material must remain distinct from other reported accusation episodes.

· · ·

REP-28. Mourning: fidelity in time, with an endpoint

Follow the argument RulingLegal reasoningScripture

Division 28: Mourning.

Ruling and reason for disagreement. Ibn Rushd separates who must observe iḥdād, which waiting periods require it, and what conduct it excludes. Mālik restricts obligatory mourning to widowhood; Abū Ḥanīfa and al-Thawrī also require it for irrevocable divorce; al-Shāfiʿī recommends it there. The reports about adornment and eye treatment are interpreted through their prohibitory or permissive force, not through a generalized theory of grief. Bidāya Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.123

How the legal argument works. · . These notes identify the relevant mechanism or comparative control; later maxims do not establish Ibn Rushd’s historical vocabulary.

Text and reported setting. limits the widow’s waiting period and then removes blame for her honourable decisions about herself. distinguishes allusive proposals from secret commitments, acknowledges what people may think, and joins God’s knowledge of inward states with forgiveness and forbearance.

Ethical force of the passage. The passage honours the ended relation without making it a perpetual veto over the survivor’s future. Desire for a new relation is acknowledged; the form and timing of acting upon it are regulated. Divine knowledge reaches concealed arrangements, while forgiveness and forbearance prevent the mere presence of a thought from being equated with a prohibited contract.

How the commentators read it. Ibn ʿĀshūr places widowhood here after the provisions for divorce and nursing, within the ordering of disrupted family relations. The case therefore concerns continuity of care and legitimate future agency, not only calculation of an interval.
