Part IV.A. Zakāt, ownership and distributive relations

Revision 3 placement: this is the detailed wealth-and-rights bridge. Its inclusion follows the object of these questions—ownership, liability, debt and other persons’ claims—while the main worship chapter supplies the shared ritual and formative orientation.

Continuous commentary on the opening and first division of Bidāya I, printed/PDF pp.244–250, beginning at Kitāb al-zakāh and stopping before the division on taxable kinds of wealth. The burial material above the opening on p.244 is not covered. Z001–Z020 are working question-units; each may include several positions and subsidiary rules. Rates, asset classifications, timing in its separate division, and recipient categories require later installments.

The primary framework: generosity and participation in wealth

Ibn Rushd’s closing synthesis explicitly places zakāt under the cultivation of sakhāʾ, generosity, and opposition to bukhl, while also placing it under al-ishtirāk fī al-amwāl, participation or sharing in wealth. The two descriptions must remain together. A transfer can serve another person’s claim even where the payer’s disposition is defective; an inwardly generous motive does not determine the exact legal incidence of the duty. The technical rules examined here explain how those relations are constituted. Bidāya, Arabic II, p.476.

The central interpretive question is not merely “How does giving make me better?” It is: whose wealth, under what control, bearing whose prior claims, becomes subject to what duty, discharged by which person, and with what consequence if circumstances change? The virtue of the payer, the right of the recipient, the agency of a guardian, the responsibility of a collector and the power of a ruler are connected without being identical.

This yields a trans-individual account of formation. Law can sustain conditions in which people who cannot themselves perform the act still have rights and obligations mediated by others. It can also limit a well-intentioned claim on a person whose apparent wealth is already committed. “Alchemy” here includes the formation of a just relation among persons, not only an interior change in the hand that gives.

Repentance, the poor person’s due and limits on collection

Setting. addresses people who acknowledge mixed conduct. Ibn ʿĀshūr relates the offering to repentance after failure to join the Tabūk expedition and its common expenses. The Study Quran records both an expiatory reading tied to that episode and a reading of as obligatory zakāt.

The passage. joins taking an offering, cleansing and growth in the giver, and the Prophet’s prayer as reassurance. God is Hearing and Knowing. says God accepts repentance and receives offerings; places deeds before divine knowledge of both hidden and visible.

Its ethical argument. Wealth is one medium of a repaired relation, but payment and reconciliation are not identical. A person acknowledges failure, gives, and receives prayer rather than being reduced to the amount collected. Divine reception relativizes public reputation and the size of the gift; it does not abolish the recipient’s material claim.

What the commentary explains. Ibn ʿĀshūr explains cleansing as removing the blameworthy condition (takhliya) and tazkiya as acquiring virtues (taḥliya). He connects reassurance to the repentant person’s unsettled heart. The Study Quran preserves the dispute between the specific expiatory offering and obligatory alms, then explains how the Prophet’s prayer brings gladness, peace and mercy. This prevents an undifferentiated use of the occasion to settle all later fiscal questions. Its mediated report of al-Rāzī on purification remains an attribution through that editorial work.

· · ·

Setting. Muslim19 places the instruction at Muʿādh’s dispatch to Yemen: teaching, prayer and alms are presented in sequence to the community he is to encounter.

The passage. The levy is taken from the wealthy and returned to the poor; the collector must avoid taking their best property and must fear the supplication of the wronged person, between whom and God there is no barrier.

Its ethical argument. The moral test runs in two directions. Owners must discharge the poor person’s due; an officer enforcing that due must not turn lawful collection into an injury. The final warning gives the person exposed to public power a claim before God which administrative rank cannot silence.

What the commentary explains. Nawawī derives a duty for the ruler to warn governors against injustice. He explains that the collector should take neither the owner’s choicest property nor accept the worst: the middle quality protects both sides. He also preserves differing readings of “their poor,” so the phrase cannot by itself establish an uncontested prohibition of transferring alms elsewhere. These distinctions belong inside an account of zakāt’s formative and civic effects.

·

Z001–Z002. Obligation, the five inquiries and the ordinary liable subject

Z001. Ibn Rushd treats zakāt’s obligation as established by Book, Sunna and agreement. He organizes the subject into five inquiries: who owes it; which wealth bears it; amounts and thresholds; when it is due; and to whom it is due and in what amount. This structure is itself philosophically important. Duty is a relation among agent, material object, measure, time and beneficiary. No one element supplies the full particular rule. Bidāya, Arabic I, p.244.

Z002. The agreed central case is the free, Muslim, mature, sane owner of a threshold amount through complete ownership. The subsequent disagreements concern minors, mental incapacity, slavery, protected non-Muslims and incomplete ownership, including debt and endowed capital. Mention of mental incapacity in this initial list does not supply a separate, fully attributed ruling in the immediate minor discussion. That comparison remains to be tracked elsewhere rather than invented. Bidāya, Arabic I, p.245.

The standard case must not be misread as a statement that every listed condition is universally necessary, since the following disputes ask whether some may be absent. Nor does the list identify all recipients or all forms of public contribution. The legal object is a specified duty, not “taxation” in an undifferentiated modern sense.

At the universal practical level, the jurist needs an account of obligation, ownership, capacity and sources. Instrumental inquiry determines how texts and comparisons bear on the edge cases. Particular fiqh determines liability under a described condition. Administrative action then establishes whether the condition obtains and carries out collection or distribution. These are the levels distinguished in the methodological volume, now visible in a single legal division. Ibn Rushd / Akl edition, PDF pp.129–132, al-Ḍarūrī §§2–9.

Principles in this argument. The five inquiries organize a particular practical field. Uṣūl supplies classifications and warranted inference; establishing whether this owner possesses the qualifying wealth is a further operation. The later definitions distinguish condition, cause and impediment without certifying that every disputed ownership or capacity feature belongs in one agreed category.

Z003. Wealth belonging to a minor: can the recipient’s right precede the owner’s maturity?

Positions. The affirmative position is attributed to ʿAlī, Ibn ʿUmar, Jābir and ʿĀʾishah among Companions, and Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, al-Thawrī, Aḥmad, Isḥāq, Abū Thawr and others. A position excluding the minor’s property is attributed to al-Nakhaʿī, al-Ḥasan and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr. Abū Ḥanīfa and his followers distinguish produce from other property, imposing the relevant duty on the former. Another group distinguishes cash from other property. Bidāya, Arabic I, p.245.

The explicit sabab. Does the legal zakāt resemble worship such as prayer and fasting, requiring maturity, or a right of the poor in the wealth of the rich, for which the owner’s maturity is not decisive? Ibn Rushd expressly says he does not at that moment know the basis of the intermediate asset distinctions. We must preserve that admission. A modern explanation of agricultural taxation might be a research hypothesis, but cannot be attributed to him as the supplied cause. Bidāya, Arabic I, p.245.

Ontology and burden. The poor-right account locates the obligation in a relation involving wealth, not solely in the owner’s capacity to perform worship. It does not declare the child morally blameworthy for non-payment. A guardian’s capacity mediates the action. The worship account preserves a correspondence between the kind of demand and the mature subject’s responsibility. It does not deny the value of helping poor people through other warranted means.

The Muwaṭṭaʾ supplies concrete controls: a report of ʿĀʾishah paying zakāt on the property of orphans under her care; reports of investing orphan property; and Mālik’s allowance of investment by a trustworthy person without treating that person as guaranteeing every loss. A report from ʿUmar urges productive use so zakāt does not deplete the property. These show the connection between distributive duty and responsible estate management without proving that every guardian historically succeeded. .

Principles in this argument. The stated resemblance to worship or to a poor person’s right is the primary cause of disagreement. The Ḍarūrī asks whether an indicated general meaning actually licenses the move, or whether the local argument remains a rival assimilation of zakāt to worship or to an enforceable right; Ghazālī’s distinction between finding a criterion and verifying it prevents the child’s age from concealing the prior dispute over what kind of obligation zakāt is. Ibn Rushd’s admitted uncertainty about intermediate asset distinctions remains unfilled.

Z004. Protected non-Muslims and the Banū Taghlib report

Most jurists in this account do not impose zakāt on protected non-Muslims. A group, including al-Shāfiʿī, Abū Ḥanīfa, Aḥmad and al-Thawrī, accepts the reported doubling for the Christians of Banū Taghlib on the precedent of ʿUmar; Ibn Rushd knows no Mālikī statement here. He suggests that the jurists treated the precedent as received authorization, while observing that general principles oppose it. Bidāya, Arabic I, p.245.

The Arabic explicitly refers to doubling what is taken from Muslims. The supplied English paragraph’s wording about an “equal” amount is inadequate as the controlling statement of this quantity. The doubling terminology was checked on the Arabic page image. The historical basis, classification and scope of the arrangement need independent primary investigation. A distinctive arrangement with a named group cannot establish a general claim that all non-Muslims owe twice the Muslim rate. Bidāya, English I, PDF p.266, printed p.284.

This case resists reducing zakāt to an economic function that could be assigned identically to everyone. Religious status, the identity of an obligation and political agreements matter. At the same time, it resists treating public finance as wholly insulated from inherited political precedent. The operative axis is general principle and specific authorized arrangement, not inward spirituality versus material interest.

Principles in this argument. A specific reported arrangement requires an account of its authority against general principles. The Ḍarūrī’s requirement of a warranted specification is the relevant methodological control, not a licence to infer fiscal exceptions directly from a desired political benefit. The report’s attribution and transmitted authorization still need the independent checks stated here.

Z005–Z006. Enslaved persons, control of wealth and incomplete ownership

Z005. Three positions are reported: no zakāt on the enslaved person’s wealth; liability upon the master; or liability upon the enslaved person. Mālik, Aḥmad and Abū ʿUbayd occur in the first group; al-Shāfiʿī as reported by Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Thawrī and Abū Ḥanīfa in the second; Abū Thawr and others in the third. Ibn ʿUmar is cited in more than one report and should not be forced into one unqualified position. Z006. Most who deny liability on the enslaved person’s property also deny it on the mukātab’s property until freedom; Abū Thawr imposes it. Bidāya, Arabic I, pp.245–246.

The cause is whether complete ownership exists and where. One reasoning locates ultimate ownership with the master. Another finds neither person in full possession of the relevant ownership: the master lacks the enslaved person’s immediate control, while the latter is subject to the master’s power of taking. A third gives weight to practical disposal and the general address encompassing free and enslaved subjects. Bidāya, Arabic I, p.246.

The legal ontology is therefore a bundle of distinguishable powers: title, possession, disposal and vulnerability to another’s taking. Modern terminology can help distinguish them, but should not be attributed to Ibn Rushd as a developed modern theory of property rights. The important primary fact is that “has wealth” does not settle who bears the duty.

The formative account also becomes morally difficult. A person can be treated as capable of worship and property-related action while subject to domination. The rule’s allocation may protect against double liability, recognize agency or preserve the master’s claim, depending on the argument. None makes the institution of slavery a transparent embodiment of vocation or spiritual rank. The project needs a separate critical account of how such statuses constrain the very agency that virtue theory presupposes.

Principles in this argument. For both ordinary enslavement and mukātaba, the first dispute concerns the legal meaning of complete ownership; the next concerns who satisfies it. These are different from merely counting assets. The general address enters one reported argument, while a later condition/impediment taxonomy describes the architecture without deciding the disputed allocation.

Z007. The debtor: when apparent possession is not wealth free of prior claims

Ibn Rushd describes a person whose debt consumes the relevant wealth while property subject to zakāt remains in hand. Al-Thawrī, Abū Thawr, Ibn al-Mubārak and others deduct debts, imposing zakāt only if the remainder reaches the threshold. Abū Ḥanīfa’s account exempts non-grain wealth through debt but not grain. Mālik’s account concerns cash, with the qualification that other goods sufficient to discharge the debt can leave the cash liable. A contrary position does not let debt remove liability at all. Bidāya, Arabic I, p.246.

The explicit cause reverses the minor case’s effect. If zakāt is a right in wealth, the creditor’s earlier claim can take priority: what appears to be the debtor’s wealth is already due to another. If zakāt is worship, possession can be the relevant sign of obligation despite debt. The passage also states an argument about priority of God’s right. Ibn Rushd judges relief of the debtor closer to the law’s purpose, invoking collection from the rich and return to the poor, since the debtor in this case is not rich. Again he says he lacks a clear basis for the intermediate asset distinctions. Bidāya, Arabic I, p.246.

The same conceptual account—poor people’s right in wealth—supports inclusion for minors and exclusion for a debtor. The outcome depends on the network of claims, not on a permanent tendency toward stricter or easier rulings. Nor can a school’s agreement with a result prove that its entire theory of zakāt is exhausted by one branch of Ibn Rushd’s explanation.

Attas’s indebtedness has a suggestive but limited relation here. Existential indebtedness to God cannot be used to cancel the human creditor’s concrete claim simply by declaring the divine debt “higher.” The primary text contains a juridical dispute about that very relation. The broader metaphysics must respect the determinations of the legal science rather than bypass them. Attas, Prolegomena, PDF pp.27–29.

The Muwaṭṭaʾ gives direct Mālikī controls for debt equal to cash, goods sufficient to discharge debt, and the creditor’s treatment. It also reports a direction associated with ʿUthmān to pay debts at the tax season so claims can be settled. These passages connect the abstract distinction to coordinated accounting practices. .

Principles in this argument. The poor-right comparison has a different implication here because a creditor’s prior claim changes the relation. This illustrates why a common ethical theme cannot mechanically predict inclusion or exclusion. The Ḍarūrī’s benefit restriction also requires us to distinguish Ibn Rushd’s actual purposive argument from our wider claim that the rule can educate justice. The right/debt comparison is not certified as indicated semantic extension: the particular expression and wider intended predicate still need to be shown.

Subsidiary maxims. The non-liability maxim concerns establishing an alleged debt; it does not erase a proved debt simply to increase the zakāt base. Nor does the payer’s wish to relieve poverty extinguish a creditor’s established claim. The precise priority between claims remains the disputed substantive question.

Z008. A real debt and a merely asserted debt are not the same evidentiary object

Abū ʿUbayd accepts the debt exemption when the debt is known, but not solely on the owner’s uncorroborated assertion. Ibn Rushd expressly says this is not disagreement with deducting debt; it is disagreement about whether to trust the claimant’s statement in the same way as the statement of wealth. Bidāya, Arabic I, pp.246–247.

The normative proposition and its ascertainment must have different records. One jurist can accept the entitlement yet require another method of proof. This is an exact instance of why general practical science, particular rule and concrete determination cannot be collapsed.

For virtue, truthful disclosure and responsible trust are the relevant dispositions. For the institution, verification protects both recipients and honest debtors if applied fairly, but can become burdensome or selective. For the common good, the question is not maximal collection but warranted collection. The developmental analysis asks whether the community possesses reliable witnesses, accounts and accessible adjudication, and whether officials themselves are trustworthy. No metaphysical conviction about the claimant supplies the missing public evidence.

Principles in this argument. This is a particularly close application of the rule/instance distinction: accepting debt as a ground of exemption does not establish that this asserted debt exists. Ghazālī’s examples of probable factual assessment clarify the operation; they do not determine whether this claimant’s unsupported declaration is legally sufficient proof.

Subsidiary maxims. The subsidiary maxims distinguish an unsupported allegation, a remote imagined objection and a concrete reason to doubt particular evidence. They do not all favor the same party. The compilation itself records school disagreement in its evidence-based-doubt example; it therefore cannot decide Abū ʿUbayd’s proof requirement by universal slogan.

Z009. The creditor’s receivable: time, possession and the origin of the claim

One position waits until the money is received and a new year passes; the Arabic attributes this to one Shāfiʿī opinion and al-Layth, or the implication of his opinion. Another requires payment for past years upon receipt. Mālik requires one year’s zakāt for a debt originating in an exchange, even after several years, while an inherited claim begins its year upon receipt. He notes further school detail. The page image confirms al-Layth in this Arabic witness. The English substitutes Abū Thawr for al-Layth in the first attribution; this discrepancy remains for another-edition control and should not be silently harmonized. Bidāya, Arabic I, p.247; Bidāya, English I, PDF p.268, printed p.286.

The practical object is an enforceable or expected claim separated from present possession. Ownership can continue while use is unavailable. The competing temporal accounts give different weight to continuing title, actual recovery and the claim’s origin. The child, debtor and creditor cases therefore do not pose the same “ownership” problem: each separates a different pair of powers or relations.

The Muwaṭṭaʾ supplies Mālik’s one-payment rule and a reported administrative correction concerning property taken by an official: an initial direction to collect for accumulated years is revised to a single collection because the owner lacked use. The report is particularly valuable for connecting wrongful deprivation with fiscal assessment, though its status as a transmitted report must remain distinct from an extant administrative record. .

Under developed commerce, many persons’ assets can be others’ debts; under political decline, recovery may become insecure. A legal order preserving confidence in claims can sustain exchange. A rule that taxes unrecovered wealth without the accepted warrant can aggravate loss. Those are causal hypotheses whose historical strength needs records of debt enforcement, collection and actual asset use.

Principles in this argument. Continuing title, actual access and a new annual period are different candidates for the operative condition. Istiṣḥāb cannot settle the matter until the relevant prior status and alleged change are identified. The Ḍarūrī’s discussion of changed qualities warns against treating the continued existence of a receivable as proof of unchanged annual liability.

Z010. Endowed fruit: a recipient class cannot simply be treated as another rich owner

Mālik and al-Shāfiʿī impose zakāt on fruit whose capital is endowed; Makḥūl and Ṭāwūs do not. A third position distinguishes named beneficiaries from the poor generally, imposing in the former case and not the latter. Ibn Rushd criticizes imposing it on the poor as a class: ownership is incomplete and the beneficiaries are an indeterminate category of those to whom zakāt is directed, not those from whom it is taken. Bidāya, Arabic I, p.247.

This is a sophisticated account of institutional property. An endowed asset has continuing productive capacity, but the beneficial relation is not identical to ordinary full ownership by one wealthy individual. The designated recipient group and the purpose of the arrangement matter. Treating every producing asset as if the same subject owned it would miss the point.

Principles in this argument. The legal problem concerns whether this institutional beneficiary relation instantiates the ownership required by the obligation. Ghazālī’s manāṭ distinctions help separate disagreement over that criterion from factual assessment of a particular endowment. A benefit to the poor alone does not establish every exemption; the text’s account of ownership and recipient class does the legal work.

Z011. Rented land: land, crop or their conjunction?

Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, al-Thawrī, Ibn al-Mubārak, Abū Thawr and others assign the agricultural obligation to the crop’s owner; Abū Ḥanīfa and his followers assign it to the landowner. Ibn Rushd frames the cause as whether the due belongs to land, crop or both. He strikingly says that it is in reality related to both, while no reported position assigns it jointly in that manner. The undisputed case unites land and crop in one owner; separating them requires identifying the more appropriate bearer. Bidāya, Arabic I, pp.247–248.

The majority attach liability to the item in which zakāt is assessed, the crop. Abū Ḥanīfa attaches it to the basis of the obligation, the land. This is not mere verbal formalism: an agricultural product depends on several causally relevant factors, but liability has to be allocated to a person. The causal explanation of production and the legal assignment of duty are therefore distinct.

The case refines Mahdi’s causal framework. Material, productive and institutional causes can jointly explain a good without each bearing an identical legal burden. A four-cause map alone cannot tell the collector whom to charge. Uṣūl must supply the relevant rule of attribution. Mahdi, Philosophy of History, PDF pp.238, 264, 273.

For virtue, the issue is justice between landlord, cultivator and recipients. For social development, it concerns differentiated production: landownership and cultivation need not reside in one person. More complex cooperation requires more precise attribution. The actual economic burden may be shifted through rents or contracts, but that is an empirical matter, not established by identifying the legally liable person.

Principles in this argument. The relevant question is the legal attachment of the due to land or crop, not the complete causal explanation of agricultural production. Ghazālī expressly distinguishes a legally designated sign from an intrinsic necessitating cause. This comparison disciplines the four-cause analysis without attributing Ghazālī’s theology of legal signs to Ibn Rushd. A legal attachment is not automatically a semantic universal; that further claim needs a textual indication, distinct from the observed production process.

Z012–Z013. Land changing hands across fiscal and religious categories

Z012. When kharāj land comes to Muslims, the majority retain zakāt alongside kharāj; Abū Ḥanīfa and his followers do not combine them. The same land/crop distinction explains the disagreement: if both charges are on land, combination is denied in the stated argument; if one concerns land and the other produce, they can coexist. Z013. When ʿushr land passes to a dhimmī, the majority in this account impose no such due, while Abū Ḥanīfa converts its category to kharāj land. Ibn Rushd challenges the apparent asymmetry: why does the reverse transfer not equally convert kharāj land to ʿushr land on that reasoning? Bidāya, Arabic I, p.248.

The object is not land as physical soil alone. Its legal history, current holder and fiscal category enter its practical identity. This creates continuity for public claims across private transfers but also opportunities for asymmetry and burden. A complete philosophy must examine the fairness and proof of that continuity, not merely celebrate law’s capacity to classify.

Upward result. Legal consistency is itself a research question. Ibn Rushd’s criticism prevents the master synthesis from making every received distinction transparently harmonious. The reader must be allowed to see where the author thinks a position fails to follow its own principle.

Principles in this argument. These cases test the persistence and transformation of a fiscal category. The Ḍarūrī’s analysis of continuity requires an argument that the change in holder does, or does not, alter a legally relevant quality. The later certainty maxim cannot by itself preserve one land category and transform the reverse case; Ibn Rushd’s consistency challenge therefore remains substantive.

Z014. Zakāt set aside and lost: five different ontologies of responsibility

Ibn Rushd collects five positions: no compensation; compensation in all cases; compensation for negligence but not without it; compensation for negligence, otherwise assessment on the remainder; and proportional sharing of the surviving wealth between owner and recipients. The familiar Mālikī distinction concerns prompt action without negligence versus delayed performance; Abū Thawr and al-Shāfiʿī are associated with assessment of the remainder absent negligence. Bidāya, Arabic I, pp.248–249.

The explicit cause is the owner’s resemblance to a debtor, trustee, partner, or someone whose wealth has diminished before obligation. A debt in the person’s liability can survive loss of particular goods. A trust can perish without liability absent fault. A partnership can distribute loss proportionately. Reassessment of the residue treats the remaining taxable base as decisive. These are not decorative comparisons; they generate different material outcomes. The practical-causal consequences concern loss and recourse, while the legal ontology determines whose claim survives. A teleological concern for just distribution can illuminate the alternatives without deciding whether the obligation is debt, trust or partnership.

This is perhaps the clearest statement of juridical morphology in the opening zakāt chapter. The same material loss is differently constituted by the relationship in which it occurs. Calling the payer a steward, debtor or partner is not interchangeable religious rhetoric. Each category has legal consequences and requires an argument.

The institutional needs are concrete: safe storage and transport, competent agents, evidence of timely segregation and an intelligible standard of negligence. More specialized administration can reduce accidental loss and also introduce intermediaries through whom funds disappear. The framework must therefore analyze both the custodian’s virtue and the institution’s incentives and accountability.

Principles in this argument. Debtor, trustee and partner are rival legal assimilations, not equivalent names for stewardship. The Ḍarūrī’s reclassification of much analogy asks which legally relevant relation warrants each extension and whether that relation is indicated by the revealed expression. Debtor/trustee/partner comparisons cannot be certified as semantic extension merely by citing that framework. Its criticism of weak resemblance prevents us from assigning all five outcomes one transparent common cause.

Subsidiary maxims. The subsidiary rule about unproved later changes explains why alleging an accident differs from proving discharge of an established debt. The necessity/rights pairing also prevents a benevolent purpose from selecting a liability regime. The text’s debtor, trustee and partner comparisons still determine which presumption is relevant.

Z015–Z016. Loss before possible payment and loss after avoidable delay

Z015 concerns partial loss after obligation but before performance was possible: one position assesses the remainder; another treats owner and recipients as partners sharing the loss. Z016 concerns an actor able to pay who delays until part is lost: Ibn Rushd reports agreement, as far as he thinks, on liability, with the Mālikī livestock qualification where the collector’s arrival completes the condition of obligation. His epistemic qualification must remain in the record. Bidāya, Arabic I, p.249.

These are different temporal cases, not repetitions of Z014. Ability intervenes between an abstract due and culpable delay. The collector’s arrival also shows that the actualization of some obligations may include a public function. The institution is not merely an external enforcer added after a wholly private liability has already been settled.

For personal development, the rule can train timely discharge rather than indefinite good intention. For justice, it separates unavoidable exposure from risk created by the obligated person’s delay. For civilization, it asks whether collection is actually available and orderly. A missing or predatory collector affects practice; the legal consequences still depend on the adopted doctrine. We cannot turn an administrative failure into personal blame without first determining which conditions were fulfilled.

Principles in this argument. Ability, avoidable delay and the collector’s arrival concern distinct conditions in the reported positions. The capacity discussion helps frame why unavoidable non-performance differs from culpable postponement; it does not settle the tax rule without its own evidence. Preserve Ibn Rushd’s qualification of the reported agreement, rather than upgrading it to unqualified ijmāʿ.

Z017. Death with unpaid zakāt: estate liability and testamentary direction

Al-Shāfiʿī, Aḥmad, Isḥāq and Abū Thawr are reported as requiring payment from the estate’s principal. Another position requires a testamentary direction and limits payment to the disposable third. Within the latter there is disagreement about priority over other bequests when the third is insufficient; Ibn Rushd reports both positions from Mālik and identifies the testamentary treatment as well known. Bidāya, Arabic I, p.249.

The Muwaṭṭaʾ supplies a precise control: Mālik gives unpaid zakāt priority over other bequests within the third when instructed, likens it to debt for that purpose, and commends a family’s voluntary payment where no instruction was left without making it obligatory on them. This shows that an analogy with debt can operate in one respect without erasing the testamentary limitation. .

The practical object now crosses a person’s death. Does the obligation survive as a prior estate claim, or require a validly expressed disposition within the protected shares of others? Heirs and recipients become distinct bearers of possible claims. The analysis cannot attend only to the deceased’s inward intention; it must ask which living persons bear the consequence.

Principles in this argument. The Muwaṭṭaʾ comparison with debt operates in a specified respect and alongside a testamentary limitation. The Ḍarūrī’s graded account of extension is a check against importing every consequence of ordinary debt from a partial resemblance. The obligation’s survival and its enforceable estate route remain separate legal propositions. The partial debt resemblance remains a partial comparison; no independently indicated universal importing all debt rules has been demonstrated.

Z018–Z019. Selling or gifting wealth after zakāt becomes due

Z018: sale. Abū Thawr allows the collector to take the due from the property, with the buyer having recourse against the seller. Al-Shāfiʿī’s reported position annuls the sale. Abū Ḥanīfa gives the buyer an option to affirm or rescind, with the agricultural due taken from the produce. Mālik places zakāt on the seller. The printed Arabic, checked on the image, reads al-muṣaddiq, the collector; the English description of the actor who takes the zakāt needs care. Bidāya, Arabic I, pp.249–250; Bidāya, English I, PDF pp.271–272, printed pp.289–290.

The explicit cause is whether sale resembles destroying or removing the taxable substance, so liability remains in the disposer’s obligation, or selling something to which another already has a right, so the due remains attached to the asset. Whether the sale is annulled is a further sales-law problem, which Ibn Rushd himself cross-references. Z019: gifts present the same type of question, but he does not give a full separate attribution list here. The record must cross-link the gift question without filling missing positions from speculation. Bidāya, Arabic I, p.250.

This is an excellent example of law’s interdependence across books. A zakāt rule cannot be fully explained without sale validity, recourse and third-party rights. The buyer’s good faith, the recipient’s due and the seller’s control are all in play. A transaction can transfer title without necessarily extinguishing every pre-existing claim.

At the civic level, predictable answers support exchange and protect third parties; uncertain or opportunistic collection can burden a buyer after the price has been paid. The economic effect of each rule depends on disclosure, remedies and enforcement. Legal validity and the actual fairness of a market are connected but distinct objects of research.

Ibn Rushd then explains that he has omitted some fine school distinctions, many of which are difficult to explain and described as involving istiḥsān. This sets a fundamental boundary for “all rules”: an exhaustive Bidāya commentary must cover every rule in this book, but it cannot be represented as covering every rule in the schools. His own selection is purposeful and acknowledged. Bidāya, Arabic I, p.250.

Principles in this argument. The primary analogy concerns destruction of an asset versus transfer of property encumbered by another’s right. Sale validity is a further question. The prohibition/invalidity discussion is relevant to that further inquiry only if its appropriate ground is established in the sales cross-reference; it cannot be used to invent a missing invalidity argument for the gift variant. The local comparisons are recorded as such; their reformulation as an indicated universal remains unproved.

Subsidiary maxims. Substance rather than a transaction’s label helps ask whether a transfer actually removes an asset, transfers an encumbered right or preserves a personal claim. An anti-evasion maxim cannot automatically invalidate every post-obligation sale: neither dishonest purpose nor its prescribed legal consequence is established merely by chronological sequence.

Z020. Withholding payment, faith and political coercion

The closing question concerns refusal to pay without denial of obligation. Ibn Rushd reports opposed treatments associated with Abū Bakr and ʿUmar, including the status of captives, and identifies the majority with ʿUmar’s treatment in his account. He relates the disagreement to whether īmān, as opposed to kufr, consists in assent alone or requires acts, with the majority’s special place for verbal testimony. The surrounding historical claims must be verified against their own primary reports before being adopted as a settled reconstruction of the early conflicts. Bidāya, Arabic I, p.250.

This case is indispensable to a theory of acknowledgement. Failure to perform what one recognizes as obligatory does not, on the majority account here, simply make the person a disbeliever. A philosophical progression from recognition to acknowledgement to adab cannot be converted into a juridical power to declare everyone lacking perfected conduct outside the community. Moral defect, fiscal refusal, political resistance and denial of belief are different descriptions.

The inner/outer question is equally exact. Verbal testimony is an act with a public form, while belief is inward. The text discusses the believer’s judgment before God as well as the legal classification. We must not collapse these registers or treat a ruler’s coercive success as proof that assent or virtue has been produced.

Principles in this argument. The classifications of refusal, denial and enforced performance must remain distinct from the cultivation of voluntary acknowledgement. The Ḍarūrī supplies an explicit agency/coercion inquiry. The later limit on inspiration supplies a separate control: an official cannot substitute an alleged reading of another’s inner state for the public grounds required for a legal judgment.

Giving, dignity and self-deception

Setting. is the extended giving sequence immediately before the ribā passage. It moves through images of growth and loss, motives and quality of gifts, concealment and publicity, guidance, and the poor who do not press their requests.

The passage. The fruitful grain is followed by prohibitions on reminders and injury. Kind speech can be better than a gift that humiliates; display can make giving barren. Fear of poverty confronts the promise of divine bounty. The passage includes the hidden poor, and ends with giving by night and day, secretly and openly, under divine reward.

Its ethical argument. Giving is judged through its source, object, manner and effect on the recipient. A transfer can relieve material need while the giver uses it to impose inferiority. The promised increase challenges a calculation in which every departure from possession is loss, but it is not a guarantee of a larger immediate bank balance.

What the commentary explains. The Study Quran’s summary of al-Rāzī at explains that reminding recipients of their neediness destroys the virtue of the gift, and that even an awkward request should meet patience. At it interprets the barren rock and fertile garden through differing motives and fruit. At it reports al-Rāzī’s account of how unwillingness to part with anything valued can expand into a more pervasive refusal of good. Its discussion distinguishes public giving that encourages others and makes help visible from secret giving that receives no social prestige. At the recipient’s restraint requires attentiveness from the giver; mere absence of a persistent request does not establish absence of need. These mediated explanations make generosity a differentiated practice rather than a label for any payment.

· · · · · · · · · · · · · · · · · ·

The Iḥyāʾ adds a directly relevant account of failure in giving. Its zakāt discussion warns against self-praise, injury to recipients and regarding one’s contribution as great. It directs attention to lawful and worthy property and to needs concealed by reluctance to beg. Elsewhere in the same discussion, it connects provision with the recipient’s opportunity for worship and speaks of the giver as an intermediary. The supplied English translation needs Arabic control for exact formulations, but its treatment clearly distinguishes financial transfer from the fullest ethical performance of giving. .

This supplies the missing affective and social detail in a bare “zakāt forms generosity” claim. The agent may comply while cultivating superiority; the recipient may receive while being humiliated; the administrator may collect while damaging trust. The alchemical operation must therefore include how wealth is earned, relinquished, delivered and received. A right should not have to depend on the donor’s enjoyment of moral prestige.

There is also a tension to retain. Ghazālī’s advice on preferring certain recipients belongs to his account of spiritually fruitful giving. It is not a warrant to deprive other legally entitled categories of their rights. His inward pedagogy and the Bidāya’s liability rules answer related but different questions. The complete commentary must eventually compare the actual recipient chapter before claiming that all preferences fit without friction.

Zakāt through the stages and conditions of civilization

What the whole opening division establishes

Zakāt’s virtue-teleology is enacted through a differentiated architecture of capacity, title, control, priority, time, evidence, transfer and jurisdiction. Its formative subject is sometimes the payer, sometimes a guardian or official, and often a network of persons whose relations are made more just. The recipient’s material good has independent significance; it is not merely a device for improving the rich person’s soul.

The chapter also identifies limits to our knowledge: unexplained intermediate distinctions, disputed attributions, partly omitted school details and historical reports needing verification. These limits belong inside a rigorous philosophy of law. They prevent the higher synthesis from claiming to know more than the legal and historical evidence permits.

Coverage status. The opening and first division have been read continuously and their identified questions interpreted. The detailed asset, rate, year and recipient divisions are not yet covered here. The Arabic/English discrepancies on Banū Taghlib, al-Layth and the collector require critical collation; the early withholding narratives require their own historical dossier. No claim of completed interpretation of the entire zakāt book is made.

Part IV.B. Exchange, ribā and uncertainty

Revision 6. Targeted ribā/deferred-exchange reconstructions at II129–135 and II147 precede the retained detailed unseen-sale dossier. These are not a complete sales chapter. The G001–G005 source boundary is: Arabic II 155, from the division between visible and absent objects, to II 156, immediately before the next issue on delayed delivery. English II printed pp.187–188, PDF pp.191–192. G001–G005 separate the principal operations within this passage. Earlier double-sale and loss-allocation material on II 155, and subsequent delivery and harvest questions, remain outside this installment. The general statement on much/little gharar at the top of II 155 is used as an adjoining interpretive control.

The scriptural argument: gain, need and reciprocal responsibility

The preceding giving sequence explains why the exchange passage asks what counts as gain and loss: it condemns a gift that humiliates, contrasts display with fruitful giving, and challenges fear-driven possessiveness. The Study Quran’s summary of al-Rāzī makes the link to character explicit: refusing to part with what one values can grow into wider avarice. This supplies the ethical background, while the following ribā definitions and disagreements require their own evidence.

· · · · · · · · · · · · · · · · · ·

Setting. follows the sustained discussion of giving at . Ibn ʿĀshūr records a Thaqīf debt-settlement occasion for but explicitly makes parts of his historical reconstruction conditional on its correctness.

The passage. The passage rejects the equation of trade with ribā; contrasts the effacement of ribā with the increase of charity; calls believers to taqwā and abandonment of outstanding ribā; preserves the principal so neither party wrongs the other; gives the distressed debtor respite and commends remission; then recalls the day on which each soul receives its due without injustice.

Its ethical argument. The sequence tests what a person calls gain. An accounting increase can accompany an ethically destructive relation, whereas giving can be described as increase before God. The creditor must relinquish a forbidden increment without losing the legitimate principal. Taqwā becomes specific conduct towards another person’s need; the final return makes present power over a debtor answerable to a judgment neither party controls.

What the commentary explains. Ibn ʿĀshūr rejects a merely formal explanation of the sale/loan difference and tests other explanations before proposing a distinction grounded in the borrower’s typical need: lending should relieve hardship, while charging for that relief can intensify it. He expressly considers borrowing to expand a business, so his account is not a simple equation of all borrowers with destitution. At he says taqwā comes before the specific command because it grounds obedience and restraint. The Study Quran explains the pre-Islamic renewal of matured debts through an added obligation and distinguishes this from the same-kind commodity exchanges treated in hadith. Its summary of preserves both release from the increment and the creditor’s claim to principal. Neither overview settles the disputed commodity predicates investigated by Ibn Rushd.

· · · · · ·

Setting. In Muslim1586, Ṭalḥa proposes to complete the other side of a currency exchange when his attendant returns; ʿUmar intervenes with the received restriction.

The passage. The report links the named exchanges to reciprocal delivery. The practical setting is a delay that a participant treated as permissible, followed by correction from someone who knew the report.

Its ethical argument. A good intention or a reputable counterparty does not make the timing immaterial. Knowledge becomes a public corrective to an otherwise ordinary-looking transaction. Compliance here can train responsiveness to a limit on gain, but the report alone does not establish either participant’s whole character.

What the commentary explains. Nawawī explains Ṭalḥa’s proposal through lack of knowledge of the particular rule, not a wish to evade it. He disputes a purported consensus that the currencies must already be physically present: on his view they can be brought during the same session before separation. He preserves the difference between immediate delivery after the contract and delivery before the parties separate. The commentary therefore supplies both the encounter’s human intelligibility and a disputed legal interpretation of its temporal requirement.

· ·

Ribā: an intended universal investigated through the realities of exchange

The existing unseen-sale analysis needs a wider account of how relevant universals are found. In the ribā discussion, the reported restriction to the named commodities treats the particular as intended particularly; the majority take the named cases as indicating a more general meaning, then disagree about what it is. This restates the introduction's classification. It does not make the candidates equally secure. The Ḍarūrī treats the proposed food, staple and measurement predicates as weak contextual indicators whose exact justification remains conjectural. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.129–132 Bidāya, Arabic I, printed/PDF p.4 al-Ḍarūrī §267, PDF pp.304–305

The practical predicates differ. A Shāfiʿī argument connects the food wording to edibility; Mālikī explanations add storability, or storability and staple use, with variants explicitly retained; the Ḥanafī argument considers measurement by volume or weight together with sameness of kind in the relevant prohibition. Different rules concern excess and deferment, and monetary goods receive their own treatment. These statements identify the arguments being assessed here; they are not an exhaustive reconstruction of all the school's ribā rules. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.129–135

On II131 the Mālikī argument already invokes protection of wealth and the necessities of livelihood while interpreting the list of commodities. On II132 Ibn Rushd judges the measurement rationale more persuasive from the direction of meaning: justice in transactions involves approximate equality; money makes unlike useful things commensurable; identical measured goods with similar uses stand differently from exchanges between goods serving different needs. He uses the example of a horse worth fifty and clothing of equal value to distinguish equality of value from equality of count. He then considers avoidance of extravagance and the purpose of monetary valuation; II133 calls the combination of measurement and food a good meaning because food is necessary to subsistence. We must preserve both his preference and this further qualification. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.131–133; pp.131–132 images checked

Here the levels of universality genuinely interact. Semantic: what common meaning does the wording indicate? Practical-causal: how do measurement, differences of use and a unit of account organize exchange? Teleological: what constitutes just commensuration and protection against excessive disadvantage? Ethical-economic understanding participates in discriminating between interpretations; it is not merely an edifying story attached to a rule already derived. Yet the teleology does not prove every empirical premise, such as the degree to which qualities and uses within a measured kind are equivalent, or establish every positive prohibition by itself.

This corrects two opposite errors. Ribā cannot be explained here simply as ordinary case-to-case transfer; Ibn Rushd classifies these extensions through intended general meaning. But it also cannot be reduced to a lexical exercise: his preference depends on an account of human need, use, valuation and justice. Nor should the passage become a modern equation between ribā and every unequal market price. The precise category, permitted form and evidentiary route remain indispensable.

Deferred exchange: a causal route is not a semantic inclusion

Ibn Rushd explicitly explains Mālik's restriction of deferred animal exchanges with identical benefits through sadd al-dharīʿa: such an arrangement can function as a loan returning a benefit. Differences between a milk-producing and a meat animal matter in the reported account because the uses differ, not simply because the names differ. He sets this beside al-Shāfiʿī's and the Ḥanafīs' use of different reports, and reconstructs Mālik's position as a reconciliation. He then considers evidence on which the restriction would be an independent rule rather than a blocking-of-means rule. That alternative must remain visible. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.134–135 Nyazee II, PDF pp.168–169, printed pp.164–165

The causal argument is exchange now → obligation of a greater later return without a relevant difference of use → the prohibited benefit-bearing loan structure. Assessing it needs knowledge of what the animals are for and what the transaction accomplishes. Calling all deferment suspect would erase the text's distinctions. Calling the rule merely “more cautious” would hide the contested economic object. The counterinterpretation asks whether a transmitted substantive rule, rather than a prediction of evasion, governs the result.

Arabic II147 gives a more explicit circumvention scenario. A request for ten dinars to be repaid at twice that amount is replaced by a named commodity sale concluded before the seller acquires the commodity; the subsequent acquisition supplies an object worth approximately the requested advance. Ibn Rushd explains that one account treats this as a route to ribā, another through inability to deliver and gharar. He specifies the prohibited form in the school where the parties settle the price before the acquisition, while acknowledging further details he does not give there. We must not use this compressed discussion as a ruling on every deferred sale or every later product carrying the same name. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF p.147; image checked

The philosophical object is the whole sequence of acts, not one isolated transfer. Its economic result, prior arrangement, ownership and delivery differ from an ordinary sale. The causal universal concerns how a sequence can reproduce a prohibited result; the normative authority comes from the prohibition and the contested law of means. Good intentions and contractual labels alone settle neither. The public formative task is intelligible, accountable exchange; its inverse is expertise deployed to conceal the operative relation. Legal scrutiny can discipline that expertise, but excessive suspicion can also obstruct useful credit and trade. Those consequences need independent historical evidence before becoming claims about an actual city's prosperity or decline.

Gharar: applying a degree criterion without inventing a numerical science

In the unseen-sale passage below, the shared rule about much and little gharar is already a legal criterion; the dispute concerns which category description or a later option produces. Description, sensory knowledge, stability before delivery and a usable right to withdraw are different practical mechanisms. Their assessment draws upon knowledge of things and institutions. It is consequently possible for the uncertainty to remain at application or practical judgment, rather than at discovery of a new semantic universal. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.155–156

A modern probability or expected-loss model could test a proposed mechanism, but the text does not supply such a numerical threshold. Nor is the protective purpose proof that every later option removes the relevant gharar. The higher good of fair cooperation helps frame the disagreement; it does not determine whether knowledge must precede commitment. This is the substantive problem developed in G001–G005, and the reason their divergent allocations of power must survive the broader synthesis.

What the prohibition means for the unseen object

Setting. Muslim1513 transmits Abū Hurayra’s report prohibiting pebble sales and gharar sales; it does not supply a detailed encounter or a securely dated first occasion.

The passage. The report names prohibited forms of sale. Nawawī reconstructs three meanings of the pebble transaction: the throw selects the object, terminates the option, or itself concludes the sale.

Its ethical argument. Each reconstruction exposes a different way commitment can outrun intelligible choice. Yet ordinary cooperation cannot wait for exhaustive knowledge of every feature. The ethical problem is warranted reliance under workable conditions, not elimination of all uncertainty.

What the commentary explains. Nawawī calls the prohibition a major organizing principle of sales, then explains why some uncertainty remains tolerable. A house’s foundations cannot ordinarily be inspected; the stuffing of a coat is incidental to what is bought; a month’s lease may run for twenty-nine or thirty days; use of bathwater varies. He brings together need, the difficulty of avoiding uncertainty and its smallness. He explicitly says disagreement over an absent object can arise because one jurist treats the uncertainty as negligible and another does not. This is direct commentary on the report relevant to G001–G005, not a generic commendation of honest trade.

·

Truthful exchange: blessing and the information another party needs

This report concerns disclosure in exchange; it does not independently settle whether the absent object has been described sufficiently. That difference is the practical question of G001–G005.

Text and situation. Ḥakīm ibn Ḥizām’s report connects the parties’ option with truthful disclosure and says concealment and falsehood remove the transaction’s blessing. The report states a transactional practice; it does not narrate an identifiable sale with a dated occasion. Its place in the option chapter does not reduce its ethical content to the duration of withdrawal.

What the commentary explains. Al-Nawawī explains disclosure reciprocally: each must explain what the other needs to know about defects and other relevant matters in the goods and the price. Truthfulness includes what is said about the price and both countervalues. He glosses blessing through increase and growth. This is relevant to cost disclosure in murābaḥa, but does not itself decide whether transport, processing or storage count as recoverable cost; those require Ibn Rushd’s separate analysis.

The practical meaning. A sale is a relation between agents whose ability to choose depends partly on information held by the other. Profit can coexist with a damaged relation when that information is deliberately withheld. Blessing is a theological evaluation, not an empirical prediction that honest sellers always earn more.

·

Giving more back: generosity, debt and the limits of a public fund

The repayment encounter sharpens the preceding ribā discussion: an added benefit voluntarily given and a benefit stipulated as the price of credit have different normative forms.

Text and situation. The Prophet directs repayment of a borrowed camel with a better one and praises excellence in repayment. In a related report, a creditor speaks sharply; the Prophet allows the claimant to speak. One version mentions camels arriving as alms. That creates a real question: a custodian of charity cannot simply use it to finance personal generosity.

What the commentary explains. Al-Nawawī calls better repayment a noble disposition and distinguishes it from a benefit stipulated in the loan. He records a disagreement with Mālik about adding quantity rather than quality. He then confronts the charity-fund difficulty: his preferred reconciliation is that the better camel was bought from a recipient who had acquired it, and only then given as the Prophet’s own property; he supports this through the version directing purchase. He also reads the creditor’s speech as ordinary forceful pursuit of a right. These are substantive conditions on generosity, not an exemption of a revered borrower from accountability.

The practical meaning. “Giving back in fullness” requires two distinctions. A voluntary addition is different from an increase demanded as the price of a loan; spending one’s own property generously is different from spending property entrusted for specified recipients.

·

G001. Whether description can supply sufficient knowledge

Positions. Ibn Rushd gives the better-known of al-Shāfiʿī’s two opinions as prohibiting sale of the absent object, whether described or not. Mālik and most Medinan jurists permit description where the object’s qualities are not expected to change before possession. Abū Ḥanīfa permits sale of an absent particular object without description, with an option when it is seen. The existence of two Shāfiʿī opinions must remain visible even though this passage develops the better-known one. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.155–156; Bidāya, English II, PDF pp.191–192, printed pp.187–188

Sabab and uṣūl. Does the lesser knowledge afforded by description count as effective ignorance and excessive gharar, or as tolerable slight gharar? Ibn Rushd places al-Shāfiʿī and Mālik on different sides of this classification. The issue is degree and legal effect of a deficiency, not a rejection of practical reason by one side. The adjacent general statement says jurists agree on prohibiting great gharar and permitting little, while differing over cases between them. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.155–156

At the vertical level, truthful exchange can be acknowledgement enacted in speech and property relations. The absent thing is not thereby a symbol of metaphysical absence. The result for the master theory is precise: law forms relations of warranted reliance, while the extent of warrant remains contested.

Principles in this argument. The local sales criterion is avoidance of the disqualifying gharar; the contested point is what description establishes. The Ḍarūrī makes sales a domain in which relevant indicators can be more evident, without making this particular disagreement disappear. Ghazālī’s application distinction helps locate the knowledge question only after the legally sufficient criterion has been adopted.

Subsidiary maxims. The compilation’s need maxim is a later comparative question, not a warrant to infer the school’s reason: does a recognized commercial need justify a particular tolerance? Its examples of distinct contracts cannot establish the validity of this absent-object sale. Remote speculation about loss also differs from the relevant gharar actually identified by the doctrine.

G002. The option of sight: a later decision can change the present risk

Primary difference. Abū Ḥanīfa’s account permits the buyer to affirm or reject on seeing the object, even when a description was given and the object conforms. Mālik makes the conforming described sale binding. On the reported Shāfiʿī position, it never validly formed in either case. Ibn Rushd explains that Abū Ḥanīfa regards the option as removing the relevant gharar even without prior sight; Mālik treats the ignorance accompanying lack of description as affecting formation itself. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.155–156

Ontology of the operation. An option is a legal power distributed over time, not just an inward feeling of reassurance. The question is whether later choice adequately controls the risk of the earlier act. The three arrangements concern prevention, qualified initial commitment and revisability. Calling them simply strict, moderate and easy would erase their different structures.

The alchemical change is from an impulsive or ignorant assent to a legally ordered sequence of seeing, choosing and bearing consequences. Accountability before God does not remove the need for a usable remedy. The feedback is that formation can be built into the architecture of a transaction rather than demanded entirely before it begins.

Principles in this argument. The option changes the legal configuration of consent and exposure. It is therefore part of the argument that relevant gharar has been removed, not merely a prediction that the buyer will probably be satisfied. This is an assessment of a legal arrangement against the adopted gharar criterion; it need not be the discovery of a new semantic universal. The Ḍarūrī comparison asks for the exact operation and its warrant, not an automatic relabeling as qiyās.

Subsidiary maxims. An option can be examined as a means of preventing or removing a specified injury to consent. The preventive maxim adds no automatic proof that this particular option is sufficient; that remains the issue in the primary dispute. The formative operation is making the buyer’s later informed choice legally effective.

G003. An internal Mālikī variant prevents a fixed school essence

Ibn Rushd records permission within the school to sell the absent thing without description on condition of the option of sight, locates it in the Mudawwana, and notes ʿAbd al-Wahhāb’s rejection of it as contrary to the school’s principles. This is an internal disagreement reported by Ibn Rushd; the underlying Mudawwana passage has not yet been independently collated. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.155–156; Bidāya, English II, PDF p.192, printed p.188

The consequence is methodological and practical. A legal tradition contains arguments about what counts as its own coherent operation. The jurist learns neither by collecting isolated permissions nor by giving the school a permanent psychological temperament. He must examine the transmitted position, the proposed principle and the alleged conflict between them.

Shaʿrānī’s differentiated severity and alleviation can prompt a question about whom a permitted operation serves, but cannot settle this school-internal validity dispute through the physician analogy alone. No text in this passage assigns the variant to a stronger or weaker spiritual patient. Spiritual preference must not silently become authority to reconstruct the school’s conditions. al-Shaʿrānī, Mīzān I, printed/PDF pp.73–74,98

The case feeds upward by limiting “perspectival differentiation”: it can illuminate why alternatives matter after their warrants have been established; it cannot erase a jurist’s claim that an alternative conflicts with governing principles.

Principles in this argument. A differing report within one school must be evaluated through its actual criterion, not a permanent school personality. Ibn Rushd’s distinction between excusable disagreement and universal correctness also limits the proposed “alchemical styles”: a meaningful orientation does not immunize an attributed position from error.

G004. Why description is sometimes a substitute and sometimes insufficient

Qualifications. In Mālik’s account, description replaces inspection because of absence, difficulty in unfolding/display, or danger of damage through repeated display. Ibn Rushd mentions sale by a descriptive list, while excluding the weapon left in its case and folded cloth where inspection is required. Abū Ḥanīfa still requires identification of the genus. The permission is therefore not a sale of an utterly unspecified nothing. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF p.156

Meaning. The physical object and the act of showing it belong within legal reasoning. A requirement designed to improve knowledge can damage the commodity if repeated display is destructive. Conversely, concealment that can readily be removed is not treated identically to unavoidable absence. The governing distinction is between an appropriate substitute and avoidable ignorance.

The institution needs shared standards and credible testimony about conformity. Specialization may improve those capacities while making buyers more dependent upon experts. Political or commercial concentration can increase the power of those controlling information. No regime-stage label substitutes for examining that relation.

The alchemical operation is to make speech an accountable mediation of material reality. In Attas’ terms this can be read as acknowledgement of the thing and another person’s due; the legal conditions remain those of the source. The result qualifies a universal theory of transparency: adequate knowledge need not always be immediate sight, but an authorized substitute must answer to a definite practical limitation. Attas, Concept of Education, PDF pp.10–12

Principles in this argument. Whether a description substitutes for inspection requires inquiry into the legally relevant features it conveys and the features left uncertain. Ghazālī’s known-criterion/instance distinction is useful for that assessment. It supplies no universal rule that all descriptions are adequate; the sales criterion and its contested scope remain controlling.

G005. Existing now, remaining the same and having been seen before

Further rule. Ibn Rushd distinguishes uncertainty about qualities from uncertainty whether the absent object exists at the time of the contract. Proximity of absence and security against loss matter, with immovable property as an example of relative security. Mālik also allows a sufficiently recent prior sight where change is not feared. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF p.156; Bidāya, English II, PDF p.192, printed p.188

Object and inference. Knowledge has a temporal index. A true description at an earlier time may cease to warrant a present commitment if the object can change or perish. The legal distinction is therefore not merely described versus seen: sight too can become stale. The operative inquiry includes the durability of the object and continuity of the conditions under which it was known.

The chapter’s upward finding is that law’s practical science must analyze time, matter, knowledge and remedial powers together. A theory concerned only with inward honesty would miss these structural conditions; one concerned only with economic efficiency would miss the norm governing what may be made binding. The remaining sales, ribā and gharar material now has priority for the same detailed method.

Principles in this argument. The existence of the object, persistence of its qualities and present legal sufficiency of earlier sight are three propositions. Istiṣḥāb can illuminate a continuity argument, but physical persistence is not automatically an adequate legal proof of unchanged quality. The Ḍarūrī expressly distinguishes continuity after a relevant quality changes; the maxim of certainty does not remove the need to identify the actual evidential baseline.

Subsidiary maxims. An unproved change, uncertain timing of a known change and a factual assumption shown false are different situations. The subsidiary maxims expose those differences; none should be applied to cancel the significance of earlier sight without showing which situation actually obtains. Effects on a completed contract require a further rule.

Representative route: exchange and cooperation

Revision 14 · 4 October 2026. Selected studies across every editorial division; exact source spans below delimit the selection. These are representative interpretations, not chapter-completion or elementary-rule counts.

Quoted scriptural clauses below are selected working translations from the cited Arabic. Exegetical views are named; the paragraph labelled “Its ethical argument” is the manuscript’s close reading of the passage and its surrounding clauses. The purple note gives the full explanation and exact sources. A related passage does not become the direct evidence for a ruling merely by being placed beside it.

Exchange brings legal meaning into objects that are partly conventional and partly material: descriptions, measures, future benefits, skills, custody, time and risk. Ibn Rushd’s explicit explanations of disagreement remain the first account. A wider interpretation becomes useful only after identifying what changes between the rival arrangements—who must disclose, who may withdraw, who receives partial benefit and who carries loss.

The common product must also be distinguished from the common good. Partnership and cultivation can yield a surplus while concentrating insecurity in the weaker participant. Maritain’s account helps test whether the shared undertaking benefits persons as participants rather than consuming them as resources. This is a comparative criterion, not an attribution of his vocabulary to Ibn Rushd. Maritain, The Person and the Common Good, PDF pp.14–17

REP-29. Exchange: intelligible justice without a universal theory of every restriction

Division 29: Sales including riba and gharar.

Ruling and reason for disagreement. The retained sales module distinguishes extending the named ribā commodities through an indicated meaning from an independently asserted analogy, then compares proposed grounds such as food, storability and measurement. It also preserves the unseen-sale disagreement over when description or an option adequately addresses uncertainty. These are separate practical objects and separate warrants. Bidāya Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.129–132,155–156

How the legal argument works. · · . These notes identify the relevant mechanism or comparative control; later maxims do not establish Ibn Rushd’s historical vocabulary.

Giving more back: generosity, debt and the limits of a public fund

Text and setting. The Prophet directs repayment of a borrowed camel with a better one and praises excellence in repayment. In a related report, a creditor speaks sharply; the Prophet allows the claimant to speak. One version mentions camels arriving as alms. That creates a real question: a custodian of charity cannot simply use it to finance personal generosity.

The ethical argument. “Giving back in fullness” requires two distinctions. A voluntary addition is different from an increase demanded as the price of a loan; spending one’s own property generously is different from spending property entrusted for specified recipients.

He records a disagreement with Mālik about adding quantity rather than quality. He also reads the creditor’s speech as ordinary forceful pursuit of a right. These are substantive conditions on generosity, not an exemption of a revered borrower from accountability.

Scope of this reading. The purchase sequence is the commentator’s harmonization of variants. It must not be presented as wording found in every narration. This dossier concerns repayment, not the separate contract of a loan for use.

Truthful exchange: blessing and the information another party needs

How the commentators read it. Al-Nawawī explains disclosure reciprocally: each must explain what the other needs to know about defects and other relevant matters in the goods and the price. Truthfulness includes what is said about the price and both countervalues. He glosses blessing through increase and growth. This is relevant to cost disclosure in murābaḥa, but does not itself decide whether transport, processing or storage count as recoverable cost; those require Ibn Rushd’s separate analysis.

Scope of this reading. The connection to murābaḥa is a bounded application of the report’s ethical argument, not a claim that this report supplies the technical definition of cost.

Direct context and explanation. follows the sustained discussion of giving at . Ibn ʿĀshūr records a Thaqīf debt-settlement occasion for but explicitly makes parts of his historical reconstruction conditional on its correctness. Ibn ʿĀshūr rejects a merely formal explanation of the sale/loan difference and tests other explanations before proposing a distinction grounded in the borrower’s typical need: lending should relieve hardship, while charging for that relief can intensify it. He expressly considers borrowing to expand a business, so his account is not a simple equation of all borrowers with destitution. At he says taqwā comes before the specific command because it grounds obedience and restraint. The Study Quran explains the pre-Islamic renewal of matured debts through an added obligation and distinguishes this from the same-kind commodity exchanges treated in hadith. Its summary of preserves both release from the increment and the creditor’s claim to principal. Neither overview settles the disputed commodity predicates investigated by Ibn Rushd.

· · · · · · · · · · ·

Direct context and explanation. Muslim1513 transmits Abū Hurayra’s report prohibiting pebble sales and gharar sales; it does not supply a detailed encounter or a securely dated first occasion. Nawawī calls the prohibition a major organizing principle of sales, then explains why some uncertainty remains tolerable. A house’s foundations cannot ordinarily be inspected; the stuffing of a coat is incidental to what is bought; a month’s lease may run for twenty-nine or thirty days; use of bathwater varies. He brings together need, the difficulty of avoiding uncertainty and its smallness. He explicitly says disagreement over an absent object can arise because one jurist treats the uncertainty as negligible and another does not. This is direct commentary on the report relevant to G001–G005, not a generic commendation of honest trade.

REP-30. Currency exchange: immediacy, equality and the discipline of settlement

Follow the argument RulingLegal reasoningScripture

Division 30: Currency exchange.

Ruling and reason for disagreement. Ibn Rushd organizes ṣarf around identifying delay, identifying equivalence, and suspected means to the prohibited forms. He reports the general requirement of equality and immediate exchange for gold with gold or silver with silver, while preserving the contrary early report from Ibn ʿAbbās about excess. His classification asks what actually counts as each condition rather than assuming the words settle their application. Bidāya Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.194–195

Direct context and explanation. In Muslim1586, Ṭalḥa proposes to complete the other side of a currency exchange when his attendant returns; ʿUmar intervenes with the received restriction. Nawawī explains Ṭalḥa’s proposal through lack of knowledge of the particular rule, not a wish to evade it. He disputes a purported consensus that the currencies must already be physically present: on his view they can be brought during the same session before separation. He preserves the difference between immediate delivery after the contract and delivery before the parties separate. The commentary therefore supplies both the encounter’s human intelligibility and a disputed legal interpretation of its temporal requirement.

REP-31. Salam: financing future provision through determinate commitments

Follow the argument RulingLegal reasoningScripture

Division 31: Salam.

Ibn Rushd: summary of the ruling and disagreement. The Ibn ʿAbbās report places the instruction in Medina, where people advanced payment for later dates. Measure, weight and term are specified. Ibn Rushd reports agreement for measured and weighed goods, restriction to those goods by Dāwūd and others, and the majority's extension to describable goods, with a further dispute about animals. Generalizability and adequacy of description are distinct questions. Bidāya Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.201

Text and reported setting. Bukhārī2239–2241 situates advance payment in Medina, where people paid ahead for produce over two or three years. The instruction specifies known measure, known weight and a known term.

Ethical force of the passage. The parties cooperate across time: one receives resources before delivery, and the other relies on future performance. Naming a measure and term makes that reliance answerable and reduces opportunities to exploit incompatible expectations. It does not eliminate harvest risk or prove every later credit instrument permissible.

How the commentators read it. Ibn Ḥajar explains why local measures must be specified when they differ and preserves disagreement over whether salam is a concession for need or a contract intelligible within the general rules. The concrete wisdom is coordination under delayed performance; its legal classification remains disputed.

Ruling and reason for disagreement. The majority permit a stipulated option; opponents invoke uncertainty and contest the validity or general scope of the Ḥabbān report. Among those permitting it, Mālik measures duration by the time needed to examine the object; Abū Ḥanīfa and al-Shāfiʿī limit it to three days; other reported positions allow an agreed longer term. Ibn Rushd keeps general admissibility distinct from duration. Bidāya Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.209
