Text and reported setting. Bukhārī2117 concerns a man repeatedly deceived in sales who is told to stipulate that there shall be no deception. The often-associated three-day provision belongs to additional reports, not this short wording.

Ethical force of the passage. The encounter recognizes that a person can enter a transaction willingly yet be vulnerable through limited market competence. An ethical market cannot treat the more skilful party’s ability to exploit that weakness as sufficient justification for doing so.

How the commentators read it. Ibn Ḥajar explains the formula as alerting the other party to the buyer’s lack of expertise, discusses the additional three-night reports and records objections to generalizing the dispensation. The commentary thus brings the buyer’s particular condition into view without making every disappointing bargain proof of incapacity or deceit.

REP-34. ʿAriyya: a concession whose beneficiary is disputed

Follow the argument RulingLegal reasoningScripture

Division 34: Ariyya sale.

Ruling and reason for disagreement. The schools differ over what ʿariyya denotes, who receives its concession, and its conditions. In Ibn Rushd's account, Mālik relates it to a prior gift and a restricted reacquisition; al-Shāfiʿī admits a wider class of small exchanges with immediate delivery; Aḥmad places the concession differently; Abū Ḥanīfa reads the transaction outside an exception to the forbidden sale. Quantity, delay and subject matter cannot be collapsed into one rule. Bidāya Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.216–217

How the legal argument works. · · . These notes identify the relevant mechanism or comparative control; later maxims do not establish Ibn Rushd’s historical vocabulary.

Text and reported setting. The ʿariyya reports concern date-fruit and an exceptional exchange involving estimation. Ibn Ḥajar preserves several practical settings: a gift whose collection becomes burdensome, access to fresh fruit and relief of a recipient’s difficulty.

Ethical force of the passage. A concession can preserve the real benefit of giving when the original arrangement creates an obstacle to use. But its wisdom depends on identifying who needs relief and what burden is removed; a generic appeal to generosity cannot dissolve the restrictions intended to prevent ribā.

How the commentators read it. Ibn Ḥajar compares Mālik’s and al-Shāfiʿī’s explanations and their differing conditions concerning the parties, estimation and delivery. These accounts are rival reconstructions of the practical situation, not pieces of a single undisputed origin story. Their differences help explain why the permitted form itself remains contested.

REP-35. Hire and lease: future service as a real practical object

Follow the argument RulingLegal reasoningScripture

Division 35: Hire and lease.

Ruling and reason for disagreement. Against a reported minority objection that future benefits do not yet exist, Ibn Rushd defends hire through scripture, prophetic practice and their ordinarily realizable character. He cites nursing remuneration, the Moses marriage-and-service narrative, and the hiring of a skilled guide for the Hijra. A future benefit's present non-existence is not by itself the relevant uncertainty. Bidāya Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.220

How the legal argument works. · . These notes identify the relevant mechanism or comparative control; later maxims do not establish Ibn Rushd’s historical vocabulary.

Text and reported setting. recommends Moses as strong and trustworthy after his help at the watering place. The proposed agreement in 28:27 distinguishes eight years from two additional voluntary years and says, “I do not wish to make hardship for you.” The Hijra guide report concerns a different event: trusted expertise hired for a dangerous journey.

Ethical force of the passage. Competence serves the work; trust concerns how one uses that competence in another’s interest. The employer’s refusal to impose hardship and the distinction between what is due and what is volunteered give the arrangement its ethical shape. Effective skill alone is not fidelity, and generosity must not be silently converted into an additional compulsory term.

How the commentators read it. Ibn ʿĀshūr reads the recommendation as a general insight emerging from observed conduct. Ibn Ḥajar draws from the Hijra the permissibility of relying on a trustworthy non-Muslim guide for the service concerned. Professional trust here rests on relevant capacity and dependability, not an inference that the parties possess identical spiritual standing.

REP-36. Reward for a result: uncertainty and uncompensated labour

Follow the argument RulingLegal reasoningScripture

Division 36: Jual wages.

Ruling and reason for disagreement. Juʿl concerns a benefit whose attainment is uncertain. Ibn Rushd reports Mālik's conditional permission, Abū Ḥanīfa's rejection and two positions from al-Shāfiʿī. More strikingly, he explains why a result-contingent arrangement becomes unjust if the promisor benefits from partial work yet owes nothing because the full result was not achieved. The ship example tests the boundary between juʿl and ordinary hire. Bidāya Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.235–236

Text and reported setting. occurs in Joseph’s narrative: an announcement concerns a missing cup, offers a camel-load for its return and includes the announcer’s guarantee. It is not a general discourse explaining every condition of a reward contract.

Ethical force of the passage. The publicly specified reward gives another person a reason to undertake work whose success is uncertain. Its narrative use does not settle whether a failed or partially successful worker is owed anything. The related labour passage supplies an ethical control: agreed service and freely added service must remain distinguishable.

How the commentators read it. Ibn ʿĀshūr reads the proclamation within the episode of the missing royal measure. Its narrative location matters because a jurist’s use of a statement from an earlier prophetic story requires further argument; the commentator’s narration is not by itself the operative uṣūl mechanism.

REP-37. Qirāḍ: sharing uncertain gain without making the worker an insurer

Follow the argument RulingLegal reasoningScripture

Division 37: Qirad.

Ruling and reason for disagreement. Ibn Rushd reports agreement on the basic profit-sharing arrangement, its pre-Islamic practice and Islamic acceptance, and its concession from otherwise uncertain hire for people's accommodation. The worker receives an agreed proportion of profit and does not guarantee capital lost without transgression. Disagreement remains over what counts as transgression, valid capital and impermissible conditions. Bidāya Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.236

How the legal argument works. · · . These notes identify the relevant mechanism or comparative control; later maxims do not establish Ibn Rushd’s historical vocabulary.

Qirāḍ: a worker’s risk, public property and privileged access

Text and setting. The Muwaṭṭaʾ reports that Abū Mūsā advanced public money to ʿUmar’s two sons to trade with on their return from Iraq. ʿUmar asked whether the other soldiers had received the same opportunity. After dispute about the gain and the sons’ assumed liability, the transaction was treated as qirāḍ and the profit divided. This is a Companion-era administrative encounter, not a Prophetic utterance. The account exposes the conjunction of family connection, office, finance and commercial work.

The ethical argument. The problem is not only whether productive skill deserves reward. The opportunity itself may be unequally distributed through power. A remedy must reckon both with the community’s capital and with work already undertaken.

How the commentators read it. Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr expressly reads ʿUmar’s intervention as protective judgment for the Muslims because the recipients were his sons and had been favoured. His next discussion distinguishes entrusted capital from an insured debt: the worker does not guarantee accidental loss without wrongdoing, consumption or neglect. He records disagreement about an invalid guarantee condition and about travel expenses. He even prefers an argument against automatically charging the worker’s expenses to the capital, because this can consume capital and make the shares uncertain. Thus a shared contract can sustain cooperation while leaving the allocation of its burdens disputed.

Scope of this reading. Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr grounds permissibility in established practice and reported agreement; this is not a fabricated direct hadith foundation. Neither his agreement claims nor every chain has been independently audited. The institutional analogy with preferential state credit is an interpretation, not an identity of systems.

REP-38. Musāqāh: productive cooperation within an unequal historical setting

Follow the argument RulingLegal reasoningScripture

Division 38: Musaqah.

Ruling and reason for disagreement. The majority permit the arrangement on the basis of the Khaybar reports; Abū Ḥanīfa rejects it in the account given here. Ibn Rushd records objections based on uncreated produce, uncertain hire, possible historical status and conflicting agricultural reports. He also distinguishes scope: palms alone, palms and vines, or a wider class of rooted crops. Bidāya Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.244–245

How the legal argument works. · . These notes identify the relevant mechanism or comparative control; later maxims do not establish Ibn Rushd’s historical vocabulary.

Text and reported setting. Muslim1551 records work at Khaybar in return for a share of the produce, with related versions discussing allocations and the arrangement’s continuation.

Ethical force of the passage. The practical good depends on land and knowledgeable labour cooperating. Merely possessing the resource does not supply the skill needed to make it fruitful. This observation identifies a condition of production, not a moral endorsement of every relation of power surrounding the historical arrangement.

How the commentators read it. Ibn Ḥajar highlights the workers’ knowledge of cultivation when discussing their employment. The agreed produce share coordinates distinct contributions whose benefit emerges through a growing season. Whether a particular allocation distributes risk and reward justly still requires the legal conditions and the actual circumstances; agricultural expertise alone does not answer it.

REP-40. Preemption: neighbourly harm and the purchaser’s acquired claim

Follow the argument RulingLegal reasoningScripture

Division 40: Preemption.

Ruling and reason for disagreement. Mālik and al-Shāfiʿī restrict the primary right to an undivided partner; the Iraqi account extends a hierarchy through shared access to the adjacent neighbour. Ibn Rushd compares apparently competing reports and the extent of harm from partnership and neighbourhood. He also gives the counterweight: property should not be removed from its possessor or purchaser without a warranted exception. Bidāya Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.256–257

How the legal argument works. · . These notes identify the relevant mechanism or comparative control; later maxims do not establish Ibn Rushd’s historical vocabulary.

Preemption: shared property, notice and the limit of a neighbour’s claim

Text and setting. Jābir’s reports concern an undivided property and a partner’s opportunity to take the offered share. They distinguish an opportunity to buy from an absolute bar on another’s sale. No single original dispute is narrated in these versions. The repeated practical setting is sale within an existing property relation.

The ethical argument. One person’s disposal changes the circumstances in which another person must inhabit or use a shared place. Preventing that harm must be weighed against the seller’s disposal and the purchaser’s acquired claim; the phrase “neighbourly good” alone cannot settle the boundary.

How the commentators read it. Al-Nawawī states the proposed wisdom as removal of harm from a partner, explaining the special importance of immovable property. He records the disagreement over adjacency after partition, and over property that cannot usefully be divided. His own school reads prior notification as recommended rather than treating every sale without it as prohibited. He also distinguishes permission to sell from the later survival of a preemption claim. The report therefore requires analysis of entitlement, notice and waiver as different acts.

Scope of this reading. The explanation of harm is not a demonstration that every harmful neighbourhood change gives preemption. The contrary Ḥanafī position remains substantive.

REP-41. Partition: a share that can no longer be used

Follow the argument RulingLegal reasoningScripture

Division 41: Partition.

Ruling and reason for disagreement. Ibn Rushd contrasts partition that preserves useful shares with division that destroys or changes their utility. He records several Mālikī positions alongside other jurists. The argument places the scriptural recognition of a share, however small, beside the prohibition of harm. A bathhouse is a pointed example: equal division of material may abolish the function of the whole. Bidāya Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.265–266

Text and reported setting. assigns both men and women an obligatory share, whether the estate is small or large. later says that people do not know which parents or children are nearer in benefit to them, and concludes with divine knowledge and wisdom.

Ethical force of the passage. The passage challenges a distributor’s claim to know whose value justifies exclusion. The shares are not a prize awarded after measuring an heir’s virtue or usefulness. The reference to divine knowledge marks a limit on the family’s power to replace an entitlement with its own ranking of persons.

How the commentators read it. Ibn ʿĀshūr places within protection of women and orphans whose resources stronger relatives could retain. Wāḥidī’s Jābir narrative and the widow-and-daughters narrative are retained separately; the latter’s naming discrepancy is not silently harmonized.

REP-42. Pledges: security that does not erase a trust

Follow the argument RulingLegal reasoningScripture

Division 42: Pledges.

Ruling and reason for disagreement. The pledge discussion begins from and asks about the pledgor, object and secured claim. The dispute over an undivided share concerns whether possession can be achieved. Another difference concerns an object initially seized wrongfully: Mālik allows its conversion into a pledge with the owner's authorization, while al-Shāfiʿī retains the original liability unless it is first returned. Bidāya Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.272–273

How the legal argument works. · . These notes identify the relevant mechanism or comparative control; later maxims do not establish Ibn Rushd’s historical vocabulary.

A pledge across religious difference: obligation, ownership and provision

Text and setting. ʿĀʾisha reports that the Prophet bought food on credit from a Jewish seller and pledged his iron armour. The exchange takes place in settled life, which is why it matters for reading the travel setting of the Qurʾānic pledge passage. The report does not state a definitive motive for choosing this seller.

The ethical argument. The seller’s enforceable ownership and claim remain real despite religious difference and the buyer’s religious authority. Security enables provision; it does not turn a creditor into the moral inferior of a borrower.

How the commentators read it. Al-Nawawī draws out recognition of the other party’s property, the permissibility of transactions with protected non-Muslims, and the use of a pledge in town as well as on a journey. He treats the report as controlling the contrary inference from the verse’s travel condition. He lists possible explanations of the seller’s selection—showing permissibility, availability of surplus food, or avoiding burdening Companions who might refuse payment—without establishing one as the narrated fact. He also distinguishes this transaction from supplying weapons to a hostile army.

Scope of this reading. This explains the report’s setting and commentary; it does not generalize the medieval protected status into modern equal citizenship, or decide every question of a pledge’s growth and loss.

REP-43. Interdiction: protection ordered toward practical agency

Follow the argument RulingLegal reasoningScripture

Division 43: Interdiction.

Ibn Rushd: summary of the ruling and disagreement. Ibn Rushd distinguishes reaching maturity from showing sound judgment in managing property (). Mālik and al-Shāfiʿī permit a judge to impose restriction on an adult whose wastefulness is established; Abū Ḥanīfa rejects initiating restriction on adults. The first argument extends the protection of minors to anyone displaying the relevant imprudence. The opposing argument treats minority as the operative impediment and maturity as the usual sign of reason and sound judgment. The reach of protection, and what warrants removing a person’s control, are therefore disputed. Bidāya Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.279–281

How the legal argument works. · . These notes identify the relevant mechanism or comparative control; later maxims do not establish Ibn Rushd’s historical vocabulary.

Text and reported setting. commands return of trusts to their owners and just judgment, ending with God as hearing and seeing. considers reliance on personal trust where documentary security is absent: the entrusted person must discharge the trust and fear God his Lord; testimony must not be concealed, and concealment makes the heart culpable.

Ethical force of the passage. The two endings address the gap between an obligation and another person’s ability to enforce it. The trusted holder must not treat the absence of a record as permission to retain what is owed; the witness must not make the truth disappear through silence. God’s hearing, seeing and knowing deny that an undetectable breach becomes morally nonexistent. The reference to the heart concerns deliberate suppression of truth, not a substitute mystical method of proving a claim.

How the commentators read it. Ibn ʿĀshūr reads as addressing everyone entrusted with something and everyone judging, with delivery to the rightful recipient at its centre. He notes the weak chain of the Kaʿba-key occasion rather than treating it as certain. On he explains that an unsecured debt is called a trust to intensify responsibility: lack of pledge or witnesses does not diminish what is owed. This is related to deposit, though a debt and custody of a particular object remain different legal relations. Al-Rāzī distinguishes trusts owed to God, to other people and to oneself. His examples include truthful speech, uncorrupted measures, rulers’ justice, and scholars refusing to recruit ordinary people into partisan error; self-trust requires not sacrificing enduring good to appetite or anger. He also records al-Qāḍī’s narrower reading of this verse as returnable property. On , his preferred explanation is reciprocal: the creditor has dealt well with the debtor by trusting him, so the debtor must not answer that kindness with denial or delay. A witness can prevent that confidence from being exploited. The Study Quran places at the opening of a passage on authority and reports a reciprocal reading: rulers are first charged with justice, then subjects with obedience in 4:59. Its broader account includes deposits, borrowed or found property and spiritual responsibilities. This is the editors’ synthesis of several commentators; its report of the Kaʿba-key occasion must be read alongside Ibn ʿĀshūr’s criticism of the chain. The Study Quran also extends responsible authority to household and body, and reads the paired names Hearing and Seeing as affirming divine knowledge. Its suggestion about hearing’s primacy and the creative command is presented as a possibility, not an established explanation of the deposit rule; this manuscript does not use it to derive a legal or alchemical conclusion. On , The Study Quran distinguishes unsecured trust from a pledge and then connects concealed testimony with accountability for what is inward. It also records the broader reading that troubled the Companions. Its discussion distinguishes being called to account from necessarily being punished; passing thoughts must not be equated with deliberately hiding a claimant’s evidence.

· · · · · · · ·

Direct context and explanation. belongs to the sequence on orphans, property and dower. It combines withholding unrestricted control, provision, honourable speech, testing judgment, timely return and accountability for the guardian. Ibn ʿĀshūr reads the reference to “your wealth” through the connected livelihood of the community: another’s property sustains hiring, exchange, giving and inheritance. Crucially, his explanation of honourable speech addresses the guardian’s irritation at requests. The guardian should not insult, should teach better management where possible, and should remind the person that the money remains theirs and is being preserved for their benefit. The Study Quran records several meanings of sound judgment and ages of maturity; its compression of legal positions must be checked against Ibn Rushd’s disagreement over maturity, sound judgment and restriction. It is useful here for seeing the range of interpretation, not for replacing that disagreement with one uniform test.

· · · · ·

Detailed continuation. capacity. These retain their own open attribution and commentary checks.

REP-44. Insolvency: preserving claims without demanding the impossible

Follow the argument RulingLegal reasoningScripture

Division 44: Insolvency.

Ruling and reason for disagreement. The majority in Ibn Rushd's account permit judicial restriction and sale to satisfy creditors; Abū Ḥanīfa and others are reported as preferring confinement until the debtor disposes of the property. Ibn Rushd calls the former more equitable. He separately treats genuine absence of assets and the temporary suspension of collection, while distinguishing an unproved plea of insolvency from an established condition. Bidāya Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.284–286,293

How the legal argument works. · · . These notes identify the relevant mechanism or comparative control; later maxims do not establish Ibn Rushd’s historical vocabulary.

Text and reported setting. gives respite until ease and commends remission; the next verse recalls return to God and recompense without injustice. Bukhārī2287 calls a person’s delay in paying, when able, wrongdoing.

Ethical force of the passage. The distinction is between inability and refusal. Mercy to the former and accountability for the latter are mutually necessary: indiscriminate coercion destroys the distressed person, while indiscriminate indulgence permits one person to retain another’s resources. The final accounting prevents either creditor’s power or debtor’s concealment from becoming the measure of right.

How the commentators read it. Ibn ʿĀshūr situates respite after the prohibition of ribā and recovery of principal. Ibn Ḥajar interprets the ability relevant to wrongful delay as effective ability to pay, not merely the public label of wealth. The practical inquiry is therefore into actual means and impediments.

· · · ·

REP-45. Settlement: agreement and unresolved truth

Follow the argument RulingLegal reasoningScripture

Division 45: Settlement.

Ruling and reason for disagreement. Mālik and Abū Ḥanīfa permit settlement where liability is denied; al-Shāfiʿī rejects it in the account here. The objection is taking money without a valid countervalue; the opposing account treats the ending of litigation and avoidance of an oath as a benefit. Ibn Rushd also preserves restrictions preventing a settlement from licensing otherwise prohibited exchange. Bidāya Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.293–294

How the legal argument works. · . These notes identify the relevant mechanism or comparative control; later maxims do not establish Ibn Rushd’s historical vocabulary.

Text and reported setting. permits settlement where a woman fears her husband’s withdrawal. “Settlement is better” is immediately followed by the statement that souls are attended by possessiveness, and then by an appeal to iḥsān and taqwā under God’s knowledge of action.

Ethical force of the passage. The text itself names the obstacle to peace: attachment to one’s own portion. It does not say that any settlement, however extracted, is good. In this setting the question is whether an adjustment can preserve a relationship without disguising coercion. God’s knowledge concerns the actual generosity or self-interest beneath the signed terms.

How the commentators read it. Ibn ʿĀshūr treats the verse as permission for an adjustment under marital strain and preserves differing explanatory reports. Reconciliation remains possible without making continued marriage obligatory in every case.

·

REP-46. Surety: standing beside another person without losing one’s limits

Follow the argument RulingLegal reasoningScripture

Division 46: Surety.

Ruling and reason for disagreement. Ibn Rushd distinguishes financial guarantee from a guarantee of appearance. The latter is contested, and its consequences when the person disappears differ: producing the person or paying, confinement, or an obligation qualified by knowledge and ability. General reports, the Joseph narrative and the analogy to other forms of liability pull in different directions. Bidāya Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.295

How the legal argument works. · . These notes identify the relevant mechanism or comparative control; later maxims do not establish Ibn Rushd’s historical vocabulary.

Surety: taking responsibility without substituting one person for another

Text and setting. In Salama’s funeral report, Abū Qatāda undertakes a deceased person’s unpaid debt. The surrounding guarantee chapter also includes reports about securing a person’s appearance. Ibn Ḥajar distinguishes the funeral accounts and their differing amounts. The later change when public resources become available is part of the transmitted sequence; the initial refusal of the Prophet personally to lead the prayer was not a refusal of all funeral prayer.

The ethical argument. A volunteered undertaking can make another’s outstanding claim recoverable. But the form of responsibility matters: a financial guarantor may owe payment, whereas the person guaranteeing an accused person’s appearance does not thereby owe the accused’s bodily punishment.

How the commentators read it. Ibn Ḥajar explicitly distinguishes the guarantee report from transfer of debt, despite their proximity in the chapter arrangement. He reports disagreement about recourse against an estate and describes the guarantee as a serious undertaking rather than ceremonial sympathy. In discussing guarantees of appearance, he records the distinction between money and a bodily penalty, along with disagreement over disappearance and death. He also challenges an inference about discretionary punishment drawn from a Companion’s act where the report does not expressly state its legal category.

Scope of this reading. The additional appearance reports have their own chains and cannot be collapsed into the funeral event. The ethical usefulness of surety does not settle whether every proposed form is valid.

· ·

Related scriptural comparison. The following passage illuminates a neighbouring good; the direct report or legal tradition is treated above.

Text and reported setting. occurs in Joseph’s narrative: an announcement concerns a missing cup, offers a camel-load for its return and includes the announcer’s guarantee.

Ethical force of the passage. The publicly specified reward gives another person a reason to undertake work whose success is uncertain. Its narrative use does not settle whether a failed or partially successful worker is owed anything.

How the commentators read it. Ibn ʿĀshūr reads the proclamation within the episode of the missing royal measure. Its narrative location matters because a jurist’s use of a statement from an earlier prophetic story requires further argument; the commentator’s narration is not by itself the operative uṣūl mechanism.

The full explanation, remaining distinctions and source passages are in the adjacent Context & commentary note.

· ·

The surrounding Qurʾānic argument. In the same Joseph narrative, turns to the brothers’ request that one of them replace the detained brother for their elderly father’s sake. Ibn ʿĀshūr explains the reply as refusal to take someone over whom no such claim exists: compassion for the father does not itself justify a substitute detention. The surrounding narrative, including Joseph’s concealed plan, must remain visible. This is related illumination for discussions of guarantee and substitution, not a transparent precedent from which every later surety rule can be read off.

REP-47. Transfer of debt: a new route to payment and the problem of consent

Follow the argument RulingLegal reasoningScripture

Division 47: Transfer of debt.

Ruling and reason for disagreement. Ibn Rushd presents ḥawāla as an accepted exception from debt-for-debt exchange. He records disagreement over whose consent matters and whether the instruction to follow a transfer to a solvent debtor is obligatory. He later contrasts transfer with guarantee when the substituted debtor becomes insolvent, preserving Mālik's exception for deception and Abū Ḥanīfa's different recourse. Bidāya Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.299–300

How the legal argument works. · . These notes identify the relevant mechanism or comparative control; later maxims do not establish Ibn Rushd’s historical vocabulary.

Text and reported setting. Bukhārī2287–2288 pairs condemnation of delay by someone able to pay with an instruction concerning transfer to a solvent payer.

Ethical force of the passage. The moral centre is the creditor’s ability to obtain what is owed. A transfer that genuinely facilitates payment differs from a manoeuvre that merely moves the burden beyond reach. The comparison concerns the effect on another person, not just formal discharge of the first debtor.

How the commentators read it. Ibn Ḥajar distinguishes effective ability to pay from reputation for wealth, explains how transfer can facilitate recovery and prevent delay, and rejects an asserted consensus about the command’s force. Helping payment and compelling acceptance are therefore separate propositions; their relation must be argued.

·

REP-48. Agency: delegation and what cannot be done by another

Follow the argument RulingLegal reasoningScripture

Division 48: Agency.

Ruling and reason for disagreement. The agency chapter distinguishes the principal, agent and delegable act. It enumerates transactions and related acts while separating bodily worship from financial or other acts admitting representation. Its compressed attribution of restrictions on a healthy present person's agency requires comparison with school discussions of litigation; it should not be generalized into a ban on ordinary commercial delegation. Bidāya Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.301

How the legal argument works. · . These notes identify the relevant mechanism or comparative control; later maxims do not establish Ibn Rushd’s historical vocabulary.

Giving more back: generosity, debt and the limits of a public fund. Al-Nawawī calls better repayment a noble disposition and distinguishes it from a benefit stipulated in the loan. He records a disagreement with Mālik about adding quantity rather than quality. He then confronts the charity-fund difficulty: his preferred reconciliation is that the better camel was bought from a recipient who had acquired it, and only then given as the Prophet’s own property; he supports this through the version directing purchase. He also reads the creditor’s speech as ordinary forceful pursuit of a right. These are substantive conditions on generosity, not an exemption of a revered borrower from accountability.

·

Text and reported setting. recommends Moses as strong and trustworthy after his help at the watering place.

Ethical force of the passage. Competence serves the work; trust concerns how one uses that competence in another’s interest. The employer’s refusal to impose hardship and the distinction between what is due and what is volunteered give the arrangement its ethical shape.

How the commentators read it. Ibn ʿĀshūr reads the recommendation as a general insight emerging from observed conduct. Ibn Ḥajar draws from the Hijra the permissibility of relying on a trustworthy non-Muslim guide for the service concerned.

The full explanation, remaining distinctions and source passages are in the adjacent Context & commentary note.

Part V.A. Capacity and the limits of protection

Detailed social-law draft, revision 7. C001–C004 examine Arabic II 279–281, from the beginning of Kitāb al-ḥajr through selected central issues concerning release and rushd. The section on the unprovided-for male beginning at the bottom of II 281 and continuing on II 282 is excluded. The full procedural variants concerning executors and the concluding discussion of unmarried women need a further position-level audit; this installment does not certify the whole passage complete. English parallels include PDF pp.338–341, printed pp.334–337. Pivotal Arabic claims at II 281 have been checked on the image.

The universalities must remain distinct throughout this dossier. A general address concerning maturity or sound judgment has a semantic scope; a person’s ability to preserve property is a practical fact; protection and responsible agency are final goods. None licenses converting a contested legal qualification into a natural essence of the person. Comparisons between prayer, ownership and legal capacity require their own ground, and may remain residual assimilations where no intended universal is indicated.

The marriage comparison now puts a further limit on the meaning of rushd. At II12 Ibn Rushd distinguishes sound judgment in wealth from sound judgment in choosing matrimonial suitability. A restriction in one sphere therefore cannot automatically disqualify a person in another, nor does competence in either sphere establish moral excellence. K027 also preserves the discrepancy between the Bidāya’s enslaved-guardian attribution and Qudūrī. Capacity, imposed legal status and acquired virtue must remain separate objects throughout this dossier. Bidāya Arabic II, printed/PDF p.12

The owner’s dignity and the guardian’s accountability

Setting. belongs to the sequence on orphans, property and dower. It combines withholding unrestricted control, provision, honourable speech, testing judgment, timely return and accountability for the guardian.

The passage. Property is a means of sustaining life. Those not entrusted with its management must still be fed and clothed and addressed honourably. Orphans are to be tested; once the requisite maturity and sound judgment are found, property is returned. Guardians must not consume it in anticipation of that moment; God suffices as Reckoner.

Its ethical argument. Protection is judged partly by the relation it creates. A guardian can preserve an asset while humiliating its owner or delaying independence for personal advantage. The speech, provision and release clauses prohibit treating the protected person as merely a defective manager. The final divine reckoning subjects the protector’s own use of power to judgment.

What the commentary explains. Ibn ʿĀshūr reads the reference to “your wealth” through the connected livelihood of the community: another’s property sustains hiring, exchange, giving and inheritance. Crucially, his explanation of honourable speech addresses the guardian’s irritation at requests. The guardian should not insult, should teach better management where possible, and should remind the person that the money remains theirs and is being preserved for their benefit. The Study Quran records several meanings of sound judgment and ages of maturity; its compression of legal positions must be checked against Ibn Rushd’s actual disagreements in C001–C004. It is useful here for seeing the range of interpretation, not for replacing that disagreement with one uniform test.

· · ·

C001. Initiating interdiction against a mature prodigal

Rule and arguments. Ibn Rushd reports agreement on interdiction over orphans below maturity, then disagreement over initiating it against rational adults who squander wealth. Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, Medinan jurists and many Iraqis permit judicial initiation when prodigality is established and the person has had an opportunity to answer. Abū Ḥanīfa and others oppose initiation against adults. Among those resisting it, Ibn Rushd distinguishes rejection after maturity altogether from continuation of restrictions originating in minority; Abū Ḥanīfa’s terminating age of twenty-five is recorded even where prodigality persists. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.279–280; Bidāya, English II, PDF pp.338–339, printed pp.334–335

Those permitting initiation identify prodigality as the relevant meaning in the minor’s restriction and extend the rule where that meaning persists. Their evidence includes release upon discerned rushd. The opposing account invokes the report of Ḥibbān ibn Munqidh, who is given a three-day option because he is deceived in sales rather than placed under interdiction. Ibn Rushd also reconstructs an argument making minority the legally operative category, normally accompanying deficient judgment and diminished accountability. His tentative introduction to that reconstruction must not become an unqualified quotation from a school. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.279–280

Practical ontology. Interdiction changes a person’s powers over property and the legal standing of transactions; it is not merely advice to behave prudently. The debate asks whether an observed substantive defect permits renewed restriction of an adult, or whether adulthood creates a status whose ordinary effect is not reversed by the exceptional prodigal. A particular option is a narrower intervention than general restriction. Withholding assets is also distinguished in the opposing argument from nullifying sales.

Principles in this argument. The argument about extending protection from minority to adult prodigality asks which quality carries the legal ground. This is analytically a discovery-of-ground problem, not merely factual detection of prodigality. The Ḍarūrī requires warrant for the extension; the later harm maxim cannot independently authorize restriction of a competent adult’s agency. Finding a candidate ground does not yet show that revelation indicates it: adult protection may remain a contested assimilation rather than established semantic extension.

Subsidiary maxims. Preventing harm and bearing a private burden for public protection supply questions for the comparative analysis, but neither independently grants the power of interdiction. A protection that transfers equivalent injury to the restricted person also needs scrutiny. The public-official maxim is a preliminary normative control, not the source of this particular jurisdiction.

C002. Release, sex and the evidence of competence

Primary differences. For males with fathers, the discussion joins maturity and discerned rushd, while later examining their definition and presumptions. Most jurists give females the corresponding rule of menstruation and discerned rushd. The well-known report from Mālik continues paternal authority until marriage, consummation and discerned rushd; another report agrees with the majority. Among his followers, intervals of one, two and seven years after consummation are reported. Ibn Rushd calls those interval-based opinions weak: they fail to require the textual criterion of rushd and competence can be present before the fixed period. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.280–281; Bidāya, English II, PDF p.340, printed p.336

The argument associated with Mālik in this passage ties the recognition of a woman’s competence to experience with men. This is a historical claim embedded in the rule’s justification; the commentary must not restate it as a universal psychological fact. The internal counterpositions and Ibn Rushd’s criticism make scrutiny part of the primary evidence itself.

Principles in this argument. Establishing legally required competence differs from proving it in this person. Ghazālī’s application analysis clarifies why observation and experience may matter after the standard is set. It cannot validate every historical sex or status proxy as an accurate measure of competence; those proxies remain objects of critical assessment.

C003. Unknown competence and the relation of finding to status

Presumptions and procedure. In the discussion of a mature male whose rushd or safah is unknown, Ibn Rushd gives opposing Mālikī presumptions: continuation of safah until rushd becomes evident, and recognition of rushd until safah becomes evident. For a person under an executor, the well-known view requires release; the role of the father’s appointment, another appointing authority, the judge’s permission and evidence of competence generates further variants. Ibn al-Qāsim’s account makes known rushd or safah decisive rather than the mere continuation or lapse of guardianship. Ibn Rushd rejects as weak the view that makes all acts ineffective despite evident rushd until formal release, saying that the effective consideration is rushd rather than the judge’s ruling. This is a local argument, not a rejection of judicial authority generally. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF p.281

The two levels. One question concerns how to act when competence is unknown; another concerns the relation between actual competence and an institutional status once it is known. The first allocates the burden of uncertainty. The second asks whether legal form recognizes a practical capacity or constitutes an indispensable additional condition. Combining them as “formality versus freedom” would conceal their different triggers.

Principles in this argument. A presumption depends on what status was previously established and on what legally counts as release. The Ḍarūrī’s distinct forms of continuity and Jamʿ’s later taxonomy prevent “certainty defeats doubt” from deciding the contested baseline. The difference between actual competence and a formal act of release must be argued, not resolved by the slogan.

Subsidiary maxims. Do not begin with “initial non-liability” where a legally imposed status is already established. Equally, continuation cannot preserve a status against evidence that its relevant ground has ceased. What ends with an excuse is prospective permission under that ground; whether a formal release is also required is still the case’s substantive dispute.

C004. Is rushd financial competence or also religious rectitude?

Definition and cause. Mālik understands rushd here as developing and properly managing wealth; al-Shāfiʿī also requires religious rectitude. Ibn Rushd expressly frames the disagreement in terms of whether the name rushd applies to someone who lacks rectitude in religion. The issue is the scope of a legally operative term, not a disagreement over whether religion matters at all. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF p.281

The alchemical result is not that law manufactures a perfected person before allowing property agency. It is that jurists disagree over how much moral formation a particular legal capacity presupposes. The distinction between juridical authority and wilāya is essential here: a finding about a release criterion is not certification of spiritual realization. This case directly corrects any master thesis that silently equates legal competence, virtue and sanctity.

Principles in this argument. The scope of rushd must be established before an individual is tested against it. The Ḍarūrī’s account of apparent meaning and warranted interpretation helps frame the semantic dispute; Ghazālī’s application distinction then separates the chosen standard from evidence that it is met. Financial skill and moral rectitude are not interchangeable simply because both are valuable.

Part V.B. Found property and foundlings

Continuous commentary on Bidāya II, printed/PDF pp.304–310, beginning at Kitāb al-luqaṭah and ending before Kitāb al-wadīʿah. This includes the attached foundling discussion. The preceding agency material on p.304 and the deposit material beginning on p.310 are outside this installment. L001–L033 and N001–N008 are working question-units, not a final count of every proposition or school position.

The argument of the chapter as a whole

A found object lies between possession and ownership, care and appropriation, individual initiative and public authority. Its owner is absent but remains a person with a claim. The finder can rescue it, misappropriate it, expose it to new danger, incur expense, misunderstand the duty of notice or deliver it to an impostor. The object itself may survive, perish, defend itself or depend on immediate human care. These differences constitute the chapter’s practical ontology.

Consequently, its governing virtue is not generic generosity. Justice to an absent person must be joined to prudent care, truthfulness about custody, and restraint from unnecessary intervention. Generosity may support unpaid service or charity after notice, but it cannot by itself license giving away someone else’s property. The civilizational achievement at stake is a social world in which a person’s absence does not make that person’s rights disappear.

This is also a direct test of the alchemical model. A thing encountered as an opportunity for gain can become an occasion for acknowledging another’s claim. But possession does not automatically transform the finder into a good person. Undertaking care can itself be rash or self-serving; in some conditions leaving an object alone better realizes its owner’s good. The law forms a capacity to distinguish these operations, rather than simply multiplying occasions for intervention.

The encounter behind the distinction between intervention and restraint

Setting. In Muslim1722, a questioner asks about lost valuables, then a stray camel and a sheep. The answers change with the object’s vulnerability and ability to survive.

The passage. The finder records the valuables’ identifying features and announces the find. The camel has means of movement and watering; the sheep is exposed to being taken or eaten. The owner’s subsequent claim remains relevant.

Its ethical argument. Intervention is not inherently more caring than restraint. Accurate attention asks whether taking charge actually protects this particular good. For property, recording and announcement preserve another’s relation to the thing while temptation to appropriate it is present.

What the commentary explains. Nawawī explains that knowledge of the container and tie distinguishes a genuine claimant from a false one and keeps the find from becoming confused with the finder’s property. He connects the camel’s treatment to its bodily capacities. He also distinguishes school positions on whether identifying features alone compel delivery; on his school’s account they do not always replace the required proof. The story thus supplies an intelligible purpose without erasing the disagreement over the means of achieving it.

·

L001. Whether taking custody is preferable, disfavoured or obligatory

Primary positions. Ibn Rushd attributes preference for taking custody to Abū Ḥanīfa and al-Shāfiʿī: a Muslim should preserve a fellow Muslim’s property. He attributes dislike of taking custody to Mālik, Aḥmad and others, with reports from Ibn ʿUmar and Ibn ʿAbbās. Reasons include the warning about a believer’s stray property and fear of failure in announcement or of transgression. Those favouring custody interpret the warning as directed against taking for benefit, rather than taking to announce. A further group requires taking custody. Bidāya, Arabic II, p.304; Bidāya, English II, PDF p.372, printed p.368.

Sabab and inferential form. The disagreement is not over whether another’s wealth deserves protection. It concerns the norm governing an intervention that creates new responsibilities, together with the interpretation of a warning report. One side emphasizes a positive duty of preservation; another gives weight to the risks created by assuming custody; another reaches obligation. The exact threshold for obligation cannot be reconstructed from a generic beneficence principle alone.

Principles in this argument. Interpretation of the warning and the purpose of taking are prior to assigning the act its normative force. The Ḍarūrī’s interpretive burden is relevant to those readings. Removal of harm is a later organizing maxim, but it cannot decide in advance whether taking custody or leaving the object creates the greater legally relevant danger.

Subsidiary maxims. The preventive and lesser-harm maxims distinguish active care from indiscriminate intervention. They require a real comparison of the object’s exposure, the finder’s competence and the risks custody introduces. A general permission to use things cannot convert another’s property into an unowned resource.

L002. Public trust and the ruler’s justice change the practical situation

Ibn Rushd reports a contextual scheme introduced as something that has been said; he does not attribute it indiscriminately to every jurist named above. With trustworthy people and a just ruler, the original disagreement applies. With untrustworthy people and a just ruler, taking is obligatory. With trustworthy people and an unjust ruler, leaving is preferable. When both people and ruler are untrustworthy or unjust, the finder chooses according to the stronger expectation of the object’s safety. Bidāya, Arabic II, pp.304–305; Bidāya, English II, PDF p.372.

Surrounding people Ruler Reported practical judgment What must be assessed
Trustworthy Just Original disagreement remains Benefit of care against the finder’s risk of failure
Untrustworthy Just Take custody Exposure to private appropriation, with a trustworthy public setting
Trustworthy Unjust Prefer leaving The danger introduced by bringing the property into a predatory institutional setting
Untrustworthy Unjust Follow the stronger expectation of safety Comparative risk; neither action is secured by a general presumption

In this case the principal variable is practical-causal: what is likely to happen to the property under the stated public conditions? Its protective end is teleological, but no newly recovered semantic universal is stated as the source of the four branches. The scheme itself is reported doctrine, its application is situated assessment, and our explanation of the risks is reconstruction. These must remain three separate claims.

The last column is our explanation of the scheme’s structure. The text supplies the judgments and the standard of likely safety; it does not narrate exactly how an unjust ruler would seize each object. The distinction matters. We have primary evidence of institutional conditions entering practical judgment, not an archival record of a specific confiscation.

Feedback into the master theory. A city is not merely the final aggregate produced by already formed persons. Its institutions are also conditions affecting what a responsible act can be. Formation is reciprocal: law can teach care, while predatory institutions can turn a normally protective intervention into a danger. This is stronger and more precise than assigning muʿāmalāt generally to “urban maturity.”

Principles in this argument. The text itself makes public conditions relevant; our mapping to taḥqīq al-manāṭ identifies the subsequent assessment of those conditions. It does not authorize rewriting a rule whenever a commentator predicts benefit. Read the later harm maxim alongside the Ḍarūrī’s warning against unconstrained interest reasoning: identifying safety under a transmitted scheme differs from inventing a new scheme.

Subsidiary maxims. The reported four-condition scheme makes the comparison of actual dangers concrete. The later lesser-harm formulation helps describe its last branch; the public-office maxim asks whether an institution serves its entrusted end. Neither permits us to turn predicted civic benefit into unrestricted administrative power.

L003–L004. Pilgrimage and Mecca: special space, continuing notice

L003 records Ibn Rushd’s special restriction concerning pilgrims’ found property. L004 records the Meccan restriction allowing collection for the purpose of proclamation, including two transmitted wordings whose grammar affects the relation between collector and announcer. He then attributes to Mālik perpetual announcement for both categories. The restrictive statement and the permitted announcing function must be retained together; the passage should not be paraphrased simply as “no one can ever touch lost property in Mecca.” Bidāya, Arabic II, p.305.

The special spatial norm prevents routine appropriation after the ordinary interval from being assumed. A gathering with mobile participants presents an obvious practical problem: an owner may leave and return only later, while the finder’s locality differs from the owner’s. That is a plausible explanation of why continued notice protects persons across distance; the passage itself grounds the exception in transmitted evidence and does not explicitly give this demographic explanation as its legal cause.

The civilizational object is a sacred meeting place serving persons beyond a single household or settled neighbourhood. Preservation requires information across time and movement. Specialized announcers, repeated gatherings and recognizable public places can make that possible; disruption can make it difficult. The difficulty does not by itself abrogate the rule.

Principles in this argument. The specific sacred-place evidence restricts the ordinary rule. The Ḍarūrī’s account of specification describes the legal operation; a demographic explanation of mobile pilgrims remains a proposed rationale, not the specifying proof. Neither hardship nor the symbolism of the centre can independently shorten the transmitted announcement duty.

L005–L007. Who can become the custodian?

L005: the stated qualifications. The initial description is a free, Muslim adult, because taking custody is a form of wilāyah. Bidāya, Arabic II, p.305.

L006: a non-Muslim finder. The passage records disagreement in al-Shāfiʿī’s school and Abū Ḥāmid’s statement that permission in dār al-Islām is the stronger position. The location is part of the account; it cannot be dropped to produce an unrestricted cross-context rule. L007: an enslaved person or a fāsiq. Two positions are reported, explained through absence of qualification for authority on one side and the generality of the found-property reports on the other. Bidāya, Arabic II, p.305.

The ontology of office controls the inference. If finding creates an authority requiring an antecedently qualified holder, exclusion follows from disqualification. If the general direction to finders is operative without that restriction, a wider class may undertake custody. These positions cannot simply be called trust versus distrust, because legal status and moral reliability are distinct grounds of exclusion in the discussion.

Principles in this argument. The general found-property reports and the proposed qualifications of custodial authority are competing legal considerations. The Ḍarūrī requires a warranted restriction of general language. Jamʿ’s definitions help distinguish a qualification of office from a condition of moral responsibility; neither proves that legal status always measures actual trustworthiness.

L008–L010. Objects that need rescue and objects that do not

L008 records the chapter’s general object: a Muslim’s property exposed to loss, in inhabited or uninhabited land, including inanimate objects and animals. That is the scope of this presentation, not proof that non-Muslim property has no protection elsewhere in the law. L009 distinguishes camels, which are left, from sheep, which are collected. L010 concerns cattle: al-Shāfiʿī is reported as assimilating them to camels; Mālik to sheep, with disagreement also reported from him. Bidāya, Arabic II, p.305.

The central report identifies the camel’s own capacities to move, reach water and feed until its owner finds it. It identifies the sheep’s exposure to appropriation or predation. The classification is therefore not a purely nominal division of animal species: capacities relevant to survival explain the practical contrast in the report. The cattle question asks to which practical kind an intermediate case belongs. .

The civilizational scale changes the question’s facts. Settlement, enclosures, traffic and predation can alter what “safe if left” means. The chapter later explicitly raises different times of justice, so contextual inquiry is not wholly imported. It does not follow that every change in circumstance licenses replacing a fixed category without an accepted legal argument. A change in the facts under an adopted criterion differs from changing the criterion itself. The Ḍarūrī’s warning about variable benefit and Bidāya’s allowance for situational scrutiny jointly discipline this distinction; neither an immutable social setting nor unlimited adaptation should be assumed.

Principles in this argument. The cattle comparison requires identifying which features of camel or sheep carry the protection rationale. Because the report states the camel’s capacities and the sheep’s exposure, an indicated wider criterion is plausible; the attribution of the cattle positions alone does not prove that each jurist reasons through that criterion. Semantic extension, rival assimilation and application must therefore be separately tested. The Ḍarūrī’s graded indications distinguish relevant similarity from nominal resemblance. Once a capacity criterion is adopted, knowledge of animals and terrain enters its application. “Remove harm” summarizes the concern but cannot by itself choose the category or action.

Finding property: preserve the means of knowing its owner

Bājī’s explanation supplies a direct Muwaṭṭaʾ commentary for the following announcement and identification questions. Its alternatives should be read before assigning a uniform spiritual meaning to the longer period.

Text and situation. The report commands the finder to know the container and fastening and to announce the find. Al-Bājī draws attention to the difference between knowing identifying details and announcing those details publicly. His commentary includes Mālikī instructions for keeping identifying information private and announcing as one is able, without abandoning ordinary work. It compares the one-year report with versions mentioning repeated years.

What the commentary explains. Al-Bājī explains that broadcasting the details would teach a dishonest claimant how to describe the object. He defends identification as evidence because people cannot have witnesses to every coin they carry; an inflexible witness demand could defeat most recovery. He preserves detailed disagreement about partial or mistaken descriptions. For the longer announcement period he offers two routes: prefer the report without the narrator’s doubt, or distinguish the minimum taught to a questioner from extra scruple encouraged in Ubayy. He also gives a practical reason for a year: news ordinarily travels in that interval.

The practical meaning. The finder must make the loss publicly discoverable while keeping the claim test useful. Secrecy and publicity here serve different parts of the same act of restitution. More disclosure is not invariably more just.

·

L011–L014. Announcement, benefit and the absent owner after a year

L011: ordinary duration. Ibn Rushd reports agreement on a year’s announcement for property of consequence, with the stated animal exception. The Arabic says ghanam here; the English’s “cattle” should not be allowed to expand or shift that exception without collation. Smaller and perishable objects receive further distinctions below. Bidāya, Arabic II, p.305; Bidāya, English II, PDF p.373, printed p.369.

L012: poor finder, charity and the returning owner. The provincial jurists named in the passage allow the poor finder to consume after the period and allow charitable disposition in the stated alternative. If the owner returns after charity, the owner may ratify it and receive its reward or demand compensation. Consent remains legally relevant after a well-intentioned act on another’s property. Bidāya, Arabic II, pp.305–306.

L013: wealthy finder and large sums. Mālik and al-Shāfiʿī permit the wealthy finder’s use; Abū Ḥanīfa restricts the route to charity in the English account and the surrounding Arabic argument. Al-Awzāʿī directs substantial wealth to the treasury. The supplied Arabic’s first compressed sentence about Abū Ḥanīfa is awkwardly printed with an “or” after negating consumption. Read with the explanation that follows, it must not be turned into a prohibition of charity; the independent school text and another Arabic edition remain controls to obtain. Bidāya, Arabic II, p.306; Bidāya, English II, PDF p.374, printed p.370.

L014: surviving compensation. All the named non-literalist positions are reported as retaining compensation when the finder consumes and the owner returns; the literalists are excepted. Ibn Rushd then lays out three inferential configurations: privilege the general prohibition of another’s property without consent and permit only charity subject to the owner’s response; treat the report as an exception allowing complete appropriation; or permit use with an accompanying obligation to compensate. Bidāya, Arabic II, p.306.

The charity configuration protects against the finder converting another’s misfortune into private enrichment. But charity itself is subject to the absent owner’s right; a desirable public end does not automatically cancel consent. The complete-appropriation reading emphasizes the authorized exception after a fulfilled public process. None can be understood merely by assigning one school to altruism and another to individualism.

Principles in this argument. For L011, the duration rests on its transmitted basis, not a general maxim. For L012–L014, the operative question is how the particular permission relates to the general protection of another’s property: specification, a permission preserving compensation, or a fuller transfer. The Ḍarūrī requires the scope of that exception to be argued. The intention maxim cannot turn an unauthorized charity into the absent owner’s consent.

Subsidiary maxims. Permission to consume, the holder’s consent and compensation are separate legal determinations. The necessity/rights and consent maxims give precise later controls for this distinction, but must also face the literalist exception recorded here. They cannot suppress that exception merely because a continuing claim suits the proposed alchemical account.

L015–L021. Proof of ownership: signs, testimony, memory and oath

L015: the initial requirement. The text’s formulation refuses delivery to a claimant who cannot identify the relevant container and tying cord. This should not be generalized to exclude every independently proven claim in every procedural setting. It is the baseline for the dispute that follows. L016: are identifying signs sufficient? Mālik accepts them; Abū Ḥanīfa and al-Shāfiʿī require bayyinah. Ibn Rushd describes the conflict between the usual evidentiary requirement for a claim and the apparent implication of the report. Bidāya, Arabic II, pp.306–307.

The interpretive question is what the command to know the object’s identifying features is for. It may preserve its distinction from other property in custody, or furnish the basis for recognizing its owner. A report variant that explicitly directs delivery upon description matters. An uncertain contrary possibility does not by itself displace an established principle. Notice also must not be confused with broadcasting all the secret identifying features: knowing the identifiers and publicizing the find are different acts. The English rendering of the opening report can obscure that difference. Bidāya, Arabic II, pp.305, 307; .

L017: coins and number. In the Mālikī discussion, description of the coins and their number accompanies the container and cord, with support claimed from a report variant. Ignorance of the number does not defeat a claim when the two identifying features are known; nor does stating a larger number. L018: stating fewer produces two positions. L019: ignorance of the coins’ description despite knowing the two main identifiers also produces disagreement; erroneous description is distinguished from acknowledged ignorance. The precise referent of the pronoun in the sentence about an erroneous description needs another-edition or commentary control. It should not be silently replaced with an English parenthetical as if the Arabic were unambiguous. Bidāya, Arabic II, p.307.

L020: one identifier known, the other unknown. The passage reports refusal until both are known; delivery after investigation; and a distinction between admitting ignorance, which calls for investigation, and giving a wrong description, which does not justify delivery. The page image reads ʿarafa, knew, in the opening case; the English sentence beginning with “makes an error in one” should not replace it. Its rendering of istibrāʾ as declaring oneself absolved also needs correction or at least clarification: in this context the issue is checking or clearing up the claim before delivery, not a spiritual release of the finder from accountability. Bidāya, Arabic II, p.307, page image checked; Bidāya, English II, PDF p.375, printed p.371.

L021: oath. When adequate signs are given, Ibn al-Qāsim permits delivery without an oath, while Ashhab requires one. This is a separate layer of assurance; it must not be folded into whether the signs are probative at all. Bidāya, Arabic II, p.307.

Why the detail matters philosophically. These rules analyze imperfect memory rather than a fiction of omniscient ownership. Knowing a container but forgetting a count, understating and overstating, and admitting ignorance versus confidently misdescribing are not treated as automatically equivalent. The absent person’s right must become publicly recognizable through finite signs. That is a highly specific instance of the project’s “normative meaning-disclosure”: a material feature becomes evidence within a legitimate inferential setting.

The competing goods are avoiding wrongful delivery and avoiding a proof requirement that can prevent a true owner from recovering. The signs-based approach makes practical knowledge of the object effective; the additional-evidence approach strengthens formal protection against imposture. Neither is simply spiritual intuition versus rational procedure. Both are public epistemic methods.

Feedback. Legal certainty is not one psychological sensation. It depends on the relevant object, accepted signs and authorized procedure. A theory that praises “certainty” without specifying these conditions cannot explain why jurists disagree over the same description.

Principles in this argument. Two stages require distinct records: what the report authorizes as evidence (especially L015–L016), and how imperfect descriptions, memory and an additional oath satisfy an adopted evidentiary standard (L017–L021). The apparent-meaning discussion concerns the first; Ghazālī’s instance analysis illuminates the second. Certainty is a later control on unsupported displacement of an established position, not proof that only direct certainty can justify delivery. The debate itself permits different kinds of warranted probability.

Subsidiary maxims. In L015–L020, remote imagined alternatives, evidence-supported doubt and demonstrated descriptive error are different defects. In L021, requiring an oath is separate from whose intended meaning would govern an oath if demanded. The subsidiary formulations help divide these questions; their later compilation is not independent proof of the Mālikī positions.

L022. Consuming a sheep in the wilderness: what happens to the owner’s claim?

The jurists are reported as allowing the finder to consume a stray sheep in a remote, uninhabited place. Most require compensation if the owner appears; Mālik’s best-known position does not, though another report from him does. The reason is again the relation between the report’s apparent permission and the general protection of property. Ibn Rushd explicitly observes that Mālik here gives the wording more force than in the ordinary property that must first be announced. Bidāya, Arabic II, p.307.

That comparison is a direct falsifier of a crude school stereotype. We cannot first label Mālik “general principle over text” and then use that label to explain every case. The relative strength of this wording and the different object matter. The available good is no longer indefinite preservation of an intact asset: the animal is exposed to death or appropriation in a setting far from recovery mechanisms.

The guaranteed-value position allows immediate benefit while preserving an eventual claim. The non-guaranteed position reads the authorization as a fuller exception under these conditions. The formative possibilities differ: one emphasizes remaining answerable for value after a permitted act; the other emphasizes accepting a bounded permission where preservation is precarious. It would be unwarranted to describe the latter as contempt for ownership or the former as failure to recognize providence.

Principles in this argument. The particular permission and the general property right must be reconciled at the level of their legal indications. A proposed benefit from consuming a vulnerable animal does not itself decide surviving compensation. Ibn Rushd’s own comparison with L014 checks the scope of each interpretation and falsifies a fixed school stereotype.

Subsidiary maxims. The maxim that necessity does not simply extinguish another’s right clarifies the compensation question, but it does not settle it: Mālik’s reported non-guarantee position resists that unqualified application. The useful comparison asks how the particular permission relates to the owner’s claim; the case must be allowed to qualify the maxim’s scope.

L023–L026. Value, perishability and proportionate effort

The Mālikī synthesis divides objects by whether they can be preserved in custody and whether they are endangered when left. Within the preservable-but-endangered category, L023 concerns things so trivial that the owner would not seek them: no announcement is required in the main account, while Ashhab prefers it. The report concerning a date on the road is adduced. L024 concerns something small but useful: announcement is required, with disagreement between a year and some days. L025 concerns substantial value: a year’s announcement. Bidāya, Arabic II, pp.307–308.

The distinctions concern a relation between value, likely pursuit and the burden of a recovery process. A small object is not metaphysically valueless; the question is what practical responsibility follows under these circumstances. The owner’s likely concern matters. The category should therefore not be mechanically equated with a modern currency amount.

Shabana’s history of custom provides a useful control: recurrence or widespread practice is not by itself sufficient for legal legitimacy; customs receive differentiated recognition through proofs, interpretation and later maxims. Our inference that assessments of triviality depend partly on social experience must not become the claim that custom can simply cancel property rights. Shabana, Custom in Islamic Law, PDF pp.179–181, printed pp.167–169.

L026: perishables outside and within settlement. What cannot be preserved may be consumed by rich or poor; two compensation positions are recorded, the better-known Mālikī one denying liability. For rapidly perishing goods in town, the passage records no liability, liability, and a distinction between charity without liability and personal consumption with liability. Bidāya, Arabic II, p.308.

The urban distinction is philosophically revealing. The material decay is similar, but the social setting may offer different possible recipients and means of care. The text records the differing consequences without fully articulating every rationale. We may therefore ask whether accessible charitable distribution changes the moral character of personal consumption, but must label that a reconstruction to test, not Ibn Rushd’s explicit sabab.

The virtues are justice, practical care and measured generosity. The common good includes preventing waste without erasing ownership. In a prosperous city, storage, markets and charitable networks can expand feasible options; in breakdown, the same food may perish before any institution can act. These conditions explain why a serious legal philosophy needs material knowledge. They do not prove that one position is historically caused by a particular storage technology.

Principles in this argument. For L023–L025, customary judgments of significance can help assess whether an owner would seek the object; the later custom maxim is a control on that assessment, not permission to relabel useful property as trivial. For L026, perishability and available alternatives enter the application, while compensation remains a separate rule. Neither removing harm nor avoiding hardship automatically determines who absorbs the loss.

Subsidiary maxims. Perishability does not warrant unlimited consumption. Measure, the end of an excuse, possible substitutes and surviving claims are distinct inquiries. These later maxims explain why rescue may preserve value, consumption or charitable benefit in different legal forms without proving that every proposed substitution or disposition is authorized.

L027. Camels again: whether a rule of restraint changes in unjust times

The Mālikī account prefers leaving self-sufficient animals on the transmitted evidence, while requiring announcement if they are taken. One position makes this preference general for all times; another confines it to times of justice and prefers collection in unjust times. This is a direct dispute over whether changed public conditions affect the practical operation of the rule. Bidāya, Arabic II, p.308.

The Muwaṭṭaʾ contains a relevant reported change in administration: camels left to range in ʿUmar’s time were, under ʿUthmān, to be announced and then sold, with the price retained for a returning owner. It also reports a finder whose camel-related burden interfered with work on his farm and who was told to release it where found. These are primary transmitted reports of practice and advice, not a modern observer’s measurements. .

The sale-and-retained-price practice distinguishes preservation of the identical animal from preservation of its owner’s economic claim. It also differentiates private rescue from public administration. Simon’s essential coordination function of authority offers a comparison: even well-intentioned persons can need an institution to coordinate common action and make a binding practical determination. That is different from saying authority exists only because people are vicious. Simon, Nature and Functions of Authority, PDF pp.27–29, printed pp.15–17.

Principles in this argument. The relevant distinction is between applying a warranted protective criterion under changed security and claiming unrestricted power to replace a transmitted rule. The Ḍarūrī’s benefit limits are therefore as important as Ghazālī’s application analysis. The reported difference over unjust times cannot be erased by announcing that all law simply follows benefit.

Subsidiary maxims. Changing security conditions require assessment of prevention and possible substituted preservation, such as retaining value after an authorized sale. The scope and duration of any exceptional action remain bounded. These maxims cannot identify every change of time with an abrogation of the received norm.

L028–L029. Loss in custody and the role of witnesses

L028 records the agreement that a finder who takes witnesses to the collection is not liable merely because the object perishes in custody. L029 concerns the absence of witnesses. Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, Abū Yūsuf and Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan deny liability without negligence even absent witnesses; Abū Ḥanīfa and Zufar impose liability when the unwitnessed object is lost. The first argument classifies the object as a deposit or trust whose nature is not changed simply by failure to witness. The second invokes a report directing the finder to take trustworthy witnesses. Bidāya, Arabic II, p.308; Bidāya, English II, PDF p.377, printed p.373.

The ontology is the boundary between amānah, custody on trust, and ḍamān, guaranteed responsibility for loss. A finder can be responsible for careful conduct without guaranteeing every outcome. The witnessing position gives an additional public act a decisive protective role. This is not a contrast between caring and not caring; it is a contrast in how a care relationship becomes legally secured.

The formative effect of witness-taking can be a public commitment that resists later appropriation or false denial. The trust-based position can protect useful volunteer action from being converted into insurance against every accident. Both protect social cooperation in different ways; both can be abused. A false trustee can exploit the presumption of trust, while an opportunistic owner can exploit an exacting proof requirement to impose an unwarranted loss.

The chapter makes possible a more precise account of “social trust”: it is not simply high public morality. It is a relation among duties of care, proof, presumptions and liability. Different arrangements allocate the risk of uncertainty differently. A city with formal witnesses but predatory officers may be less trustworthy than a community with less paperwork and effective accountability; that proposition is a historical hypothesis, not a ranking supplied by these jurists.

Principles in this argument. The trust classification and the report requiring witnesses compete over the conditions of liability. The local deposit distinction provides a controlled cross-reference; it does not prove that every trust allegation is conclusive. The witnessing rule is a substantive evidentiary condition in one account, not merely a useful extra manifestation of a universal virtue. The primary task here is reconciliation of a substantive report with a trust classification, not the automatic recovery of a single semantic universal.

L030. The finder’s intention and the possibility of returning the object

The Mālikī account separates three intentions. Taking in order to appropriate entails liability, while the text notes that this intention may be known only from the finder. Taking as a finder creates a trust with duties of preservation and notice. Taking provisionally to ask nearby people whether the object is theirs, without either appropriation or assuming the full custodial undertaking, permits returning it to the same place if they deny ownership, without liability in the school agreement reported here. Bidāya, Arabic II, p.309.
