The same bodily act—picking up a garment—can therefore instantiate different legal relationships. This is a direct non-ritual counterpart to the ablution intention problem. Intention does not operate only as an inner devotional adornment. It can help constitute the object of practical judgment: an attempted theft, a custodial undertaking or a provisional act of identification.

The distinction also sets an epistemic limit. An actor can be answerable for a concealed appropriative purpose without a court automatically possessing proof of it. Inward accountability and public adjudication remain distinct. A theory of spiritual transparency would destroy precisely the limit the text recognizes. Powers’ account of legal intention provides a useful modern comparison, but the primary paragraph here is sufficient to establish this particular distinction. Paul Powers, Intent in Islamic Law, PDF pp.30–33, for the broader problem of acts and intention; Bidāya, Arabic II, p.309.

Principles in this argument. This is the clearest non-ritual use of the later intention maxim in the current dossiers: appropriating, undertaking custody and provisional inquiry can give the same physical taking different legal meanings. The primary warrant remains this Bidāya paragraph. The maxim explains the pattern across fields; it does not give a court knowledge of an undisclosed purpose.

Subsidiary maxims. The difference between inward intention and enforceable verbal scope becomes especially useful here. The finder’s concealed intention may constitute personal wrongdoing while remaining unavailable to public proof. The later compilation itself differentiates inward accountability from others’ claims, so it must not be used to abolish that boundary.

L031. Can an undertaken trust be put down again?

For a finder who has already assumed custody, Ibn al-Qāsim imposes liability if the object is returned to where it was found. Ashhab denies it if returned to the same place, but imposes it if placed elsewhere, comparing the matter with deposit. The finder’s report of accidental loss is accepted without oath unless suspicion arises. These are three distinct determinations: withdrawal from an undertaking, relocation and the evidentiary status of a loss report. Bidāya, Arabic II, p.309.

The stricter account makes the undertaken relationship enduring; the other permits a restoration of the prior situation under a place condition. This can be read as a disagreement about what changes when care begins. Is the owner now entitled to continued protection from this particular finder, or can the finder restore the object’s earlier exposure without creating a new injury? The text gives the comparison with deposit; the fuller relational explanation is our reconstruction.

Principles in this argument. Ashhab’s deposit comparison must be evaluated for the specific feature allegedly permitting restoration of the earlier situation. Continuing responsibility cannot be inferred merely from the physical possibility of putting an object down, nor dissolved by good intention. The local trust distinction and the Ḍarūrī’s account of legally relevant extension organize this inquiry. An indicated universal has not been demonstrated for Ashhab’s comparison; retain the reported analogy without silently promoting it to one.

L032. An enslaved finder who consumes the property

Mālik distinguishes consumption before the year, where liability attaches to the enslaved person’s body and the master may surrender or redeem the person, from consumption after the year, where the obligation is a debt on the person and does not attach in that manner. Al-Shāfiʿī’s reported distinction turns on the master’s knowledge: with knowledge the master is liable; without it the liability attaches to the enslaved person. The Muwaṭṭaʾ directly supplies the Mālikī before/after-year account. Bidāya, Arabic II, p.309; .

The technical distinction has severe human consequences and must not disappear into an agreeable metaphor of differentiation. The legal order here recognizes an enslaved person’s acts and debts while also treating that person as subject to another’s property rights. Preserving an owner’s claim can therefore expose another human being to transfer. An intellectually honest virtue reading must analyze that conflict rather than presuming every legal mechanism embodies an uncomplicated common good.

The timing distinction also shows that the year changes the juridical kind of permitted use and resulting liability. It is not merely an arbitrary waiting period. The master-knowledge distinction introduces responsibility through knowledge of another’s act. These are rich questions of agency and allocation, but the passage’s briefness does not warrant inventing the full rationale of every school.

Principles in this argument. The year and the master’s knowledge function as different legally relevant conditions in the reported accounts. The later taxonomy makes that distinction explicit without inventing a missing sabab. “Matters depend on intentions” does not settle liability based on time or another person’s knowledge, and a general harm maxim cannot make the severe human consequences of these historical rules disappear.

L033. Who bears the expenses of preservation?

The majority treat the finder as voluntarily preserving the object and deny recourse to the owner for expenditure. The Kufan position permits recourse when the judge authorized the expense. The passage does not provide a complete definition of reasonable expenses or all emergencies; those require related chapters and school controls. Bidāya, Arabic II, p.309; Bidāya, English II, PDF p.378, printed p.374.

This rule joins generosity, consent and jurisdiction. The owner did not necessarily request the service. A well-meant expenditure cannot automatically create a debt against an absent person. Judicial authorization provides a different route: a public office can establish an accountable basis for intervention. The physician analogy reaches a limit here too. A helper’s belief that something benefits another person is not itself a right to charge that person.

The formative possibility under voluntary care is service without appropriation of a financial claim. The authorized-expense route can enable preservation that a poor finder could not otherwise afford. These goods can conflict in practice. If every finder must bear every cost, valuable rescue may not occur; if every finder can charge freely, owners may be exploited. The primary distinction locates a mediating institutional act rather than resolving the matter solely by exhorting better character.

Al-Qarāfī’s later separation of fatwā, adjudication and administrative acts makes a useful control: a general answer about what is permissible is not identical to a judge’s particular authorization producing consequences for another person. Simon’s account of authority as coordinating common action provides a philosophical comparison for the same need, without erasing differences in jurisdiction. al-Qarāfī, Criterion, PDF pp.79–82; Simon, Nature and Functions of Authority, PDF pp.27–29.

This is a precise case of the city producing responsible agency. Accessible, trusted adjudication can make a costly good act possible; predatory or inaccessible adjudication can make it impracticable. Conversely, juristic controls on reimbursement help keep the city from converting all care into private extraction.

Principles in this argument. An expense that preserves property and an enforceable reimbursement claim are different legal objects. The Ḍarūrī’s restriction on free-standing benefit reasoning prevents a helper’s useful act from automatically creating another person’s debt. The judge’s authorization changes the warranted institutional relation; applying that route requires facts about authorization and expenditure.

Subsidiary maxims. A benefit conferred without request does not automatically establish a reimbursement debt. Initial non-liability therefore illuminates one side of the comparison; valid judicial authorization supplies a different possible basis. Public benefit is a limit on the use of office, not a substitute for showing that authorization occurred.

N001–N008. The foundling: analogy with property reaches its limit

The next short section deliberately changes the object from lost property to a child without a carer. Some procedural analogies continue, but the human subject must not be treated as simply another luqaṭah. Bidāya, Arabic II, pp.309–310.

N001: rescue as a collective obligation. Al-Shāfiʿī is reported as making collection of the unprotected foundling a communal obligation. The practical good is preservation of a dependent human life. Unlike the self-sufficient camel, the child cannot simply be left to find resources. Unlike an object with an identifiable absent owner, the child’s proper future cannot be described merely as return of property.

N002: witnesses against enslavement. The obligation to take witnesses is disputed by analogy with found property, but the specified danger is enslavement. A procedural act serves the child’s status and future freedom, not just the finder’s defence against liability. The same formal technique has a different human good as its object.

N003: who counts as a foundling? The text identifies the young minor and records hesitation in the Shāfiʿī account concerning a discriminating minor. Developmental capacity matters to the need for this form of guardianship. It is not a metaphysical judgment of lesser humanity.

N004: qualifications of the carer. The account requires freedom, probity and sound practical management, excludes the enslaved person and mukātab, distinguishes religious affiliation and guardianship, and removes custody from the fāsiq or spendthrift. These are historical legal qualifications and proxies for fitness, not an assertion that social status guarantees care. The religious distinction is asymmetric in the account: a Muslim may take a non-Muslim foundling, while a non-Muslim is not granted custody of a Muslim child. This raises questions about protection, communal identity and authority that cannot be resolved by a generic appeal to vocation. Bidāya, Arabic II, pp.309–310.

N005: wealth, maintenance and recourse. Wealth is not a condition of the finder’s qualification; maintenance is not thereby imposed on the finder, and voluntary expenditure does not establish recourse. This separates willingness and fitness to rescue from private financial capacity. It also leaves a real institutional question: who supplies continuing support? The short section does not answer that in full. The research must locate the relevant treasury, maintenance and guardianship rules rather than fill the gap with a reassuring assumption.

N006: religion attributed by place. A foundling in Muslim territory is assigned the legal status of Islam in this presentation. Place supplies a public presumption when personal history is unknown. N007: religion through parents. Mālik’s account follows the Muslim father; al-Shāfiʿī and Ibn Wahb follow whichever parent becomes Muslim. The report concerns legal attribution, not a claim that the child has already made an informed act of faith. This distinction is essential for separating juridical status, education and inward acknowledgement. Bidāya, Arabic II, p.310.

N008: freedom and walāʾ. Ibn Rushd records a view that the child is the finder’s slave, a view that the child is free with walāʾ to the finder, and the Mālikī view of freedom with walāʾ to the Muslims. He judges the legal foundations to support the latter unless a sound report supplies a specifying exception, mentioning a report about a woman inheriting from her foundling. Walāʾ here is a legal affiliation with consequences such as inheritance; it is not wilāyah as saintly realization. The terminology itself guards against a false vertical synthesis. Bidāya, Arabic II, p.310.

These eight questions belong together. Rescue, proof, developmental capacity, carer qualification, funding, attributed religious status and freedom form the legal morphology through which a vulnerable human being enters a durable social world. A city’s virtue is tested by whether it can make that entry possible without exploitation. The practices can train adults in care and justice; the beneficiary’s good is not reducible to the rescuers’ moral improvement.

Maritain helps keep the child’s own good central; Attas helps articulate responsible placement without reducing a person to utility; Farabi supplies the question whether cooperation aims at true felicity rather than the interests of a dominant group. These remain distinct comparative frameworks. None entitles us to conceal the restrictive or contested historical classifications in the primary passage. Maritain, Person and Common Good, PDF pp.14–17; Attas, Concept of Education, PDF pp.10–12; al-Fārābī, Perfect State, PDF p.244, account of cooperation.

Principles in this argument. N001’s rescue duty requires its stated legal warrant; the harm maxim alone does not determine its communal form. N002 uses a procedural analogy whose human object is protection from enslavement, not return of an asset. N003–N004 distinguish legally chosen qualifications from actual fitness; N005 separates care from reimbursement. N006–N008 concern public status and its grounds, not inward belief or spiritual worth. The manāṭ and condition distinctions help analyze these different operations. Neither the property analogy nor one maxim should be spread across all eight propositions as a common proof. The procedural comparison in N002 is not yet established as semantic extension, and its classification cannot decide the distinct questions in the other seven propositions.

Subsidiary maxims. For the foundling, preventing injury concerns a person’s life and future agency. A substitution that preserves an asset’s exchange value cannot simply be carried over to that human object. For N005, the duty of care and the creation of a debt for expenses still need separate warrants; neither general need nor public benefit supplies the missing institutional detail.

From rules to civilizational processes

The chapter’s upward feedback

The law of found property develops a civic capacity to care for persons who are absent or unable to protect themselves. It does so through differentiated acts: take, leave, preserve, announce, investigate, return, compensate, authorize, spend and refrain. The act that best protects can change with material capacities and political trust. Intention can constitute a relationship, while public proof limits what an institution may assert about it. Charity remains answerable to ownership; office remains answerable to purpose; custody remains answerable to the person cared for.

That is its alchemical meaning in a defensible sense: opportunity for appropriation can become acknowledged responsibility, and isolated goodwill can become a competent, publicly accountable practice. Its vertical horizon lies in accountability and the ordering of action toward a good beyond possession. The passage does not disclose a secret metaphysical correspondence for every container, cord or numerical interval. Its philosophical depth lies in the disciplined mediation of person, object, knowledge and institution.

Source and coverage cautions. The named narrator in the supplied Bidāya report differs from the Muwaṭṭaʾ’s Zayd ibn Khālid; another-edition collation is required. The rich-finder Arabic sentence, some pronoun referents and the interpretation of istibrāʾ need further textual control. The English loses or alters several distinctions and is not the sole base. The chapter has now been read continuously with its subsidiary questions identified, but a position-by-position critical audit against additional school sources remains unfinished. These L and N records therefore denote interpreted questions, not a certified exhaustive critical edition.

Part V.C. Deposits, trust and proof

Detailed social-law draft; scriptural commentary revised 4 October 2026. D001–D004 cover the opening evidentiary sequence of Kitāb al-wadīʿah, Arabic II 310–311, stopping before the sentence on stipulating a guarantee. English II printed pp.375–376, PDF pp.379–380. Both Arabic page images have been inspected. The subsequent rules on guarantee, unauthorized use, travel, re-deposit, customary care and profits remain priorities for the detailed continuation, not material deemed covered by this opening analysis.

The revised inference framework prevents the trust analogy from doing more than the text warrants. The relevant issue is which legal consequences accompany acknowledged custody, not whether trust is generally a virtue. Practical knowledge of opportunities for loss or fraud helps explain evidentiary burdens; it does not settle the authority of an oath or witnesses. Until the difficult Arabic transition is collated, no indicated semantic universal should be asserted as a completed explanation of the passage.

The entrusted thing, the unseen act and the responsible heart. commands return of trusts to their owners and just judgment, ending with God as hearing and seeing. considers reliance on personal trust where documentary security is absent: the entrusted person must discharge the trust and fear God his Lord; testimony must not be concealed, and concealment makes the heart culpable.

The two endings address the gap between an obligation and another person’s ability to enforce it. The trusted holder must not treat the absence of a record as permission to retain what is owed; the witness must not make the truth disappear through silence. God’s hearing, seeing and knowing deny that an undetectable breach becomes morally nonexistent. The reference to the heart concerns deliberate suppression of truth, not a substitute mystical method of proving a claim.

Ibn ʿĀshūr reads as addressing everyone entrusted with something and everyone judging, with delivery to the rightful recipient at its centre. He notes the weak chain of the Kaʿba-key occasion rather than treating it as certain. On he explains that an unsecured debt is called a trust to intensify responsibility: lack of pledge or witnesses does not diminish what is owed. This is related to deposit, though a debt and custody of a particular object remain different legal relations. Al-Rāzī distinguishes trusts owed to God, to other people and to oneself. His examples include truthful speech, uncorrupted measures, rulers’ justice, and scholars refusing to recruit ordinary people into partisan error; self-trust requires not sacrificing enduring good to appetite or anger. He also records al-Qāḍī’s narrower reading of this verse as returnable property. On , his preferred explanation is reciprocal: the creditor has dealt well with the debtor by trusting him, so the debtor must not answer that kindness with denial or delay. A witness can prevent that confidence from being exploited. The Study Quran places at the opening of a passage on authority and reports a reciprocal reading: rulers are first charged with justice, then subjects with obedience in 4:59. Its broader account includes deposits, borrowed or found property and spiritual responsibilities. This is the editors’ synthesis of several commentators; its report of the Kaʿba-key occasion must be read alongside Ibn ʿĀshūr’s criticism of the chain. The Study Quran also extends responsible authority to household and body, and reads the paired names Hearing and Seeing as affirming divine knowledge. Its suggestion about hearing’s primacy and the creative command is presented as a possibility, not an established explanation of the deposit rule; this manuscript does not use it to derive a legal or alchemical conclusion. On , The Study Quran distinguishes unsecured trust from a pledge and then connects concealed testimony with accountability for what is inward. It also records the broader reading that troubled the Companions. Its discussion distinguishes being called to account from necessarily being punished; passing thoughts must not be equated with deliberately hiding a claimant’s evidence.

Qushayrī first requires people’s property to be returned without having been damaged. He then treats the heart as something entrusted by God: betrayal is to claim it as one’s self-owned possession, and the inward secret is betrayed through self-regard. In judgment he demands equal treatment of near and distant parties and excludes revenge prompted by concealed resentment. The link across levels is responsible use of what one holds—property, attention or authority—rather than appropriation for the self.

· · · · · · · ·

From meaning to formation. Al-Rāzī’s account supplies a concrete reciprocal practice: the debtor answers another’s confidence with truthful repayment; the custodian answers entrusted possession with preservation and return. Qushayrī extends the test to attention and authority: can either be exercised without being appropriated to one’s importance or resentment? In the project’s comparative vocabulary, fixatio would mean fidelity becoming dependable precisely when concealment is possible, and ablatio the abandonment of an appropriative habit through actual restitution. These are possible changes in the practitioner. The owner’s immediate good—recovery of property—is distinct and may be secured even when the holder acts reluctantly. At the level of household or city, repeated reliable conduct can support delegation and cooperation; a favourable evidentiary presumption alone cannot establish that this formation has occurred.

D001. Return to the depositor: does entrusting custody also settle proof of return?

Primary rule and variants. Ibn Rushd begins with agreement that deposit is an amāna rather than property automatically guaranteed by its holder, apart from a reported exception from ʿUmar. The Mālikī argument links restoration of trusts with the absence of a requirement of witnessing. A custodian’s statement of return, with an oath when disputed, is therefore ordinarily accepted. The well-known Mālikī qualification concerns an originally witnessed deposit: the depositor may have entrusted preservation without waiving proof of return. A report from Ibn al-Qāsim, together with Abū Ḥanīfa and al-Shāfiʿī, accepts the custodian more broadly even in that situation. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF p.310; Bidāya, English II, PDF p.379, printed p.375

The Arabic passage’s short sentence between “it is the analogy” and the difficulty of dividing amāna needs another-edition collation; the supplied translation does not remove the difficulty. The reconstruction here rests on the clearly stated positions and distinction between trusting preservation and accepting proof of return, not on a silently corrected negation.

Object and mechanism. Physical control differs from ownership, and trust in custody differs from certainty about a later delivery. The legal relation gives statements different evidentiary standing. The disagreement is about how far that standing extends when an initial act used witnesses. It is not a psychological choice between trusting all people and distrusting all people.

Public and vertical goods. Usable custody enables travel, work and preservation across absence. It needs credible accounts and remedies. During specialization, more transfers can increase the need for records; in declining trust, excessive liability can deter service while inadequate proof can permit abuse. These are hypotheses about conditions, not facts deduced from a handbook. The vertical reading is acknowledgement of another’s enduring right, not certification that an oath reveals the inner person. The case feeds upward by showing that moral trust becomes institutionally useful through specified limits.

Principles in this argument. The trust relation does not automatically answer what proves its discharge. The local Bidāya distinction is primary; the certainty maxim is only a later check on the move from established entrustment to alleged return. The party entitled to a presumption must be established by the adopted proof doctrine, not selected by the analyst’s preferred outcome.

Subsidiary maxims. The initial-liability maxim asks whether the alleged duty has been established; the later-change maxim concerns alleged discharge after an obligation or entrustment is admitted. They cannot be collapsed into a single presumption favoring whichever party seems trustworthy. The adopted custody and proof doctrine fixes the correct starting point.

D002. Delivery to another person: authorization and evidence are separate questions

Positions. For onward delivery, Mālik requires evidence, with the guardian’s witnessed restoration of an orphan’s assets supplying the comparison; otherwise the custodian bears liability when receipt is denied. Ibn Rushd records an alternative derivable within the school. In the reported Mālikī account, the proof requirement is not removed simply because the depositor ordered the delivery. Abū Ḥanīfa accepts the custodian’s account with an oath where delivery was to the person designated by the depositor. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.310–311; Bidāya, English II, PDF pp.379–380, printed pp.375–376

What changes. There are now at least three epistemic positions: the owner who entrusted, the custodian who claims to have delivered and the recipient who denies receipt. Authorization answers whether the transfer was instructed; it does not by itself prove the transfer happened. The analogy asks whether the original entrustment extends to the intermediary in a way that supports the custodian’s account.

The institution needs witnesses or an accepted account, accessible adjudication and an intelligible chain of authority. Kin networks can make informal agency workable while obscuring transactions to outsiders; larger urban relations may require more explicit evidence. No universal evolution from oral trust to written distrust is established. The alchemical operation is the transformation of a private instruction into publicly accountable action. Divine accountability supplies an ethical horizon; it does not remove the third party’s right to contest the alleged fact.

Principles in this argument. The analogy with a guardian’s delivery is an argument about a specific relation of entrustment, authorization and proof. The Ḍarūrī’s method requires that common relation to carry the extension. It supplies no warrant for silently repairing the short Arabic justification whose reading remains uncertain in this witness. A common relation is only a candidate ground until its indication is shown; the source uncertainty prevents a definitive semantic classification.

D003. Acknowledged receipt followed by loss: how far does one amāna extend into another?

Variants and express cause. Where the onward recipient admits receipt but claims loss while holding as a trusted intermediary, Ibn al-Qāsim has two reported positions. One releases the delivering custodian through the recipient’s acknowledgement; another requires proof of the delivery or production of the property. Ibn Rushd expressly relates the broader family of disagreements to amāna strengthening a claimant’s statement with an oath. Those equating the intermediary’s trust with the original custodian’s accept its further evidentiary consequences; those regarding it as weaker do not release the first holder on the recipient’s account alone. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF p.311; Bidāya, English II, PDF p.380, printed p.376

Relational ontology. This is no longer simple denial of receipt. One person’s acknowledgement can support another person’s release while the property itself is absent. The system therefore needs an account of whether credibility passes through the chain and who bears the failure if it does not. Trust is a legally articulated relation, not a substance automatically transmitted by proximity to a good person.

The vertical orientation is constrained by epistemic humility: public adjudication uses designated reasons under uncertainty. A claimed spiritual insight into either intermediary’s character cannot replace the indicated form of proof. Mūsā–Khiḍr here functions as a limit on private certainty, not a rival method of deciding custody.

Principles in this argument. Acknowledged receipt changes what remains to be proved, but the subsequent loss claim still depends on the legal reach of amāna. Ghazālī’s distinction between rule and instance helps organize that change. Procedural signs of credibility are not automatically the same kind of qarīna as a linguistic indicator in the Ḍarūrī; the comparison must retain that difference.

D004. Personal liability rather than fiduciary custody

Further distinction. Ibn Rushd then treats delivery that places the asset against a person’s dhimma—for example, in a loan or an advance for a commodity—rather than leaving it held simply as an amāna. If the recipient’s financial responsibility is sound, the delivering holder is released in the reported school account; where it is impaired, two opinions occur. This compressed passage needs fuller school controls before all conditions of the arrangement can be reconstructed. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF p.311; Bidāya, English II, PDF p.380, printed p.376

Practical meaning. The form of the recipient’s holding changes the route of recourse. A fiduciary account of accidental loss and an obligation attaching to a dhimma do not have the same structure. Thus “the money has been passed to someone else” is an inadequate description of the legal event. Universal practical categories organize the possible obligations; instrumental reasoning determines their analogies; particular fiqh identifies the effect of this transfer.

Principles in this argument. Classifying the holding as a personal obligation rather than fiduciary custody is prior to applying the consequence of loss. The chapter’s distinction governs that classification. The later presumption of continuity can describe persistence of an established debt, but cannot establish a debt that the facts and substantive law have not yet shown.

Subsidiary maxims. A known personal debt and an alleged later payment illustrate the shift from initial non-liability to proof of discharge. That shift is explicit in the compilation’s debt example. It clarifies the local distinction without turning every custodian into a debtor who guarantees accidental loss.

From private trust to the city

The four questions build a sequence: custody, alleged return, onward delivery, subsequent loss and the change into personal liability. Every transition alters the evidentiary positions. The common good is not maximal confidence but justified and usable confidence, with neither owner nor custodian exposed to arbitrary demands.

The jurist’s work is consequently a civilizational activity. It formulates the distinctions that let service extend beyond immediate personal presence. The city in turn supplies teachers, witnesses, offices and conditions of credibility. Al-Qarāfī’s normative differentiation of fatwa and judicial or administrative action and Hallaq’s historical overview help identify those functions, but neither establishes how this particular rule was enforced in a particular place. Documents and cases must supply that evidence. al-Qarāfī, Criterion, PDF pp.79–82; Hallaq, Introduction, PDF pp.17–23

The next deposit installment must examine what happens when the custodian uses the asset, travels, delegates custody, forgets or profits. Those rules will test whether the trust reconstructed here actually controls action when the holder has opportunities for advantage. They remain uncompleted.

Representative route: trust, succession, criminal law and judgment

Revision 14 · 4 October 2026. Selected studies across every editorial division; exact source spans below delimit the selection. These are representative interpretations, not chapter-completion or elementary-rule counts.

Quoted scriptural clauses below are selected working translations from the cited Arabic. Exegetical views are named; the paragraph labelled “Its ethical argument” is the manuscript’s close reading of the passage and its surrounding clauses. The purple note gives the full explanation and exact sources. A related passage does not become the direct evidence for a ruling merely by being placed beside it.

The later books put the thesis under its hardest tests. A person may be protected without acting, inherit without being virtuous, obtain release from an inherited status institution, or suffer a wrong whose remedy cannot restore what was lost. Those effects are not lesser versions of inward purification. They are different legal and human goods.

The closing virtue passage gives a normative horizon for the sequence. It does not resolve every attribution, redeem every historical institution or show that punishment produces reform. The Makhzūmī narrative’s aftermath, qasāma’s evidentiary difficulties and inheritance independent of personal righteousness are substantive controls on that horizon.

REP-49. Found property and foundlings: care without appropriation

Follow the argument RulingLegal reasoningScripture

Division 49: Found property and foundlings.

Ruling and reason for disagreement. L001–L033 and N001–N008 distinguish property capable of return to an owner from a found child whose immediate safety cannot await identification. Their boundaries and reported differences remain in the original module. One representative contrast is the tension between taking charge to preserve a good and claiming a power over it that preservation does not confer. Bidāya Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.304–310

How the legal argument works. · . These notes identify the relevant mechanism or comparative control; later maxims do not establish Ibn Rushd’s historical vocabulary.

Finding property: preserve the means of knowing its owner

Text and setting. The report commands the finder to know the container and fastening and to announce the find. Al-Bājī draws attention to the difference between knowing identifying details and announcing those details publicly. His commentary includes Mālikī instructions for keeping identifying information private and announcing as one is able, without abandoning ordinary work. It compares the one-year report with versions mentioning repeated years.

The ethical argument. The finder must make the loss publicly discoverable while keeping the claim test useful. Secrecy and publicity here serve different parts of the same act of restitution. More disclosure is not invariably more just.

How the commentators read it. Al-Bājī explains that broadcasting the details would teach a dishonest claimant how to describe the object. He defends identification as evidence because people cannot have witnesses to every coin they carry; an inflexible witness demand could defeat most recovery. He preserves detailed disagreement about partial or mistaken descriptions. For the longer announcement period he offers two routes: prefer the report without the narrator’s doubt, or distinguish the minimum taught to a questioner from extra scruple encouraged in Ubayy. He also gives a practical reason for a year: news ordinarily travels in that interval.

Scope of this reading. The differentiated-scruple explanation is al-Bājī’s proposed reconciliation. It supplies a precise comparison with al-Shaʿrānī’s differentiated human states, not proof that all conflicting rulings express spiritual ranks. The transmission and evidentiary alternatives remain real.

· · · · · · · ·

Direct context and explanation. In Muslim1722, a questioner asks about lost valuables, then a stray camel and a sheep. The answers change with the object’s vulnerability and ability to survive. Nawawī explains that knowledge of the container and tie distinguishes a genuine claimant from a false one and keeps the find from becoming confused with the finder’s property. He connects the camel’s treatment to its bodily capacities. He also distinguishes school positions on whether identifying features alone compel delivery; on his school’s account they do not always replace the required proof. The story thus supplies an intelligible purpose without erasing the disagreement over the means of achieving it.

REP-50. Deposit: being trusted and proving what happened

Follow the argument RulingLegal reasoningScripture

Division 50: Deposits.

Ibn Rushd: summary of the ruling and disagreement. Ibn Rushd presents a deposit as an entrusted holding rather than a guarantee against every loss. He then distinguishes safeguarding it from proving its return. The well-known Mālikī position requires proof of return where the original handover was witnessed, while accepting the custodian’s account of destruction. Al-Shāfiʿī, Abū Ḥanīfa and one report from Ibn al-Qāsim reject that distinction. The disagreement asks whether the manner of entrusting property changes the evidential force of the custodian’s word; neither position makes actual betrayal impossible. Bidāya Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.310–311

REP-51. Loans for use: generosity that permits the borrower to rely on it

Follow the argument RulingLegal reasoningScripture

Division 51: Loans for use.

Ruling and reason for disagreement. Ibn Rushd treats lending a usable object as a good act and reports disagreement over recall. Abū Ḥanīfa and al-Shāfiʿī allow the lender to recover it at will; Mālik's predominant account binds an agreed period or an ordinarily useful period. Liability is separately disputed through the Ṣafwān report and rival reports and classifications. Bidāya Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.313

How the legal argument works. · . These notes identify the relevant mechanism or comparative control; later maxims do not establish Ibn Rushd’s historical vocabulary.

A loan for use: returning a thing and guaranteeing its loss

Text and setting. Anas’s report describes the Prophet borrowing Abū Ṭalḥa’s horse during alarm in Medina. The loan permits use without transferring ownership. Ibn Ḥajar places the report in the gift sequence because a loan for use gives a benefit while retaining the thing itself. The public alarm gives the borrowed capacity a concrete shared purpose.

The ethical argument. Access to another’s useful thing can support common life without acquisition. But the obligation to return what remains and an obligation to compensate accidental loss are not the same proposition.

How the commentators read it. Ibn Ḥajar explicitly challenges an inference from the saying that a borrowed thing is to be returned to an unconditional guarantee of loss: entrusted goods must also be returned, yet that does not by itself settle compensation when they perish. He discusses the separate report “the hand owes what it takes” with its disputed transmission question. He retains different Mālikī/Ḥanafī and majority rules. The inward lesson of faithful use therefore cannot be used to manufacture consensus about liability.

Scope of this reading. The horse encounter is directly explained. The other reports are comparative evidence assessed by Ibn Ḥajar, whose judgment is not relabelled as an independent authentication here.

·

Text and reported setting. Q107 moves from denial of judgment to driving away the orphan and failing to encourage feeding the poor, then condemns ostentatious prayer and withholding small useful assistance.

Ethical force of the passage. The argument concerns an incoherence in life: religious display coexists with refusal of accessible care. The opening reference to judgment places ordinary treatment of vulnerable people within ultimate accountability. The criticism is not that owning a household implement is wrong, but that one’s relation to possessions makes even modest help unavailable.

How the commentators read it. Ibn ʿĀshūr explains the borrowing of ordinary implements as assistance that costs little to provide; withholding it discloses extreme stinginess. He records the alternative interpretation of māʿūn as zakāt and distinguishes deliberate neglect of prayer from involuntary forgetfulness.

REP-52. Usurpation: responsibility for setting harm in motion

Follow the argument RulingLegal reasoningScripture

Division 52: Usurpation.

Ruling and reason for disagreement. Opening a cage and a bird's subsequent flight is Ibn Rushd's representative of disputed causal responsibility. Mālik imposes liability whether or not the opener actively drives the bird out; Abū Ḥanīfa does not in the account here; al-Shāfiʿī distinguishes active inducement. A wrongfully dug pit supplies another example. The issue is the relation between initiating a condition and the subsequent cause of loss. Bidāya Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.316

REP-53. Restitution: restoring title without erasing another’s work

Follow the argument RulingLegal reasoningScripture

Division 53: Third party title and restitution.

Ruling and reason for disagreement. Ibn Rushd distinguishes recovery of a small part, most or all of an object, and changes in its value. In the Mālikī account, a building or planting added by the possessor produces alternatives concerning payment, retention or shared interests; a different recovery rule follows where the purchased remainder was never separately agreed. Restoring title is not a single material operation. Bidāya Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.325,327

REP-54. Gifts: affection, favouritism and the claims of children

Follow the argument RulingLegal reasoningScripture

Division 54: Gifts and related endowment questions.

Ruling and reason for disagreement. The Nuʿmān ibn Bashīr report confronts unequal gifts to children. Ibn Rushd reports validity with disapproval among the majority, rejection by the Ẓāhirīs, and a Mālikī distinction involving all the property. He explains the tension between the prohibition and reasoning from a person's power to give to outsiders. Return of a gift is separately limited, including where third-party claims have arisen. Bidāya Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.327–328,332

How the legal argument works. · . These notes identify the relevant mechanism or comparative control; later maxims do not establish Ibn Rushd’s historical vocabulary.

Text and reported setting. Muslim1623 records a parent seeking the Prophet’s witness to a gift for al-Nuʿmān. The response refuses to witness injustice and calls for fairness among children.

Ethical force of the passage. The parent’s power to give is exercised within a relationship capable of being damaged by favouritism. A gift does not become ethically self-justifying because it is voluntary: the excluded children also experience what it says about their standing in the family.

How the commentators read it. Nawawī distinguishes the recommendation or obligation of equal treatment from the legal validity of an unequal gift, and discusses different accounts of equality between sons and daughters. The moral criticism must not be collapsed into automatic contractual invalidity, nor validity treated as proof that no injustice occurred.

REP-55. Bequests: Godward giving includes those who remain

Follow the argument RulingLegal reasoningScripture

Division 55: Bequests.

Ruling and reason for disagreement. The one-third limit is grounded in the Saʿd report. Ibn Rushd also asks whether a bequest to an heir can be validated by the other heirs: is the restriction intelligible through their claim or an independent devotional limit? The reported positions divide accordingly. Different questions about the beneficiary, the asset and its use must remain separate. Bidāya Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.334–335

Text and reported setting. Muslim1628 places Saʿd’s wish to dispose of wealth within grave illness.

Ethical force of the passage. The encounter corrects an opposition between lofty giving and ordinary responsibility. Care for dependants is itself capable of being devotion.

How the commentators read it. Nawawī makes intention decisive in explaining how habitual acts such as providing food for one’s wife become obedience. He also reads the passage through the needs of relatives.

REP-56. Inheritance: which relationships receive a determinate share?

Follow the argument RulingLegal reasoningScripture

Division 56: Inheritance.

Ruling and reason for disagreement. Ibn Rushd distinguishes recognized categories of heirs from disputed distant kin. Mālik and al-Shāfiʿī are reported as refusing inheritance to the latter; Iraqi and other positions admit them, with further differences over the method. The dispute opposes the need for a specific warranted allocation to broader scriptural kinship indications and further transmitted evidence. Bidāya Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.338–339

How the legal argument works. · . These notes identify the relevant mechanism or comparative control; later maxims do not establish Ibn Rushd’s historical vocabulary.

Text and reported setting. assigns both men and women an obligatory share, whether the estate is small or large.

Ethical force of the passage. The passage challenges a distributor’s claim to know whose value justifies exclusion. The shares are not a prize awarded after measuring an heir’s virtue or usefulness.

How the commentators read it. Ibn ʿĀshūr places within protection of women and orphans whose resources stronger relatives could retain. Wāḥidī’s Jābir narrative and the widow-and-daughters narrative are retained separately; the latter’s naming discrepancy is not silently harmonized.

REP-57. Manumission: liberation and the creditor’s competing claim

Follow the argument RulingLegal reasoningScripture

Division 57: Manumission.

Ruling and reason for disagreement. The selected dispute concerns a debtor's manumission before judicial restriction. Mālik and others consider property already committed to creditors; the Iraqi account allows disposition until formal interdiction. Ibn Rushd distinguishes the underlying reason for restriction from the judge's act recognizing it. The favourable character of release does not dissolve other parties' claims. Bidāya Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.366

How the legal argument works. · . These notes identify the relevant mechanism or comparative control; later maxims do not establish Ibn Rushd’s historical vocabulary.

Text and reported setting. calls for contractual emancipation where good is known and assistance from “the wealth of God which He has given you.” It also prohibits compelling women under one’s power into prostitution for worldly gain. The Barīra report distinguishes a prophetic command from an intercession she may decline.

Ethical force of the passage. The description of wealth challenges an owner’s claim to autonomous disposal; material assistance is part of making release possible. The same verse condemns extracting profit through another person’s coerced body. Barīra’s refusal shows another dimension: restored agency must include the ability to decline a desired relationship, even when someone honoured recommends it.

How the commentators read it. Ibn ʿĀshūr explains the practical importance of earning capacity, reliable performance and instalments, and favours the obligatory reading of the command to contract while recording disagreement. Ibn Ḥajar preserves the variants concerning Mughīth’s status and reconstructs their chronology. Neither his reconstruction nor this ethical reading erases the coercive background of the historical institution. The Study Quran records the obligatory and recommended readings of contractual emancipation, explains “good” through honesty or earning capacity, and compares different accounts of material assistance. It therefore helps identify alternatives to be checked, rather than supporting a claim that all exegetes agree with Ibn ʿĀshūr’s preferred obligation. The Study Quran’s account of the prohibition of coerced prostitution places the concluding forgiveness with the women compelled, following its cited Ṭabarī interpretation. The moral division is between exploitation by the coercer and the compromised agency of the coerced person, not a shared presumption of guilt.

REP-58. Contractual manumission: making a route to freedom usable

Follow the argument RulingLegal reasoningScripture

Division 58: Contractual manumission.

Ruling and reason for disagreement. Ibn Rushd explicitly contrasts strict exchange with a contract whose purpose involves generosity and reduced contention. He uses this to explain tolerance of limited uncertainty in the consideration. A stipulated immediate payment from a person with no available assets raises another question: preserve the undertaking and give workable instalments, or invalidate the defective arrangement? The opposing accounts reason about its purpose differently. Bidāya Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.374–375

REP-59. Freedom promised after death: reliance across time

Follow the argument RulingLegal reasoningScripture

Division 59: Manumission at the owners death.

Ruling and reason for disagreement. Tadbīr is distinguished from an ordinary revocable bequest by some jurists and identified with it by others. Ibn Rushd follows the consequences of the particular formula and intention, then treats debts and divided ownership. The text itself preserves tension between broadly worded agreement about debt and a later reported difference; a simplified consensus statement would be unsafe. Bidāya Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.388–389,392

How the legal argument works. · . These notes identify the relevant mechanism or comparative control; later maxims do not establish Ibn Rushd’s historical vocabulary.

Promised freedom and the narrator’s unspoken circumstances

Text and setting. Jābir reports the sale of a person whose owner had promised freedom after his own death, while owning no other property. The proceeds were returned to that owner. The report’s setting includes poverty; other versions invoked by commentators add debt. These details affect whether the act is taken as a general permission or a particular intervention.

The ethical argument. A promise can create reliance without settling its legal revocability. The effect must be described separately for the person promised freedom, the owner lacking provision and any creditor. Their interests cannot be merged into a single story of liberation.

How the commentators read it. Al-Nawawī reads the report as general permission to sell before the owner’s death, defending the Shāfiʿī position. He reports Mālikī and Ḥanafī resistance and the explanation through debt; he also reports Qāḍī ʿIyāḍ’s reading through care for an owner who had retained nothing. He rejects some restrictive explanations. His further lesson about a ruler preventing harmful dispositions therefore sits beside, rather than abolishes, a genuine disagreement over the report’s reach.

Scope of this reading. The disagreement is preserved. Modern moral assessment must also register that relief for one party is obtained here by continued enslavement of another. Calling the transaction formative does not answer that objection.

Text and reported setting. calls for contractual emancipation where good is known and assistance from “the wealth of God which He has given you.” It also prohibits compelling women under one’s power into prostitution for worldly gain.

Ethical force of the passage. The description of wealth challenges an owner’s claim to autonomous disposal; material assistance is part of making release possible. The same verse condemns extracting profit through another person’s coerced body.

How the commentators read it. Ibn ʿĀshūr explains the practical importance of earning capacity, reliable performance and instalments, and favours the obligatory reading of the command to contract while recording disagreement. Ibn Ḥajar preserves the variants concerning Mughīth’s status and reconstructs their chronology.

REP-60. The mother of an owner’s child: a moral argument inside a status system

Follow the argument RulingLegal reasoningScripture

Division 60: Slave women bearing their masters children.

Ruling and reason for disagreement. Ibn Rushd reports disagreement over sale of an umm walad, the competing early precedents and the weakness attributed to two prophetic reports invoked for prohibition. He then argues for recognizing the status across acquisition histories because selling the mother of one's child is contrary to noble character. This is explicit ethical reasoning in the primary juristic text, not merely our retrospective lens. Bidāya Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.392–394

How the legal argument works. · . These notes identify the relevant mechanism or comparative control; later maxims do not establish Ibn Rushd’s historical vocabulary.

Motherhood within slavery: reports, public judgment and an incomplete emancipation

Text and setting. The Muwaṭṭaʾ records ʿUmar’s ruling against selling, gifting or bequeathing a woman who has borne her owner’s child, with freedom following his death. Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr sets this beside earlier permissions of sale and differing reports from Companions. He distinguishes the securely attributed public ruling from proposed Prophetic reports that he judges weak.

The ethical argument. Protection against alienation changes a person’s future and the family’s continuity, but does not grant immediate freedom or erase coercive dependence. A history of improved protection is not yet a history of complete recognition of agency.

How the commentators read it. Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr explicitly criticizes the chains of reports that would make the child itself the immediate liberating cause. He reports ʿIkrima’s appeal to obedience to those in authority as support for ʿUmar’s ruling, and versions in which ʿAlī revises an earlier view. He explains that language likening the woman to a free person in this discussion concerns sale; other status effects remained those of slavery until the owner’s death. This sharply limits an otherwise attractive claim that biological motherhood automatically transformed the whole juridical person.

Scope of this reading. The transmission judgments and historical attributions are those of Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr. No fresh consensus is inferred from a preferred later outcome. The woman’s own experience is largely absent from these reports.

Criminal conduct, injury and judgment: a map of the later book

These studies belong to the second volume’s Kitāb al-jināyāt, followed by the book of judgments. “Criminal law” is a useful finding aid, not an assertion that these categories reproduce a modern code. A private claim, compensation, a specified penalty and an official’s discretion have different structures.

REP-61. Offences: classify the injury before interpreting its repair

Follow the argument RulingLegal reasoningScripture

Division 61: Offences introduction.

Ruling and reason for disagreement. The introduction distinguishes injuries to bodies, sexual relations, property, reputation and prohibited consumption, with further differences among taking by force, theft and related acts. Ibn Rushd introduces retaliation through specified agent, act and injured person because justice is the object sought. The taxonomy is not reducible to one generic mechanism of punishment. Bidāya Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.394–395

How the legal argument works. · . These notes identify the relevant mechanism or comparative control; later maxims do not establish Ibn Rushd’s historical vocabulary.

Text and reported setting. states retaliation while speaking of remission by a brother, honourable pursuit and good payment, calling the relief a mercy from the Lord. addresses people of understanding: in retaliation there is life, “so that you may acquire taqwā.”

Ethical force of the passage. The moral argument is restraint of killing and of the revenge that follows it. Recognition of an enforceable claim prevents aggression from becoming costless; remission and fair payment open a path beyond reciprocal destruction. Calling the other a brother prevents the wrong from making him simply subhuman. The life-preserving claim is a stated purpose, not an empirical guarantee about every penal system.

How the commentators read it. Ibn ʿĀshūr contrasts proportionate redress with feuds in which status justified taking additional lives. He distinguishes an established claim from an obligation upon each person to exact it, preserving waiver as an explicit alternative.

REP-62. Homicide: command, coercion and divided responsibility

Follow the argument RulingLegal reasoningScripture

Division 62: Retaliation for homicide.

Ruling and reason for disagreement. The selected disagreement concerns the commanding person and the direct killer, especially under coercion. Ibn Rushd records liability of one, the other or both, and explains the competing resemblance of the coerced person to a choosing agent and to an instrument. He does not treat the fact of an order as a sufficient account of agency. Bidāya Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.395–396

Murder, accident and quasi-intentional killing

The practical classification. Ibn Rushd reports agreement on intentional and accidental killing and a dispute over a middle category, shibh al-ʿamd. He attributes acceptance of the middle category to the majority of the regional jurists and its general rejection to Mālik’s well-known position, while retaining a limited parent–child qualification and another reported possibility. The direction of that parent–child qualification is not developed here: Nyazee’s compressed formulation requires collation with the following family-liability discussion before being relied upon. Bidāya Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.397–398; p.397 image checked Bidāya English II, PDF pp.485–486, printed pp.481–482

Ibn Rushd distinguishes accounts concentrating on the implement from al-Shāfiʿī’s account of an intended blow with an unintended death; he calls the latter distinction good. This is not merely a scale from severe to lenient punishment. It differentiates an intention to act, an intention to injure or kill, the usual effects of the means, and the death that actually occurs. Different accounts of that practical object produce different consequences. The surrounding pages on command and coercion add the separate question of which agent is responsible. Bidāya Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.396–398

Setting. distinguishes accidental killing and different communal relations; follows with the grave warning concerning intentional killing. These passages concern liability and accountability, not only deterrence.

Text and reported setting. Accidental killing carries requirements of emancipation and compensation, with specified distinctions and remission; inability receives a stated alternative. Intentional killing is placed before divine anger and judgment.

Ethical force of the passage. A death is not exhausted by the killer’s subjective account. The victim’s family, the wrongdoer’s responsibility and the conditions of peace all remain in view. Conversely, the gravity of the warning should not become a claim that human judges possess complete knowledge of intention or can determine a person’s final destiny.

How the commentators read it. The Study Quran summarizes disagreement over what outward act warrants an inference of intended killing, including death following an intended assault with a normally nonlethal implement. It then records the debate over forgiveness, connecting the possibility of repentance with and other passages, and attributing to Ṭabarī and al-Rāzī arguments that preserve that possibility. These are mediated reports. Ibn Rushd’s directly read Arabic II397–398 supplies the more precise legal distinction: human judgment uses outward acts and circumstances because intentions are fully known to God; the intermediate classification belongs to our judgment, not an uncertainty in divine knowledge.

· · · ·

The hadith does not remove the source problem. Ibn Rushd adduces the report associating quasi-intentional killing by whip, stick or stone with an enhanced compensation, but immediately relays Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr’s criticism of its transmission as unstable. The manuscript therefore does not present that report as an uncontested proof or build its formative interpretation on the assumption that every detail is securely transmitted. A new independent commentary-and-chain study of this particular report remains open. Bidāya Arabic II, printed/PDF p.398, report and transmission criticism

REP-63. Injury: when a matching response cannot be safely matched

Follow the argument RulingLegal reasoningScripture

Division 63: Retaliation for injury.

Ibn Rushd: summary of the ruling and disagreement. Ibn Rushd distinguishes intentional injury from accidents and disputed intermediate acts. Even where retaliation is recognized, the possibility of equivalence and the risk of killing matter. His examples include injuries where exact matching of diminished sight or hearing is not practicable. In such cases the legal response cannot simply imitate the original physical act. Bidāya Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.405,407

The surrounding Qurʾānic argument. explicitly recalls what was prescribed in the Torah. Ibn ʿĀshūr places its equal retaliation against reported status-based disparities, then explains matching bodily injury as conditional on avoiding a greater injury; otherwise compensation becomes relevant. His account of voluntary remission is especially important: it can remove resentment and preserve lives and bodily capacities, whereas an official’s cancellation of another person’s right is not that person’s forgiveness. The commendation of remission therefore does not nullify the underlying judgment. This is a direct exegetical account of proportion, repair and agency, with a historical setting reported by the commentator.

REP-64. Compensation for death: a claim borne by a social group

Follow the argument RulingLegal reasoningScripture

Division 64: Compensation for homicide.

Ruling and reason for disagreement. The compensation chapter begins from and distinguishes kind, amount, timing and bearer of liability. The later threshold dispute on II427 asks how much accidental-injury liability the ʿāqila bears: Mālik, Abū Ḥanīfa, al-Thawrī and al-Shāfiʿī are reported with different boundaries. Ibn Rushd contrasts a general starting rule with claimed established practice. Bidāya Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.409,427

How the legal argument works. · . These notes identify the relevant mechanism or comparative control; later maxims do not establish Ibn Rushd’s historical vocabulary.

Compensation and the attempt to speak an injury out of existence

Text and setting. The reports of violence between women of Hudhayl describe a death and the loss of a fetus. A relative contests compensation for a life that had not eaten, spoken or cried; the Prophet rejects his rhymed objection. Versions differ over the instrument and some pronouns. The narrative distinguishes the victim’s inheritance from the group charged with compensation. Al-Nawawī explains these difficulties rather than silently merging the versions.

The ethical argument. The verbal objection would make the loss disappear from public accounting. Shared compensation can redirect kinship from shielding one’s own side toward meeting a claim, but it also distributes a burden to people who did not themselves strike the blow.

How the commentators read it. Al-Nawawī explains that the censure is not a ban on eloquence: it is directed at strained speech used to defeat an owed judgment. He interprets the reported small stone or pole through the category of quasi-intentional killing, while marking the differing liability rules for the fetal loss. He explains the fixed amount in part by the dispute that uncertainty would otherwise produce. The original prescribed payment is an enslaved person or its legally assessed equivalent; that feature cannot be omitted from a moral account of the institution.

Scope of this reading. The instrument’s smallness is the commentator’s interpretation, not a detail common to all report wordings. Kin liability, the payer of fetal compensation and the status system remain contested or ethically difficult features, not proof of achieved solidarity.

Related scriptural comparison. The following passage illuminates a neighbouring good; the direct report or legal tradition is treated above.

Text and reported setting. distinguishes accidental killing from deliberate killing, combines compensation to the family with expiation, recognizes possible remission and provides fasting where freeing a believing slave is beyond means. It ends with divine acceptance of repentance, knowledge and wisdom.

Ethical force of the passage. Accident changes culpability without making the lost life or surviving family’s claim unreal. Compensation and expiation answer different dimensions of the event; neither makes a life interchangeable with a price. The provision for inability makes return and responsibility practicable under differing means.

How the commentators read it. Ibn ʿĀshūr reads the passage as turning from conflict with enemies to restraints on killing within the community, and carefully distinguishes intention from accident. The differences over collective liability and the identities of those who bear it remain juristic questions.

The page image reads al-qawad (retaliation) in the preliminary contrast with assessed compensation, where the OCR wrongly gives al-ʿaql. This account follows the image. REP-66. Qasāma: protecting life when ordinary proof is absent

Follow the argument RulingLegal reasoningScripture

Division 66: Qasama.

Ruling and reason for disagreement. Ibn Rushd records both acceptance of qasāma and its rejection. Opponents invoke the need to swear from knowledge, the ordinary distribution of proof and the danger of taking life through oaths. The accepting account treats it as a transmitted exception serving protection of otherwise unproved deaths. Ibn Rushd tests that rationale against theft and highway violence rather than accepting the benefit formula without examination. Bidāya Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.427–428

How the legal argument works. · . These notes identify the relevant mechanism or comparative control; later maxims do not establish Ibn Rushd’s historical vocabulary.

Text and reported setting. Muslim1669 describes a man found dead at Khaybar, the family’s accusation, proposed oaths and their refusal to swear without the requisite knowledge. The account ends with compensation provided by the Prophet.

Ethical force of the passage. The encounter brings two goods into tension: a killing must not disappear without concern for those harmed, but indignation and suspicion must not become knowledge the claimant does not possess. The refusal to swear marks a limit on what desire for redress can authorize.

How the commentators read it. Nawawī records disagreement over admitting qasāma and over whether it can support retaliation or compensation. Mere accusation is insufficient. The eventual provision in the report addresses an unresolved loss without proving that the accused party’s guilt has become known. Its relation to general public compensation rules requires further argument.

REP-67. Zinā: uncertainty, coercion and the danger of a false finding

Follow the argument RulingLegal reasoningScripture

Division 67: Zina.

Ruling and reason for disagreement. The selected closing passage treats pregnancy alongside a claim of coercion or marriage. Ibn Rushd reports a stricter evidentiary requirement in Mālik's account and acceptance of the uncorroborated claim against imposing the penalty in the accounts of Abū Ḥanīfa and al-Shāfiʿī. He states that a coerced woman is not liable to the penalty, then separately asks about financial redress. Bidāya Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.440

The direct text and its disputed interpretation

Setting. stands near the beginning of the sūra’s treatment of sexual wrongdoing and accusation. Muslim1690 interprets a promised way mentioned in . The report supplied here does not give a securely dated single first occasion.

Text and reported setting. states a penalty, warns against allowing pity to suspend its application, invokes belief in God and the Last Day, and requires a group of believers to witness it. The following accusation provisions sharply constrain what may be asserted about another person.

Ethical force of the passage. The passage confronts a difficult relation between feeling and public obligation; its aim cannot simply be redescribed as kindness. The legal account must first establish the act, agent, applicable category and proof. The warning against selective pity does not prove an allegation or warrant increasing a penalty out of zeal.

How the commentators read it. Ibn ʿĀshūr distinguishes the involuntary feeling of compassion from allowing it to cancel or reduce what he takes to be a binding judgment. He interprets the warning through a claimed restorative purpose, and cites a report condemning both excess and deficiency; that report’s chain is not independently assessed here. Nawawī on Muslim1690 preserves alternatives between explanation and abrogation of , disagreement over combining penalties, and differences over exile. These are substantive disagreements about the relation of texts, not merely levels of severity. They do not settle the separate pregnancy/coercion proof question on Bidāya II440.

· · · ·

The related protection against accusation. The following explanation concerns qadhf; it illuminates the neighbouring concern for proof and reputation, and is not the source of the pregnancy rule.

Text and reported setting. demands evidence for sexual accusation and specifies consequences for its absence. immediately makes room for repentance and repair, ending with forgiveness and mercy.

Ethical force of the passage. The sequence protects reputation from unanswerable speech while refusing to identify a person permanently with a past wrong. Repair is more than a declaration of changed inward feeling: public damage gives the restoration of credibility a social dimension. The precise effect of repentance on testimony remains disputed.

How the commentators read it. Ibn ʿĀshūr reads the provision against the circulation of sexual slurs and emphasizes that the feminine grammatical form does not imply a different moral standard for men’s sexual wrongdoing.

REP-68. Qadhf: whether repentance restores a public voice

Follow the argument RulingLegal reasoningScripture

Division 68: Qadhf.

Ruling and reason for disagreement. The chapter disputes both indirect accusation and restoration of testimony after repentance. For the latter, Mālik and al-Shāfiʿī extend the exception in to the refusal of testimony; Abū Ḥanīfa restricts it to the judgment of wrongdoing. Ibn Rushd argues that continued testimonial exclusion after the removal of that defect is difficult to align with other legal principles. Bidāya Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.441,443

REP-69. Drinking offences: a predicted effect does not fix a penalty

Follow the argument RulingLegal reasoningScripture

Division 69: Drinking offences.

Ruling and reason for disagreement. Ibn Rushd distinguishes prohibited substances, the degree of consumption, penalty amounts and modes of proof. The argument attributed to ʿAlī relates intoxication to disordered speech and false accusation; competing forty- and eighty-lash accounts remain. The Ḍarūrī control makes the crucial distinction: a predicted sequence is not itself a textual universal prescribing an identical number. Bidāya Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.443–445

How the legal argument works. · . These notes identify the relevant mechanism or comparative control; later maxims do not establish Ibn Rushd’s historical vocabulary.

Setting. Ibn ʿĀshūr places in a sequence of increasingly explicit restrictions. He reports Saʿd’s account of a drinking gathering in which rivalry between emigrants and helpers ended in injury. Muslim1706 separately reports differing punitive practices and consultation under ʿUmar.

Text and reported setting. links avoidance to flourishing and names enmity, hatred, and obstruction of remembrance and prayer. The closing question asks whether the hearers will desist. The next verse recalls the Messenger’s responsibility to communicate clearly.

Ethical force of the passage. The named harms connect inward distraction with relations between people. The call asks for an understood change in conduct. It gives a moral orientation for restraint, but does not supply a numerical penalty by itself or prove that every instance of enforcement reforms desire.

How the commentators read it. Ibn ʿĀshūr reads the staged address as preparing hearers through explanation, initially acknowledging what they perceived as benefit before clarifying the greater harm. Nawawī on Muslim1706–1707 distinguishes forty as a fixed amount with a possible discretionary addition, the view he favours, from the view making eighty the fixed penalty. He also sees consultation as a practice of judges and muftis. A social explanation of intoxication thus coexists with disagreement about public authority’s precise limits; it cannot be substituted for the relevant transmitted evidence.

· · · · ·

REP-70. Theft: equal treatment and identifying the actual act

Follow the argument RulingLegal reasoningScripture

Division 70: Theft.

Ruling and reason for disagreement. The Makhzūmī woman's report is disputed as a precedent for denial of borrowed property. Some take the denial as the operative act; others distinguish it from theft and read the account as mentioning both. Ibn Rushd relates that reading to the ordinary classification of entrusted possession and to different report wordings. The anti-favouritism sermon does not eliminate the need to identify the offence. Bidāya Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.445–446

How the legal argument works. · . These notes identify the relevant mechanism or comparative control; later maxims do not establish Ibn Rushd’s historical vocabulary.

Text and reported setting. speaks of theft and a deterrent punishment under divine might and wisdom. The next verse turns to repentance and repair, with forgiveness and mercy. In the Makhzūmī report, attempted intercession raises the question of unequal treatment by social rank.

Ethical force of the passage. The neighbouring verse prevents punishment from becoming the person’s total identity. The hadith’s rebuke concerns an institution whose severity falls on the weak while powerful offenders receive exemptions. Equal answerability and the possibility of a repaired life are both present; neither supplies permission for private punishment.

How the commentators read it. Ibn ʿĀshūr takes the command as addressed to those with public authority. Ibn Ḥajar brings the report’s aftermath into view: the woman repented, married, and continued to bring needs through ʿĀʾisha. This matters ethically because the narrative does not end with exclusion from social concern. It does not establish that every penal aftermath historically achieved reintegration.
