REP-71. Public violence, rebellion and apostasy: distinct objects of judgment

Follow the argument RulingLegal reasoningScripture

Division 71: Hiraba.

Ruling and reason for disagreement. Ibn Rushd records agreement on armed road obstruction outside a town and disagreement about urban cases. Mālik includes them; al-Shāfiʿī's account follows the capacity for overwhelming force and includes a town where government is weak; Abū Ḥanīfa restricts the category differently. This is unusually explicit attention to actual political conditions within classification. Bidāya Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.454–455

How the legal argument works. · . These notes identify the relevant mechanism or comparative control; later maxims do not establish Ibn Rushd’s historical vocabulary.

Text and reported setting. treats violent predation and corruption in the land; distinguishes repentance before capture and ends with divine forgiveness and mercy.

Ethical force of the passage. The passage combines protection from organized violence with a distinction that makes timing and voluntary cessation consequential. The reach of that exception, especially concerning victims’ claims, still needs juristic analysis. Neither the severity of the offence nor the hope of mercy makes personal vengeance a form of public justice.

How the commentators read it. Wāḥidī retains both the violent episode and Qatāda’s separately transmitted statement connecting revelation to it. Ibn ʿĀshūr favours the ʿUrayna account and discusses its relation to earlier punishment, while recording competing settings. His conclusion is an interpretation of the reports, not an independent confirmation of the occasion chain.

· · ·

Armed conflict within the community and the work of reconciliation

The juridical distinction. After ḥirāba, Ibn Rushd treats fighters acting on an interpretation, taʾwīl, separately. A ruler’s response during active conflict and after its end is not identical. The passage reports disagreement about treatment of captives, calls to repent, and liability for killings; property still identifiable in another’s possession is to be returned. Its discussion of belief also distinguishes an asserted denial from a consequence an opponent draws from someone’s doctrine but that person does not affirm. Ibn Rushd records disagreement about declaring unbelief on that latter basis. Neither a common penalty heading nor a claim of religious error makes ordinary predation, interpreted rebellion and apostasy the same practical object. Bidāya Arabic II, PDF pp.458–459; p.458 checked as an image

Reconciliation after conflict: justice binds the victor too

Text and setting. begins with reconciliation, permits action against an aggressing party until it returns, and then commands a further just reconciliation. Believers remain brothers; the command to fear God and hope for mercy addresses the whole community. Ibn ʿĀshūr links the passage with verification of reports at . He records different quarrel narratives and identifies a chronology difficulty in attaching the verse to the early encounter involving Ibn Ubayy. The occasion is therefore reported and debated, not established as one certain event.

The ethical argument. Stopping aggression does not complete the work of peace. Those who have surrendered can be left humiliated and resentful; the victorious side and the mediators remain responsible for the terms of return. The aggressor’s wrong does not make the other side’s conduct automatically just.

How the commentators read it. Ibn ʿĀshūr distinguishes the verse’s ordinary sense of aggression from the later technical category of rebellion. He recommends intervention before conflict fully erupts, then reads the second reconciliation as necessary because a defeated group feels broken and the other victorious. He explains the closing taqwā as binding aggressors, victims and interveners according to their different duties. He also preserves legal disputes about losses in interpretive rebellion and warns that the historical reports are partisan. These legal distinctions prevent the rhetoric of brotherhood from erasing responsibility.

Scope of this reading. The verse is a basis used in the later law of rebellion, not a transcript of every technical rule. Qushayrī’s inward analogy is a different interpretive operation from identifying which public party has aggressed.

· · ·

Apostasy, coerced profession and the limit of the formation thesis

What Ibn Rushd actually reports. The opening case is a male apostate apprehended before fighting. Ibn Rushd reports agreement on a death penalty in that case, then disagreement about women, invitation to repent and related conditions. Abū Ḥanīfa’s exclusion of women and the opposing appeal to general wording display a real difference in scope. This wording prevents the present manuscript from explaining his doctrine away as punishment only for armed treason. His assertion of agreement is reported as his assertion; an independent school census has not been completed. Bidāya Arabic II, PDF p.459; opening sentence checked as an image

Religious coercion, public status and the limit of outward judgment

Text and setting. The report cited by Ibn Rushd concerns punishment for changing religion. In Bukhārī6922 it is transmitted within Ibn ʿAbbās’s response to ʿAlī’s punishment of a group. instead states no compulsion in religion, relates this to the distinction of guidance from error, and describes faith through grasping a firm handhold. These are distinct texts and settings. Ibn Ḥajar reports competing identifications of the punished group. Ibn ʿĀshūr records different occasions for , including parents attempting to compel their children; he also gives his own historical account of the verse’s relation to warfare.

The ethical argument. The historical law’s coercive protection of public affiliation and the inward reality of faith must be examined separately. Neither a compelled profession nor successful state discipline demonstrates recognition, acknowledgement or certainty. Conversely, recording the jurists’ coercive doctrine is necessary to understand the text rather than replacing it with a preferred modern reconciliation.

How the commentators read it. Ibn Ḥajar retains the punishment doctrine and its disagreements about women and repentance, while excluding an unproved inward change and a profession extracted under compulsion from the report’s simple generality. Ibn ʿĀshūr explains faith as involving evidence, an opportunity to consider and choice. His interpretation of no compulsion nevertheless retains expansion of Islamic political authority and jizya; it is not a doctrine of modern religiously neutral government. He distinguishes his chronology from earlier abrogation and restriction readings. These source arguments expose a tension requiring analysis; they do not provide a warrant to claim that Ibn Rushd restricted apostasy to armed treason.

Scope of this reading. Ibn Rushd expressly treats a male apostate apprehended before fighting. The project must not erase that sentence. The report’s variants and all school doctrines have not received a new independent transmission audit. The inward reading below is not an alternative criminal methodology.

· · · · ·

REP-72. Judgment: competence, public effect and the virtues of common life

Follow the argument RulingLegal reasoningScripture

Division 72: Judgment proof and concluding virtues.

Ibn Rushd: summary of the ruling and disagreement. The judicial opening disputes required juristic competence and eligibility, including the reported positions on women judging. The later attention cases distinguish a judge's condition from the effect of a judgment. The closing passage explicitly orders practical sunan toward virtues, names generosity and sharing in zakāt, and connects social practices to the necessities of common life. These statements establish a virtue horizon without certifying the justice of every institutional exclusion. Bidāya Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.460,474–476

al-Ḍarūrī · method · Arabic / Englishal-Ḍarūrī: the jurist’s qualifications and bounded competence

How the legal argument works. · · . These notes identify the relevant mechanism or comparative control; later maxims do not establish Ibn Rushd’s historical vocabulary.

An oath, a hidden reservation and another person’s right. Al-Nawawī gives his school’s detailed distinction: in an authorized judicial oath the judge’s intended matter controls, so equivocation does not avoid the oath. Outside that setting, a reservation can affect whether the oath is broken; nevertheless it is impermissible to use it to cancel someone’s rightful claim. He then reports more differentiated Mālikī accounts, including whether the oath was demanded or volunteered and whether deceit was intended. His account preserves the difference between the oath’s technical effect and the wrong of depriving another.

·

A commander’s instructions: governing without claiming divine omniscience. Al-Nawawī explains the need to teach commanders what is obligatory, permitted and forbidden, together with care for their followers. On taking a fortress under one’s own judgment, he says the warning supports those who hold that an investigator can miss the true ruling; he preserves the opposing answer that revelation could still correct the judgment during the Prophet’s life. On an undertaking in God’s name, he explains the danger of subordinates breaking a pledge whose gravity they do not understand. He also records incompatible school allocations of revenue and the scope of jizya, rather than extracting a uniformly benign administrative doctrine.

·

Fitness for office and justice across the household and city. Al-Nawawī says the warning particularly concerns inability to perform the office’s tasks. He distinguishes the incapable appointee from the capable but unjust one, and both from the competent person who governs justly. His explanation of the neighbouring praise expressly includes rule, judgment, market supervision, orphan property, alms, endowments and family rights. The description of responsibility concerns preserving and advancing the good of what is entrusted, in religious and worldly matters.

·

Text and reported setting. commands return of trusts to their owners and just judgment, ending with God as hearing and seeing.

Ethical force of the passage. The two endings address the gap between an obligation and another person’s ability to enforce it. The trusted holder must not treat the absence of a record as permission to retain what is owed; the witness must not make the truth disappear through silence.

How the commentators read it. Ibn ʿĀshūr reads as addressing everyone entrusted with something and everyone judging, with delivery to the rightful recipient at its centre. He notes the weak chain of the Kaʿba-key occasion rather than treating it as certain.

The full explanation, remaining distinctions and source passages are in the adjacent Context & commentary note.

· · · · · · · ·

Direct context and explanation. Muslim1713 reports a dispute brought before the Prophet, including a version in which disputants are heard at Umm Salama’s door. Nawawī explains that judgment proceeds by accessible testimony and oath, while God knows hidden matters. He distinguishes a judgment correctly following its evidentiary duty from culpable false testimony and from an error of juristic reasoning. He reads the Prophet’s ordinary public procedure as a model that others can follow. He records the majority position that a judgment does not inwardly make forbidden acquisition lawful, then disputes Abū Ḥanīfa’s differently delimited position concerning marital cases. He also says the reference to a Muslim’s property is not a permission to take the protected property of a non-Muslim.

·

Direct context and explanation. Muslim1717 preserves Abū Bakra’s written instruction to his son, who was judging in Sijistān, based on the Prophetic prohibition of judging while angry. Nawawī extends the concern to intense hunger, excessive fullness, worry, joy, bodily urgency and other preoccupations that disrupt deliberation. He explains the risk as loss of the sound consideration needed for the ruling. He nevertheless distinguishes acting in a prohibited condition from the validity of a judgment that actually conforms to the law. This explains the purpose of the prohibition on judging while distracted without merging professional discipline with the legal effect of the decision.

·

Detailed continuation. judicial attention. These retain their own open attribution and commentary checks.

Part V.D. Judicial attention and public effect

Detailed social-law draft, revision 6. J001–J002 examine the judge’s condition at Arabic II 474–475, from the opening inquiry into when the judge decides through Ibn Rushd’s proposed invalidity argument concerning anger. English II printed pp.570–571, PDF pp.574–575. The surrounding testimony, insolvency, execution and property-restraint rules are separate uncompleted dossiers.

Public knowledge and the condition of the judge

Setting. Muslim1713 reports a dispute brought before the Prophet, including a version in which disputants are heard at Umm Salama’s door.

The passage. One litigant may present a stronger argument than another. The Prophet warns that an award of another person’s right on that basis is a portion of fire, not an inward entitlement.

Its ethical argument. Speech, proof and office mediate public judgment; success before them does not erase a concealed wrong. The warning addresses the beneficiary as well as the judge: procedural victory can become an occasion for greater moral responsibility rather than vindication.

What the commentary explains. Nawawī explains that judgment proceeds by accessible testimony and oath, while God knows hidden matters. He distinguishes a judgment correctly following its evidentiary duty from culpable false testimony and from an error of juristic reasoning. He reads the Prophet’s ordinary public procedure as a model that others can follow. He records the majority position that a judgment does not inwardly make forbidden acquisition lawful, then disputes Abū Ḥanīfa’s differently delimited position concerning marital cases. He also says the reference to a Muslim’s property is not a permission to take the protected property of a non-Muslim.

·

Setting. Muslim1717 preserves Abū Bakra’s written instruction to his son, who was judging in Sijistān, based on the Prophetic prohibition of judging while angry.

The passage. The prohibition concerns judgment while anger impairs the person charged with deciding between others.

Its ethical argument. A judge’s state becomes a public concern because another person bears the cost of impaired attention. The duty is not simply to suppress visible emotion; it is to preserve the capacity to hear, understand and decide.

What the commentary explains. Nawawī extends the concern to intense hunger, excessive fullness, worry, joy, bodily urgency and other preoccupations that disrupt deliberation. He explains the risk as loss of the sound consideration needed for the ruling. He nevertheless distinguishes acting in a prohibited condition from the validity of a judgment that actually conforms to the law. This gives J001–J002 an account of the rule’s purpose without merging professional discipline with the legal effect of the decision.

·

Fitness for office and justice across the household and city

The report distinguishes being personally devout from being able to discharge an entrusted role. That distinction bears on formation of a judge before the narrower question of judging in anger.

Text and situation. Abū Dharr requests office and is warned of his weakness for its demands. Neighbouring reports praise those who judge justly in government, family and what they administer, and censure rulers who impose hardship. Personal esteem and affection accompany the refusal of office. The report does not infer incapacity from lack of piety.

What the commentary explains. Al-Nawawī says the warning particularly concerns inability to perform the office’s tasks. He distinguishes the incapable appointee from the capable but unjust one, and both from the competent person who governs justly. His explanation of the neighbouring praise expressly includes rule, judgment, market supervision, orphan property, alms, endowments and family rights. The description of responsibility concerns preserving and advancing the good of what is entrusted, in religious and worldly matters.

The practical meaning. Different functions require different capacities. A spiritually serious person may be unfit for administration; a technically capable officer still has to exercise justice. Household care, guardianship and public office share responsibility without becoming interchangeable authorities.

·

An oath, a hidden reservation and another person’s right

A judicial oath makes the relation between private intention and public claim especially clear. This is a direct report-commentary chain for that neighbouring question, not additional evidence about anger.

Text and situation. The report locates the oath’s meaning in what the person requiring it can accept as truthful. A variant speaks of the intention of the person administering the oath. Al-Nawawī’s principal application is a judicial oath in a claim, where a litigant privately intends a meaning different from the judge’s. He separately discusses nonjudicial oaths.

What the commentary explains. Al-Nawawī gives his school’s detailed distinction: in an authorized judicial oath the judge’s intended matter controls, so equivocation does not avoid the oath. Outside that setting, a reservation can affect whether the oath is broken; nevertheless it is impermissible to use it to cancel someone’s rightful claim. He then reports more differentiated Mālikī accounts, including whether the oath was demanded or volunteered and whether deceit was intended. His account preserves the difference between the oath’s technical effect and the wrong of depriving another.

The practical meaning. An inward intention is morally significant without becoming a private power to dissolve a publicly owed truth. The question is whose practical reliance the words have engaged.

·

A commander’s instructions: governing without claiming divine omniscience

The commander’s instructions provide a comparison for the qualified judge’s epistemic position: a decision must be made without representing it as knowledge of God’s hidden judgment.

Text and situation. Burayda’s report places a commander’s personal taqwā and care for those accompanying him before military instructions. It forbids treachery and misappropriation and concludes by distinguishing the commander’s own undertaking and judgment from God’s. This is a reported pattern of commissioning commanders, not a single dated siege. It also distinguishes migration, military participation, revenues and the offer of jizya.

What the commentary explains. Al-Nawawī explains the need to teach commanders what is obligatory, permitted and forbidden, together with care for their followers. On taking a fortress under one’s own judgment, he says the warning supports those who hold that an investigator can miss the true ruling; he preserves the opposing answer that revelation could still correct the judgment during the Prophet’s life. On an undertaking in God’s name, he explains the danger of subordinates breaking a pledge whose gravity they do not understand. He also records incompatible school allocations of revenue and the scope of jizya, rather than extracting a uniformly benign administrative doctrine.

The practical meaning. Public power has an inward discipline and a public limit. The person commanding must care for subordinates and honour undertakings; that responsibility does not make his judgment identical with divine knowledge. His office remains answerable precisely where its decisions are consequential.

·

J001. Anger and other impediments to understanding

Primary requirement and extension. Ibn Rushd invokes the report prohibiting judgment while angry. Mālik includes thirst, hunger, fear and comparable impediments to understanding. The legally significant question is the judge’s availability for understanding when acting; the extension follows the impediment, not merely a list of undesirable emotions. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.474–475; Bidāya, English II, PDF pp.574–575, printed pp.570–571

The sciences in operation. The three universalities clarify different contributions: the proposed semantic scope is impairment of understanding; the practical-causal premise concerns the effects of anger, hunger or fear; the teleological end is just adjudication. A general psychological likeness does not itself confer legal authority. Universal practical knowledge supplies the conception of a binding norm and competent office. Instrumental discernment considers a transmitted prohibition and its extension through an intelligible meaning. Particular fiqh addresses the judge in the specified condition. Actual judgment then requires situated knowledge of the dispute. None of these levels can be replaced by the proposition that justice is good.

Simon’s account of prudence helps distinguish correct acting from mere technical facility; Ghazālī’s account of presence offers a comparison for the difference between continuing an outward operation and attending to it. Their relation is analogical. The judge’s evidentiary authority does not become the authority of a spiritual director. Simon, Critique of Moral Knowledge, PDF pp.28–31,67–68;

Principles in this argument. Extension from anger to other impediments requires identifying the legally relevant impairment; assessing whether it occurs in this judge is a separate act of practical judgment. The Ḍarūrī’s indicated-meaning account and Ghazālī’s manāṭ distinction therefore belong at different steps. A later control is unusually close: al-Shāṭibī discusses the same anger example through both meaningful scope and the psychological fact of disturbance. His terminology must remain his; it cannot prove that Ibn Rushd used the later account. Muwāfaqāt I, PDF pp.77–78, printed pp.42–43 Jamʿ’s account of practiced juristic competence adds the institutional formation needed to perform those steps responsibly. Reading impairment as an indicated general meaning is our supported reconstruction; the later parallel does not turn that classification into an explicit statement in this Bidāya passage.

Subsidiary maxims. Prevention concerns impairment before it damages judgment. Public benefit conditions the official’s work, while the private burden of postponement or recusal needs a warranted comparison with the threatened injury. The maxims guide these questions; they do not establish a diagnosis of impairment or authorize coercive measures absent the relevant jurisdiction.

J002. A correct judgment by a judge in a prohibited condition

Position and qualification. Ibn Rushd says that, as far as he knows, jurists agree that a correct judgment issued in one of these conditions takes effect. He then proposes a possible contrary argument for anger specifically: the express prohibition might imply the invalidity of the prohibited act. The qualification on agreement and the conjectural form of the alternative must remain. The alternative is not assigned to a named madhhab in this passage. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF p.475; Bidāya, English II, PDF p.575, printed p.571

Three assessments. The judge’s conduct, the correctness of the result and its public effect are distinct objects of evaluation. A theory of formation that makes every inward defect dissolve a correct judgment would endanger established rights. A theory that considers only the result would fail to explain the prohibition regulating the judge. The reported account holds the distinction together; the proposed alternative reopens the relation between prohibition and effect for the expressly named case.

The vertical limit is decisive: accountability before God does not make legal effect depend on another person’s unverifiable estimate of spiritual perfection. Public knowledge remains finite and warranted. The alchemical model must therefore form agents while allowing institutions to function before all agents are perfected. This is one of the clearest links from detailed fiqh upward to the theory of the city.

Principles in this argument. The prohibited condition and the judgment’s legal effect must be separately established. This is a direct point of contact with the Ḍarūrī’s prohibition/invalidity discussion and Jamʿ’s later map of its disagreements. A correct result cannot simply erase misconduct, while misconduct cannot automatically undo other people’s adjudicated rights. The later distinction between excusable error and judgment finality further prevents institutional effect from being mistaken for universal truth.

Subsidiary maxims. Correction of a demonstrated error must be distinguished from revisiting a judgment simply because another qualified view is available. A maxim rejecting disproved probability addresses the first concern; the rules governing finality and reversal address the second. The law’s institutional operation cannot be derived from either slogan in isolation.

The witness sequence at II17–18 supplies a reciprocal comparison. Public announcement and admissible judicial proof are distinct functions; legal probity may also operate through an outward presumption rather than knowledge of inner virtue. The judge’s cognitive fitness is therefore one element in a distributed process of knowing, alongside witnesses, parties and rules about what their statements can establish. This does not add a new judgment rule to J001–J002; it corrects any implication that good adjudication consists only in the judge’s concentration. Bidāya Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.17–18

Judgment and the formation of virtue

Immediately after the surrounding judicial material, Ibn Rushd distinguishes norms adjudicated by judges from norms outside that jurisdiction and then introduces the virtues of the soul. That placement makes a powerful structural comparison possible: law is wider than enforceable judgment, while judgments serve a formative order they do not exhaust. It does not prove that every procedural detail is transparently deduced from a named virtue. Read together with the ribā and illness-marriage passages, however, the conclusion shows why final goods can also illuminate the act of judging itself. Virtue is a horizon within practical discernment as well as a possible result of disciplined practice; neither role eliminates the requirement for a proximate legal warrant. Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.46–47,131–133 Bidāya, Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.475–476

The completed book must trace this relation throughout testimony, proof, liability, penalties and office. This installment establishes only the cognitive-condition example and its disputed consequences. It relocates the strongest question of concentration from repetitive ritual commentary to a concrete public act in which another person’s rights depend on the quality and limits of knowing.

Part VI.A. Principles at the point of use

Revision 9, 1 October 2026. This register makes the operative legal reasoning visible. The notes distinguish what a source actually says from our application of it to a Bidāya question. They do not replace each case’s primary sabab al-ikhtilāf.

Reading key: Ḍ = Ibn Rushd’s al-Ḍarūrī; M = al-Ghazālī’s al-Mustaṣfā; J = al-Subkī’s Jamʿ al-Jawāmiʿ; Q = fiqh maxim or its historical classification; B = a local Bidāya criterion. “Later control” is not an attribution to Ibn Rushd. “Analytical comparison” identifies our mapping between texts.

In the HTML reader, hover, focus or click a short reference to see its full name, kind, warrant, limitation and source page. In Markdown, follow the reference to its complete entry here. Each source link identifies the exact local witness; PDF links in the reader also open at the indicated page.

Source and attribution rules

The Ḍarūrī references use the primary Arabic/French text in Akl’s edition, not his later interpretive commentary unless expressly stated. Mustaṣfā references marked M use the full Arabic file, not the partial English translation. Jamʿ entries cite the matn; its editor’s illustrative footnotes are separate. Kızılkaya is a modern study. The five maxims are verified directly in Jamʿ, rather than cited solely through that study.

A reported analogy is not automatically an indicated universal or a shared legal cause; a known criterion is not its proved instance; a legal cause is not a physical efficient cause; an ethical effect is not a legal proof. These distinctions govern the annotations below.

DR-SCI · al-Ḍarūrī: practical generality and instrumental inquiry

Short reference: Ḍ: sciences. Kind: Rushdian primary — classification of sciences.

Knowledge terminating in action may be universal and remote from action or particular and proximate to it. A further instrumental inquiry regulates correct thought. Ibn Rushd singles out the third of the Mustaṣfā’s four divisions as this instrumental core.

Limit: The entire historical discipline of uṣūl is not identical to this narrower core; fiqh contains rules for kinds of acts, not only judgments of unique events.

Source: al-Ḍarūrī §§2–9; Akl Arabic/French text, PDF pp.128–133, printed pp.118–123.

DR-AG · al-Ḍarūrī: agency, capacity and obligation

Short reference: Ḍ: agency. Kind: Rushdian primary — conditions of obligation.

Ibn Rushd gives agency a real causal relation to action and rejects obligation to perform the impossible; the following discussion differentiates coercion, omission and the conditions of responsible action.

Limit: This does not decide every property liability of a minor or dependent person: liability, capacity for personally obedient action and liability mediated through a guardian require separate arguments.

Source: al-Ḍarūrī §§54–59; PDF pp.158–161, printed pp.148–151.

DR-QIY · al-Ḍarūrī: reclassification of most juristic qiyās as indicated meaning

Short reference: Ḍ: indicated universal. Kind: Rushdian primary — inferential method.

After reporting the original/branch/common-cause definition, Ibn Rushd says most operations called qiyās are not qiyās in his strict classification: a particular expression and authorized context indicate a wider normative meaning, under which another instance is established by ijtihād or perception.

Limit: Do not classify every reported analogy this way. Show the indication of the intended universal; otherwise retain residual resemblance or an unresolved classification. Semantic warrant does not exclude knowledge of reality or make an inferred universal certain.

Source: al-Ḍarūrī §§257–261; PDF pp.298–301, printed pp.288–291.

DR-RANK · al-Ḍarūrī: unequal strengths of inferential indication

Short reference: Ḍ: indicators. Kind: Rushdian primary — assessment of proof.

The discussion differentiates a fortiori indication, equivalence, suitability supported by legally recognized benefit, and weaker resemblance. Their probative force is not uniform; suitability itself has degrees.

Limit: Indicated extension can remain conjectural: §267 treats the rival ribā predicates as weak contextual indications. Do not equate textual mediation with certainty, or every occurrence of qiyās al-shabah with the residual category of the Bidāya introduction.

Source: al-Ḍarūrī §§262–267; PDF pp.302–305, printed pp.292–295.

DR-MAS · al-Ḍarūrī: benefit is not an unrestricted source

Short reference: Ḍ: benefit limits. Kind: Rushdian primary — limits of interest-based inference.

Istiḥsān and istiṣlāḥ need a warranted legal basis rather than approval by taste. In §266 Ibn Rushd rejects inference from an indeterminate generic interest: benefits vary with circumstances, and this can become legislation instead of derivation.

Limit: Generic benefit alone does not authorize a positive rule. Read this strict criticism alongside Bidāya II46–47, where Ibn Rushd also warns that refusing benefit consideration can facilitate injustice and calls for evidenced situational judgment. Their exact reconciliation remains a research problem.

Source: al-Ḍarūrī §§172–174 and §266; PDF pp.242–243 and 304–305.

DR-DOM · al-Ḍarūrī: the visibility of indicators differs across domains

Short reference: Ḍ: domains. Kind: Rushdian primary — domain-sensitive inference.

§268 says indications differ in manifestness across kinds of obligation. Necessary affairs, exemplified by sales and marriage, make them more evident; the discussion contrasts fixed penalties and expiations and reports Abū Ḥanīfa’s restriction of analogy there.

Limit: This is not a prohibition on reasoning in all worship, nor an assurance that every transaction has a transparent benefit. Do not replace the passage’s actual examples with a comprehensive ritual/social binary.

Source: al-Ḍarūrī §268; Arabic/French PDF pp.306–307, printed pp.296–297; Arabic page image checked.

DR-IST · al-Ḍarūrī: distinct uses of istiṣḥāb

Short reference: Ḍ: continuity. Kind: Rushdian primary — presumption and continuity.

The discussion distinguishes original non-liability, persistence of general or univocal evidence until a modifier, continuity in recurring circumstances, and the disputed persistence of a previously agreed status after a relevant quality changes.

Limit: The established baseline and the alleged change must be identified. Physical persistence does not automatically establish unchanged legal status, and a change in a relevant quality can reopen inquiry.

Source: al-Ḍarūrī §§169–170; PDF pp.240–241, printed pp.230–231.

DR-AM · al-Ḍarūrī: general expression and warranted specification

Short reference: Ḍ: general/specific. Kind: Rushdian primary — textual scope.

General wording can intend a restricted class. Restriction requires evidence and assessment of relative indication; the discussion includes controversy over general and particular evidence and their chronology.

Limit: Neither a general ethical purpose nor a preferred result automatically specifies a revealed general expression. A claimed exception needs its own warrant.

Source: al-Ḍarūrī §§217–219; PDF pp.272–275, printed pp.262–265.

DR-ZAH · al-Ḍarūrī: apparent meaning and interpretive burden

Short reference: Ḍ: apparent meaning. Kind: Rushdian primary — linguistic indication.

An expression’s preponderant meaning supplies an operative starting point; departure from it requires countervailing evidence. Greater initial clarity calls for a correspondingly stronger reason to depart.

Limit: This does not make every literal reading certain or eliminate context. A juridical reconstruction of a relationship is not always a dispute about a single word.

Source: al-Ḍarūrī §§196–199; PDF pp.260–263, printed pp.250–253.

DR-NAHY · al-Ḍarūrī: prohibition and legal invalidity

Short reference: Ḍ: prohibition/effect. Kind: Rushdian primary — normative force and validity.

The argument relates prohibition to the act itself, a relevant quality or an external matter and to the account of what the prohibitive form signifies. Invalidity cannot be treated as an unqualified synonym for prohibited conduct.

Limit: One must identify what is forbidden and why that affects, or does not affect, the legal effect. This register supplies a method of analysis, not a blanket validation of prohibited transactions or judgments.

Source: al-Ḍarūrī §§253–254; PDF pp.296–297, printed pp.286–287.

DR-FIL · al-Ḍarūrī: what a prophetic act establishes

Short reference: Ḍ: prophetic acts. Kind: Rushdian primary — Sunna and indication.

An act that explains an utterance takes its legal determination from the explained utterance. For an act without an established explanatory or specifically prophetic status, Ibn Rushd requires context rather than inferring a determinate obligation from occurrence alone; conflicting explanatory acts require comparison.

Limit: This differs from simply declaring all acts obligatory or all recommended. The Bidāya’s report of other jurists’ positions must not be mistaken for Ibn Rushd’s own preferred rule in al-Ḍarūrī.

Source: al-Ḍarūrī §§276–279; PDF pp.312–315, printed pp.302–305.

DR-ERR · al-Ḍarūrī: determinate truth and excusable error

Short reference: Ḍ: error. Kind: Rushdian primary — ijtihād and correctness.

Ibn Rushd rejects universal correctness of conflicting conclusions in the relevant disputed legal questions. Legal discourse and its indicators have a determinate bearing; immunity from sin is distinct from immunity from error.

Limit: Plurality can be legally managed and spiritually interpreted without making all incompatible propositions equally true. This is a substantive disagreement with Ghazālī, not a difference to harmonize away.

Source: al-Ḍarūrī §§288–295, especially §§290, 293, 295; PDF pp.320–325.

MS-MAN · al-Mustaṣfā: taḥqīq al-manāṭ — determining the criterion in the instance

Short reference: M: application. Kind: Ghazālian primary comparison — application of a known rule.

Ghazālī distinguishes a known criterion from probable identification of its instance. His examples include sufficiency in maintenance of relatives, valuation of destroyed goods, appointments and witness reliability. Such particular judgments cannot all be exhaustively specified in texts.

Limit: His maintenance example concerns relatives, not specifically the disputed spousal quantities in M003. It illuminates applying an adopted adequacy rule; it does not settle whether the legally correct rule is adequacy or a prescribed quantity.

Source: al-Mustaṣfā, third quṭb, introduction to investigation of causes; printed pp.437–438, PDF pp.439–440.

MS-TAN · al-Mustaṣfā: tanqīḥ al-manāṭ — removing irrelevant accompanying features

Short reference: M: refinement. Kind: Ghazālian primary comparison — refinement of a stated ground.

A ruling can be attached to an event with incidental features. Removing features known to be irrelevant extends the ruling; uncertainty about a feature’s relevance can itself cause disagreement. The Ramadan expiation example distinguishes obvious incidental features from disputed extensions to eating.

Limit: Refinement of a ground, discovery of a ground and assessment of an instance are distinct operations. Naming all three qiyās conceals a difference Ghazālī expressly discusses.

Source: al-Mustaṣfā, printed pp.438–439, PDF pp.440–441.

MS-TKH · al-Mustaṣfā: takhrīj al-manāṭ — inferring an unstated ground

Short reference: M: finding the cause. Kind: Ghazālian primary comparison — discovery of a legal cause.

Where a text supplies the ruling and its subject without stating the ground, the jurist investigates the relevant quality. Ghazālī contrasts this contested operation with assessment of a known criterion and refinement of a stated event.

Limit: A later label is an analytical comparison, not proof that Ibn Rushd called a specific Bidāya dispute takhrīj. It must not be confused with historical or psychological explanation of why a jurist preferred a view.

Source: al-Mustaṣfā, printed pp.437–439, PDF pp.439–441, especially PDF p.441.

MS-IMA · al-Mustaṣfā: a ruling attached to a suitable description

Short reference: M: indication by context. Kind: Ghazālian primary comparison — implicit indication of a ground.

The attachment of a ruling to a suitable description can indicate explanation without an explicit causal particle. Ghazālī also insists that a fortiori inference depends on understanding the relevant context and purpose, not merely observing a lesser and greater act.

Limit: An interpreter’s preferred purpose is not sufficient evidence that the text attached its ruling to that quality. This is not automatically mafhūm al-mukhālafa.

Source: al-Mustaṣfā, printed pp.412–413, PDF pp.414–415.

MS-MAF · al-Mustaṣfā: no automatic contrary rule from a qualifier

Short reference: M: contrary inference. Kind: Ghazālian primary comparison — disputed implication.

In the discussion beginning at PDF p.415, Ghazālī defines contrary implication and rejects deriving exclusion merely from the presence of a qualifier. Additional evidence or contextual indication is needed; he records other jurists’ acceptance.

Limit: Do not cite Ghazālī as endorsing every inference later taxonomies call mafhūm al-mukhālafa. A dispute over an inferred exchange relationship may not be contrary implication at all.

Source: al-Mustaṣfā, printed pp.413–415, PDF pp.415–417.

MS-ERR · al-Mustaṣfā: correctness under the jurist’s warranted probability

Short reference: M: qualified correctness. Kind: Ghazālian primary comparison — position opposed by Ibn Rushd.

Ghazālī explicitly defends every qualified mujtahid’s correctness in the relevant probabilistic inquiries. He treats the legal cause as a divinely designated sign, not an intrinsic necessitating cause; its benefit need not be transparent to the investigator.

Limit: This does not license unqualified opinion, negligence or treating every factual assertion as true. Do not assimilate this doctrine to Ibn Rushd’s contrary account or to Shaʿrānī’s later spiritual harmonization.

Source: al-Mustaṣfā, discussion of the possibility of legal qiyās; printed pp.441–442, PDF pp.443–444.

J-DEF · Jamʿ al-Jawāmiʿ: proofs, inference, investigator and detailed fiqh

Short reference: J: definitions. Kind: Later primary control — disciplinary taxonomy.

The opening matn defines the discipline through general proofs, modes of inference and the inferer, and defines fiqh through practical legal rulings acquired from detailed evidence. The subsequent definitions distinguish ruling, cause, condition, impediment and validity.

Limit: This is al-Subkī’s later taxonomy. It neither supplies Ibn Rushd’s historical terminology nor erases the Ḍarūrī’s instrumental analysis.

Source: Jamʿ al-Jawāmiʿ, opening matn, printed/PDF pp.13–15.

J-NAHY · Jamʿ al-Jawāmiʿ: disagreements over prohibition and invalidity

Short reference: J: prohibition/effect. Kind: Later primary control — validity taxonomy.

The matn records divergent accounts of whether and how prohibition entails invalidity, distinguishing worship and transactions and whether the prohibition concerns an internal, inseparable or external matter.

Limit: This is a map of contested accounts, not one agreed maxim that prohibited conduct has no legal effect. The editor’s examples below the matn are not al-Subkī’s own examples.

Source: Jamʿ al-Jawāmiʿ, printed/PDF pp.43–44.

J-FIL · Jamʿ al-Jawāmiʿ: explanatory, ordinary and specifically prophetic acts

Short reference: J: prophetic acts. Kind: Later primary control — Sunna taxonomy.

The matn distinguishes ordinary bodily acts, acts explaining revelation, specifically prophetic acts and acts whose status is known or unknown; it records competing answers for the last category.

Limit: An observed act and an obligation are not synonymous. This later arrangement clarifies the alternatives without replacing Ibn Rushd’s own account.

Source: Jamʿ al-Jawāmiʿ, printed/PDF pp.61–62.

J-IST · Jamʿ al-Jawāmiʿ: persistence and the alleged change

Short reference: J: continuity. Kind: Later primary control — istiṣḥāb.

The matn distinguishes original absence, persistence of general/univocal evidence and an established status, and rejects persistence of a former consensus as decisive in the newly disputed condition while reporting disagreement.

Limit: The claimant must identify an established prior state and the absence of an adequate modifier. A slogan about certainty cannot choose the disputed baseline for us.

Source: Jamʿ al-Jawāmiʿ, printed/PDF p.108.

J-ILH · Jamʿ al-Jawāmiʿ: inspiration and public proof

Short reference: J: inspiration. Kind: Later primary control — limit of legal evidence.

The matn acknowledges inspiration bestowed on some elect persons but denies it probative authority because an uninfallible person cannot be assured of the reliability of inward suggestions; it notes dissent among some Sufis.

Limit: This is the later text’s legal-epistemic position, not a denial of spiritual life or a historical statement about Khiḍr. It supports a limit on substituting private experience for publicly warranted judgment.

Source: Jamʿ al-Jawāmiʿ, printed/PDF p.111, paragraph preceding the concluding maxims; page image checked.

J-MAL · Jamʿ al-Jawāmiʿ: practiced sciences as juristic malaka

Short reference: J: juristic formation. Kind: Later primary control — qualifications of judgment.

The matn reports the author’s father describing the jurist as possessing these sciences as malaka, knowing the major legal principles and practicing them until able to understand the Lawgiver’s intent. The surrounding passage lists evidential and linguistic competences.

Limit: An intellectual/legal malaka is not by itself moral virtue or spiritual realization. This is a later normative account of formation, not evidence that every historical judge had these qualifications.

Source: Jamʿ al-Jawāmiʿ, printed/PDF p.118, matn attribution to al-shaykh al-imām.

J-ERR · Jamʿ al-Jawāmiʿ: error, reward and stability of judgment

Short reference: J: truth and finality. Kind: Later primary control — ijtihād and adjudication.

The matn records rival doctrines of correctness, prefers one correct answer in the relevant dispute while allowing reward for excusable error, and then distinguishes the rule against overturning judgments in matters of ijtihād, subject to specified exceptions.

Limit: Institutional finality does not certify every ruling as metaphysically true. The beginning of the reversal rule at p.120 must not be used without its continuation for a complete account of exceptions.

Source: Jamʿ al-Jawāmiʿ, printed/PDF pp.120–121; taṣwīb/taḫṭiʾa and non-reversal discussion.

Q-CERT · Certainty and doubt — اليقين لا يرفع بالشك

Short reference: Q: certainty. Kind: Later primary control — cross-chapter fiqh maxim.

An established certainty is not removed merely by doubt. The matn’s wording is lā yurfaʿ, not a silently substituted quotation of lā yazūl. Jamʿ attributes the first four maxims to al-Qāḍī Ḥusayn; the intention maxim is introduced separately with qīla, “it is said.”

Limit: Identify what is established, what is doubtful and whether the alleged evidence is merely doubt. It does not determine every evidentiary burden or forbid acting on warranted probability.

Source: Jamʿ al-Jawāmiʿ, concluding maxims of Book V, printed/PDF p.111; matn, not editorial examples; page image checked.

Q-HARM · Removal of harm — الضرر يزال

Short reference: Q: harm. Kind: Later primary control — cross-chapter fiqh maxim.

Harm is to be removed; this is a cross-chapter legal orientation whose concrete means are determined by the relevant doctrine. Jamʿ attributes the first four maxims to al-Qāḍī Ḥusayn; the intention maxim is introduced separately with qīla, “it is said.”

Limit: It does not establish that intervention always reduces harm, authorize uncompensated injury to a third party, or erase a specific rule.

Source: Jamʿ al-Jawāmiʿ, concluding maxims of Book V, printed/PDF p.111; matn, not editorial examples; page image checked.

Q-EASE · Hardship and facilitation — المشقة تجلب التيسير

Short reference: Q: hardship. Kind: Later primary control — cross-chapter fiqh maxim.

Hardship calls for legally recognized facilitation. Jamʿ attributes the first four maxims to al-Qāḍī Ḥusayn; the intention maxim is introduced separately with qīla, “it is said.”

Limit: Ordinary inconvenience does not automatically cancel an obligation; the occasion, form and limit of relief require source-specific demonstration.

Source: Jamʿ al-Jawāmiʿ, concluding maxims of Book V, printed/PDF p.111; matn, not editorial examples; page image checked.

Q-CUSTOM · Custom as a determinant — العادة محكمة

Short reference: Q: custom. Kind: Later primary control — cross-chapter fiqh maxim.

Recognized custom has a determining role in legal assessment. Jamʿ attributes the first four maxims to al-Qāḍī Ḥusayn; the intention maxim is introduced separately with qīla, “it is said.”

Limit: Prevalence does not by itself legitimate a practice or override textual evidence. Custom can supply an assessment within a rule without becoming an unrestricted source of new rules.

Source: Jamʿ al-Jawāmiʿ, concluding maxims of Book V, printed/PDF p.111; matn, not editorial examples; page image checked.

Q-INT · Matters and their purposes — الأمور بمقاصدها

Short reference: Q: intention. Kind: Later primary control — cross-chapter fiqh maxim.

The legal character of a matter can depend on its purpose or intention. Jamʿ attributes the first four maxims to al-Qāḍī Ḥusayn; the intention maxim is introduced separately with qīla, “it is said.”

Limit: Not every consequence turns on a concealed intention, and a court needs warranted evidence. Intention, the Lawgiver’s purposes and civilizational results are not interchangeable meanings of maqāṣid.

Source: Jamʿ al-Jawāmiʿ, concluding maxims of Book V, printed/PDF p.111; matn, not editorial examples; page image checked.

Q-TYPE · Uṣūl principle, fiqh maxim and chapter-specific ḍābiṭ

Short reference: Q: kinds of rule. Kind: Modern historical/conceptual control.

Kızılkaya distinguishes principles concerning proofs and derivation from maxims concerning juristic acts and statuses, and broad maxims from more local ḍawābiṭ. He also documents variation in terminology and exceptions to apparently general propositions.

Limit: Use this as a modern historical analysis, not a universal medieval definition or primary evidence for Ibn Rushd’s vocabulary. A short formula is not automatically a self-sufficient proof.

Source: Necmettin Kızılkaya, Legal Maxims in Islamic Law (Brill, 2021), printed pp.17, 23–26, 36–41; PDF pp.29, 35–38, 48–53.

B-GHR · Bidāya: when uncertainty prevents a sale

Short reference: B: gharar criterion. Kind: Rushdian primary — local sales criterion, not a universal maxim.

The unseen-object discussion makes the decisive issue whether the available description or later option removes the relevant uncertainty. Schools and reports differ about what supplies adequate knowledge.

Limit: This register’s short label is editorial. Do not turn it into a verbatim maxim or infer that every nonzero uncertainty invalidates every contract.

Source: Bidāyat al-mujtahid, Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.155–156; absent-object issue only.

B-AMANA · Bidāya: fiduciary custody and personal liability

Short reference: B: trust/liability. Kind: Rushdian primary — local juridical distinction.

The opening deposit sequence differentiates trust, disputed proof of return or onward delivery, and an obligation in the person’s liability. Those classifications change how a claimed delivery or loss affects the claim.

Limit: Trust does not make every assertion conclusive; liability in the person is not extinguished merely by a custodial loss. This is an editorial précis of a local distinction, not an exceptionless quoted maxim.

Source: Bidāyat al-mujtahid, Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.310–311, before stipulated guarantee.

Expansion from the user-supplied qawāʿid compilation

The following entries supplement the five broad maxims. They are later comparative controls, with the compilation’s detailed argument distinguished from index-only leads. The 91-entry catalogue preserves every numbered entry of its index, including duplicates and disputed questions. These are not 91 independently verified, universally accepted rules.

Q-SUBSTANCE · Contractual meaning and the label used

Short reference: Q: contract substance. Kind: Later comparative control — fiqh maxim or disputed formulation, compilation body checked.

The compilation gives priority to the transaction’s actual juridical meaning over its nominal label; an exchange called a gift can still be a sale. This concerns what the parties constitute, not only a hidden motive.

Limit: Do not infer that all formal requirements are dispensable. The same page’s footnote records differences over taḥlīl marriage that qualify its sweeping main-text assertion about invalid purpose. A Bidāya rule still needs its own attribution and proof.

Source: Legal Maxims of Islamic Jurisprudence: A Translated Compilation, user-supplied PDF pp.57, 58; modern compilation, not an independently collated medieval witness.

Q-INTSCOPE · Can intention restrict or extend the wording of an undertaking?

Short reference: Q: intention and scope. Kind: Later comparative control — fiqh maxim or disputed formulation, compilation body checked.

The compilation presents a disputed question, including distinctions between inward accountability and enforceability against others. Intention’s effect on verbal scope is not uniform across the reported schools.

Limit: The English examples contain awkward or apparently inconsistent formulations. Use the differentiated question as a control; do not adopt each example as a verified school rule or equate this with technical specification of revelation.

Source: Legal Maxims of Islamic Jurisprudence: A Translated Compilation, user-supplied PDF pp.59, 60; modern compilation, not an independently collated medieval witness.

Q-OATHPARTY · Whose intended meaning governs a demanded oath?

Short reference: Q: whose oath meaning. Kind: Later comparative control — fiqh maxim or disputed formulation, compilation body checked.

The oath-taker, the person demanding an oath and the judge occupy different roles. The compilation records competing qualifications concerning equivocation, entitlement to demand an oath and the judicial occasion.

Limit: This is a disputed procedural formulation, not permission to deceive by a concealed intention. It does not settle the separate question whether an oath must be required at all.

Source: Legal Maxims of Islamic Jurisprudence: A Translated Compilation, user-supplied PDF pp.63, 64; modern compilation, not an independently collated medieval witness.

Q-HASTE · Wrongfully accelerating a benefit can defeat entitlement

Short reference: Q: premature acquisition. Kind: Later comparative control — fiqh maxim or disputed formulation, compilation body checked.

The maxim addresses attempts to obtain a legally timed benefit prematurely and associates that wrongful route with deprivation of the sought benefit.

Limit: It is not a penalty for every prompt action or a self-executing universal forfeiture rule. Identify the prohibited means, intended benefit and particular doctrine before applying it.

Source: Legal Maxims of Islamic Jurisprudence: A Translated Compilation, user-supplied PDF pp.66, 67; modern compilation, not an independently collated medieval witness.

Q-NONLIABILITY · Al-aṣl barāʾat al-dhimma — initial freedom from liability

Short reference: Q: initial non-liability. Kind: Later comparative control — fiqh maxim or disputed formulation, compilation body checked.

A debt or other liability must be established; an unsupported allegation or a person’s bare suspicion is not enough to create it.

Limit: Once a debt is established, its persistence raises a different presumption. This is not a finding of factual innocence in every moral sense, nor a rule that every claimant must use the same kind of proof.

Source: Legal Maxims of Islamic Jurisprudence: A Translated Compilation, user-supplied PDF pp.74; modern compilation, not an independently collated medieval witness.

Q-ACCIDENT · An adventitious quality or event is not presumed without a basis

Short reference: Q: unproved change. Kind: Later comparative control — fiqh maxim or disputed formulation, compilation body checked.

The compilation distinguishes an established condition from an alleged later addition or alteration. Its debt example treats alleged payment as requiring proof after the debt has been established.

Limit: The source’s phrase “occasional descriptions are not reliable” is misleading if it means such qualities never count. The issue is the evidential presumption of non-occurrence, subject to a legally sufficient contrary showing.

Source: Legal Maxims of Islamic Jurisprudence: A Translated Compilation, user-supplied PDF pp.76, 77; modern compilation, not an independently collated medieval witness.

Q-NEAREST · An undated new event is presumptively attributed to the nearer time

Short reference: Q: timing of an event. Kind: Later comparative control — fiqh maxim or disputed formulation, compilation body checked.

The maxim supplies a default for uncertain timing of an event already known to have happened; it does not simply decide whether the event occurred.

Limit: Do not apply it against adequate contrary evidence or use it to supply the time of an event whose legal relevance has not been established. Its chapter-specific exceptions require verification.

Source: Legal Maxims of Islamic Jurisprudence: A Translated Compilation, user-supplied PDF pp.78; modern compilation, not an independently collated medieval witness.

Q-PERMISSION · The default status of things: a qualified permissibility inquiry

Short reference: Q: default permission. Kind: Later comparative control — fiqh maxim or disputed formulation, compilation body checked.

The compilation argues for permissibility as the ordinary baseline for things while treating prescribed worship separately. It presents the issue as a question before advocating a position.

Limit: This does not authorize any invented ritual, settle the validity of every contract, or erase specific prohibitions. Distinguish an object’s use from the legal constitution of a transaction involving it.

Source: Legal Maxims of Islamic Jurisprudence: A Translated Compilation, user-supplied PDF pp.79, 80, 81; modern compilation, not an independently collated medieval witness.

Q-REMOTE · Lā ʿibra bi-l-tawahhum — remote conjecture does not defeat a warranted basis

Short reference: Q: remote conjecture. Kind: Later comparative control — fiqh maxim or disputed formulation, compilation body checked.

Bare imagined possibilities do not by themselves displace an established legal or evidential basis. The example concerns unfounded objections after creditors have established their claims.

Limit: This is not a denial of credible risk or a demand for certainty in every practical judgment. Read it with Q-EVIDDOUBT, which concerns a possibility supported by evidence.

Source: Legal Maxims of Islamic Jurisprudence: A Translated Compilation, user-supplied PDF pp.83; modern compilation, not an independently collated medieval witness.

Q-FALSE · A conjecture shown to be erroneous loses its authority

Short reference: Q: disproved probability. Kind: Later comparative control — fiqh maxim or disputed formulation, compilation body checked.

Once adequate evidence reveals that a probable assessment was mistaken, the earlier probability cannot continue to justify prospective action merely because it was once sincerely held.

Limit: The effect on completed payments, judgments or compensation is a further doctrinal question. Discovered error and retrospective legal invalidity must not be equated automatically.

Source: Legal Maxims of Islamic Jurisprudence: A Translated Compilation, user-supplied PDF pp.84; modern compilation, not an independently collated medieval witness.

Q-EVIDDOUBT · A possibility grounded in evidence can undermine a purported proof

Short reference: Q: supported doubt. Kind: Later comparative control — fiqh maxim or disputed formulation, compilation body checked.

The compilation contrasts an evidentially grounded objection with merely imagined doubt. Its example concerns a suspected deathbed acknowledgement and expressly attributes a restrictive position to Abū Ḥanīfa rather than all jurists.

Limit: Do not quote the short formula as “any possibility defeats any proof.” Its scope and school disagreement are essential, and the example’s full primary doctrine remains to be collated.

Source: Legal Maxims of Islamic Jurisprudence: A Translated Compilation, user-supplied PDF pp.87; modern compilation, not an independently collated medieval witness.

Q-NECESSITY · Necessity can authorize a specifically bounded exception

Short reference: Q: necessity. Kind: Later comparative control — fiqh maxim or disputed formulation, compilation body checked.

The compilation distinguishes necessity that permits an otherwise forbidden act, coercive excuses with different legal effects, and acts for which necessity does not supply the claimed permission.

Limit: Necessity must be real and legally relevant. The modern examples in this compilation are not adopted as present-day advice or as Ibn Rushd’s rules. Read this with limits of measure, duration and others’ rights.

Source: Legal Maxims of Islamic Jurisprudence: A Translated Compilation, user-supplied PDF pp.95, 96, 97; modern compilation, not an independently collated medieval witness.

Q-MEASURE · Al-ḍarūra tuqaddar bi-qadrihā — relief is measured by necessity

Short reference: Q: limits of relief. Kind: Later comparative control — fiqh maxim or disputed formulation, compilation body checked.

An exceptional permission extends only as far as the necessity warrants; its extent and any specified temporal boundary matter.

Limit: Permission is not an unlimited transfer of authority to the actor. Neither the actor’s confidence nor a generally beneficial end establishes the measure; the legally relevant facts and grounds must be shown.

Source: Legal Maxims of Islamic Jurisprudence: A Translated Compilation, user-supplied PDF pp.98, 99; modern compilation, not an independently collated medieval witness.

Q-END · A permission dependent on an excuse ends with that excuse

Short reference: Q: end of excuse. Kind: Later comparative control — fiqh maxim or disputed formulation, compilation body checked.

A special dispensation does not persist solely because it was once available when its legally relevant occasion has ceased.

Limit: The consequence for an act already begun or completed requires its own rule. Do not convert loss of permission for future conduct into automatic retroactive invalidation.

Source: Legal Maxims of Islamic Jurisprudence: A Translated Compilation, user-supplied PDF pp.100; modern compilation, not an independently collated medieval witness.

Q-NEED · Ḥāja can receive a necessity-like legal treatment

Short reference: Q: public or particular need. Kind: Later comparative control — fiqh maxim or disputed formulation, compilation body checked.

The compilation distinguishes need from necessity but explains a necessity-like treatment in some cases of public, occupational or particular need. It gives transactional examples and conditions on the claimed need.

Limit: Need is not identical to luxury or convenience. The status of salam, hire, brokerage and other examples must be checked in their own doctrines; a generic commercial need does not validate every uncertain exchange.

Source: Legal Maxims of Islamic Jurisprudence: A Translated Compilation, user-supplied PDF pp.101, 102, 103; modern compilation, not an independently collated medieval witness.

Q-RIGHTS · Al-iḍṭirār lā yubṭil ḥaqq al-ghayr — necessity does not simply extinguish another’s right

Short reference: Q: rights survive necessity. Kind: Later comparative control — fiqh maxim or disputed formulation, compilation body checked.

The compilation distinguishes permission to take protective action from the survival of another person’s compensable claim. It also records disagreement over compensation when defending against an animal.

Limit: This is a check against treating emergency benefit as gratuitous appropriation. It does not prove compensation in every case: the stated school differences and the source of danger can change the result.

Source: Legal Maxims of Islamic Jurisprudence: A Translated Compilation, user-supplied PDF pp.104, 105; modern compilation, not an independently collated medieval witness.

Q-SUBSTITUTE · When the original performance is unavailable, an authorized substitute can become due

Short reference: Q: authorized substitute. Kind: Later comparative control — fiqh maxim or disputed formulation, compilation body checked.

The compilation organizes substitution where the ordinary means or performance is unavailable and differentiates the timing and conditions of alternatives.

Limit: The maxim does not itself invent the substitute. Whether money, another act or deferred performance is authorized must come from the applicable doctrine; material similarity or an attractive outcome is insufficient.

Source: Legal Maxims of Islamic Jurisprudence: A Translated Compilation, user-supplied PDF pp.106, 107, 108; modern compilation, not an independently collated medieval witness.

Q-PREVENT · Harm is to be prevented to the extent possible

Short reference: Q: preventive care. Kind: Later comparative control — fiqh maxim or disputed formulation, compilation body checked.

Prevention concerns a threatened injury before it occurs, unlike removal of an injury already present. The compilation relates the formulation to protective institutions and restrictions.

Limit: Feasibility is not blanket authority to intervene. The likelihood, gravity, competence and legal warrant of the intervention require examination; preventive power can itself produce harm.

Source: Legal Maxims of Islamic Jurisprudence: A Translated Compilation, user-supplied PDF pp.114, 115; modern compilation, not an independently collated medieval witness.

Q-EQUALHARM · Removing one harm does not by itself authorize an equal harm

Short reference: Q: harm by harm. Kind: Later comparative control — fiqh maxim or disputed formulation, compilation body checked.

The maxim constrains the means of protection: transferring an equivalent destructive burden to another person is not justified simply by a wish to escape injury.

Limit: It must be read with the rules for lesser unavoidable harm, compensation and public authority. Similar bodily or financial magnitudes do not alone establish juridical equivalence.

Source: Legal Maxims of Islamic Jurisprudence: A Translated Compilation, user-supplied PDF pp.117; modern compilation, not an independently collated medieval witness.

Q-LESSERHARM · Where an unavoidable choice remains, the lesser harm can be borne

Short reference: Q: lesser harm. Kind: Later comparative control — fiqh maxim or disputed formulation, compilation body checked.

The compilation gives several formulations for choosing the less harmful course where competing harms cannot both be avoided.

Limit: First establish that the alternatives are genuinely unavoidable and within the actor’s authority. This is not unrestricted aggregation of welfare or a warrant to discard another’s right whenever a larger benefit is predicted.

Source: Legal Maxims of Islamic Jurisprudence: A Translated Compilation, user-supplied PDF pp.118, 119; modern compilation, not an independently collated medieval witness.

Q-PUBLICHARM · A bounded private burden may avert a public harm

Short reference: Q: public harm. Kind: Later comparative control — fiqh maxim or disputed formulation, compilation body checked.

The formulation distinguishes the range of affected persons and includes examples about regulating incompetent practitioners and public economic conditions.

Limit: The maxim alone does not establish jurisdiction, proportionality, due process or compensation. The compilation’s examples need separate school and historical verification; a ruler’s description of an interest as public is not sufficient.

Source: Legal Maxims of Islamic Jurisprudence: A Translated Compilation, user-supplied PDF pp.120; modern compilation, not an independently collated medieval witness.

Q-AVERT · Preventing harm has priority in the stated conflict with obtaining benefit

Short reference: Q: harm and benefit. Kind: Later comparative control — fiqh maxim or disputed formulation, compilation body checked.

The maxim gives priority to avoiding the relevant harm when the harmful and beneficial effects cannot be separated in the contemplated act.

Limit: Do not elevate this abbreviated formulation into “any harm always outweighs any benefit.” The catalogue itself includes a competing consideration where a stronger positive ground can matter; the legal comparison and relative weight must be established.

Source: Legal Maxims of Islamic Jurisprudence: A Translated Compilation, user-supplied PDF pp.121, 122; modern compilation, not an independently collated medieval witness.

Q-CONSENT · An established right cannot simply be appropriated without its holder’s permission

Short reference: Q: another’s right. Kind: Later comparative control — fiqh maxim or disputed formulation, compilation body checked.

The compilation reports Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr’s formulation about a person’s established right and a transmitted example in which permission to give another person precedence is requested.

Limit: This is a reported earlier formulation mediated by the compilation. Public authority, necessity, incapacity and other legally established exceptions require their own arguments; the formula is not a universal veto over all jurisdiction.

Source: Legal Maxims of Islamic Jurisprudence: A Translated Compilation, user-supplied PDF pp.13, 14; modern compilation, not an independently collated medieval witness.

Q-PUBLICFUNCTION · The exercise of authority over subjects is conditioned by maṣlaḥa

Short reference: Q: public office. Kind: Later comparative control — reported maxim, preliminary catalogue control.

The compilation introduces this maxim in its classification of the genre and repeats it as catalogue entry 60. It provides a useful normative question about the end of public office.

Limit: The checked witness here is an introductory example and index, not a full doctrinal treatment. A claimed public benefit cannot validate an otherwise unwarranted power or replace the Bidāya’s explicit reason. Primary qawāʿid and jurisdiction texts remain controls.

Source: Legal Maxims of Islamic Jurisprudence: A Translated Compilation, user-supplied PDF pp.5, 135; modern compilation, not an independently collated medieval witness.

DR-RES · al-Ḍarūrī: the limit of transfer without textual indication

Short reference: Ḍ: residual qiyās. Kind: Rushdian primary — restriction and criticism of inference.

The Ẓāhirī objection that legal statuses are not natural essential qualities bears upon transfer from an original whose expression does not indicate the relevant ground; §273 gives wine-drinking and false accusation penalties. Contextually indicated meaning is treated differently.

Limit: This is not a denial of all rational knowledge of goods. The connection to al-Fārābī’s rhetorical exemplum is a separately attributed reconstruction through Akl, not wording of this passage.

Source: al-Ḍarūrī §§272–275, Arabic/French PDF pp.308–311; compare Bidāya Arabic I p.4.

J-QIY · Jamʿ: the four pillars of legal analogy

Short reference: J: fourfold qiyās. Kind: Later primary control — alternative taxonomy.

The matn defines qiyās by equality in the ruling’s cause and explicitly names four pillars, then treats original, original ruling, branch and cause. Its conditions also distinguish a proof that already includes the branch.

Limit: This later schema does not establish Ibn Rushd’s terminology or historical dependence. Do not identify its various accounts of ʿilla with a single natural efficient cause.

Source: Jamʿ al-Jawāmiʿ, matn, Book IV, PDF pp.80–84; editorial footnotes separate.

B-ILL · Bidāya: illness-marriage, benefit and evidence of circumstances

Short reference: B: illness and judgment. Kind: Rushdian primary — situational practical judgment.

Ibn Rushd rejects the gift assimilation as inconsistent, warns against quasi-legislation through remote benefit and injustice through rigid outward form, and directs qualified trustworthy scholars to examine evidence of good intent or injury. Medicine illustrates trained judgment without a fixed formula for all situations.

Limit: The text does not give an unrestricted power to override law, a complete court procedure, or certainty about hidden intentions. The tension with al-Ḍarūrī §266 must remain visible.

Source: Bidāya Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.46–47: illness impediment; ends in the opening two lines of p.47.

B-SADD · Bidāya: sadd al-dharāʾiʿ and contested consequences

Short reference: B: foreseeable means. Kind: Rushdian primary — reported means–ends reasoning.

Illness-divorce is explained through blocking deprivation of inheritance; deferred animal exchange through preventing a benefit-bearing loan. Ibn Rushd criticizes expansive inheritance effects and also considers an independent transmitted basis for the commercial restriction.

Limit: A causal route to a prohibited end is different from semantic extension or mere resemblance. Attributing this argument to Mālik is not Ibn Rushd’s unqualified endorsement of every application.

Source: Bidāya Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.82–83 and 134–135.

B-RIBA · Bidāya: practical and teleological discrimination among ribā predicates

Short reference: B: justice in exchange. Kind: Rushdian primary — assessment within derivation.

After reporting rival general meanings, Ibn Rushd uses justice, approximate equality, valuation, differentiated use and avoidance of extravagance to favor the measurement rationale from the direction of meaning, while also praising a measurement-and-food rationale.

Limit: This is not a proof that every positive ribā detail follows from justice, or that all empirical assumptions hold universally. The wider classification of the chapter remains to be audited.

Source: Bidāya Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.129–133; especially pp.131–133.

DR-BAY · al-Ḍarūrī: clarification until need versus beyond need

Short reference: Ḍ: timely clarification. Kind: Rushdian primary — language, timing and warranted assent.

Sections 188–194 distinguish circumstances in which further specification may await the time of need from postponing clarification beyond that time. Section 194 rejects the latter; the preceding analysis does not endorse either blanket position about all delayed clarification.

Limit: Public need is not a license to invent missing detail. Bidāya II10–12 uses expected clarification and transmission as a probable argument concerning guardianship, not as a demonstrated archive of early practice.

Source: al-Ḍarūrī §§188–194, Arabic/French PDF pp.252–259; especially §194, PDF pp.258–259.

B-AUTH · Bidāya: a duty to prevent does not confer exclusive matrimonial power

Short reference: B: duty and authority. Kind: Rushdian primary — interpretation of legal relations.

A prohibition of obstruction or of an unlawful marriage can bind relatives, rulers or Muslims without establishing an exclusive guardian power to constitute marriage. Permission, personal pronouncement and corrective oversight require distinct analysis.

Limit: This local argument does not abolish all guardianship. Ibn Rushd’s conclusion is a qualified disjunction, and the detailed grounds and ranks remain contested.

Source: Bidāya Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.10–12.

B-RANK · Bidāya: binding priority, a guardian’s claim and non-waivable validity

Short reference: B: rank and ratification. Kind: Rushdian primary — the reason for different remedies.

The remote-guardian dispute turns first on whether the rank is legally binding and then on whether it concerns a waivable guardian’s claim or a divine right affecting validity. Rescission, validity and ratification are distinct reported outcomes.

Limit: The classification is part of a particular dispute. It does not establish that every divine right is treated identically across law or that every defect can be cured by approval.

Source: Bidāya Arabic II, printed/PDF p.14, guardian order and rival contracts.

B-PUBLIC · Bidāya: witnessed form, announcement and prevention of denial

Short reference: B: publicity and proof. Kind: Rushdian primary — form and means–ends reasoning.

The witness dispute distinguishes a condition at contracting from completion before consummation, prescribed form from prevention of denial, and announcement from the requirements of admissible testimony. The schools also disagree about what counts as secrecy.

Limit: Purpose does not by itself derive every witness qualification. Agreement among three authorities is not unanimous consensus; the Abū Thawr dissent and criticism of the consensus argument remain part of the evidence.

Source: Bidāya Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.17–18, ending before the dower chapter.

B-COMP · Bidāya: financial rushd is not matrimonial rushd

Short reference: B: domain competence. Kind: Rushdian primary — disanalogy of practical capacities.

In evaluating assimilation to property guardianship, Ibn Rushd distinguishes sound judgment in wealth from sound judgment in choosing matrimonial suitability. The practical object matters to the competence required.

Limit: The distinction does not prove that money is irrelevant to marriage, that no capacity transfers between fields, or that an eligible guardian has acquired moral virtue.

Source: Bidāya Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.12–13, financial rushd and probity.

B-MUK — Mushāḥḥa and mukārama: the practical relation governs tolerated indeterminacy

Type: Rushdian primary — local cause of disagreement

Principle: In the unspecified-servant dower dispute, Ibn Rushd asks whether marriage is assimilated to transactions governed by exacting bargaining or to dealings governed by generosity and honour. That characterization affects tolerable specification.

Scope: A local dispute, not a rule that all uncertainty is harmless in marriage. Other dower cases retain limits, valuations and remedies.

Source: Bidāya Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.21–22

B-EQV — Shared money and a shared word do not establish an operative likeness

Type: Rushdian primary — criticism of an analogy

Principle: Ibn Rushd rejects assimilating minimum dower to the theft threshold through a supposed monetary making-licit of a bodily member: punishment and injury differ in meaning from marital pleasure and affection. A valid analogy needs relevant likeness and a ruling attached on account of that likeness.

Scope: His critique is stronger than saying the objects have different final ends; he also denies the indicated common basis of the proposed transfer. The critique must not erase the text’s own other exchange analogies.

Source: Bidāya Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.19–20

B-OATH — Role-defined burden or evidentiary strength of the appearance

Type: Rushdian primary — explanation of procedural disagreement

Principle: In disputed intercourse and dower claims Ibn Rushd asks whether the defendant’s oath is assigned through a fixed procedural role or a reasoned assessment of the stronger claim. Agreement on an oath formula need not determine the parties’ roles.

Scope: The comparison concerns legal proof, not access to the hidden event itself. His preference for the wife’s statement on unpaid dower survives his recognition of the rival customary presumption.

Source: Bidāya Arabic II, printed/PDF pp.23,30–31

S-TRIAD — Discernment, concentration and affective conformity

Type: Modern spiritual-philosophical comparison — Schuon’s explicit doctrine

Principle: Understanding, concentration and conformity concern intelligence, will and the living soul; the Way requires discernment, concentration and goodness together. Known truth must engage volition and affective character.
